The non-dualism of Śiva has attained perfect consistency precisely where the path of correct reasoning, as instructed by the eminent teachers beginning with the venerable Somānandanātha, has been brought under one's own control.
Spreading forth from Kashmir with its manifest fragrance and delighting all lands, it attained universal veneration—unseen in any other country—like a stream of saffron. || 1 ||
Cross quickly the ocean of saṃsāra; place your feet firmly in the supreme state, which is overflowing with the bliss of eternal light.
Contemplate the nectar-like essence of the realization of non-duality as taught by Śiva.
[It is] that which, through its forcefully manifesting correct reasoning, causes an internal leaping-up [of realization]. || 2 ||
Now begins the Śrīmad Bhagavadgītā,
accompanied by the commentary composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha.
The First Chapter.
Salutation to You, the Supreme Self, whose infinite names and forms are illuminated by Your own light, and whose body is pure consciousness, devoid of name and form. (1)
That which, like the surface of a crystal, assumes a variegated appearance through its intermingling with the rising diversity of the various rays of the perceivers—
such is the essential nature of all things.
May He shine forth in His own form within the sky of the heart, which has become serene as the veil of clouds of conceptual construction has dissolved, for the sake of all worlds. || 2 ||

Since the manifestations of the world— the various words of the extensive doctrines of different philosophical systems— are unable to exist outside of that which is like the sky, possessing an immeasurable and stainless expanse; therefore,
that very Brahman alone is the supreme [reality]— such is the view of the great seer, the son of Parāśara.
May the virtuous, whose minds are perpetually fixed [on Him], meditate for the sake of severing their bonds.

In the midst of all the wise, alas, only a few noble ones have truly achieved their life's purpose, for they alone among the world’s bees perceive the specific excellence of the qualities of these verses of the Gītā; indeed, it is they who dance upon the lotuses of Fortune.
Those who are connoisseurs of flavor in tasting the honey from the lotus-like hands [of the Lord]. || 4 ||
These *vṛttis* were indeed composed by many who were naturally profound, possessed of intense exertion, whose meditative absorptions were never fruitless, and who were endowed with stainless wisdom.
What more could one like me say here? And what indeed can I do in this matter?
For we are but mockers here to those who are deluded, acting as friends to their own intellects. || 5 ||
Because it is clear, everyone enters this [teaching], thinking it is easy to traverse;
yet once entered, one who has not reached its bottom falls here due to its profundity.
Thus, for a person wishing to cross the ocean of the meaning of the Gītā:
I shall fashion this fearless boat for the sake of reaching the meaning of the sentence.
Who, even if mature, is capable of awakening those whose minds are utterly deluded, hostile, and arrogant, by means of refuting their views and discourses that are eternally opposed to one another?
[Only one who possesses] the grace of the Lord, manifested through an excess of devotion, by way of [accepting] their very tenets as established.
In this [work], there is a certain person to be instructed whose impurities of all doubt have been almost entirely swallowed up. || 7 ||

Indeed, herein is the instruction on the four aims of human life (caturvarga), which is scattered throughout the vast expanse of various scriptures such as the Vedas, the Vedānta siddhāntas, the immortal Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas.
For the sake of making it easy for those to be instructed— whose wisdom and other faculties have been diminished by the passage of time—

the Blessed Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, or rather the Supreme Lord himself manifesting in that form, composed this history known as the Mahābhārata, having condensed it according to its essence. And therein also:

Anticipating that even though liberation (apavarga)— the supreme human goal and most desirable object— is taught in the various sections on the dharma of liberation through diverse methods of exposition, it might still be impossible for those of limited intellectual capacity to comprehend it correctly, [the author proceeds].

For the instruction of all suitable people, there exists this treatise known as the *Gītā*, spoken by the Blessed One; it is composed of a discourse in the form of a dialogue between friends transmitted through the sequence of history, characterized by a flow of speech that is both clear and profound, and is captivating even to those of the most tender intellects, as it establishes the means to liberation (*apavarga*).
He established [this doctrine], the conclusion of which is the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all spiritual treatises (*adhyātma-śāstra*), namely: "All this is indeed the Self.
For it was from this very [source] that the Supreme Seer [declared this] in this very *Mahābhārata*.

Having described the nature of that [Lord] both collectively and individually by means of this hymn to the Blessed One entitled *Gītastavarāja*, which flows from the exceedingly pure intellect perfumed with the joy of the ultimate reality experienced during the state of unsurpassed *samādhi* attained at the moment of renouncing the body— even so, in the conclusion:
Salutation to that Self of All, in whom is everything, from whom is everything, who is everything, who is everywhere, and who is eternally composed of all.

The very meaning which he indicated in that verse as being the summary of the supreme essence has been encapsulated here in this section. And thus, those who are skilled in discerning the ultimate truth explain this verse in the following manner: to him...
Salutation to the Self of all, whose essential nature is conveyed by the five words distinguished as qualifiers, and who is the Self of everything—
by resorting to both modes of interpretation, [it refers] to the Self alone, the supreme cause.
By this term, the Supreme Lord’s actual non-duality and state of being without a second are established. As it has been said here:
"He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me..."
"I am never lost to him, nor is he ever lost to me" (6.31).
Thus,
[he sees] the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self.
"He whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives the same everywhere" (6.30), and so forth.

To whom? To Him—to whom [the word] "to whom" (*tasmai*) refers. Although there is oneness, these [passages] characterized by the word *yat* (which) establish His unsurpassed sovereignty, such as omniscience and the like.
The qualifiers are explained in sequence. Among them, salutation to that Blessed One,
in whom this entire multitude of entities— which consists of an infinite variety of utterly distinct appearances—
attains its respective self-nature solely by being bound to the state of being perceived.

The meaning is: "that which, abiding in the nature of the self-luminous subject—which consists solely in being the single cognizer pervading all states such as pleasure and so forth—manifests itself as this very multiplicity by virtue of its power. The connection is: "salutation to that [Self]. By this...

By means of this qualifying attribute, which is intent on establishing the Lord’s status as the sole perceiver of the entire multitude of all objects of cognition, the attribute of omniscience—or a particular power—of the Self, the Lord, is established. This very point has been stated here [in the verse]: "Omniscience [is] the one Self... (k, g).
By designating [the Lord] as "the one omniscient one" (sarvajñam ekam), the Blessed One stated:
"And I am seated within the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss" (Gītā 15.15).
By such passages as these,
and likewise by "All beings abide in Me" (9.4),
etc., the doctrine of multiple knowers is refuted; for [if it were so], knowledge would be merely momentary.

The doctrine that the knower is an error [of perception] has been refuted, as has the doctrine that the body alone, qualified by consciousness, is the knower. Now, let it be granted that there exists some one omniscient being by whom all this that is perceived is sustained; however, from what was this entire world produced which is perceived by him?

To dispel the doubt as to who its creator is, and for the purpose of establishing that He alone is the creator of all, he provides the qualification: "from whom all [proceeds]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "from whom—from this one Creator—all this effect originates. By this...
By the reasoning to be stated hereafter, the fact that the one Reality already mentioned is the creator of all has been established. And so it was said by the Blessed One in this very place:
"By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded" (9.4).
By such passages as these, and likewise by "There is nothing that exists without Me, whether moving or unmoving" (10.39),
and so forth; and furthermore:
Even from the words of Savyasācin, whose supreme speech is renowned through his contemplation of the Cosmic Form (vaiśvarūpya) seen with divine vision awakened by the grace of the Blessed One,
it follows that there is no other creator of the universe than You alone.

"Also by such [statements] as: 'He is the Ordainer, the Disposer, the All-pervading One, and the Lord' (11.47). By this, the doctrine that the Omniscient One is not an agent is also refuted. Now, one might raise the objection: 'If He is the creator of all, upon what does He rely when He creates this? In order to dispel this doubt—"
To demonstrate that she possesses universal agency without any external substrate, he provides another qualification:

"He who is all. The meaning is that although this effect has issued forth as a manifold variety of diverse entities by virtue of its universality, it is not distinct from that very reality characterized as previously described.
(5) Salutation to Him!
By this, it is established that He is independent of any other material cause (*upādāna*) existing apart from His own mere will. And this has been stated right here by Arjuna’s own words:

"O All-pervading Lord, since You Yourself are indeed the agent of everything, therefore all this is You alone. (11.48), and so forth. By this, the doctrine that agency is dependent upon material causes such as Māyā or Prakṛti is refuted.
Now, let it be granted that its agency is indeed without any substrate;

however, why does this effect—which manifests as a variety of fragile entities mutually distinct from one another—not produce a modification of its own essential nature? To this he says: "And he who [is] from all sides..."
"Salutation to that One alone who shines forth within every object of knowledge. By this [it is meant]:
it is precisely in the state of delusion produced by His wondrous power of *māyā* that all this work of the transmigrating person is perceived as manifold.

However, when this entire world of effects is examined by one who is awakened, possessing the divine eye consisting of *vidyā* (knowledge) opened by the power of grace from the supreme cause, it has been established that nothing whatsoever appears apart from that single reality (*ekatattva*).
This is just as [it is perceived] by one characterized by the various specific causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*) of those respective objects.
Bracelets, earrings, armlets, and so forth, when perceived by the world of ordinary people and others, appear as mutually distinct entities whose nature is essentially subordinate gold; however,
when they are examined by those who have developed a desire to know their true nature, all of them [are seen as such].

Just as not even a single atom is perceived apart from the single nature consisting of gold, which possesses distinct individualities such as bracelets and other ornaments that have become subordinate qualities, so too, when effects— which appear distinct during the state of *māyā*— are reflected upon in the state of awakening, they are found to be nothing other than that [single reality].

It has been established that, in reality, nothing whatsoever is perceived apart from the nature of pure consciousness (*viśuddha-saṃvin-mātra*) within all entities; thus, even as this entire effect manifests in such a manner, it does not bring about even the slightest modification of the agent's own essential nature.
This very point has been stated right here [in the Gītā] with the words:
"He is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable" (2.25), and so forth.
By this, even the doctrine that [the Self] is subject to the contact of adventitious limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*) is refuted. Now, one might object:

Even though this is so regarding its state as an effect, let it be granted that this Self is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*); however, when this [Self] does not initiate an effect, what is its nature?
In order to dispel such a doubt and to establish that it is always the essence of all things, [the author says: p. 6) ...
He states another qualification: "and who is eternally composed of all.

In the manner established by the previously mentioned qualifications, he who is eternally—that is, constantly—composed of all (*sarvamaya*), whose very nature is everything (*sarvātmaka*); to him, salutation. By this [it is shown that] even while he is manifesting...

In this collection of works characterized by the wondrous forms of infinite deities, even the debate regarding the purpose of the Lord— the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, eternally complete and never departing from its supreme purity— has been resolved. As it has been said:
"O Pārtha, there is nothing for Me to do; yet, even so, I engage in action. (3.21) Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"Actions do not taint me, nor do I have any desire for their fruits.
He who understands me thus is not bound by actions.
(4.14) And so forth. [He is] the one who is all, the omniscient, the creator of all, and devoid of material cause.

"Free from limiting conditions, it eternally manifests as the self of all. By this verse, one should understand that the very nature of the Supreme Lord, the Self—which was propounded there by the Great Sage—is here encapsulated as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thus, its essential character is as follows:
The Blessed One, whose sole instrument is His own will, like the creation of a lord of yogis,
like objects in a dream, or like the various manifestations fashioned in a kingdom of the mind,
has for His purpose nothing other than unsurpassed play that is unique to Himself— this which is so exceedingly wonderful.

It paints the variegated picture of the universe; it should also be understood that the process regulated by His very will alone is subsumed within this treatise. For, because His agency depends solely upon His own will, it is that supreme reality itself which [acts] in the primary sense.
The status of being the cause of the universe is established merely by the manifestation of its knowability. As the Blessed One himself has said:
"O Pārtha, know Me to be the eternal seed of all beings" (Gītā 7.10).
...and so forth; likewise:
"When one perceives the distinct existence of all beings as situated in one place, and from that very [place] perceives their expansion, then one attains Brahman" (13.31).
Thus, likewise:
"I am the father who provides the seed" (14.4); and likewise:
"I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe" (7.6),
and so forth. Consequently, the very nature of that [Self], as it has been explained,
is the world, characterized by the universal mark of being merely an object of cognition (*vedyatva*).
It manifests in two ways, consisting of nature (prakṛti) in its gross and subtle forms, distinguished as the insentient and the sentient.
As it has been said: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect..."
This nature of mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold.

"O mighty-armed one, know that this is My lower nature; but other than this, know My higher nature, which is the soul (jīva), by which this world is sustained. (7.5). And regarding these two natures, even that gross distinction consisting of insentient matter, [one should understand it] as being of the nature of the cause.

And that very Lord manifests Himself in two ways through the nature of the effect (*kāryātmanā*). In this regard, because every object of knowledge (*vedya*) has its essential form ultimately determined as consisting of pleasure and so forth,
there exists a single, pervasive universal (*sāmānya*) composed of the three qualities (*guṇatrayamaya*), such as *sattva*, which persists as a commonality.
It manifests that [Prakṛti] as its intermediate cause;

and it manifests as an effect that which, having followed through the sequence from Mahat down to Earth, has evolved into the form of bodies consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects, as well as into the form of objects such as sound and the rest.

As it was said by me: "Under my supervision, nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving" (9.10). Furthermore, that differentiation which consists of consciousness is also [to be understood] in terms of the demonic creation and the divine creation.
First, it manifests in two ways, as stated in such passages as:
"There are two types of creation of beings in this world, the divine and the demonic" (16.6), and so forth. Among these, the demonic creation is of two kinds, distinguished as inferior and superior.

Of these two, there is the inferior asuric creation, consisting primarily of the quality of *tamas* with *sattva* and *rajas* completely submerged, which takes the form of barbarians (*mleccha*) and the like, and which he will later refer to by the name "rakshasa. In comparison to that, the other is slightly superior, being human in nature and dominated by *tamas* accompanied by a trace of *rajas*.
Those who possess such characteristics as described,
and whose engagement and withdrawal people do not understand, are of the nature of Asuras;
in them neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truthfulness is found.
"They say that this world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord; born of mutual interaction, it is insignificant and causeless. (16.8), and so forth.
...hating [Me] and full of envy" (16.18).

Thus far. Since the Blessed One has spoken even of His own pastimes as having them as their object, He says of those who hate Him: "Those cruel haters, the lowest of men among all beings in the cycle of rebirths, I—"
I cast them incessantly into the inauspicious realms of the Asuras alone.
"Having entered an asuric womb, deluded from birth to birth, they do not reach Me at all, O son of Kuntī, but from there they go to the lowest state" (Gītā 16.20).
Thus, the asuric creation is of two kinds. Now, the divine creation—

First, it manifests in two modes according to the distinction between gods and humans. Within that, too, the mode consisting of the gods and so forth is twofold. One is the nature of specific deities such as Indra, who are appointed to various ritual actions and whose tenure lasts until they have fulfilled their respective offices.

Having passed the time until the conclusion of its own office, it transforms back into its own cause. The second [state] consists of the experience of mere pleasure resulting from various rites such as sacrifices performed while in the human state;
experiencing enjoyment in those various other worlds until the exhaustion of the fruits of its own karma.

Having passed through time again and again, one returns to the field of action (*karmabhūmi*). This [creation], though possessing both forms, is primarily characterized by the qualities of sentient beings (*sattvaguṇa*). Thus, due to the gradations and the infinity of these specific qualities, the infinity of all distinct types of creation is to be understood. Even that which takes human form is part of the divine creation (*daivasarga*).

It is of two kinds. Among them, one is that in which the quality of *rajas* (passion) is predominant, accompanied by a trace of *sattva* (purity); because it is oriented toward the path of worldly activity (*pravṛtti-mārga*), when the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, [the mind functions] under the influence of the quality of *rajas* accompanied by a trace of *sattva*.
One for whom ritual action— such as sacrifice, charity, and austerity— as enjoined by the three Vedas and other scriptures is the sole primary concern, experiences the cycle of transmigration;
it is with reference to such a person that the definition was stated, beginning with the phrase "on account of being unfit for knowledge."
O descendant of Kuru, the intellect characterized by resolute determination is indeed one;
for the intellects of those lacking such determination are many-branched and infinite.
O Pārtha, those who are unwise, who delight in the ritualistic discourse of the Vedas and who assert that "there is nothing else," utter this flowery speech.
Those whose nature is desire, who look toward heaven, who long for the fruits of birth and action, are intent upon various ritual acts directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and power.
"For those who are deeply attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds are carried away by that [attachment],
the intellect characterized by resolute determination is not established in meditative absorption" (2.45).
Likewise, with reference to the fact that it is merely action that is prescribed, it was said:
The knowers of the three Vedas, drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven; they,
having reached the holy world of the Lord of the Gods—
They enjoy divine pleasures in heaven.
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world,
they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted;
thus do those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas proceed.
"Those who desire objects of desire obtain [only] coming and going.

(9.22) Thus, with regard to them, the Blessed One has also spoken of his own sport of action through this very [verse], since it is solely by the will of the Lord that they now experience such a state of transmigratory existence. This is the second [point].

The divine creation consisting of humans (manuṣyātmaka-daivasarga), which is dominated by *sattva* accompanied by a trace of *rajas*, [is described] because it is rendered motionless by the wind of powerful conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), due to the two preceding [qualities], *kula* and *sthairya*. (p. 10)
Because the veil of the multitude of terrible obstacles, such as doubt, is being dispelled by devotion and faith,
he is indicated here as one for whom the great festival of the vision of the proximate Supreme Lord has been manifested, precisely because he possesses the characteristics thus described.
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge,
charity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, non-attachment, absence of backbiting,
compassion toward all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness.
"Energy, forgiveness, fortitude, contentment, non-malice, and freedom from arrogance— these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with the divine nature" (Bhagavad Gītā 16.3),
and so forth. For it is precisely such a person as this [who is meant].
He is embraced here as the subject of the instruction on the supreme secret, which is the theme propounded in the section concerning *prārabdha*. As it is said:
"In this way, I taught the imperishable Yoga to Vivasvat" (4.1).
Having begun with these words, [the Lord said]: "This very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today;
for you are My devotee and My friend, and this is the most supreme secret. (4.3)
and so forth; likewise, "Thus, four kinds of virtuous people always worship Me" (7.16), and so forth;
and likewise, at the conclusion of the section:
"Listen to me briefly regarding how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman;
O son of Kuntī, I shall explain in brief that which is the supreme culmination of knowledge. (18.50) Thus begins [the discourse].
"Being equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me;
through devotion he comes to know Me—who I am in truth. (18.55).
Likewise, He also speaks regarding the objects of faith and so forth:
"One endowed with faith, self-controlled, and with senses restrained, attains knowledge;
having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace before long" (4.39). Likewise:
"Those who possess faith and are free from malice are liberated from all sins" (3.31);
likewise,
"those devotees who have faith and regard Me as the Supreme are exceedingly dear to Me" (13.20).

And so forth. Thus, while the various types of creation remain established, the nature of that human form of the divine creation— which was just explained and which has been adopted as the subject matter of this instruction— is now briefly set forth.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O Sañjaya, on the field of dharma, Kurukṣetra, where all the kṣatriyas had assembled, what did my sons and the Pāṇḍavas do?
Sañjaya said:
Having seen the Pandava army drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana then approached the Teacher and spoke these words.
Behold, O Teacher, this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
arrayed by the wise son of Drupada, your own disciple.
Here are heroes, great archers equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna:
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the heroic King of Kāśī; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaivya, the bull among men. || 5 ||
And Yudhāmanyu, the valiant, and the heroic Uttamaujas, as well as the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī—all of them were indeed great car-warriors (mahārathas). || 6 ||
But as for those who are distinguished among us, O best of the twice-born, listen to them;
I shall name those leaders of my army for your information.
In this great army, all those who are leaders esteemed as heroes are present:
yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Jayadratha. (8)
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and the heroic son of Somadatta, as well as many other heroes, have renounced their lives for my sake. (9)
Wielding various weapons and missiles, and skilled in various modes of warfare,
this army of theirs, protected by Bhīṣma, is indeed inexhaustible.
This army, protected by Bhīṣma, is indeed sufficient;
they stand stationed according to their respective divisions in all the strategic positions.
"Indeed, all of you together must protect Bhīṣma alone;
for the elder of the Kurus, the grandfather, will produce joy in him. (12)
Having uttered a lion’s roar loudly, the majestic one blew his conch shell;
then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns [resounded].
Suddenly they were struck down, and that sound became tumultuous;
then [the two of them] stood upon a great chariot yoked with white horses.
Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava likewise blew their two divine conchs:
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, and Dhanañjaya blew the Devadatta. || 15 ||
Vṛkodara, the performer of terrible deeds, blew his great conch, Pauṇḍra;
and King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya.
Nakula and Sahadeva, Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka, the great archer Kāśya, and the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki, as well as the great archer of the Pañcālas and the five sons of Draupadī. || 18 ||
And the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā blew his conch shell separately from the others;
that sound rent asunder the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The tumultuous noise resounded through both the sky and the earth.
Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra standing firm, he whose banner bears the monkey [Arjuna]— (20)
O lord of the earth, when the clash of weapons had begun, the son of Pāṇḍu raised his bow and then spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa.
Arjuna said:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies, so that I may behold those who have taken their stand, desiring to fight. (22)
"With whom must I fight in this undertaking of war? I shall observe those who have assembled here, ready to fight. (23)
Desiring to do what was pleasing to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle, Sañjaya said:
"O Bhārata, having been thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, Hṛṣīkeśa... (24)
Having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies,
in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and before all the rulers of the earth.
He said, "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here.
There, Pārtha saw his fathers and grandfathers standing.
[He saw] teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, as well as friends,
fathers-in-law, and well-wishers, on both sides of the two armies.
Beholding all those kinsmen standing there, that son of Kuntī,
overcome by supreme compassion and sinking down, spoke this.
Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, having seen these kinsmen standing here eager for battle,
my limbs fail me and my mouth is parched.
Trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end; the Gāṇḍīva bow slips from my hand and my skin is burning all over. (30)
(14) Nor am I able to remain steady;
my mind seems to reel, O Keśava, and I behold adverse omens.
Nor do I foresee any good from killing my own kin in battle;
I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
O Govinda, what need have we for sovereignty, what need for enjoyments, or what need for life itself—
for the sake of which we desired sovereignty, enjoyments, and pleasures?
These who stand here in battle— teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers— have renounced both their lives and their wealth.
Maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives—these I do not wish to slay, O Madhusūdana, even though they are killing me. (35)
"Even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, O Janārdana, what joy could there be for us after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, let alone for the sake of the earth? (36)
"By killing these aggressors, we would only incur sin ourselves;
therefore, we ought not to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who are our own kinsmen. (37)
O Mādhava, how indeed could we be happy after killing our own kin, even if these men, their minds overwhelmed by greed, do not see [the wrongness of it]? (38)
How is it that we have not recognized the fault caused by the destruction of our lineage and the sin of betraying our friends, so as to turn away from this evil? (39)
O Janārdana, clearly perceiving the evil resulting from the destruction of a lineage, [we see that] upon the destruction of a lineage, the eternal family traditions perish. (40)
When dharma is destroyed, adharma indeed overcomes the entire family;
and from the prevalence of adharma, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family become corrupt. (41)
O Vārṣṇeya, when women are corrupt, a mixture of castes arises;
this intermixture leads only to hell for both the destroyers of the lineage and for the lineage itself.
For their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water, due to these faults of the destroyers of the lineage who cause the intermixture of castes. (43)
The eternal laws of caste and the laws of family are destroyed, O Janārdana, when the laws of family are destroyed for those people. (44)
"We have heard that residence in hell is certain;
alas, we have resolved to commit a great sin! (45)
If, out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty, you are prepared to slay your own kinsmen—should you, with weapons in hand, strike me while I am unarmed and offer no resistance? (46)
"It would be more secure for me if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were to slay me in battle.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down upon the seat of his chariot.
Casting aside his bow and arrow, his mind agitated by grief [he reflected]:

"Indeed, since the Supreme Lord— the creator of all, whose essential nature has been established here— is eternally devoid of the loss of his agency, it is well-established that his power of action (kriyā-śakti) is ever-present."

Since even those individual souls (*jīvas*) whose sense of difference is manifested by the power of His *māyā* are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), identical with Him, they likewise remain forever inseparable from His power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Thus, it is impossible to abandon actions in their entirety.
For those [acts] enjoined by the scriptures,
which have been refined by the knowledge to be described— the cause for suppressing their power to bind—

one should perform them according to one's capacity, in the order of the primary (mukhya-kalpa) and secondary (anukalpa) rites, with due regard for the predominant [factors] such as place, time, and circumstance.

And it is precisely the performance of all that constitutes the subject matter of this instruction, according to the prescribed rule, which is the cause for attaining liberation characterized by absorption into the nature of ultimate reality; this is the teaching intended here. Therefore, for any qualified person, in any [circumstance]...

While it remains impossible to avoid even a terrible action when it is enjoined by the scriptures, [the Lord] addresses Arjuna— who is characterized by being the subject of such a terrible action and who possesses the qualifications of one fit for liberation through instruction.
The preeminent sage begins to instruct this secret, whose author is the Blessed One;
therein, the passage beginning with "On the field of dharma" (p. 16) and ending with "What did they do, Sañjaya? [is presented].

The words of Sañjaya, prompted by the questions of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— beginning with "Having seen the army of the Pāṇḍavas" and ending with "the tumultuous noise resounded"— [describe] the entire armies of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, who had assembled and were frantic with the resolve to slay one another.

Because they indicate the exertion and intensity of the battle between the formidable warriors, these [verses] have the purpose of demonstrating the severity of the action; they are explained by their very utterance (*nigadavyākhyāta*). Likewise, beginning with "Then, seeing them drawn up in array" (*atha vyavasthitān dṛṣṭvā*), the words of Arjuna are indeed those spoken by Sañjaya.
The introductory sections on the inspection of the armies, beginning with "between the two armies," etc., are easy to understand.

Following that, even the words of Hṛṣīkeśa spoken by Sañjaya have clear meanings. Then, the section concerning Arjuna, beginning with "There Pārtha saw them standing" and ending with "sinking down, he spoke," [is presented].
The speech of Sañjaya, consisting of the act of beholding the circle of kinsmen such as fathers and grandfathers, is also clear in meaning. Therefore,
[the grief] arising from the ignorance of the reality that is to be negated by the instruction at hand regarding those kinsmen, such as fathers and grandfathers...

Having seen these kinsmen of Arjuna— who was despondent regarding the fruit of battle, filled with doubt about his duty, overcome by an onset of compassion, and designating unrighteousness itself as righteousness— [the Lord spoke] the words beginning with "O Kṛṣṇa" and ending with "that would be more conducive to my welfare."

The statements that set forth the false knowledge easily accessible to the human nature are indeed self-explanatory. Consequently, the speech of Sañjaya beginning with "Having thus spoken to Hṛṣīkeśa... has its meaning already established; such is the purport of the first chapter.
It has been explained; indeed, not word-for-word for fear of prolixity.
O Lord, for those who meditate upon that [teaching] which is the prologue to the dramatic performance of the method for bestowing grace upon the worthy— the first chapter of the Gītās—
their mind, moistened by the nectar of divine flavor, blossoms with burgeoning curiosity.
May the assembly, with due respect, fix their close attention upon this.

Thus ends the first chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the syntactical connection of the meaning of the words, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.

In certain parts of this historical section, the completion of the sage’s discourse is seen to occur sometimes with six quarters (pādas) and sometimes with half a verse; such instances are observed here and there. Therefore, in this case:
In various contexts throughout that work, it should be understood in exactly this manner. Now,

in order to introduce the words of the Blessed One— which indicate the commencement of the instruction on the ultimate truth (paramārtha) and which arose because he desired to inspire Arjuna, who was thus overwhelmed and agitated by the power of delusion— [the following is said].
Saṃjaya said: To him who was thus overcome with compassion, whose eyes were clouded and filled with tears,
and who was sinking down, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 1 ||
That which the Blessed One said then, he spoke thus:
"Whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis, O Arjuna? It is un-Aryan, it leads away from heaven, and it brings infamy."

From what cause, or for what reason, does this defilement— consisting of delusion, which causes exhaustion through the performance of one's own duties that ought to be performed in such a manner— afflict you, sir, in this adversity?

O Arjuna, when a crisis has arisen and arrived—what kind of dejection is this? It is "resorted to by the ignoble" (anāryajuṣṭam), meaning practiced by the undisciplined; for that very reason, it is "not leading to heaven" (asvargyam), which is opposed to the attainment of heaven, and "causing infamy" (akīrtikaram), meaning productive of reproach. This connection of the words is quite clear. However, regarding this specific meaning:
Incorporating this [meaning], the Blessed One said: here the word "Arjuna" is not intended merely as an address to the person so named,
but rather for the purpose of indicating the weight of his qualities— such as noble lineage, wisdom, and prowess— which reside within him.

The word "you" (tvam) is also employed as a designator of the Self, whose essential nature is in reality free from the impurities of delusion and the like; therefore, in actual fact, there is no connection between you— who you truly are— and this stain of delusion, just as there is none between light and darkness.
This is utterly impossible; thus, the phrase "how has this come upon you? (p.
18) contains an implicit meaning. For this very reason, it was stated that "this sin is practiced by the ignoble, those who do not know reality, and the wicked," and so forth. || 2 ||
In this very sequence, in order to qualify this [statement], he said:
"Do not yield to unmanliness, O son of Kuntī; this is not worthy of you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe! (3)

O scorcher of foes! O producer of fever in the hearts of enemies, do not yield to cowardice or the conduct of a base man; for such a thing, fit only for those of little courage, is not possible in you, whose greatness consists of virtues such as prowess renowned throughout the world. Therefore, [abandon] that which is trivial and insubstantial.

Abandoning this weakness of heart and emaciation of spirit, arise and take up the effort in the praiseworthy task of battle that has been set before you. Here too, the use of the word *tvad* (you) should be understood as encompassing the previously mentioned meaning, as should the use of the word *klaibya* (weakness).
"By way of internalizing the state of being devoid of discrimination"— thus, other qualifiers should also be applied in this manner.
Now, at present,
because he lacks the wisdom capable of discerning the true nature of the Self and the non-Self, [he perceives] only the body and so forth.
Perceiving [the enemy] as his own self,
Arjuna spoke in order to prohibit— by pointing out the faults— the undertaking of battle which results in the great sins of killing one's preceptor and others.
How, O Madhusūdana, slayer of enemies, shall I fight against Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle with my arrows, when they are both worthy of worship?

O Madhusūdana! In what manner and by what means sanctioned by the scriptures shall I cause my grandfather Bhīṣma and my preceptor, the Brahmin Droṇa, to be struck back in combat with arrows in battle? Or rather, the accusative case may be explained as being used in connection with the word *prati*.

And the root *yudh* is indeed intransitive; the use of the *parasmaipada* here is Vedic. It should be understood similarly elsewhere as well. Since those two [the parents] are the supreme benefactors who bestow knowledge, name, and wealth, and whose hearts must be satisfied even at the cost of one's life, they alone deserve worship. In this regard, by this—

By the question "How? (katham), Arjuna indicated his intention that the Lord’s presentation of the desire to abandon the battle at hand as being base is indeed improper, because it contradicts the Dharma. || 4 ||
(19) Then he said: "Indeed,
rather than slaying my high-souled gurus,
it would be better even to lead a life of begging here in this world."
But I would not, for the sake of wealth or desire, enjoy pleasures stained with blood after having slain my gurus. || 5 ||
Since by avoiding battle the slaughter of my elders is avoided,

and since it would be praiseworthy for me to consume even alms-food without having killed them, I, who am desirous of dharma, will not slay them for the sake of those desired sense-objects nourished by their blood.
In equal splendor. || 5 ||
Moreover,
we do not know which of these two would be better for us: whether we should conquer them, or whether they should conquer us.
Those very ones, by slaying whom we do not wish to live, stand before us, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

We do not know this very thing: which of these two objects would be more significant—that is, more weighty—for our purpose? He asks: "Of which two objects?"—namely, whether we might conquer those adversaries and overcome them, or whether they [might conquer] us.
They would treat us with contempt. He states the reason for not knowing which of these two outcomes is more grievous:
because those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our brothers, whom we do not wish to keep alive even for a moment due to the loss of our kinsmen after having slain them—those very men stand before us.

[They] remained [silent]. What is meant by this? If we were to kill the Kurus, what would be the greatness of that side, since its fruit would be nothing but suffering? And thus, by implication, this would have been said: if they were to defeat us, that side would be the greater one.
Now, having established that the performance of ritual combat (samarakarma) must be avoided because it obstructs dharma and happiness, [the author],
fearing the fault of conceit regarding his own scholarship, [addresses] the Blessed One...
Proclaiming himself to be full of doubt, he said:
"With my nature overwhelmed by the defect of pity, and with my mind confused regarding dharma, I ask you."
Tell me that which is the best, upon which I may rely;
I am your disciple, instruct me who have taken refuge in you.

"O Blessed One, because my own nature has been impaired by the fault of miserliness and by the wretchedness born from the injury of my kinsmen, and because the duty of a Kshatriya has been destroyed, my mind is utterly bewildered regarding the teachings of the Dharma and the conduct prescribed by the scriptures; thus, with a doubting heart, [I have come] to you..."

I ask you this: therefore, please point out with certainty and without doubt that matter which would be for my ultimate good and most praiseworthy; for I am your disciple, one who is to be instructed by you. Thus, being a true teacher, instruct and enlighten me, who have approached you in this manner. || 7 ||
Furthermore,
I do not perceive that which might dispel this grief of mine, which withers the senses.
Having obtained on earth a sovereign, prosperous kingdom, and even lordship over the gods.

For this reason, I do not consider anyone other than you to be one who might dispel my grief— that is, my sorrow— and which grief is such that it withers and torments the senses, both internal and external organs. Having done what?
"Even having obtained a vast sovereignty over the earth free from all adversaries—

or rather, to say this is too little— even having attained the lordship of the gods, for one whose very nature is afflicted by the defect of miserliness, there would be nothing but sorrow; therefore, instruct me."
Thus, the priority of the action of obtaining (*avāpti*) should be understood with reference to the action of grieving (*śocana*), and not with reference to the action of removing (*apanodana*);
for if it were so [understood], there would be the fault of a discrepancy in the agent (*bhinnakartṛkatva*) and a lack of syntactic coherence (*samanvayābhāva*). (p. 21)
The defect in meaning would be difficult to avoid. || 8 ||
Then, in order to demonstrate Dhananjaya’s firm resolve to abstain from battle,
Saṃjaya said:
"Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes— "
Having said to Govinda, "I will not fight," he indeed became silent.
O descendant of Bharata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of both armies.
The meaning of these two verses is already understood; however, "hṛṣīkāṇi" refers to the senses, and their "īśa" is the Lord who controls them. They call "guḍākā" sleep;
its "īśa" is one who is not to be overcome by it—thus this epithet of Arjuna is to be explained. || 10 ||
Thus, desiring to turn Arjuna— who had abandoned his resolve for battle due to the delusion of ignorance—
back toward his own duty through the instruction of perfect knowledge,
the Blessed One spoke.
Your inner self being afflicted by human frailty, you have lost consciousness due to being overwhelmed by despondency and delusion; yet,
seized by compassion, you look upon your kinsmen.
Nor those who have not reached the mouth of Death. || 11 ||
Due to the absence of instruction, at present your intellect is not suited to the unfolding of the divine creation;

with your inner self afflicted by human nature— characterized by an abundance of doubt and erroneous knowledge— and because of the lack of recognition, the true nature of your real Self has been obscured.

The word "you exist" (*vartase*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Because your defeat—the destruction of your capacity—has been wrought by despondency born of grief, by dejection consisting of a lack of resolve, and by delusion which is the cause of erroneous cognition and mental distraction;
for that reason, you are unconscious, meaning you have lost the aforementioned right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Why?

He says that this is understood because, having observed your kinsmen who have entered the jaws of Death whose onset is difficult to ward off, you were seized by compassion— that is, you were gripped by pity and took up a state of sorrow.

[The compound] has been formed. Because [the class] beginning with *āhitāgni* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, it should be understood that there is no *pūrvanipāta* (mandatory prior placement) of the word *gṛhīta* here. Therefore, this is strictly a *bahuvrīhi* and not a *tatpuruṣa*;

for if it were the latter, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having different agents [for the two actions]. By means of this verse, [the author intends to state] what is about to be said...
The knowledge of the distinction between the body and the embodied one, which is the first thing to be established regarding the knowledge of the self, has been indicated. 11.
Since this state of regarding [the body] as a kinsman— bound to a particular configuration of the body that is utterly perishable—
is rooted in a failure to reflect upon the true nature of the embodied self, for this very reason he says:
Lamenting for those who should not be lamented, you speak as one who is not wise;
the learned do not grieve for the dead or for the living.

Like a wise man, you do not prattle like one who lacks intelligence about how the conduct of war— which culminates in the slaughter of kinsmen, elders, and others— is unrighteous and results in suffering, and thus brings ruin upon both worlds; this is not a final, settled conviction.

This very doubt is produced by the absence of knowledge that distinguishes between the body and the embodied soul. For these elders and others are not necessarily merely perishable bodies; rather, they are eternal embodied souls distinct from those bodies. Therefore, what were you doing?

Like a wise man, you do not speak out; for those who are not to be grieved for—because they are subject neither to destruction nor to suffering from the perspective of ultimate reality—are beyond the scope of lamentation. Yet, grieving for them and treating them as objects of sorrow, you consider them as such. And because these [beings] are eternal, it is precisely for that reason that you [grieve for] those whose life-force has departed.

From those various bodies, those whose vital breaths have departed and who thus partake of the designation "dead," as well as those whose breath has not yet departed and who, because their vital breaths remain within those respective bodies, partake of the designation "living"— the wise, who have realized the supreme truth, do not grieve for them.
And thus, in order to establish their eternity even during the state of individual existence (jīvāvasthā), he says:
"For never was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men."
And yet, after this, none of us shall ever cease to exist.
(23) Regarding me, whom you think to be present: "I was never non-existent.
By means of the double negative, this establishes precisely what is under discussion—the existence in prior time.
It does not mean that I come into being after having not existed; rather, having existed previously, I exist now as well.

Just as I am, so too you, appearing as present at this moment, certainly existed previously; you did not come into being after having not existed. And just as you are, so too all these kings, appearing as present, certainly existed previously, and not...

Furthermore, there is the coming into being of these [elements] after not having existed. Nor is it the case that none of us at all will cease to exist immediately after this body; rather, we shall certainly continue to exist. By this, [it is shown that] for the world of living beings established through the distinction between "you" and "I," [existence persists] throughout the three periods of time.

Because of the possibility of existence, he asserts its permanence. However, the designation of [the self] as the agent of actions such as "I was" and so forth is caused by the delusion of grammatical coreferentiality with a body characterized by perishability; it does not belong to that which is permanent.
The designation as "the origin of beings" and so forth is thus justified. || 13 ||

Now, one might raise the following ill-conceived doubt: "Since the living being (jīva) residing in the body is perceived as possessing agency, knowledge, and so forth, how can it be eternal if that [body] is destroyed?
To dispel this doubt by demonstrating an example perceived through direct observation, he says:
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this. 14.
In this body, which is grasped by the notion of "I am," just as there are for this embodied soul—

the experiencer of that body— the three states of childhood (the state of being a child), youth (the state of being young), and old age (the state of being aged), which are impermanent, so too [is the body].

Being considered as the source of the elements (*bhūtādi*), it is connected [to them]; likewise, by that very same illustration, the attainment of another body from this body is already established for that Self which pervades both bodies. In that regard, one who does not know reality falls into delusion, thinking that the embodied self perishes upon the destruction of the body.
The fool thinks it has perished; however, the wise man, a scholar who knows reality, is not deluded in that regard.

He does not think it is destroyed by the destruction of the body, but understands it to be eternal. What is meant by this? Just as there is no destruction of the self when states such as childhood perish.
The cognizer considers himself to be one and enduring; likewise, while connecting various bodily associations through the states of past and future,
every single cognizer connects the stages of infancy and so forth through the states of past and future.

The awakened one constantly perceives the Self. Through these gross states, such as childhood and so forth, it should be understood that the subtle states residing within them—such as waking and the rest—are also being described. For indeed, among those [states], which possess mutually distinct forms...

While these [states] proceed, characterized by arising and perishing, the Self— endowed with the single characteristic of being the perceiver, possessing a nature entirely distinct from them— is established for everyone through self-awareness as existing by virtue of its pervasiveness. || 14 ||

Thus, having introduced the ultimate non-duality of the Self by means of demonstrating the logical possibility of the distinction between the body and the embodied being as being unified through illusion,
[the author now explains] the reason why all living beings are deluded regarding the nature of the Self as it has been established, perceiving it otherwise.
Having first explained that [the world] proceeds in such a manner, the Lord speaks in order to teach the means for its cessation:
"But the contacts with the senses, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting, coming and going, and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata. (15)

The term *mātrā* refers to the capacities of the sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*artha*), which are so called because they "measure" (*mīyante*)—that is, they serve as the means for the cognizer, who is distinguished by his embodied nature, to determine the objects of cognition.
The term *sparśa* refers to the sense objects (*indriyārtha*), because they are "touched" or perceived as objects of knowledge. And these...

They are of two kinds: those consisting of sound and so forth, which are perceived by the external senses such as the ear; and those consisting of pleasure and so forth, which are perceived solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction.
Furthermore, for the eternally existent Self in the ultimate sense, these contacts with the objects of the senses—

The connection is that they bestow cold, heat, pleasure, and pain. When associated with the body, they produce the cognitions, "I experience cold" and "I experience heat"; when associated with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), [they produce similar cognitions].
They provide the cognition: "I experience pleasure," and "I experience pain.

Consequently, by superimposing the nature of the self upon cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and so forth, they [regard these] as impermanent within the self because their intrinsic nature is subject to arising and destruction.
The meaning is that they delude all living beings by producing the delusion of permanence.
Since they, in the ultimate sense, perish every moment, therefore,
reflecting upon the Self as eternal through the reasoning already set forth, endure and bear with them, remaining surrendered to them.
Do not abandon your firm standing in the support of your own eternal and unchanging self merely because of contact with impermanent pleasure and the like; just as you,
the sole hero of the three worlds, [overcame] adversaries who were attacking with irresistible pride and arrogance.
They were endured by me— who remained firmly established in my own unshakable manly vigor and whose inner mind underwent no change even when insulted—
because they repeatedly bore the burden of contempt;
likewise, having superimposed ego upon my own nature which is naturally free from modification, those [feelings] known as "touch" were also endured.
Let the adversaries be tolerated merely by examining their inherent lack of substance and their true nature;
for this delusion is produced solely by the absence of inquiry into things as they actually exist— namely,
the superimposition of attributes such as the body and the intellect upon the Self, leading one to think, "I am emaciated," "I am full," or "I am happy."

Cognitions such as "I am suffering" arise in grammatical coreferentiality with that [Self]; however, in reality, they abide as one with its own essence and are merely touched by the powers of the external and internal organs, but not to any degree whatsoever.

They are capable of producing even a minute particle of modification in the Self; for this Self, which is like a crystal mirror, cannot be altered by proximate cognitions of pleasure and so forth, even though they flash forth as appearances similar to blue, yellow, and the like. As it has been said:
By the power of attachment, the various manifestations of the multitude of objects shine forth; yet the wise man never undergoes internal transformation, just as a mirror [remains] unclouded.
He was serene.
Thus, for this very reason, the term *mātrāsparśa* (contact with the objects) is used as a designation for the senses and their objects.
By this verse,
[the self] is shown to possess a nature that is fragile like all objects of perception, similar to states such as childhood or waking.

Even in states such as pleasure that pertain to all living beings, it has been established that the Self is one, eternal, and all-pervading, endowed with the single nature of being a conscious experiencer. And yet, this does not entail the consequence that when one individual experiences pleasure and so forth, everyone must experience pleasure and so forth; for:

Cognizing subjects (*pramātṛ*), which are merely appearances of mutual differentiation manifested through *māyā*, constantly perceive themselves as mutually distinct; however, this is not the case for the ultimate, supreme subject (*para-pramātṛ*). For in that [supreme subject], there is always, everywhere, and in every way a nature devoid of all distinction, being one alone.
All this is interconnected, as it has been stated—
beginning with "I take refuge in Him, the creator of beings"—
and so forth.
In that eternal, extended, and firm thread, the entire universe—
composed of both the existent and the non-existent— is woven together within the All-Creator, whose limbs are the universe itself.
Thus [ends the section]. 15.

Thus, in order to demonstrate that when such a nature exists, one is well-established in one's own self characterized by liberation— (in the Kaśmīra, Gauḍa, Ghaṭika, and Guptaka recensions, the reading is *suvyavasthitatvaṃ muktalakṣaṇam*)—
he says: "For those [senses], O bull among men, do not afflict that person..."
The steadfast one who is equal toward pain and pleasure is fit for immortality. || 16 ||

That person who possesses the characteristics described above—who, while abiding in the state of one seeking liberation, exists through wisdom that is exclusively focused on knowledge and free from conceptual construction;
who is therefore steadfast (*dhīra*) because he has fully understood the ultimate reality of both existent and non-existent categories; and who is therefore equal in pain and pleasure—[is the one].
When pleasure and pain are touched by a single form— namely, the mere state of being cognizable by the mind— and are thus equal,

he remains one whose internal modification is not produced by such things as pleasure and pain, which, like jars and other objects, are characterized solely by the common property of being cognizable; these [pleasures and pains] [do not affect him].

The objects denoted by the term "contact," such as sound and so forth, are impermanent because they are subject to the nature of birth and destruction; they are not the causes of erroneous cognitions such as "I am happy."
They do not cause one to fall away from the Self, which is Truth because its sole nature is to be the solitary knower distinct from them;
that [Self] leads to immortality—that is, to non-perishability by virtue of attaining identity with the Supreme Self—and thus one becomes liberated. This is the meaning. || 16 ||

Then, preceded by the presentation of arguments, he speaks in order to establish the ultimate existence of the self as having the singular nature of being a knower, and likewise to demonstrate the absence of birth and destruction for the body and so forth, which are its objects of cognition and possess those [characteristics].
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being;
the truth regarding both of these has been perceived by the seers of reality. 17.
In this world, by its very nature, that which is a non-existent thing has no being—that is, no existence—because it is non-existent;

likewise, for that which exists eternally by its own nature, there is no non-existence—that is, no destruction—because these two, existence and non-existence, are absolutely mutually exclusive like light and darkness. However,...
The end— the finality or certainty— of both these views has been seen and known by those who know reality and have directly realized the supreme truth, but not by those who do not know reality;
for the latter [possess] cognitions of objects produced by the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is inconceivable and wondrous.

Those who, failing to reflect upon the true Self, perceive the body and other objects— which lack real existence due to their being unreal and impermanent— as existing in terms of "this-ness" because they are experienced as such,
[yet] which in ultimate reality are indeed existent; [they perceive them thus].
Because the eternal reality of the Self is not recognized, they perceive it as non-existent. || 17 ||
Therefore, in order to instruct [the disciple] as to what is truly existent and what is non-existent in reality, he says:
"But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this imperishable. (18)

Between these two—existence and non-existence—know, that is, understand, that which is indestructible because it is devoid of the nature of destruction; it is existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). What is that? It is that one by which this entire collection of things, both moving and unmoving, consisting of mutually distinct appearances, is pervaded.

It is expanded when the intention is to express agency (*kartṛtva*), or it is pervaded when the intention is to express the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). For in ultimate reality, there is only one Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, who is the omniscient agent of all;
however, for the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*)—who are manifested by Him—the body and so forth alone constitute their mutual distinctions.

For those who conceive of it as a self, agency and knowledge— which have limited objects— are not real. Thus, because this reality designated as the essence of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is imperishable, being devoid of limitations such as space and time, and possesses an undecaying nature, [agency and knowledge] are of a different character from it.

No object whatsoever, whether of the nature of an action (*kārya*) or an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), is capable of effecting destruction or non-existence. For no impermanent, delimited entity has the power to destroy an eternal object whose majesty is in every way unconditioned. || 18 ||
Having established that [the Self] has the nature of a sentient being, he speaks in order to establish its nature as a non-sentient being:
"These bodies of the eternal embodied one are said to have an end; they are perishable, while [the Self] is immeasurable. Therefore, fight, O Bhārata! (19).
Because it has as its sole characteristic the undeluded state of being the perceiver throughout all bodies and in all conditions, it is eternal and indestructible;
and because it cannot be delimited by the body and so forth, it is immeasurable.

These bodies belong to the embodied Self (ātman), which is the object of such notions as "this much" and so forth; they are distinct from that [Self], mutually different, and perishable because they possess the nature of coming and going, and because they have a perishable essence; likewise, they are finite because they are delimited by space, time, and other factors.
Since these [objects] have become the objects of such measurements as "this much" and so forth, they are connected merely by the quality of being knowable; thus,

when the destruction occurs of that entity in the form of the body— which is ultimately perishable— due to the reason of its being merely an object of knowledge and so on, then [upon the destruction] of that which is connected to the Self, the Self [is also affected].

The perception of destruction is a manifestation of ignorance, and that is not possible in your case. Therefore, established in the true nature of the Self as it has been explained, and possessing the sense of "I," perform your own duty—which is difficult to avoid—by means of the reasoning to be stated hereafter; fight in the battle at hand.
One should practice thus. || 19 ||

Now, you may think: "War, being an action characterized by violence in the form of killing others, how could I engage in such a terrible deed involving the slaughter of my teachers, kinsmen, and others?
This notion of yours is merely a manifestation of delusion born from ignorance of the true nature of the Self.
For he who thinks this [Self] is a slayer, and he who thinks it is slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain. (20)
He who, under the influence of illusion, failing to reflect upon the Self— which is ultimately changeless and absolutely real—
mistakes the body, which is of a different nature, for the Self.
By superimposing bodily attributes such as killing upon this true Self, one perceives— that is, conceives of— this very Self as the slayer,
the agent of the act of killing; and likewise, one who [perceives] this very Self, characterized as described, as imperishable...
They consider [the body] to be "slain" or "injured" by superimposing the attributes of the perishable body upon it;

both of them, under the sway of delusion, have their right knowledge seized by the obsession of identifying the Self with what is not the Self, and thus they do not know the true nature of the real Self. For this reason, this...
The Supreme Self, whose very nature is the supreme, changeless pure consciousness,
always perceives all this as its own self and thus does not kill, nor is it killed;
it does not assume the agency of the act of killing based on the status of being a killer, nor does it assume the status of being the object to be killed.
The status of being the object belongs to the action of killing. || 20 ||

For these [attributes] are possible only for the individual souls (kṣetrajña), whose nature consists of conventional usage characterized by conceptual construction and erroneous cognition; they do not belong to the Supreme Self,
which is never born nor does it ever die.
Having come into being, this [Self] shall not cease to be hereafter;
it is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient.
It is not slain when the body is slain. (21)

This Self, whose characteristics have been described, is not born—that is, it does not arise—because its nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of limitations such as place, time, form, and state;
nor does it die, that is, it does not perish, because its nature is eternally unarisen. Nor...
It experiences the modification of existence (*bhāvavikāra*) in the form of the state of persistence (*sthityavasthā*) occurring within the interval between birth and death.
For those distinct states, consisting of birth, persistence, and destruction, have as their substratum impermanent entities such as the body;
indeed, those entities [manifest] when qualities (*dharma*) previously non-existent appear.
They are said to be "born" when they arise; they are said to be "destroyed" when their previously existing nature has disappeared;

and in the interval between these two, they are said to be "abiding" due to the delusion caused by the similarity in the flow of their respective conditions. Furthermore, this is a state of non-recurrence for those [phenomena], but not for the self, which is eternally existent.
There is a connection with non-existence; and because it does not deviate from the single characteristic, there is neither the manifestation nor the disappearance of another property.
By this verse, the negation of its three states characterized by birth, duration, and destruction is established.

This has been established. Now, these very modifications of being are negated of this [Self] by means of qualifiers (according to the reading *viśeṣyasya pratītiḥ*). In that regard, this Self is "unborn" (*aja*), meaning it is not produced according to the stated sequence; thus it is devoid of the modification of being characterized by birth, which is impermanence.

Likewise, by the term "eternal" (*nitya*), meaning always inseparable from its own single nature, the modification known as transformation— characterized by the appearance and disappearance of other attributes at every moment— is negated for this [Self]. By the term "constant" (*śāśvata*), meaning perpetually endowed with a complete form...

The modification characterized by increase is denied of this [Self]. For it does not undergo a modification in the form of growth after having previously been diminished, as is the case with impermanent entities. Likewise, by the term "ancient" (*purāṇaḥ*)—meaning eternally existing from time immemorial due to the impossibility of a prior limit—the modification characterized by decay is denied.

Transformation is denied; for this [Self], having become increased, does not subsequently diminish, unlike the state of the body and so forth. Likewise, when the body is being slain, this Self is not slain, because the body alone is impermanent; for that which undergoes states such as birth, the state of destruction is also possible.
By the phrase "but not of the eternal self," the modification characterized by destruction has been denied of it.

However, the sixth modification, characterized by existence (*astitva*), was previously indicated by the term "non-existence after having existed" (*bhūtvābhāva*) within the three aforementioned states; therefore, it is not mentioned now. Or else:
Some do not accept that existence [is subject] to modification; therefore, it was not mentioned. //21//
Thus, O Pārtha, how can that person— who is devoid of all modifications of being, who knows the imperishable, the eternal, the unborn, and the unchanging— be slain, or how can he slay? 22.

That person— the cognizing subject— who always, at all times, knows this imperishable Self whose nature has been thus established, how and in what manner could he be slain or destroyed, or could he slay another, since he realizes himself as non-different from that [Self]?

How does one destroy another? This state of being the agent and the object of the act of killing is established only among the unawakened *kṣetrajñas* who possess the conceit of a self bound solely to the body. || 22 ||
Now, one might object: "When the body is destroyed through killing and the like, the attributes of consciousness are no longer perceived;
therefore, when the body perishes, how can it be understood that the self is imperishable?
To dispel such delusion, its eternity is once again established by means of illustrative examples.
To strengthen this conviction, he said:
"Just as a man, having cast off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new."
In the same way, the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new. (23)
Just as a certain person, having discarded worn-out clothes that have been used, remains the same while taking up and acquiring others that are new and fit for use— by this [analogy],
it is shown that [the Self] is not [affected] by the conjunction with or separation from various bodies overcome by the manifold transformations such as birth and so forth.
It is the state of being devoid of the single characteristic of being merely the knower of that [object]. || 23 ||
This Self is indeed eternal, not touched in the slightest degree by the impermanent attributes of the body; for:
"Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it;
water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it. (24)

Weapons such as swords and the like do not cut this Self—that is, they do not divide it into two parts, just as they cannot divide the body; likewise, fire does not burn it, water does not moisten it, and the wind does not cause it to wither away. 24.
When the body is being modified by cutting and so forth, there is no contact with modification for that [Self] which is by nature changeless; for it is said:
"This is indeed uncuttable, unburnable, undissoluble, and also undrying."
It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient. || 25 ||

This self is not subject to modification through actions such as cutting; this is a restatement of what was previously explained. Likewise, qualifiers such as "eternal" and so forth, which signify indestructibility, are employed in great number to mutually support one another for the sake of strengthening comprehension.
These are to be understood. || 25 ||
And thus it is said: "This Self is unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable;
therefore, knowing it to be so, you ought not to grieve. (26)
Because it is not an object for the sense organs— such as the ear and others whose objects are manifest things like sound— it is called "unmanifest" (avyakta);
likewise, because its nature is solely that of the knower, it cannot be grasped by the internal organ even as an "this."

"Unthinkable" (*acintya*) means it cannot be made an object of thought; it is beyond the scope of the act of thinking. Likewise, because it is in no way touched by any other attribute apart from pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*), it is "unchangeable" (*avikārya*), meaning it is impossible to bring it into a state of modification. Therefore, in the manner thus described, [it is] from every respect...

Having realized this Self— which is entirely distinct from the objects within the range of all the senses and which pervades all objects by virtue of being the knower— you ought not to grieve over its destruction through the destruction of the body, nor through the resulting delusion of its destruction. 26.

Thus, although the first [section], which consists of the demonstration of the logical possibility of the distinction between the body and the embodied one, has been set forth in detail by the text beginning with "In this way, you [are not different] from the human [state]" (2/11), etc., regarding the knowledge of the non-duality of Brahman— which is the subject matter propounded throughout the entire treatise— ...

Considering that Arjuna was currently unable to grasp even the preliminary stage because it is to be understood only through a particular application of extremely subtle and pure wisdom, the Blessed One spoke in order to enlighten him by setting aside all other positions.
Or even if you consider him to be constantly born or constantly dying,
even so, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for him.

Alternatively, even if you do not understand the matter as it has been stated through the sequence of arguments taught by me, and you still consider this self to be constantly born or constantly dying— nevertheless:

Even by that reasoning, you ought not to grieve for him on account of his perishability. The purport here is this: regarding the self, two possible conceptions may be entertained—it must be either eternal or non-eternal;
a third alternative is impossible. In that regard, if [one proceeds] with the conception of its eternity...

Even if you consider this [self] to be eternally born, always arisen and devoid of destruction, nevertheless, because it is indestructible, what occasion is there for grief? Or, if through the perception of its perishability you consider this [self] to be eternally dead, lacking existence, even then, because it is eternally destroyed—

There is no ground for lamentation. Others, however, explain it thus: "Even if you consider this self to be eternal and always connected with birth and death because of its impermanence, even so, you ought not to grieve for it. (27)

Having understood this very uninterrupted flow of birth and death as being perceived by some as eternal and by others as non-eternal— even regarding this *ātman* (the reading "even regarding this *ātman*" is found in the Kaivalya-gama-pustaka)— he speaks in order to explain it:
For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died;
therefore, you should not grieve over this inevitable matter. 28.

The word *hi* indicates the reason: because for that which is born—that is, for the body itself, which undergoes the modification characterized by birth and is apprehended as the self—death, known as destruction, is certain (*dhruva*) and inevitable; and in the very same way, for that which is dead and destroyed, birth is inevitable. Of what, then, is this [certainty]?

The worldly saying that "one who is born dies, and one who has died is born"—which consists of the connection with modifications characterized by birth and death—remains established even for people who do not investigate the truth; therefore, even from the perspective of common worldly parlance, grief is simply untenable. || 28 ||
He speaks of yet another way to dispel grief:
"O Bhārata, beings have unmanifest origins, manifest middle states, and unmanifest ends; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (2.28)

(34) Because they consist of bodies which are the locus for the arrangement of the elements such as earth and so forth, all living beings are referred to here by the word *bhūta*. These very elements, beginning with the unmanifest (*avyakta*), have unperceived prior forms; likewise, they have the unmanifest as their dissolution.

They extend as far as the imperceptible. For it is not known that these were previously of such a nature, nor that they will again become of such a nature in the future; therefore, with respect to both these extremes, they are not to be grieved for. Although the manifest states are perceived in their various specific forms, [they too are not to be grieved for].

Those whose intermediate state consists of the period existing between birth and destruction are likewise not to be grieved for; for in their manifest state, the perception of stability is merely an illusion. Indeed, in whatever manner these [beings] exist...

They are conceptualized as such, and therefore they are indeed perishable.
