Whether they be momentary, or whether they be characterized by the emergence and disappearance of properties due to their nature of transformation, in every way, when these are conceptually constructed, they are simply not to be grieved over, because a single, stable form is impossible. Thus it is said.
Since bodies are understood to be merely a configuration of the elements that constitute the self, what occasion is there for lamentation? Thus, [verse 29].
Now, although this matter has been explained in many ways, because of its extreme profundity, it is impossible to retain in the mind and to put into practice; therefore,
[the Lord speaks] in order to remove Arjuna’s lack of resolve regarding this subject.
To show that this matter is to be understood through extraordinary effort, he says:
"Someone beholds this as a wonder; likewise, another speaks of it as a wonder."
And yet another hears of this as something wonderful;
but even having heard it, no one at all truly knows it.

Someone, by virtue of the ripening of preeminent merit among thousands of men, at the end of many births, perceives this very Self— whose nature has been explained as it is— in reality, through recognition, and realizes it directly. He who...
He sees it as something marvelous. (p.

35) Just as someone might occasionally, by some means, for a mere moment, see a marvelous and unprecedented wonder, in that same way, someone who has performed meritorious deeds [sees this] for a mere moment.

He sees it; likewise, someone of a similar nature, appearing as if in a wondrous form, speaks of it to another for the sake of awakening them and explains it. In the same way, someone else, being of that very same nature, hears and comprehends what is being presented by another. Someone...

Because he has not been favored by the grace of the Blessed One and his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is afflicted by ignorance, he does not know this Self—whose nature has been explained as it is—even after hearing it from someone skilled in its exposition; that is, he does not know it in its true essence. And he...

One of such a nature is indeed not fit for instruction; you, however, because you have been favored by the Lord as indicated by your collection of qualities such as devotion and faith, are truly a fit vessel for the instruction of this truth—this is the meaning of "be diligent in this. This is the intended purport here.
May there be some fortunate recipients who, through the lineage of teacher and disciple or by their own direct experience, come to realize this for themselves; yet,
this cannot happen without the dissolution of all veils of conceptual construction through the constant practice and cultivation [of meditation].
Because it is not free from impurity and because it is unstable at all times, this is merely a preliminary practice;
thus, according to the sequence described, one should correctly understand that only a rare individual—one among hundreds of thousands, someone in their final birth—could truly become such a person.
Therefore, even if you are a suitable candidate for this, you must not remain one of dull resolve.
It must be cultivated. || 30 ||
Therefore, he states the conclusion here: "O Bhārata, this embodied self in the body of everyone is eternally indestructible;
therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings. (31)

This embodied self (dehin), whose sole defining characteristic is the state of being a cognizer entirely distinct from all objects of cognition such as the body and so forth just described, [is distinguished] by the mere fact that the body is an object of cognition and he himself is the cognizer.

The Lord is the supreme subject; He alone exists as the pervasive one, eternally and perpetually present within the various forms of bodies throughout the multitude of living beings— those illusory subjects who, identifying with the mere physical body alone, mistake it for the Self.

"Indestructible" (*avadhya*) means incapable of being killed or destroyed. For when various bodies— which possess the nature of coming and going, are subject to manifold changes, and always have as their sole intrinsic nature the state of being merely objects of cognition— are destroyed, [the Self remains], as that which pervades them all and is one.

The destruction of the Self—which is Truth, whose majesty is unlimited, which has the single characteristic of being invariably associated with the state of being a knower—is impossible. Since this is so, there is certainly no occasion for lamentation regarding that which is eternal by virtue of its indestructibility. Therefore, the elements (bhūtas) possess only the nature of destruction.

Seeing that bodies—which consist of specific arrangements of the elements such as earth and so forth—are themselves understood as "possessors of bodies" (embodied beings) and are thus subject to destruction, you ought neither to grieve nor lament;
for what occasion is there for sorrow to a person of discrimination when that which was already lost meets its end? This is the meaning. || 31 ||

Then, perceiving that Arjuna was unable to accept the true nature of the Self due to the arguments already presented, the Blessed One [proceeded] by inflaming his pride, which is appropriate for the Kṣatriya caste, regarding his own duty that must necessarily be performed.
To urge him forward, he said:
"Furthermore, considering your own duty, you ought not to waver;
for there exists nothing better for a kṣatriya than a righteous war. (32)
O Pārtha, by good fortune, such a battle as this— this open gateway to heaven— has come to you Kṣatriyas through your own meritorious deeds.
But if you do not engage in this righteous battle,
then by abandoning your own duty and fame, you will incur sin.
Furthermore, people will speak of your undying infamy;
and for one who has been highly esteemed, ill-repute is worse than death. (35)
The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear; and having been highly esteemed by them, you will now meet with contempt.
Your enemies will utter many unspeakable words, reviling your prowess; what indeed could be more painful than that? (37)
(37) Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle. (38)
These seven verses have been explained by the very words [of the commentary]. || 32–38 ||

Thus, even while it remains established that one does not abandon one's own karma in any way by resorting to dharma characterized by activity, which has heaven and other impermanent fruits as its cause,
[one must resort to] dharma characterized by cessation, which is the cause for attaining the unsurpassed and eternal fruit.
To establish once again as his final conclusion the very teaching on knowledge that was under discussion— asking what fault there would be in not abandoning these— the author says:
"Having made pleasure and pain equal, and gain and loss, victory and defeat..."
Therefore, prepare yourself for battle; in this way, you shall not incur sin. || 39 ||
Proceeding in this manner, you will not incur—meaning you shall not obtain—the evil or sin that might be expected from the slaughter of kinsmen and the like. How so? First of all:

By virtue of being filled with eternal, unsurpassed bliss, [he is one] whose nature is pure universal consciousness (*sāmānyasaṃvinmātra*), which— through the firm and unshakable wisdom that has reached a state of realization free from doubt regarding the meaning as it was taught— has recognized all living beings in all their states as being pervaded by that [universal consciousness].
Having established an unartificial self-identification with the True Lord— who is devoid of any desire to attain another object distinct from His own nature—
one should abandon the erroneous cognition that characterizes the non-self, such as the body and so forth, as the Self; this error is produced by the delusion of *māyā*.

In the Self, which is the seer that remains equal toward pleasure and pain, joy and despondency— things conceived as distinct by all living beings through their respective cognitions as either to be accepted or rejected, and which perish at every moment—
the Self is characterized by the absence of any modification consisting of specific qualities, because it is connected [to objects] merely as the object of vision.

Having made them equal and devoid of distinction through right practice, and having likewise accomplished the gain and loss of desired objects such as a kingdom— which are the causes of those two— as well as victory and defeat, which are themselves the causes of those two,
making them both equal and indistinguishable in their true nature as they actually exist.

The meaning is "having ascertained. For these [states] such as pleasure and pain, being connected merely by way of being objects of cognition (*vedyatva*), are not capable of imparting even the slightest trace of modification to the cognizing Self (*ātman*). Just as blue, yellow, and so forth, being connected merely by way of being illuminated (*prakāśyatva*), [do not affect] the illuminator.

They are not capable of manifesting any particularity of light, such as blue, yellow, and so forth; rather, they are connected to it solely by way of being illuminated, in a single form. This is as follows:

The commonality of pleasure and the other [feelings] consists solely in their nature as being objects of experience (*vedyatva*). Having thus equalized pleasure and the rest, immediately after attaining this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one whose mind is well-established in this absorption [is described by] the word "fight" (*yuddha*).
"Engage in your own duty"—that is, apply yourself to it; the meaning is: perform your own duty by being established in the knowledge as previously described. || 39 ||

Having thus determined that the very synthesis of knowledge and action is what must be taught, and considering that the subject matter of knowledge has been treated as if in isolation, he now begins to speak on the subject matter of action; those same two— knowledge and action— he expresses by means of the terms *sāṃkhya* and *yoga*.
Speaking in accordance with worldly convention, He said:
"This wisdom has been declared to you in Sāṃkhya; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga, O Pārtha, by which wisdom joined, you shall cast off the bondage of action. (40)

The enumeration of things to be abandoned and things to be accepted—such as "this, the self and so forth, is real" and "this, the body and so forth, is unreal"—is *saṃkhyā*. The treatise composed concerning that [enumeration] is here called *Sāṃkhya* in its primary sense, because it possesses a name according to its actual meaning (*anvarthatayā*); [the other system] is based upon that.

Knowledge, moreover, is Sāṃkhya, but not that which was composed by Kapila and others, because its ultimate truth consists in the doctrine of a plurality of selves. Regarding that subject of Sāṃkhya, this understanding—this wisdom—has been taught to you through this treatise; by means of that wisdom, that...

*Sāṃkhya* is that which is correctly joined (*samyak yujyate*) or understood (*budhyate*). *Yoga* is the connection with the object characterized as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*), which is attainable through the aforementioned knowledge; because it has that [knowledge] as its cause, it is action itself that is designated here by the word *yoga*. For knowledge alone does not possess the quality of being the cause for a connection with the meaning of *yoga*.
It is possible; however, it will be explained in detail later that this pertains only to the action associated with that [Self].

Regarding such a yoga of action, listen to—that is, comprehend—this intellect which is about to be described, by means of which [one discerns] "What is action? What is inaction? [the true nature of action]. (Khaṇḍa-puṭa) By what [intellect does one know] the reality of action?

The reading is: "it is understood as the cause of liberation. In reality, it is action alone that is understood as the cause of liberation. For this very reason, he says: "endowed with," that is, connected to, the understanding which is about to be described, you [should perform] what is done through action.

(p. 39) You will cast off—that is, you will abandon—the bondage of lack of autonomy, which has as its object those people who are devoid of knowledge. For such a performance of action will be taught here, by means of which even that action which is the cause of bondage for all utterly deluded people becomes solely a cause of liberation.
It culminates. || 40 ||
For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that this yoga of action possesses a power distinct from yoga characterized by the cessation of mental fluctuations, he says:
"In this, there is no loss through transgression, nor is there any obstacle."
Even a very small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear.

In this context, when the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is undertaken, there is no destruction by transgression as there is in the case of yoga characterized by the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*);
for the latter must be accomplished through all the stages (*bhūmikā*) thoroughly practiced according to the prescribed sequence.

When there is a transgression characterized by skipping over the stages— consisting in the failure to attain each preceding stage before ascending to each subsequent stage— the [yoga] perishes and does not even maintain its own nature.
Such destruction, however, does not exist in this yoga, owing to the reasoning that will be explained immediately hereafter.

Likewise, when an action is performed imperfectly due to the deficiency of its various constituent parts, there arises a transgression (*pratyavāya*) consisting of diseases and the like to be experienced by the present body,
as well as the suffering of dwelling in the womb and so forth to be experienced by a future body.
The occurrence of the union with the undesired is possible; however, in this case, as before, even that does not exist,

because this dharma— consisting of the practice of one's own duties as enjoined by the scriptures and having the nature of meditative concentration— is preceded by the aforementioned knowledge and constitutes a specific form of right conduct.

Even a very slight connection with this [Self], whose nature has been experienced for even a brief moment, protects— that is, fully preserves— the practitioner, the yogin, from the fear and terror characterized by the notion of "self" in what is not-self, which is the great cause of all worldly existence.
The meaning is that it further negates even that connection. For here, while the attribute (dharma) exists,

there is the unsurpassed *samādhi*, which is the self-reflection (*pratyavamarśa*) upon one's own nature, characterized solely by the supreme manifestation (*paraprakāśa*)— the singular consciousness of the universal (*sāmānyasaṃvit*) which is the sole cause for the constant and uninterrupted manifestation of all things.

By the very fact of being manifested once (*sakṛdvibhātatva*), the complete nature that is to be accomplished is enjoined; and that which is merely manifested brings about the complete fruit. And so it will be said:
"Even at the time of death, remaining in this [state], one attains the Nirvāṇa of Brahman" (2.74).
Thus, in this case,
unlike yoga— which is characterized by the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*) achieved through stages practiced in a sequential order of earlier and later steps—
neither destruction nor transgression are possible. Nor does this present [state]...

Because the excellence of the dharma characterized by the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is being demonstrated here, it should be understood that the yoga of cessation (*nirodhayoga*) is entirely excluded; for the latter must be practiced at fixed times such as the first and last watches of the night, just like those specific ritual acts such as bathing mentioned previously.
That which has a fixed procedure is indeed included [within this]. || 41 ||

And in order to demonstrate that one such as you— who is indicated by the manifestation of qualities such as pure devotion and faith— is the qualified person for this [instruction], and not just anyone at all, he says:
O joy of the Kurus, the intellect characterized by resolute determination is indeed one;
for the intellects of those lacking such determination are many-branched and infinite.

Resolve (*vyavasāya*) is determination; that which has this as its essence (*ātman*), its very nature, is intellect (*buddhi*) of such a form. By its inherent nature, intellect possesses only a single characteristic. Determination may have real objects such as the self (*ātman*) as its domain, and it may also have unreal objects such as the body (*deha*) as its domain. In that regard:
That which has an unreal object as its domain is a semblance of certainty; it cannot possibly be a certainty at all.

Therefore, the intellects of those who lack primary discernment regarding an object that is real—those who are undiscerning—are multi-branched, cluttered with various webs of conceptual constructions even concerning a single object, and remain unresolved.

For those whose intellect has not attained firm ground in the Self, which is the ultimate reality and the sole cause for the total extinction of all desires, do not find rest anywhere as they grasp at impermanent objects, thinking, "This has been obtained; this is yet to be obtained. || 42 ||

He says that the intellect of such persons— who have set out with the sole aim of enjoying the fruits of heaven and the like— is not applicable to the supreme Dharma which has been introduced for discussion.
O Pārtha, those who are unwise, who are devoted to the mere recitation of the Vedas and who assert that "there is nothing else," utter this flowery speech. (43)
Those whose nature is desire, who look toward heaven, who long for the fruits of birth and action, are intent upon specific rituals directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and power. (44)

For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [desire], the intellect characterized by resolute determination is not established in meditative concentration. (45)

This very intellect, which is characterized by resolve and has the nature of determination, is not established— not directed— toward *samādhi*, that is, toward the application of the mind upon the ultimate reality whose characteristic is the Self, for those persons who are attached to enjoyments and power.
He is instructed because she lacks the capacity to comprehend that meaning;

for those who are intensely attached— meaning solely devoted— to the sovereignty, ownership, and excellence of desired enjoyments and sense-objects, which consists in the preeminence of excluding all other things, [for them...]

The intellect characterized by worldly resolve, which has as its object impermanent things consisting of enjoyments, does not at all take hold of the resolve that has meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as its object. Of what sort are those people—to whom the intellect is not directed toward meditative absorption? They are those who are attached to enjoyment and power. By that speech [it is said]:
By what speech [do they speak] to those whose minds have been captivated and whose hearts have been won over? By this well-known speech, which is "in flower"—

meaning it is devoid of the fruit characterized by the awakening to the ultimate truth and is joined only with the flowers that are sensual enjoyments— and which is devoted to the doctrines of the Vedas.

The ignorant speak and explain; here, the word "Veda" should be understood as referring to a specific portion of the Veda that prescribes mere ritual action devoid of knowledge. The "discourse" (*vāda*) regarding such a Veda—that is, its expression—is itself the supreme [authority].

Those for whom this is the reality are so described. For this very reason, they are "proponents of the non-existence of anything else," meaning they are habitually inclined to assert that there is no scripture other than the Veda which prescribes specific ritual acts that serve as the means for attaining results such as heaven. For this same reason, they are "unwise."

Those who, regarding an object that consists merely of transient, impure, and surpassable enjoyments produced as the fruit of rituals such as sacrifices, accept it as the fruit of the goal of human life (puruṣārtha), are not wise. For they [accept] an object contrary to this, characterized by the nature of the Self— which is indestructible, pure, and unsurpassed.

Those who perceive [objects] as fruits attain the state of being wise (*vipaścit*). For this very reason, he states their qualifiers which indicate a lack of wisdom. Furthermore, those whose nature is desire have sounds and other objects as their dear [goals].
p. 42) Those for whom the self is everything because it constitutes their very essence, and who, precisely because they are characterized by desire,

are intent on heaven— meaning those for whom heaven, as the locus of supreme enjoyments, is the highest (*para*) or most excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*) thing to be attained— and likewise those who desire the fruits of birth and action when their enjoyment is exhausted.
Birth necessarily occurs somewhere in another womb;

when that exists, there is karma consisting of merit and demerit; and when that exists, there is a fruit characterized by pleasure and so forth—those who desire to obtain these [seek] the enjoyment of power for this very reason.

The various specific actions, such as sacrifice, charity, austerity, and so forth— which serve as the means toward the various paths (the *gatis*) that result from the sovereignty over desired objects— are the different types of karma.
"Abundant" means those who are numerous; not only those attached merely to obligatory and occasional rites,
but even those who expand upon specific optional rites— by the speech that such teachers utter, for those whose minds are captivated by it.

The connection [of the words] is: "the intellect of those attached to enjoyments is not directed toward meditative absorption. The intended meaning here is as follows: those who, being themselves devoid of awakening, are devoted solely to enjoyment, are [further] praised by others of the same kind for that very purpose.

Since those whose intentions are nurtured in such a manner are driven far away from the resolve to attain the ultimate truth, how can the intellect of such persons be made subject to concentration in meditation? || 45 ||

Therefore, by your very nature, you are a fit vessel for the instruction of the consciousness under discussion; thus, O wise one, abandon this state of mind that is being scorched by the fire of words intended merely to please the ignorant (according to the reading in the Khaṇḍana-puṣpa manuscript: "a state of mind being made subservient to words").
"Be established in the knowledge as it has been taught," he said:
"The Vedas have the three qualities (guṇas) as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna!
Be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity (sattva), beyond acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self. (46)
The three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are themselves "traiguṇya" (the state of having the three qualities).

Because it consists of the intellect (*buddhi*) which is composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, that whose object or substratum is *traiguṇya* is "traiguṇyaviṣaya. Here, by a figurative usage, the class of transmigrating persons is referred to by the word *traiguṇya*.

It is said: Thus, those Vedas whose object or sphere of experience is such a state consisting of the three qualities (traiguṇya) are of that nature. For those who seek pleasure and the like are enjoined by the Vedas to perform specific ritual acts which are the means for attaining those [pleasures].

Since they do not realize as their own self the true Self— which is of a nature entirely distinct from all [else], which is omnipresent, unique, and possesses the aforementioned attributes— therefore, for them, the Self, though existing, does not exist. But you,
being free from the three qualities (*nistraiguṇya*), become possessed of the Self, having emerged from the three qualities (*nistraiguṇya*).

Transcending the three qualities (guṇatraya), this Self is connected with the qualities— such as pleasure and so forth— which consist merely of being objects of cognition, yet its sole nature is that of the cognizer; it does not possess those qualities, for in the ultimate sense, its nature is entirely distinct from them.
Reflecting upon such a one as the Self, become possessed of the Self;

that is to say, do not allow the ultimate reality of the Self—which is truly existent—to become non-existent, as it were, due to laxity in the practice of the instructions you have received. And when...
When you realize the Self as the Self, whose nature transcends the three qualities (guṇas), then become free from dualities—

freed from the pairs of opposites such as pleasure and pain, thirst, old age, death, and other afflictions. For these dualities exist only in that which is not the Self and is composed of the three qualities.

These are the causes for the notion of self regarding the body and so forth. And because you are free from the pairs of opposites (*nirdvandva*), therefore become one who is eternally established in *sattva*; that is, remain always situated in that *sattva* which is indestructible—the state of true being—and find your firm foundation therein. Being such, even though you are without acquisition or preservation (*niryogakṣema*), [remain so] regarding that which has not yet been attained.

Yoga is the attainment of an object to be attained; Kṣema is the preservation of what has been attained. One who has emerged from both of these is "niryogakṣema"; become such a one. For there is nothing whatsoever to be attained for one whose self is eternally complete and entirely free from desire.

It is possible; nor is there protection against the fear of destruction for any object that has been acquired as something unprecedented. Therefore, security and well-being (yogakṣema) are based solely upon the body and so forth, which are grasped as a semblance of a self by erroneous cognition. Thus, from that...
Become possessed of a self through the reflective awareness of a real self, by means of a cognition of the self that is free from [superimposed] exclusions. 46.

Nor [is it the case that the scriptures] are crowded with hundreds of instructions regarding the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) of specific rites enjoined for the sake of persons to be instructed who are solely intent on the performance of active duty (*pravṛttidharma*), due to their being attached to enjoyments and power.

(p. 44) It should be understood that within the family [tradition] and the Vedic scriptures, everything is to be practiced; however, a wise person should accept only so much from them as is necessary for the accomplishment of their intended purpose, characterized by the realization of the ultimate truth. Thus he says:
As much purpose as there is in a small reservoir when there is a flood of water everywhere,
so much is there in all the Vedas for a Brahmin who possesses true knowledge.

In a water source— such as a lake or a spring— in which water overflows from all sides in every direction and is abundant with moisture, whatever purpose is required by those in need, there is merely the utilization of a small portion of water sufficient to satisfy thirst and fulfill its functional purpose from a single spot.
The purpose, for one who knows, possesses discernment, and realizes Brahman— that is, for the Brāhmaṇa—

is the entire meaning of all the Vedas together with their secret portions (rahasya). For by a single portion of the scripture, the fulfillment of the purpose characterized by the attainment of the supreme reality occurs.

At that very moment, he should take from it only as much as is required; what is meant by this? Just as a thirsty person in need takes only a small amount of water—sufficient merely for the accomplishment of his own purpose—from a reservoir of water that is like the ocean, though it be overflowing with thousands of rites.

Only that which is useful is taken up, not the entire reservoir of water. In the same way, even from the Vedic scriptures— which are filled with a multitude of various objects pertaining to knowledge and action—
only that meaning which is useful for the mere understanding of reality (tattva) should be grasped by one desiring to know that reality, and not [anything else].
"The entire Vedic scripture is indeed [the authority]," so it is said. (47)
Then, having understood what is to be accepted from all the scriptures, [the Lord] spoke in order to instruct Arjuna, placing him at the forefront:
"Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits."
Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction.

Now, by virtue of the firm conviction rooted in the realization of the truth of reality just taught to you, as your cognition of the Self turns away from the impermanent body and so forth, [you perceive] that which is of the nature of the non-dual light consisting of consciousness.
For one who perceives the supreme reality as "I" through the sense of self,
let there be eligibility for action— that action which consists of specific activities to be accomplished by means of body, speech, and mind.

The qualification for that which is prescribed in the scriptures as necessarily to be performed— distinguished by the divisions of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), depending on place, time, and circumstance, consisting of various primary and secondary procedures, and categorized as obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth.

The sense is: "You possess agency; therefore, being authorized by that [agency], proceed toward the accomplishment of your own purpose. For action is invariably concomitant with embodiedness and cannot be abandoned by anyone. Furthermore, even in states such as those of an ascetic (*yati*) and so forth, some specific discipline must certainly be observed; and thus, that very [discipline]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

One attains a specific distinction in karma, similar to the rules governing the duties of different stages of life (*āśrama*); thus, the renunciation of action in its entirety is impossible. Furthermore, let it be granted that even non-renunciation may be designated as "renunciation"; however, that merely reveals one's exclusion from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
For one who is such [as described], since aversion cannot possibly exist without being an object of aversion,

it is difficult to avoid the consequence that the very mention of the renunciation of action entails passion and hatred. Furthermore, if— on account of the oneness of reality— the performance of actions according to one's own will and without restriction were itself considered renunciation, [it would follow that all worldly activity is renunciation].
Even if this is accepted, nevertheless, as before, because passion and hatred would otherwise be inexplicable,

that [state] also reveals only the lack of knowledge of reality on the part of the practitioner; thus, there remains either the state of non-action or the state of non-contradictory action, which is the supreme [state], overflowing with the unsurpassed and infinite innate bliss.

For the yogi who is intent upon the knowledge of reality and who desires to ascend to the supreme state of meditative absorption (samādhi), characterized by equality toward all while realizing the truth as the Self— both [of these positions] are untenable; therefore, let your qualification be in action alone, but not for them.

May there be no inclination toward the fruits of actions— which consist of various worldly and scriptural enjoyments sought through diverse intentions appropriate for those ignorant of the Self, and which are the causes of bondage—
for those who, due to their lack of knowledge of reality, engage in various such actions with those fruits as their objective.
While those actions of theirs are being performed, they remain in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as seeds upon the ground of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); and consequently,
when the experience of the fruits of impermanent actions has ceased, [the continuity persists] in those various [beings] in the form of diverse latent impressions.
In various other wombs, they repeatedly become the cause of that particular birth;
and birth becomes the cause of that particular karma, while karma assumes the status of being the cause of that particular fruit.

"This wheel of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), birth, and the fruits of action revolves incessantly, serving as a cause for bondage for the ignorant; therefore, do not become like an ordinary person, subject to the fruits of action.
By the method described, [understand] the fruits of actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious."
One who is such that pleasure and the like— which constitute the nature of happiness— are not the cause, meaning the instrumental factor of his birth;

being thus established in the aforementioned knowledge while performing actions, he brings them to a state where their seeds are burnt by the fire of that knowledge, characterized by the attainment of the essential nature of the Supreme Lord.

The meaning is: "Attain liberation. Furthermore, because the abandonment of action is being enjoined in a certain state, regarding that which you consider to be "inaction," let there be no attachment (*saṅga*) of yours even to such inaction; for even attachment to that is like [attachment to] another form of action.
That it is indeed the cause of bondage has already been stated previously. || 48 ||
Therefore, established in yoga, perform actions while abandoning attachment, O Dhanañjaya;
having become the same in success and failure, such equanimity is called yoga. 49.
In this context, the practice of actions prescribed by the scriptures,

characterized by steadfastness in the knowledge of the non-duality of the Self as previously described, is called *samādhi* or *yoga*. This is just as the knowledge known as *Sāṃkhya*, propounded by Kapila and others, [is distinct from] that propounded by Patañjali and others.

Perfection in Yoga is characterized by the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; likewise, perfection in the performance of action and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) constitutes perfection in the knowledge of the non-dual Self taught here. Thus, that [knowledge] is also expressed by the word "Yoga. In such Yoga, one who is established remains there, having abandoned other stages of life (*āśrama*).

Having established yourself [in this state], perform the actions as they have been described. How? By abandoning attachment—that state of mind which is intent solely on the means due to the realization that those actions are the cause for attaining their respective specific fruits—and therefore, even upon success, that is, the attainment of the fruit, [remain free from it].
And since both [the self and the object] are immutable, when that [object] is not established and is thus destroyed, one becomes equal and without distinction; for,
being established in the aforementioned knowledge, one is satisfied by the bliss born from the constant reflection upon the aforementioned reality of the Self, which is eternally perfect.

Since there is no distinction consisting of pleasure or pain arising from the fruit of action— whether that fruit be impermanent, accomplished, or unaccomplished— you should, having ascended to the state of universal equanimity,
become established in the yoga as described. For equanimity exists toward all things.
The state of being untouched by even a trace of modification amidst all conditions is called Yoga; the meaning is that the attainment of equanimity itself is its final goal (niṣṭhā). || 49 ||
For this very reason, he states the characteristic of the yogi who is established in this yoga:
"He whose undertakings here are all free from the bonds of desire, and for whom everything is offered in renunciation—he is a renouncer and he is wise. (50)

The connection is as follows: for that person who is qualified for the yoga described above, all undertakings—that is, all activities and inclinations—even those that are inevitable—become free from the bonds of desire; such a person is a renouncer (*tyāgin*). "Desire" (*āśīḥ*) refers to the longing directed toward impermanent objects of enjoyment.
That very bondage, because it is the cause of *saṃsāra*, is the bondage of desire (*āśīrbandhana*), which is a lack of independence.

"Free from the bondage of desire" (*nirāśīrbandhanāḥ*) means they are devoid of the bondage consisting of worldly enjoyment. For this very reason, all auspicious and inauspicious actions in the form of obligatory duties—

And in the case of renunciation— specifically the renunciation of the desire for fruits— it is like a collection of seeds cast into a fire for the purpose of destroying their capacity to produce fruit; one who performs obligatory duties (nityakarman) in this manner alone is a "renouncer" (tyāgin), possessed of true renunciation, and not one who acts out of fear of hardship and the like.
"One who abandons actions alone becomes a renouncer"—the reasoning for this has already been stated previously.
And such a person is one endowed with praiseworthy knowledge, not one who considers the mere abandonment of action and so forth to be knowledge. || 50 ||
Therefore, one should perform action endowed with such superior intelligence, and not merely [action] alone; thus he says:
"For action is far inferior, O Dhanañjaya, to the yoga of intelligence."
Seek refuge in the Buddha; the wretched take refuge in the causes of their fruits. || 51 ||

Because, through the yoga of the intellect—that is, through the concentration on knowledge as previously described—action devoid of that [knowledge] alone is by far superiorly inferior; it is lowly because it is devoid of knowledge and is a cause of saṃsāra, meaning it is extremely base compared to that. Therefore, in the aforementioned intellect...
Seek right knowledge as your refuge and support; the meaning is that you should rely upon it precisely because it is desired as the means [to liberation].
For those which are causes of results are merely impermanent results characterized by enjoyment.

Those for whom the cause is the motivating factor in the actions that serve as the means to achieve that [result]—they are wretched ones who perform mere ritual acts devoid of knowledge; they are miserable because of their pursuit of trivial fruits, and [their consciousness] is therefore delimited by the ego-identification with various castes, bodies, and so forth. For this very reason...
Considering themselves to be afflicted by thirst for the fruit consisting of impermanent enjoyments, they are of evil conduct. || 51 ||
Therefore, in order to explain the true nature of the knower who is distinct from that [ignorant person], he says:
"Endowed with wisdom, one casts off here both good and evil deeds;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in actions. (52)

In this system, the Self alone, the Supreme Lord, is the single reality (*tattva*). He alone, by the power of His own *māyā*, through the manifestation of objects of knowledge, is the one ultimate agent of the entire aggregate of effects.
And as He fashions this manifold effect, there exists for Him nothing other than His own mere will.
It depends neither on a material cause nor on auxiliary factors;
and although this effect appears in such a manner, it is incapable of imparting even the slightest trace of modification, because its essential nature is pure consciousness alone.

Thus, he who reflects with unwavering realization upon that single reality endowed with such eternal and unsurpassed sovereignty as being his very self— he is said here to be "endowed" or "connected" with intelligence, supreme awakening, and perfect knowledge. And he, being of such a nature—
In this context, one who is qualified for the yoga of action being taught, even while performing actions,
perceives everything with equanimity due to having entered into the state of the Lord;
he regards this as "well-done" or virtuous action because it is a cause of results such as the happiness of heaven, and that as [evil] because it is a cause of suffering.

"Evil deed" means wicked action; thus, regarding the distinction imagined by those who lack the wisdom of discernment and who perceive things unevenly—both "well-done" and "evil-deed"—the yogin, being composed in universal equanimity, abandons and relinquishes them.
For such a yogin, even an action currently being performed does not possess the characteristics of either well-done or evil-deed.

The meaning is that he resorts to duality. Thus, by this half-verse, it is taught that one who possesses the knowledge of reality must certainly perform prescribed action, and must not superimpose upon it the unreal conceptualization of "being" or "non-being. Since this is so, therefore you—

Being firmly established in the knowledge of reality as it has been described, apply yourself to yoga— that is, to meditative absorption (*samādhi*)— by means of the performance of action; that is, become disciplined through the practice of actions,
because skillfulness in performing actions consists in being grounded in the aforementioned knowledge.
In this context, that very state of acting rightly is yoga and samādhi; it is nothing else. || 52 ||
To explain this very point by means of a formal argument, he says:
"For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action, being liberated from the bondage of birth, go to the state that is free from suffering. (53)

Because for one who is always and in every way free from desire, having abandoned— that is, relinquished— through non-attachment the fruit consisting of pleasure and so forth which necessarily arises from action performed by those ignorant of reality, and because such a person is established in the Self; therefore...

Because birth is bound to karma performed with a view toward its fruits, they— being liberated from that bondage characterized by rebirth and from the lack of autonomy— are, through the absence of obstacles, [attained] to the state free from affliction (*anāmaya*).

They go to—that is, they attain—the state which is free from the defects of conceptualizing [things] as impermanent, pleasant, and so forth; that abode whose nature consists in being established in the ultimate reality.
Therefore, the connection with the preceding verse is: "Thus, being endowed with intelligence, apply yourself to yoga. (53)

And when this knowledge of reality, though explained, does not immediately take firm root in the mind because it is so exceedingly difficult to fathom, you must not become discouraged in this matter; for you will come to know it gradually— thus he says:
When you have crossed over the thicket of delusion by means of discernment,
then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.
When your intellect, confused by the various scriptural teachings, shall stand firm, resolute, and unshakable in concentrated meditation, then you will attain yoga. 55.

When, at which time, you— by means of merely realizing the validity of this taught knowledge— [shall have cast off] the thicket of delusion, that mire of ignorance consisting of the notion of "I" directed toward the body and so forth, which has been practiced since beginningless birth;

When you transcend— that is, leap over— this through the realization of their erroneous nature, then you will attain detachment (*nirveda*) and dispassion (*virāga*) toward the objects of various scriptures, which are characterized by the doubts of people who think, "This has been heard" and "This is yet to be heard."

(50) ...you will go. And because of that lack of certainty, being possessed by doubt such as "this has been heard" and "this is yet to be heard," your intellect— rendered discordant and contrary due to the unacceptability of that learning which consists in hearing various scriptures— will become determined [in its rejection].
When she, having had her doubts removed by the aforementioned knowledge of the Self, and being thus immovable— unshakable even by powerful conceptual constructions—
shall stand firm in this samādhi, attaining stability, then, by this sequence, she will attain the aforementioned yoga characterized by the samādhi of action.
You will obtain; you will attain. || 55 ||
Then, having heard the words of the Blessed One, "Your intellect shall then become steady," Arjuna spoke, not yet fully understanding the true nature of one whose wisdom is established.
What is the description of one whose wisdom is established, O Keśava, when he is situated in samādhi? What does the man of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move? (56)

O Blessed Keśava! Skill in actions is indeed called *yoga*, and unwavering discernment is called the state of one whose discernment is established (*sthitaprajña*). Now, what is the description of such a person whose discernment is established?
How does he speak? What is his explanation? For this appears to be contradictory.
Since action is defined as the activity of the three—speech, mind, and body—none of these three types of movement are possible for him. How could he speak?
He would not perform the act of speaking, because his wisdom is unwaveringly fixed upon the single reality.

Speaking, which is the activity of speech, is not possible for him. Would he go—that is, would he perform a bodily activity characterized by the action of moving? That too is not possible for him, as before. Or would he sit—would he remain with an internal state alone, having ceased the movement of speech and mind? That too is not possible for him.

It has been stated that for one engaged in yoga characterized by skill in action (*karmakauśala*), [the notion of] an agent consisting of the operation of both actions is not tenable; thus, because its essential nature cannot be determined, it was asked, "What is its verbal form?
And these three questions should be understood as referring solely to action in its general sense, where the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). || 56 ||
Now,
regarding the one whose "all undertakings" [are as described]—
as stated by the term "the wise one" (*buddhimat*) in the passage beginning at (50), p. 51— it is the one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*).
Although its true nature has already been largely explained, it was not correctly ascertained because it is difficult to comprehend;
therefore, in order to instruct Arjuna, [the Lord] speaks again, qualifying it by some particular aspect, so that he may grasp it.
The Blessed One said: "When one abandons all desires that have entered the mind, O Pārtha,
and is satisfied in the self alone by the self, then one is said to be of steady wisdom."
Indeed, in this science which is the ultimate secret of all secrets, there is perhaps one among hundreds of thousands—

a person whose single self-nature has been fully manifested through cultivation over a thousand births, and who has grasped the supreme nectar of reality, having shaken off the impurities consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*.
When only pure being remains through that [process],
the qualified person is an exceptional individual in his final birth, whose wisdom is capable of the reflective awareness of his own true nature.
He, whose firm hand was grasped by devotion and faith— those two constant companions sent by the Supreme Lord who desired to show him favor when such an opportunity had arisen—
and whose foot was firmly placed upon the ladder of knowledge as it has been described.

He has resolved to ascend to the supreme abode, which is the form of the reflection of the ultimate causal absorption; with reference to this, he will speak while designating the very reality of the Self as "I-ness."
"Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection;
and even among those who strive and have attained perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth. (7.3).
Likewise:
"At the end of many births, the one possessed of knowledge takes refuge in Me" (7.19), and so forth. When such a person practices this, he becomes one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*).
What does he practice? When [he abandons] the desires residing in the mind, which exist within the realm of volitional constructions (*saṃkalpa*)...

One abandons—that is, relinquishes completely—happiness and other fruits that result from actions performed by one who does not know reality; one does not even form a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) toward them. However, one does not abandon the actions themselves. How is this possible?
That one performs actions yet abandons their fruit. To establish this:

He states the qualification: "satisfied with the self alone by means of the self. Not everyone experiences satisfaction or joy based on their own consciousness as the locus; rather, it occurs when some previously unobtained, impermanent object that serves as a means to pleasure is acquired.

[The ordinary person] attains satisfaction only with what is impermanent (p. 52). This yogin, however, [attains it] through the mere absence of reflective awareness regarding the Self, which is the light of consciousness that is eternally present and never-setting.

As if by a great treasure that had been hidden and forgotten, yet which— because it is always perfectly full in its own majesty and because it cuts off all longing for any other object— had merely attained a state of concealment, [he was now restored] through the power of his memory being awakened once again.
Having attained this unsurpassed gain through the very truth and intrinsic nature of the self, he has obtained innate bliss. And being such as this,
how could he not [despise] those sensual pleasures which are sought by the wretched and whose nature is non-arising and non-perishing?
One should abandon it. || 57 ||

And when, being thus situated, one abandons desires even while performing all actions, then one becomes "steadfast in wisdom" (sthitaprajña)— that is, one whose intellect has attained a firm foundation in the aforementioned nature.
Having thus stated the general characteristics of one steadfast in wisdom, he speaks as follows to describe that very state in detail:
One whose mind is unperturbed by sorrows, who is free from longing for pleasures, and from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed—he is called a sage of steady wisdom. 58.

In this world, pleasure and pain— which are the fruits of karma— act as causes for the transformation of all living beings in two ways, both when they are about to be experienced and when they have been attained. However, this person of steady wisdom, whose characteristics have been described, [remains unshaken] even when such sufferings are about to be encountered.

One whose mind is undisturbed becomes indeed fearless in heart, because one has attained a firm foundation through the realization of the true nature of the self as it was described and perfected; thus,
having entered the samādhi of universal equanimity, fear likewise [ceases].

Terror arises from the inability to counteract that which causes the obstruction of happiness; likewise, anger is resentment toward such an obstructive thing when it can be countered. He in whom these have departed—that is, are gone—is called one whose wisdom is steady (sthitaprajña). || 58 ||

Having thus described the specific characteristic of one whose wisdom is steady by virtue of remaining unmodified when about to experience pleasure or pain, he speaks in order to demonstrate that same state through the absence of modification when actually experiencing pleasure or pain:
He who is without attachment everywhere, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious—his wisdom is firmly established. 59.
The yogi, having encountered various infinite varieties— whether they be means of happiness or means of suffering,
or whether they be of the nature of pleasure or of the nature of pain, or auspicious or inauspicious— (p. 53) [remains equanimous].

He does not rejoice, nor does he resort to agitation characterized by unprecedented momentary joy; for he is without attachment toward any object whatsoever, [thinking], "This is my everything; without this, everything else of mine is a cause of suffering. Attachment (*anurāga*) toward desired objects is *abhisneha*. That—

He who has not [these] is so described. Likewise, he does not hate, nor does he undergo agitation characterized by the effort to repel them. For one of such a kind, whose intellect remains well-established solely in his own eternal, unchanging Self even when the pleasant and unpleasant are encountered—of him...
Wisdom is said to be established. || 59 ||
To demonstrate that one who possesses that very action which, as a means (*upāya*), brings about such establishment of wisdom is indeed "one whose wisdom is established" (*sthitaprajña*), he says:
"When he withdraws these [senses] from all sides, like a tortoise its limbs..."
When the senses are withdrawn from the objects of the senses, one is then said to be of steady wisdom.
The word "ca" (and) indicates exclusion (*vyatireka*). When, moreover, this yogi withdraws all his sense organs— the ears and so forth— from all objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest,
he separates them from their [external] nature and makes them focused solely upon that [Self], which is of the nature of the rays of the sun of consciousness.
How so? Just as a tortoise draws its limbs within itself, making them reside solely within its own body, so too is he called one whose wisdom is steady. || 60 ||

Now, regarding the withdrawal of the senses from their objects: does this consist in the non-perception of sound and so forth, or rather, as stated here, in remaining free from modification even while sound and so forth are being perceived?
Since both these alternatives are possible—
Having first established the stability of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he speaks in order to support the very position of the reply (uttara):
"The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food."
With the exception of taste; for even this taste ceases upon seeing the Supreme.

This is stated by way of concession: it is true that for one who abstains from food—even when not consuming sound and other objects permitted by the scriptures, but rather avoiding them from afar—the desired sense-objects such as sound recede due to the absence of proximity; consequently, they do not initiate their own effects, such as passion and the like.

However, with the exception of *rasa*— that is, excluding the craving for that object, the affliction known as passion (*rāga*)— for at that time it remains either dormant or attenuated; or else, in the case of one who has reached the ultimate state of steadfastness (*paramanaiṣṭhika*), even *rasa* indeed ceases, being supreme and most excellent.

Having seen and realized the object to be attained through meditative concentration (*samādhi*); or rather, when this practitioner perceives the supreme reality through the sequence of concentration that abandons sense objects, then,
because even the "taste" for that [reality] never ceases for one who has seen it, the word *anta* (end) is used in the sense of finality (*niṣṭhā*).
This is to be explained. || 61 ||
Thus, demonstrating that even for one who has reached the highest pinnacle of concentration through the avoidance of sense objects,
there exists a deceptive form [of practice], he describes the non-deceptive concentration which consists of the enjoyment of unprohibited sense objects preceded by the aforementioned knowledge.
Establishing his own conclusion, he says:
"For even of that wise man, O son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind. (62)
Restraining those [senses] with the mind, one should sit disciplined and intent upon that; for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established. (63)
Because even for that wise and learned man who has attained fitness for the vision of the supreme reality while remaining composed and withdrawn from sense objects,
[the senses] are intent on seeking flaws and are by nature destructive, owing to their constant readiness to obstruct his knowledge.

The sense faculties, having found even a slight opportunity, forcibly and violently seize the mind and the consciousness; they draw it away even from the fruit of meditative concentration and lead it toward the objects of the senses. For such things are indeed heard of.

Yogis who have reached the culmination of the yoga of restraining sense objects may, even after a long time, have their minds overwhelmed by the senses turning toward desires. Therefore, having restrained the mind with a consciousness established in the aforementioned knowledge— having brought it under one's own control— one should remain disciplined in the reality of one's own Self, characterized as previously described.
Being concentrated in all states, being solely intent upon that and devoted to it,
he should remain with his senses fixed precisely on their engagement in perceiving sound and other objects as permitted by the scriptures.
For, in the manner described, for that yogin whose senses abide in a state of subjection and control, [his mind becomes steady].

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is said to be that which has attained a firm, immovable state. In this regard, there is this illustration: suppose there were a certain snake-charmer who, through the power of mantras, was capable of restraining serpents. When he—
If he indulges in negligence characterized by laxity in the practice of such mantras,
then those serpents, who seek out vulnerabilities, will surely destroy him. However, someone else,
because of his knowledge of the secret of the *Gāruḍa* scriptures, becomes endowed with such excellence that by those very [serpents]—

He plays with serpents as if with garlands of flowers, and they are never able to overcome him. In the same way, for that yogi who, by some skillful means, practices meditative absorption (samādhi) for a time after having abandoned the sense objects, [even] from the slightest interruption of his attention...

Having gained the opportunity, those sense objects indeed afflict the mind. However, one who is always well-established in the ultimate self as described above cannot be disturbed in any way, even while sporting with sense objects. As it has been said:
Even while dwelling in the midst of sense-objects, the wise man does not truly dwell there;
whereas the foolish man dwells even among evil objects.
Thus [ends the verse]. 63.

Now, because of the use of the comparison "like the limbs of a tortoise," the withdrawal of the senses (*saṃhāra*)—which is their restraint (*saṃyama*)—consists precisely in turning them away from sense objects; it is not otherwise than that [turning away from those sense objects]. [That withdrawal of the senses...]

Explaining otherwise— that is, in a different manner— the meaning is that "otherwise-ness" consists in the very fact that for those whose senses are liberated from passion and hatred, their active engagement itself is their withdrawal. Explaining this, he states the primary characteristic of one whose wisdom is firmly established through five verses.
In a person dwelling upon sense-objects, attachment to them arises;
from attachment, desire is born; and from desire, anger is produced. (64)
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory comes the destruction of intelligence; and from the destruction of intelligence, one perishes.

In this world, indeed, for the transmigrating person who— having his right knowledge stolen away by the inconceivable illusion (māyā) of the Supreme Lord— has come to regard the mere body as the self,
there exists the primary, imperishable, and incomparable ocean of the nectar of one's own infinite bliss, though it is ever-present.
It is true that for one who does not contemplate their own self,
there arises a longing for objects such as sound and so forth— objects which are artificial means of pleasure that result exclusively in suffering and impermanence.

For one who meditates—that is, who constantly contemplates—upon them, attachment arises; that is, a state of the mind being deeply immersed in them comes into being. From such attachment, desire—the affliction known as passion (*rāga*), which is a longing directed toward those objects—is born; it originates from that. And from that...
In objects adverse to that [pleasure], a type of affliction called hatred (*dveṣa*) arises and prevails;
and from that, delusion (*saṃmoha*)—
which consists of ignorance characterized by the lack of discrimination between self and non-self— arises, known as *moha*.
The meaning is that the affliction (*kleśa*) emerges. Consequently, memory (*smṛti*) becomes confused;

though it does not actually touch the Self which is to be remembered, it undergoes, as it were, a loss of its own nature. And from such a lapse of memory, the intellect (*buddhi*) [loses] the knowledge consisting of the determination of ultimate reality.

It perishes, that is, it becomes concealed. And for that reason, the person undergoes a destruction characterized by the state of being established in the nature of reality (satyasvarūpa). || 64–65 ||
Having established the succession of causes for the lack of firm-mindedness with reference to the transmigrating person,
[the author] now, by means of removing the veil of doubt being cast forth at the moment of the desire to favor [him], [proceeds].
In order to explain the sequence of causes for a person seeking liberation who has attained awakening— the illumination of his own true nature as it has been described— he says:
But one who moves among sense objects with senses that are free from passion and hatred, being self-controlled and having a disciplined mind, attains tranquility. (66)
In serenity, the destruction of all sufferings arises for him;
for the intellect of one with a serene mind quickly becomes firmly established. 67.
For one who is undisciplined, there is no wisdom; for the undisciplined, there is no meditative cultivation.
For one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; and for the one without peace, how can there be happiness? (68)
For when the mind follows after the wandering senses, it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters. (69)

One whose self is subject to control— meaning a person whose nature or self is dependent on that very truth which has become the object of reflective awareness— is such [a person] through those things that are under his own mastery.

Because he is manifested through his own power (*svaśaktitayā*), he moves among objects— the sense-objects— by means of the internal and external organs (*indriya*) which are the instruments (*karaṇa*) subject to his command and whose activity, maintenance, and withdrawal depend upon him; like the sun with its rays, he moves through them and attains clarity (*prasāda*).
He attains and acquires clarity (*vaiṣadya*), which consists in the absence of contact with the stains of pleasure and so forth.
For this very reason, with what kind of faculties does he move among sense objects? With those free from passion and hatred;
for passion and hatred belong to one who is attached to meditation on the mere sense objects and has forgotten the Self.
When the sense organs of a person are directed toward objects and flash forth,

he whose entire conduct regarding all knowledge and action is preceded by the reflective awareness of his own nature— which is eternally free from desire due to its being completely full— is liberated from attachment and aversion.

It has been stated that as the senses proceed toward their respective objects, one who moves among those objects with such senses attains clarity (*prasāda*). And when such clarity exists— characterized by the manifestation of one's own nature which is naturally stainless—
The destruction— that is, the complete exhaustion— of all sufferings, whether internal, celestial, or caused by other beings, which are bound to the afflictions such as passion and the like,
arises for this person, because [his mind] has become serene in the manner described.

For such a person whose mind is free from the stains of attachment and aversion, the intellect—meaning wisdom—immediately, right after becoming serene, becomes firmly established; that is, it attains an unshakable foundation everywhere and on all sides within the true Self. || 66-69 ||
Since this is so,
therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established.

Therefore, for that person whose senses have not issued forth— having been restrained— with regard to all objects of the senses, whether they be causes of happiness or causes of suffering, being free from aversion toward the causes of suffering and free from passion toward the causes of happiness;

The external and internal senses of such a person— who is thus close to attaining union (*sāyujya*) with the Supreme Lord— have been restrained; his wisdom (*prajñā*), that is, his intellect (*buddhi*), is firmly established, having found its stability within his own Self, and not like that of another whose senses are merely suppressed by a concentration characterized by feeble effort.
Because the root consisting of passion and hatred has not been uprooted, he considers the senses—which have already spread out and are capable of producing effects—to be merely restrained. || 68 ||
Therefore, in order to demonstrate the state of the awakened one, which is distinct from that of all worldly persons, he says:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch."
That in which all beings are awake is night for the sage who perceives [the truth].

In this context, it is precisely the mental state (*vṛtti*)—which consists of the determination of the light of one’s own nature that illuminates all things—that is designated by the word "night" for those in transmigratory existence; for, because they have that as their object, all beings remain as if asleep, since the power of their vision has not yet dawned. Such is the [state].
For all beings that night is night, but in that state, the self-controlled one— having restrained all his senses in the manner described— remains awake and vigilant,
perceiving through the eye consisting of pure consciousness, whose nature is fully blossomed, that very [Supreme Reality].

He remains without relinquishing [his vigilance], free from the sleep of delusion; for in this worldly course of activity, which consists merely of the grasping and discarding of sense-objects that serve as the means for pleasures and pains perishing at every moment,
all beings have their entire collection of senses seized.

As long as all living beings remain awake, they experience a state as if free from sleep due to their exclusive attention to that [limited] measure; such is the mental state of the sage, the self-controlled one, who perceives and beholds the ultimate reality of the multitude of existent and non-existent objects.
For one who is awakened, it is night; that is the "darkness" (niśā), because he lacks attention toward it. || 71 ||
Thus, with an intellect firmly established and serene in his own nature— the self-luminous essence of universal consciousness that never sets— the awakened one, like the wind,
encounters various objects of experience, whether pleasant or unpleasant, without being affected by them.

To demonstrate more clearly its true nature— that it is not led even slightly into transformation by pleasures and the like arising from contact with those [objects]— he says, by way of an illustrative simile:
"Being filled, yet established in immovability..."
Just as waters enter the ocean, so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires. (72)

That awakened, preeminent person attains—reaches—peace, which is the state of the mental fluctuations becoming motionless due to the total cessation of the agitation caused by the waves of all conceptual constructions. Who is he? He into whom desires—that is, sense objects—enter as it were.

They plunge into it indeed without any longing. How so? Just as the waters of rivers coming from various directions enter the ocean. Of what nature is it? Though being filled and replenished by those waters, it remains established in immovability.

It is the state of one's own nature, which is unshakeable and profoundly deep. By this analogy, that which cannot be led into agitation—even by sounds and other objects that are connected [to it] through the power of proximity as causes of pleasure and so forth—is called "peaceful" (*śānta*); but not otherwise.
Among those who are present there, he alone was unperturbed; as it has been said:
"Those whose minds do not undergo transformation even when the causes of transformation are present—they alone are the wise" (Kumārasambhava 1.58).
Thus it is said: "Therefore, one who desires objects of desire does not attain peace. (72)

Desiring— that is, longing for— objects of sense which are the means to pleasure through the mind alone, one does not attain tranquility merely by refraining from the activity of the senses; it is with this intention that he says:
Having abandoned all desires, the man who moves about free from longing, devoid of the sense of "mine" and without egoism, attains peace. (73)

He who, having mentally abandoned and renounced all desires without exception— the longings for desired objects such as sound and the rest— wanders among or engages with sense-objects by means of the senses, attains and reaches the peace described above. Being of what nature?

Because he has attained self-assurance through the realization of non-dual pure consciousness that is eternally satisfied, he is free from longing; he has emerged from desire, which is the greed for the pleasures of sense objects. Likewise, he is free from the sense of "mine" (*nirmama*), having departed from the conceit of possessiveness—the thought "this is mine"—regarding specific entities such as the body, the senses, and their objects.

"Departed" means that he has likewise emerged even from the limited ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which consists of the notion of "I" directed toward the body, intellect, vital breath, and so forth. || 73 ||
By this section of the text ending on page 60, [it is shown that] for a person inclined toward the path of liberation,

by virtue of the continuous practice of the knowledge of the distinction between the body and the embodied self as taught by a true guru— [a state] indicated from the very beginning by innate devotion and other unfailing signs as being possessed of an intellect fit for instruction— (The remainder of the sentence continues beyond the provided fragment.)
For one whose self-consciousness has turned away from the category of the body and so forth,
due to the sprouting of the non-dual consciousness of universal oneness, the very nature of the cognition of "I" consists of the rays of the sun of consciousness; thus,
the powers of the internal and external organs are simply projected toward the objects enjoined by the scriptures.
Having established the defeat [of the opponent] as the means for attaining the state beyond reply,
he concludes the second chapter— which sets forth the meaning that constitutes the very lifeblood of the instruction on the supreme secret revealed in the seventeenth chapter— and says:
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding even at the time of death in this state, one attains the Nirvāṇa of Brahman.
This state belonging to Brahman—the supreme reality known as the Paramātman—is established by the textual passage ending with "he who, having abandoned all desires.
By means of this [state], one abides in Brahman; thus, through the cessation of movement toward other objects, a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is established.

Therefore, having attained this [state] and having assimilated it through self-identification according to the aforementioned sequence, the diligent practitioner does not become deluded; he does not succumb to the mental aberration consisting of the notion of a self with regard to the body and other such things.
For, by remaining and resting in this state even at the time of death, at the moment of cessation, one attains *nirvāṇa*.

Due to the cessation of the agitation caused by various conceptual constructions, one attains—that is, goes toward—the supreme reality of Brahman, which is tranquil and consists of one's own essential nature; thus, one reaches identity with it. || 72 ||
In this second chapter, having affectionately grasped the Gītās— which are as deep and pure as the heart— of those beloved by the wise,
may those who savor the unprecedented nectar-essence of the bliss of embracing them [attain their goal].
May your state as men always be one that has accomplished its purpose for you who have perfected your intellects.

Thus ends the second chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meanings of the statements, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.
Then, reflecting upon the separate words of praise spoken by the Blessed One for both knowledge and action, and failing to correctly determine their purpose as a synthesis, [Arjuna said:]
Doubting which of these two might be the more worthy of being adopted,
Arjuna said to the Blessed One:
"O Janārdana, if you consider wisdom to be superior to action..."
Why then, O Keśava, do you urge me toward this terrible deed?
With these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, confusing my intellect.
Therefore, tell me with certainty that one thing by which I may attain the highest good.

"If wisdom (*buddhi*) is considered superior to action (*karman*)— as in the verse beginning, 'Action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom' (2.51)— and if knowledge (*jñāna*) is intended by you as being more excellent than action,
then for what reason [should one perform action] when all [action] is a cause of bondage?"
Since this action, being of terrible consequence, is particularly horrific—
being of the nature of battle and the cause of great sins such as the slaughter of gurus and kinsmen— you have no right to engage me in this deed. (2.48)
By such statements as these, you enjoin and urge me on; and thus,
because [your words] consist of praises for mutually contradictory knowledge and action, you seem to confuse my intellect— that is, my discernment— with this mixed or confused speech.

The meaning is: by formulating words that produce doubt while intending to provide awakening through definitive instruction, you lead me, as it were, into confusion. Therefore, from between these two—knowledge and action—one [must be chosen].
Having ascertained and decided that "this alone is to be practiced," please tell me so that, by correctly grasping one or the other,
I may attain and obtain the highest good characterized by liberation or worldly prosperity.
(62) Then, as if manifesting a reproach toward Arjuna by saying, "I have spoken one way, but you have understood it quite another," the Blessed One spoke in order to dispel his doubt.
O sinless one, I have previously declared that there are two kinds of steadfastness in this world:
through the yoga of knowledge for the followers of Sāṅkhya, and through the yoga of action for the yogis.

*Sāṃkhya* is the enumeration (*saṃkhyāna*) of the categories of objects to be accepted and rejected—such as the embodied soul and the body—which possess the characteristics as they have been explained;
those who know this are primarily called *Sāṃkhyas*. *Yoga*...
The specific practice that brings about the direct realization of the object determined by the aforementioned Sāṃkhya is [yoga];
those who possess this are primarily yogins. However, Kapila and others, as well as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, are called both Sāṃkhyas and yogins in a secondary sense.

Because those objects such as the Self (ātman) and so forth, which possess the characteristics previously described, are neither determined nor directly perceived by them, I have stated— prior to this chapter, namely in the second chapter— that for such Sāṃkhyas and Yogins there is but one steadfastness (niṣṭhā), that is, a settled conclusion.

It has been explained. Of what kind is this culmination? It is of two kinds; that is to say, it consists of two modes of prescription to be employed simultaneously, both of which culminate in a single person who practices them. In what manner is it twofold? He says: "by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, and by the yoga of action [for the Yogins]."

Regarding the term "of the yogins": here, "knowledge" refers to the realization characterized by the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the reality of the Self, whose nature is non-dual pure consciousness as previously explained; "yoga" is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) directed toward that [reality], which—even while action is present—is characterized by non-deviation from the aforementioned essential nature.

This is the declaration. By that application of knowledge, I have declared the final goal for the principal Sāṃkhyas as previously described; for they are the Sāṃkhyas who have reached the culmination, whose concentration upon the subject of the aforementioned self-knowledge remains unshaken even while they are engaged in action.
Action (*karma*) refers to those various rites enjoined by the scriptures according to one's caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*).

In this context, "yoga" means concentration (*samādhi*), which is the steadfastness in performing those rites without abandoning the aforementioned knowledge. By means of that *karmayoga*, the steadfastness of the primary type of yogis has been described. Thus [ends the description] of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*).

Because action is inseparable from the application of action, and because that application is inseparable from knowledge, I have previously declared that there is only one steadfastness (niṣṭhā) accomplished through two modes; and the text establishing that has been stated therein.
How have you forgotten this? For instance, having begun with the demonstration of the excellence of knowledge in such passages as, "Action is indeed far inferior... (2.51), and so forth.
To demonstrate that samādhi, it was said: "Therefore, apply yourself to yoga; be steadfast in action.
For that which is yoga in actions—that skill, that wisdom—is what constitutes being a man of knowledge (*jñānitva*).
