By means of this yoga of knowledge, the steadfastness of the Sāṃkhyas is established; thus it was stated there. Likewise:

Having established the necessity of performing action through such statements as, "Your right lies in action alone; therefore, engage in yoga," and so forth, [the Lord] spoke the following in order to demonstrate its reconciliation with meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action and being liberated from the bondage of action, go to the state that is free from all ailment. (2.53) Likewise:
"But one who moves among sense objects with senses that are free from attachment and aversion, being self-controlled and having a disciplined mind, attains serenity" (2.66).
By this also, the steadfastness of yogis in that [state] has been declared through the yoga of action. What more need be said?
From the verse beginning with "For action is far inferior" (2.51) up until the conclusion of the chapter,
the entire [text] is devoted to demonstrating the two kinds of steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) to be practiced by a single person.
The text has been explained there. So, what is this inconsistency of my speech on account of which this delusion of understanding has arisen in you? (3)

Now, if you think that knowledge is defined as being focused on the single object that is the characteristic of the Self as previously described, whereas action consists of activity in the form of abandoning or acquiring various objects—
then, regarding these two, knowledge and action:

"How can it be possible for two mutually contradictory things to be practiced by a single person simultaneously? To this it is said: Your failure to correctly discern the respective culminations (*niṣṭhā*) of knowledge and action is the very cause of such delusion of the intellect. Therefore, that [failure]—
"Pay close attention as it is being spoken again"—having thus reflected in his mind, he said:
"One does not attain freedom from action by merely abstaining from actions;
nor does one achieve perfection simply through renunciation. (4)

Because you have not grasped the certainty regarding the intended meaning of the appropriate combination [of action and knowledge] as it has been explained, and because you consider actions to be in every respect opposed to knowledge, this state of "niṣkarmya"—
the absence of action— which appears to you as a cause for perfection, is what a person desiring perfection [must understand].

Because of the non-commencement—that is, the non-performance—of all actions, he does not partake of [the results]; nor does he attain them by the reasoning to be stated hereafter, since scriptural actions, which are inseparable from embodied existence, are difficult to avoid. Therefore, he does not...

In this context, it is not intended that the mere non-performance of these actions constitutes their non-existence; rather, what is meant here is the induction of their non-existence by destroying their capacity to produce their own effects, characterized as bondage. Now...
The abandonment of action intended here in the context of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is merely the non-performance of prescribed duties.
Thus, from such mere renunciation alone—
which is devoid of the knowledge as it has been explained— a person does not attain perfection characterized by liberation (apavarga).
One attains and acquires prosperity.

If, in this world, the attainment of the fruit characterized by delusion were to result from the mere avoidance of prescribed actions for those devoid of knowledge, then specific states such as deep sleep and the like— which, being of the nature of delusion,
bring about a state of non-action— would be the causes of perfection; yet they are not.
Regarding the statement that the perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmyasiddhi*) does not result merely from the non-commencement of prescribed duties, he states the reason for this:
"For no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action."
For everyone is compelled to perform action, being powerless, by the qualities born of material nature.

The word *hi* indicates the reason: because no embodied being (*dehin*) ever—at any time, in any particular state, and even for a single moment, however subtle—that limb of his remains without performing action; that is, he does not experience a state of remaining while not acting.

The meaning is that it continues to exist. And thus, it is perfectly evident that in all gross states—namely childhood, youth, and old age—every embodied being remains engaged in action through mind, speech, and body; this is true even within those [subtler] states contained therein.
And in the subtle states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there is no one who does not act;
for in the waking state—
which consists of the activity of the senses occupied with grasping objects such as sound and so forth— everyone [is active].

The state of being intent upon action (*karma-niṣṭhatva*) is indeed manifest; for even in the state of dreaming, there is no cessation of the apprehension of objects, and thus no one remains in a state of non-action. However, in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), although there is an absence of the perception of objects distinct from that time, at the time of awakening—

Mental action certainly exists, because otherwise the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of objects experienced in the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion would be inexplicable. This same principle applies even to those states such as waking and so forth that pertain to yogis; for:
Because the conceptualizations of the perceived object, the perceiver, and so forth do not cease during waking and dreaming states,

and because even in the state of deep sleep, although there is at that time an absence of the perception of the distinction between the perceived, the perception, and the perceiver, upon emerging from that state—
Since the reflective awareness of such a state of meditative concentration would otherwise be impossible, no one in any of the three stages of life can exist without performing action;
thus, the connection with the preceding [verse] is that the attainment of *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action) does not result merely from the non-commencement of prescribed actions.
Thus, stating the reason for the impossibility of the non-existence of all action, he says: "He is impelled. The word *hi* indicates a reason.

Because every embodied being (*dehabhṛt*), while being entirely helpless and dependent, is impelled toward action prescribed by the scriptures by the *guṇas*—such as *sattva* and the rest—which are born of *prakṛti*, that is, produced from *pradhāna*.
And that which is invariably concomitant with embodiedness is apprehended and enjoined. For here,

the principle known as *prakṛti*— which has the nature of a cause fashioned by the will of the Supreme Lord and consists of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, transformed through their mutual relationship of subordinate and predominant— is [the object].

It initiates each respective body for all embodied beings; and because the qualities (guṇas) function through mutual inseparability, when accompanied by the quality of passion (rajas), they render every embodied being— whether dominated by sattva or other qualities— engaged in their corresponding actions, thus by means of the qualities born of primordial nature (prakṛti).
It has been stated that everyone performs action. || 5 ||

And thus, since it remains impossible for all embodied beings to effect the total cessation of all actions in any state whatsoever, there exist those yogins who, out of pride in having attained "actionlessness" (naiṣkarmya), merely refrain from undertaking prescribed actions.

Since the existence of other unavoidable actions that are inseparable from having a body entails the impossibility of attaining the state characterized by liberation (*kaivalya*), [the author] says the following in order to demonstrate that such a person is generally not a true yogi: (p. 66)
He who restrains his organs of action but sits dwelling upon the objects of the senses with his mind is a deluded soul; he is called a hypocrite.
By the reasoning already stated, since there is no cessation of mental action, that yogi who remains—

relying on the intellect of inaction (naiṣkarmya-buddhi)— while mentally recollecting and contemplating the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, with his mind or internal organ, is said to be one of false conduct; such a person is described thus.

The meaning is that the practice of yoga is indeed useless because it does not correspond with its intended result. For, by the term "organs of action" (*karmendriya*), the external instruments here—both the ears and so forth, as well as the voice and so forth—are understood;
thus, one should restrain the senses, such as the ear and the rest, which are authorized for the functions of perceiving sound and other objects.
By means of a specific effort, having restrained [the mind] from its own activity, it remains in that state for some time;
however, the attainment of the fruit of liberation—characterized by the total eradication of all afflictions (*kleśa*)—does not occur merely by that much.
For, in such a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), at most the afflictions are merely dormant.
Even if they were so, nevertheless, because they are awakened again upon emerging from that state, their non-annihilation is understood.

However, that concentration in which those afflictions, being rendered like burnt seeds, no longer possess the capacity to sprout even when an object of perception is present— this is the distinction of the yogin intended here as the subject of discussion over the previous one.
"Moving among sense objects with the senses freed from attachment and aversion," (2.66)—
recalling what was stated previously by such verses, he speaks again:
"But he who, O Arjuna, begins [action] having restrained the senses with the mind..."
He who performs the yoga of action with the organs of action, unattached, is superior.

The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. Furthermore, that yogin who is unattached and free from worldly undertakings excels—that is, he is distinguished by superiority—over the previously mentioned yogin. Who is he? He is one who, by means of the mind, has attained a firm foundation in the Self which possesses the characteristics as they have been explained.
Having ascended the state of universal equanimity with the internal organ—

that is, the intellect— one should restrain the ears and other senses from contact with defects such as passion, but not from their objects such as sound; having thus prohibited [such contact] by means of these [senses].

With the organs of action— which are devoid of contact with passion and the like— and with the senses appointed to their respective functions consisting of the apprehension of sound and so forth, he undertakes *karmayoga*; that is,
he initiates a connection (*yoga*) or union through action (*karman*), namely through the activity consisting of the apprehension of sound and other objects as enjoined by the scriptures.
He introduces [the topic]. || 7 ||
The avoidance of attachment and aversion is the means for establishing the point to be proven in this discourse,
and not the non-commencement of actions. Therefore, perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction.
Moreover, even the maintenance of your body would not be possible for you without action.
Perform and practice that specific action which is prescribed by the scripture according to the fixed divisions of caste and the divisions of life-stages; never abandon it,
for from non-action— that is, the absence of action or the abandonment of ritual performance— arises [the fault of] karma.

The performance of prescribed actions is superior and best, because for some, the mere non-commencement of actions does not cause the cessation of afflictions; thus, the misconception that there is an absence of action is not a cause of perfection. However, when action is performed through the aforementioned meditative absorption (samādhi), it leads to success.

Even when objects that cause arousal exist, it is more praiseworthy to reach a state where there is no manifestation of afflictions; moreover, while one possesses a body, the total absence of all action is not possible, because for you who are "without action"—
meaning entirely devoid of activity and like a pillar— even the mere maintenance of the body would be impossible.
Even the functioning of the body would not be established; it would not be possible.
And it is not possible for anyone to exist without the entire range of activities such as drinking, eating, lying down, sitting, walking, contracting [limbs], scratching, and so forth. || 8 ||
And thus, since the total non-existence of action is untenable, it remains established that not every action performed leads to success; therefore, he says:
"Apart from action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action."
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.

Sacrifice (*yajña*) is, in its primary sense, the worship of the deity; and that deity is none other than the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the One whose nature has been explained in such verses as: "In whom all [exists], from whom all [proceeds]" (p. 68). It is this alone.

The reality intended here is that very [reality], and its worship is the act of propitiation characterized by the reflective awareness of it as one's own essential nature (*svabhāva*), through a consciousness purified by the cultivation of the knowledge as previously explained; such is the meaning, that which has this as its purpose.
Regarding action: apart from such action—that is, performing a different kind of action while avoiding that specific type—this entire world becomes bound by action;
for even the performance of action enjoined by the scriptures is a bondage, because it results in rebirth within saṃsāra.

He for whom there is a cause of dependence is "one who is dependent. Because of being devoid of the knowledge of the reality of the Self as described, even scriptural action performed according to the rules leads only to bondage;
however, when performed with steadfastness in the realization as explained, [it leads to liberation].
The meaning is that because it is the cause of the primary sacrifice for the propitiation of the Supreme Lord, it bestows supreme accomplishment (*parasiddhi*).
And so he will say:
"That from which the activity of beings proceeds, and by which all this is pervaded..."
"By worshipping Him alone through one's own action, a human being attains perfection. (18.46).
Since this is so, therefore, for that purpose—in order to accomplish such a sacrifice—perform properly, meaning carry out correctly, the action enjoined by the scriptures of ritual.
To specify what kind of person is authorized for its correct performance, he provides the qualification "muktasaṅgaḥ" (free from attachment).

One who is "mukta" (freed) means one by whom "saṅga" (attachment)—the immersion in objects that cause defects such as passion and aversion, and the state of having a mind solely absorbed in them—is abandoned due to the absence of volitional construction (*asaṃkalpa*). Being of such a nature, [he is authorized]. By this—
Thus far, it has been established that one who desires liberation must not abandon ritual action.

Now, in order to demonstrate step by step that for no one in this world— which is the subject matter of the two-fold scriptural teachings, wherein some are concerned with the dharma characterized by worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) and some are concerned with the dharma characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*)— is the abandonment of action ever tenable:

In order to establish that even for one who is authorized in the religion of active engagement (*pravṛttidharma*), there is no abandonment of ritual action, preceded by the citation of scripture, [the Lord] said (p. 69):
"Having created all beings together with sacrifice, Prajāpati spoke in the beginning:"

By the word "prajā" (people) here, only those humans born in the land of action who lack supreme knowledge and seek heaven and so forth are intended, because it is only they who are suitable as the objects of Prajāpati’s instruction introduced in this context. Therefore, [the text says] "Prajāpati."

The Supreme Lord, having created— that is, having brought forth— the various classes of beings as described, along with the specific deities who possess authority characterized by the creation fashioned by His supreme will, together with sacrifice— meaning together with that particular ritual procedure consisting of the worship of the deities through sacrifice— instructed them in speech.
What did He say? To this he replies:
"By this you shall procreate; may this be for you a cow of plenty that grants all desired objects. (10)
"Nourish the gods with this; let those gods nourish you.
Nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good. (11)
For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you your desired enjoyments;
he who enjoys what is given by them without giving to them in return is verily a thief.

By performing this sacrifice born of your own nature, you shall procreate; that is to say, you will obtain offspring and attain growth. The grammatical form *prasaviṣyadhvam* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), and it should be understood in the same way elsewhere as well. And this—

Being performed by you, may this [rite] become a cow of plenty (*iṣṭakāmadhuk*); as the fruit of its performance, may it milk—that is, fulfill—the enjoyments such as heaven that are desired by men. To the question "What shall we do with this?", he says:
"By means of this, nourish the gods, Indra and the others."

The meaning is: "May they, being satisfied by the sacrifice performed according to the procedure taught in the scriptures, bestow upon you the state characterized by satisfaction. And furthermore, since they have been thus worshipped by you, may they, being satisfied, nourish—that is, cause you to increase.
Or rather, may they deliver you from the state of falling into hell, the animal realm, and so forth.

Thus, being devoted to the cultivation of mutual assistance, you shall attain—that is, you will obtain—the supreme good, which is prosperity according to your desire; for you have been purified by sacrifice, that is, by the ritual offering.

The gods will grant and bestow upon you the eight desired objects of desire and enjoyments. He who, having failed to offer those enjoyments given by those gods back to these gods according to the sacrificial rite, consumes those desires for himself, is indeed a thief and a robber.
The meaning is that one incurs the sin of misappropriating the property of the gods. This concludes the statement of Prajāpati; what follows is the speech of the Blessed One. || 12 ||
The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins;
but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin.

Thus, not transgressing the ordinances of Prajāpati, those who eat the food known as *vighasa*— the remnant of the sacrifice performed as described— are liberated from all sins (*kilbiṣa*) that arise from the non-performance of the daily and other obligatory sacrifices.

The meaning is that they do not become thieves by being abandoned [by others]. Furthermore, those sinful evildoers—who cook and prepare food for their own sake, for themselves, and not for the sake of the gods and others—consume only sin (agha); having abandoned the practices prescribed by the scriptures, they go only to hell.
The meaning is that they attain [it]. || 13 ||

Since all this has proceeded from the Supreme Brahman, which is designated as the Imperishable (akṣara), it must indeed not be transgressed; thus he states the sequence: "From food beings arise; from rain comes the production of food."
From sacrifice comes rain; sacrifice originates from action. || 14 ||
Know that action originates from Brahman, and Brahman originates from the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice. 15.
From food—specifically from that which is swallowed, such as tears and so forth, which serves as the cause for sustaining life—all beings, meaning all living creatures, come into being;
they obtain their existence. For the life of beings is dependent upon the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the activity of the vital breath is dependent upon food. Such being the case...

Food originates from Parjanya, the cloud; and such a Parjanya arises from sacrifice—that specific ritual consisting of the worship of deities such as Soma, Arka, Agni, Indra, and others. For when the deities are gratified in sacrifice, they impel Parjanya to bring about the abundance of rice and other grains; and he, in due time...
One produces rice and other grains through the rainy season and so forth, as it has been said:
"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings" (Manusmṛti 3.76).
Thus, such a sacrifice has its origin in action— that is,
it originates from a specific injunction consisting of a particular procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And such action has its origin in Brahman— that is, it originates from Brahman in the form of the sacred scripture (*śāstra*).
Such is that [Brahman]. By means of another Brahman, consisting of sound in the form of the Vedas and other scriptures, action that accomplishes the performance of sacrifice is taught.
And that Brahman, which consists of sound and is of such a nature, is "born from the Imperishable" (*akṣarasamudbhava*); it does not perish, it does not move, nor does it...

That from which there is emergence is "of such a nature"— namely, that whose origin is from the Imperishable (akṣara), the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause. For, according to the actual state of things, the scripture [teaches] that [the individual soul] does not abandon its own essential nature even while proceeding from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause.

Not deviating from its nature as consciousness, it flows forth—its essential form being distinct only by designation—just like light from the sun; for this very reason, it too is designated by the word "Brahman. Since this process has thus proceeded, that is the Supreme Brahman.

Established as all-pervasive, meaning as that which extends through all things, it is eternal, always remaining in its aforementioned nature; it is firmly rooted in sacrifice, for it is for the sake of that very purpose [of sacrifice] that it has come forth—indeed, the stability and abiding of that purpose lies within sacrifice. || 15 ||
Therefore,
O Pārtha, he who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion lives in vain— he whose life is sinful and who delights only in the objects of the senses.

Thus, he who in this world does not follow the wheel— the collection of categories such as the scriptures— which has been set in motion by the Supreme Lord Himself, who is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, for the sake of the play and maintenance of the universe, and which has been manifested through His devotion to the dharma characterized by worldly activity; [he does not follow it].

And he who, not following the scripture himself, does not cause other people to practice it either— he, being such a person, because he subverts the process set forth by the Supreme Lord, is "aghāyuḥ," meaning one whose life or existence is for the sake of sin alone; being thus, his [effort] is in vain.
For such a person lives fruitlessly, because,
being devoid of the knowledge of reality, they lack the supreme fruit characterized by liberation, and because they transgress the laws established by the Lord.
Furthermore, because there is an absence of inferior fruits characterized by enjoyments such as those of heaven, life itself is indeed fruitless.

Having thus established that it is impossible for a transmigrating being— who is subject to the dharma characterized by worldly activity (*pravṛtti*)— to avoid the actions prescribed by the scriptures, [the author] now [establishes] that same impossibility even for one who desires liberation and whose intellect is firmly established in the performance of the dharma characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*).
To demonstrate this, he says:
"That person who finds delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who is contented in the Self alone—for him there is no duty to be performed. (17)
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire. (18)
Therefore, always perform the duty that must be done without attachment;
for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme. 19.

In this world, every living being who desires to obtain some pleasure not yet attained develops an attachment, passion, or longing for the objects such as sound that serve as the means to that pleasure; then, when that object is obtained through a particular effort, satisfaction— the state of having one's desire fulfilled— arises.

Then there is contentment, which is the cessation of longing; these—delight, satisfaction, and contentment—are always established in the very Self, which is ever-present and overflowing with unsurpassed bliss. For that [Self], there is no dependence on any other object to be attained apart from itself.

There exists no task to be performed that serves as a means for accomplishing his own purpose, nor is such a thing possible; because he is always one whose duty is fulfilled, there is no need whatsoever for anything accomplished— since nothing was previously unaccomplished— to be adopted now as something brought into being, nor is there any need for what is unaccomplished.

Since there is no purpose or need for anything that has been abandoned because it is to be discarded, therefore, for such a yogi whose intellect is established in the Self alone, there is no dependence on any object whatsoever among all beings— whether stationary or moving— within the totality of sentient existence. This is because of the nature of the object itself.

The support (*ālambana*) is the reliance upon the object to be attained. The intended meaning here is this: for the yogi who has ascended to the stage of stable intellect previously explained, [the mind] does not [cling] through a sense of exclusivity, thinking "this is mine," out of a desire for the fruit.

(p. 73) There is no task whatsoever to be accomplished as an object to be achieved; however, for one who is established in the realized knowledge taught [here], there certainly exists the duty enjoined by the scriptures, which is common to all castes and stages of life and consists of those specific, prescribed obligations. Since this is so:

Therefore, for one who desires liberation, one's own duty— action prescribed by the scriptures such as battle— is indeed to be performed, even for one established in the knowledge of the Self. Since this is so, for that reason, being a seeker of liberation, one must perform one's own duty, which is action.
Since it is enjoined by the scriptures, you must perform activities such as battle; doing so without attachment—

meaning with a mental disposition that is not submerged in sense objects which serve as means for mere fleeting fragments of pleasure— you should carry out [your duty] properly, provided your intellect is established in the reality of the Self as it has been explained, even in the slightest degree.

Practice and perform [your duties] with heedfulness; for by performing action regulated by the scriptures while being free from attachment and unattached to worldly existence, a person desiring liberation attains—
that is, obtains— the supreme object to be reached, which is characterized by final emancipation (apavarga), and not otherwise.
Success does not come for anyone from the renunciation of action, because it has already been established that the renunciation of all actions is impossible;
or, if one renounces some actions,
there arises the manifestation of defects such as passion and hatred due to the false conceit of having renounced all actions.
Because it is difficult to ward off. || 19 ||
Right here he provides an illustration:
"For by action alone did Janaka and others attain perfection.
In this world, Janaka and others were royal sages.

Those who are well-known through the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other sources, have attained— meaning they have accepted as their own— the state of perfection characterized by the attainment of the unsurpassed human goal (puruṣārtha) through action alone, specifically through particular activities prescribed for their respective caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), such as the protection of subjects and so forth.
And so, in the Mokṣadharma,
this dialogue is heard regarding even a single substratum:
"The triple staff (tridaṇḍa) belongs to one who is liberated from the umbrella and other such [paraphernalia], and to a woman who is liberated."
Thus began the dialogue between Sulabhā and Janaka; these were the words of Janaka:
"I am happy, having attained my goal, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
free from attachment, I abide in the kingdom, yet I am superior to other tridaṇḍins."
For regarding liberation, a threefold steadfastness was observed by the great-souled ones of old:
that which is supramundane knowledge and the total renunciation of actions.
(74) Thus do people learned in the scriptures of liberation declare steadfastness in knowledge;
likewise, other sages who perceive the subtle declare steadfastness in action.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body—
he whose restraints are fixed in these three is celebrated as a *tridaṇḍin*.
Having abandoned both of these— knowledge and action alone—
this third culmination was proclaimed by that Great-Souled One.

Thus, the third [verse] has the sense of being a form of conjunction (*samuccaya*); likewise, elsewhere it is said: "In non-possessiveness there is no liberation, and in possessiveness there is no bondage.
Only through knowledge is a living being liberated from both possessiveness and its opposite."
(Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan, Chapter 325, Verse 1).
Now, he states another reason why even one who knows the truth should not abandon action:
"Even considering the maintenance of the world-order, you ought to act. (20)
Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do; whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. 21.

By the word "world" (*loka*), the people who constitute the object of instruction regarding the mere three aims of life (*trivarga*) are intended here; their "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) is the acceptance of one's own side, characterized by the practice of the meaning of the scriptures. Perceiving that [gathering] as something necessarily to be performed for the reasons about to be stated, he [the author] thoroughly...

Being awakened, you ought to perform and practice those actions prescribed by the scriptures. Therefore, whatever action a person who is superior— being greater in terms of lineage, learning, conduct, and so forth— performs or undertakes,
that very same thing, and nothing else, another person should do of their own accord.

The world acts with an intellect devoid of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; therefore, whatever object that superior person makes authoritative—establishing it as valid through his own practice—the world follows and conforms to that. Consequently, even by one who knows the ultimate truth...
Action prescribed by the scriptures must be performed in every way for the sake of the welfare of the world. || 21 ||

p. 75) Here, making himself the very example, he says: "O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me; there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I engage in action. (22)
O Pārtha, there is no task whatsoever to be performed by me for the sake of accomplishing my own purpose,

because in the three worlds and throughout the entire universe, there is nothing unobtained that was not previously acquired, nor anything yet to be obtained that must now be gained to fulfill my own will.
Nothing remains to be attained. For everyone undertakes their own task for the sake of obtaining what has not yet been obtained;

but for me, whose wisdom is established in the steadfastness of the knowledge of reality as it has been explained, there is nothing to be gained. Therefore, even being such as I am, I engage in the actions prescribed by the scriptures, just like the world.
I remain constantly diligent. By this [verse],
it is shown that for one who finds delight only in the Self—
[as stated in 3.17]— "for him there exists no duty"— (3.17).
Having begun with these words, [the Lord] says:
"Therefore, always perform the action that must be done without attachment" (3.19).
That which was stated previously refers exclusively to the person who is a practitioner of that [action], as is beyond doubt.
He has explained. || 22 ||
Now, [the Lord] says that even though he is a knower of reality, he engages in action like an ordinary person:
"For if I were not to engage tirelessly in action at any time, O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect. (23)

If I were not to act— were not to abide— even for a moment, unwearied and free from sloth, in the duties appropriate to my caste and stage of life, then all men who are entitled to action would follow the path of me,
whose conduct has become authoritative.
They should follow and pursue the path and conduct. || 23 ||
Furthermore, for this reason he says:
"These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action;
I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings. (24)

If I were not to perform the action enjoined by the scriptures as the world does, then these worlds— all the realms that serve as the substrata for the enjoyment of the fruits of various individual actions appropriate to transmigrating beings— would perish.

They would suffer destruction and ruin; for the stability of the worlds is indeed bound to their respective duties (*karma*). Furthermore, by not performing such duty, I would become the author and instigator of *saṃkara*—the mixing of the distinctions between the social orders (*varṇa*). For all men [regard] me as [the authority on] scriptural duty.

Those who follow [others] while themselves failing to perform their own respective duties as prescribed for their particular caste— practicing them at will with contradictions such as treating them as prescribed for other castes—
would fall into the state of mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇavarṇatā*). Therefore, I alone am the author of this fault of the confusion of castes.
Furthermore, because of this, I would strike down all these creatures— these transmigrating persons born in the land of action who are entitled to perform the rites enjoined by the scriptures—
and I would subject them to injury, that is, to destruction; for these creatures [depend] upon their prescribed duty.

Not practicing [virtue], they are excluded from attaining heaven and the like; because they are naturally devoid of knowledge of reality, they are cast far outside the supreme human goal characterized by liberation (kaivalya), and would undergo destruction characterized by rebirth in the states of women and animals. Thus it is.
It would be I alone who would have transgressed the rules of the cosmic play, which is fashioned by the will of the Supreme Lord. || 24 ||
Therefore,
O Bhārata, just as the ignorant act while attached to action,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.
Just as, in whatever manner, ignorant persons—
being devoid of the aforementioned knowledge of the reality of the Self and thus lacking true wisdom—
engage in ritual action consisting of sacrifices and other rites which serve as means for momentary pleasure;
Attached to worldly activity and regarding that alone as supreme,
they perform prescribed duties while considering the goals of human life to be fully accomplished by that much alone.

Just as they perform actions, so too should the wise one— the scholar of ultimate reality— perform actions in that very same manner, characterized by such diligent application, because he is established in the knowledge of truth that is perceivable within his own heart and difficult for ordinary people to discern.

One should act. Being of what nature? Unattached, because of being perpetually satisfied by the constant tasting of the nectar of unsurpassed bliss; like worldly people, one is devoid of attachment to the fruits of various actions, which consist of objects of enjoyment such as heaven and the like. For what purpose should one act in this way?

He provides this qualifying description containing a reason, saying "one should act," because he desires to effect the "gathering of the world"— that is, desiring to bring about the aforementioned gathering of the unenlightened world.
For by one who has known what is to be known, the world— which is devoid of fitness for instruction in the knowledge of reality— [is to be gathered].

One who desires to deliver others from the suffering of falling into hell and other such states should perform action in such a way that the world, following his example, does not fall away even from the fruit of heaven through the performance of its own duties. || 25 ||
He says that the instruction of the knowledge of reality to one who is unfit would result only in ruin:

"The wise man, being disciplined, should not create a disturbance of the intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should cause them to take pleasure in all actions by performing them himself with composure. (26)

The wise man, awakened and disciplined— possessing the aforementioned knowledge of the Self— while properly performing and carrying out the duties prescribed by birth and so forth according to the scriptures, [stands in contrast] to those who, at present, act solely by their own nature out of ignorance.

Because they have not been graced by the will of the Supreme Lord, those whose discriminative knowledge has not yet manifested— and for that very reason, who are attached to rituals such as sacrifices because of their addiction to enjoyments and power— are bound; for them, there is a distinction in their intellect (*buddhi*) or wisdom from that [of the liberated].
One should not cause them to fall away from their attachment; for if those ignorant ones, being truly ignorant,
were to be instructed in the knowledge of reality merely through the abandonment of ritual action, then— precisely because of that ignorance—
they would fail to find firm footing in the knowledge of reality and would instead remain attached to ritual action as a means for attaining heaven and other such rewards.
The intellect of one who has fallen away, having reached a state of division, results only in the ruin of both [worlds].

Therefore, one should cause those people of such a nature—who have grasped an attachment to all actions—to take pleasure in them; that is, one should personally serve them by promoting the performance of those very acts in which they have become attached. || 26 ||

(p. 78) Thus, in order to prevent the suspension of the world-order regulated by the will of the Supreme Lord, and to impel even the awakened person—just like the unawakened—to engage in their respective duties, the necessity of performing prescribed actions has been established. And therefore:
Since agency is exactly the same for both the awakened and the unawakened, and their actions are likewise identical,
with the only difference being the fruit caused by non-attachment— this being the established case— how can there be a difference in results when agency is equal and the actions performed are equal?

Anticipating the doubt of Arjuna, who has not yet discerned the distinction between the awakened and the unawakened, [the Lord] speaks in order to demonstrate that distinction by analyzing how a difference in results arises even when the activity of both the worldly person and the yogi is the same.
Actions performed in various ways by the qualities of nature are attributed by one whose self is deluded by egoism as "I am the doer. (27)

But he who knows the truth, O mighty-armed one, regarding the divisions of the qualities and their functions, does not become attached, realizing that "it is the qualities acting upon the objects of the qualities. (28)

In this world, whatever action— whether physical, vocal, or mental, whether prescribed by scripture or not— is performed by any agent whatsoever, that agent alone is not the sole cause; rather, [there is another].
"The locus, likewise the agent...

(18.14)—by such statements, the five categories to be described hereafter constitute the cause. And he will explain that all of these are composed solely of the primal qualities (*guṇa*) characterized as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Therefore, [they arise] from *prakṛti*.
All actions performed by the constituent qualities (guṇas) are established according to their respective parts.

How so? By way of division: a sattvic basis and other causes initiate a sattvic action; one consisting of rajas initiates a rājasic action; and one consisting of tamas initiates a tāmasic action. Thus...

Since the nature of the three *guṇas* will be explained later in the passage beginning with "Even for the agent, being free from attachment and devoid of the sense of 'I'... (18.26), it follows that agency ultimately resides in the *guṇas* alone.
One whose self is deluded by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)—that is, by the notion of a self with respect to the body and so forth—and whose true nature is unawakened, thinks:
"I alone am the transmigrating being, the sole agent. (p. 79)

He superimposes agency— which is independent of other causes such as a substratum— upon his own self, which is artificial in the form of a body and so forth. And he, superimposing the notion of "I" upon such a self that is dependent on the *guṇas*, becomes attached only to the *guṇas* and never [turns away] from the causes of bondage in *saṃsāra*.

He is liberated. The yogi who knows the truth of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the distinction between actions, and who realizes the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), [sees that] the *guṇas*—namely *sattva* and the others—exist and abide only within their own purpose, which consists of the body, the senses, and the objects; they never belong to the Self.

The qualities are not able to impart their own taint to that whose nature is solely independent and perfectly serene consciousness; thus, by being always established in the true Self, one does not cling to the qualities nor to actions—the meaning is that one does not form the notions of "I" and "mine" with respect to them. Now, what are these qualities like?
The classification [of things] and the nature of actions, as well as what the reality here is, will now be explained. Herein,
the Supreme Lord is the cause of the entire manifold universe, whose very nature is manifested by His inconceivable free will.

[This occurs] through that [power] which is called *prakṛti*—which consists solely in the non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) of the non-difference between the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) and the self (*ātman*), and is thus manifested;
and which, for that very reason, is composed of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva*, whose nature is the restriction of the activity of cognition to objects that appear as distinct;
[this occurs] through that [power] which is bound by the beginningless continuity of ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) solely by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*).

Since the entire collection of bodies, instruments, worlds, and enjoyments of living beings—who appear distinct from one another—is indeed commenced by the qualities (guṇas), everything is dependent upon the qualities;
thus, for the most part, the qualities themselves are their agents. This [is stated] with reference to the subject of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).

The classification of qualities: such living beings as they are, whatever actions they undertake, they become attached to them due to being afflicted by thirst for sensual pleasure; and because they overcome others who obstruct that [pleasure] with hatred, they become deluded, since their mental fluctuations are restricted to this much alone. Thus it is said.

Since all actions have that [ego-sense] as their object, they result in being causes for bondage to *saṃsāra* because they consist of passion, hatred, and delusion; such is the classification of those actions.
However, for yogis whose intellects are established in the true reality of the Self, the qualities [of nature] function otherwise.

And there is a distinction among the *karmas*. For instance, those qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the others exist for the sake of the *guṇas* themselves—that is, for their own purpose—by way of being the domain of transmigrating beings, in the form of the construction of the manifold world (*jagat-prapañca*); they do not [exist for anything else].

Considering that, as their very object, these [perceptions] possess no other form whatsoever apart from the mere manifestation of consciousness which is eternally non-setting, they remain solely intent upon savoring the earth of their own eternal, unsurpassed, and innate bliss.

How is it that they become attached to those [objects] which are like the time of the uneven poison-juice of passion and the like? Since these qualities manifest as objects for the yogin rather than as mere qualities, this is the "division of qualities" (guṇavibhāga) pertaining to the yogin.
And whatever actions such persons as these undertake, even while they are being performed...

Because they have been burnt by the fire of knowledge as previously described, these [actions] are not able to bring about the state of being a cause for saṃsāra; such is this classification of karma concerning the subject of the yogin. A yogin of that kind is said to be "beyond the guṇas. He will declare [this] later.
"He does not hate what has arisen, nor does he long for what has ceased;
sitting like one indifferent, he is said to have transcended the qualities.
(14.25) Thus, the true nature of these two—the division of qualities and the division of actions—is established by this very explanation.
This has been explained. || 28 ||

Having thus established the difference in results— characterized by liberation or bondage to saṃsāra— that arises when enlightened and unenlightened persons perform identical actions, [the author now addresses] the enlightened person.

In order to regulate worldly activity concerning external objects as well as activity concerning the self for one whose intellect is firmly resolved upon the practice of the synthesis of knowledge and action as previously explained, He says:
"Those who are deluded by the qualities of *prakṛti* become attached to the actions of those qualities."
One who knows the whole should not cause those dull-witted people, who do not know the whole, to waver. || 29 ||

By means of the qualities (guṇas), such as sattva and the rest, which belong to primordial nature (prakṛti) as previously defined— qualities that exist as distinct entities due to being familiar through beginningless connection, and which function both as latent impressions (vāsanā) and as the initiators of the body and so forth.

Those who are deluded— beings in the cycle of transmigration who, though consisting of such qualities themselves, have fallen into the confusion characterized by the notion of a self in the body and so forth— become attached to actions composed of those very qualities,
which are the causes for fruits such as celestial, human, or animal states, because they lack the knowledge born of discrimination.

Regarding those very [qualities] as the Supreme, they sink into them. Therefore, the Knower of the Whole (kṛtsnavid)—because his knowledge is limited by the fluctuations of the qualities (guṇaparispanda)—does not know the entire range of objects to be known, consisting of both what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted; for this very reason, he is dull-witted and of small intellect compared to the Knower of the Whole.

One who knows the reality of all that is to be known should not cause anyone to waver from that very state; rather, for the sake of removing the conflict of intellect in those who are attached to action characterized by the gunas and to its fruits, one should perform all prescribed action so as not to cause them to fall away from it. || 29 ||

Explaining how even action performed with regard to the welfare of the world results in liberation for the yogi— just as his previously mentioned performance of action through steadfastness in knowledge does— the Lord speaks by means of Arjuna’s words to reach a definitive conclusion.
Renouncing all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Supreme Self,
become free from desire and the sense of "mine-ness," and fight, rid of all feverish anxiety.

Having completely renounced— that is, having properly surrendered— all actions prescribed by the scriptures, such as sacrifice, charity, austerity, and so forth, into Me, the supreme cause and supreme teacher, with an internal mind fixed upon the Self whose true nature has been explained as it is, you shall be one indeed.

The Supreme Lord, whose nature has been explained at the outset, is the agent of all actions performed by all living beings; by His mere will, He is the creator of the manifestations of His own powers. There is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from Him.

Agentship exists in the ultimate sense; however, because it is dependent upon the *guṇas*, the identification with the body and so forth is merely the play of *māyā*. Having accomplished the rite of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) through this contemplation, one is therefore "free from expectations" (*nirāśīḥ*), being devoid of anything to be desired, and thus free from *āśis*—that is, from prayers or petitions.

Having emerged [from worldly existence], and for that very reason, being without possessiveness (*nirmama*) due to the absence of grasping toward all things— having thus departed from the attitude characteristic of worldly persons, such as "this is mine"— he is free from fever,
having become one whose entire distress, including doubt and the like, has ceased through the drinking of the nectar of the aforementioned realization.
Fight! Perform your own duty, which consists of battle, has presented itself at this opportune moment, and must necessarily be done. || 30 ||

With this much of the text, this *Upadeśasāra*, which consists essentially of the practice of the union of knowledge and action, is for the most part completed; for first of all, its introduction has been set forth.

(p. 82) Having established the nature of consciousness in the second [chapter] and considering that in the third [chapter] the performance of karma refined by that [consciousness] is necessarily to be undertaken, the Blessed One, for the purpose of demonstrating the power of his own doctrine— which is the supreme secret— [discusses] awakening and non-awakening.
He states the result:
"Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and free from carping, are liberated from all sins. (31)
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—know them to be deluded in all knowledge, ruined, and devoid of sense. 32.
Thus have I set forth my own opinion,

the very essence of all the scriptures; those men who are qualified by the scriptures and who, having correctly understood it, always follow this intention at all times— [they attain the supreme goal].

They are liberated from all sins— those evils produced by the performance of wicked deeds, rooted in afflictions such as passion and hatred which arise from ignorance and which bestow the terrible sufferings of saṃsāra— and they are not bound again.

Being of what nature? They are possessed of faith (*śraddhāvantaḥ*), endowed with that faith which consists in the possibility of attaining the aforementioned fruit, produced by a non-conceptual realization firmly rooted in my doctrine as it has been explained; for this very reason...
Those who, however, do not harbor such malice toward this view— which is characteristic of those ignorant of reality— but instead,

being obscured by the darkness of delusion and having their right knowledge eclipsed, revile this very teaching of mine as described above by attributing faults to it and so forth, and do not follow it, nor conform to it— in all [matters] regarding them...

Know those who are utterly deluded regarding all forms of knowledge— whether scriptural or otherwise— concerning the determination of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, to be especially confused, disoriented, and ruined; that is,
fallen away from both fruits characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Know that those who have reached destruction, characterized by falling into miserable states of existence, do not truly exist even though they do, because their minds lack the correct vision of the inner faculty. || 32 ||
Now, in order to establish with firm conviction the very meaning already stated, and for the benefit of those to be trained,
the author sets forth that same point through various modes of expression; he says the following to further solidify the impossibility of abandoning actions:
Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature;
all beings follow their nature—what can restraint accomplish? (33)

In this world, every embodied being is bound by *prakṛti*, which has been operating through an beginningless continuity; for everything belonging to everyone—the body, the senses, the objects, and so forth—is composed of the three *guṇas*.
Therefore, even a man who possesses knowledge, even one whose discernment between the body and the embodied self has become manifest, [remains bound] to his own...

Of that primordial nature (prakṛti)— which, having attained the state of being "one's own" through its transformation into the form of the body and so forth in various ways, has been manifested by the will of the Lord as the cause of the universe, and which consists of the three qualities (guṇas)— of that ignorance (avidyā).

He acts and conducts himself in a manner that is similar and appropriate. What is meant by this? Even one who has perceived the truth, because he possesses a body and so forth commenced by *prakṛti*, whatever action he performs through mind, speech, or body, that necessarily results in being composed of the three *guṇas*. And such an action—

It has already been established that this is unavoidable even for one possessed of knowledge. Thus, all beings go to their own nature—their own inherent disposition—and in every way they rely upon it alone;
they do not venture even to breathe or to move as something distinct from that. Therefore, restraint [is impossible].

The restriction, "I shall not perform this action prescribed for my own caste," will be utterly ineffective; for, as previously demonstrated, it is impossible to prohibit all actions, and thus such a rule would achieve nothing. Alternatively, even self-restraint is itself an action, and therefore—

Since it is the basis for rejection and acquisition, and being permeated by passion and aversion, it becomes merely material (prākṛta) due to its nature as the constituents (guṇas); thus, even in this way, restraint is ineffective. || 33 ||
Regarding this unavoidable action, he says what one who possesses knowledge and seeks liberation should do:
"Lust and hatred are seated in the object of each sense; one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries. (34)

Whatever object is the domain of a particular sense organ— such as sound for the ear and so forth— attachment and aversion are established toward each such object. For when a person perceives an object, such as sound, through a sense organ like the ear as a means to pleasure, then [attachment] arises in him toward that [object].

Attachment is established [toward an object]; however, when one perceives that very same object as something to be abandoned because it is a cause of suffering, then aversion is established toward it as it is being avoided by the sense organ— thus,
attachment and aversion are established toward every object.
One who possesses knowledge—that is, one in whom discriminative wisdom has arisen—should not, like an ignorant person, fall under the sway or subjection to those two;

for to this man of knowledge, those two, attachment and aversion, are adversaries, opposers, and enemies. Therefore, it is those very two that must be abandoned by renouncing everything, and not the objects themselves. For indeed...

When these two remain unconquered, the defeat of the objective domain is effectively accomplished. For as long as they have not been brought to a state of being wounded and mangled by the sword of knowledge as previously described, they are indeed capable of subjugating a person, even while the objective domain has been abandoned, by flourishing within him. || 34 ||
Thus, since it stands as impossible for anyone— whether awakened or unawakened— to prevent [the results] due to the power of the attainment of such qualities in all actions,
he says that dharma, characterized by the performance of one's own duty, must be practiced even by the awakened one.
One’s own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed;
death in one’s own duty is better than success in the duty of another. 35.

Whatever dharma has been prescribed by the scriptures according to the fixed requirements of one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and which is established as one's own through right conduct (*sadācāra*), even if it is deficient— meaning devoid of its own specific qualities— because it is performed according to the primary method for some reason, [it is superior] to that which is merely self-performed.
It is better—more praiseworthy—to perform one's own duty, even if it is imperfectly executed, than to practice the duty of another, which involves a different mode of conduct;
for there is an absence of the fault of sin arising from the non-performance of what is enjoined by scripture and the transgression of what is prescribed therein. Since:
Thus, while one's own duty (svadharma) is being performed, there is the attainment of auspicious fruits in the next world; therefore,
even death (nidhana) that occurs while remaining in that svadharma would be better— that is, more praiseworthy— than the prosperity arising from the duty of another, even if it is well-performed.
Even the attainment of kingship and so forth [arising] from that [action] has the nature of being a cause for results contrary [to one's desires] in another world. || 35 ||

Having heard this established conclusion of all the chapters propounded by the Blessed One— that the performance of one’s own duties as enjoined by the scriptures, through being established in the knowledge of the Self, is the cause for attaining the perfection characterized as liberation— (p. 85) [he acted accordingly].
Considering such dependence of the Self, whose true nature has been explained, to be untenable, Arjuna said:
"Then by what impelled does this person commit sin?"
Even though he was unwilling, he was forcibly constrained and compelled as if by an invasion. || 36 ||
Now, this self, whose characteristics have been thus established by the Blessed One, being impelled and urged— like a servant by a master— to perform evil deeds in the form of sin,
which result in miserable rebirths and are defilements, even though it does not desire or wish for them, is forcibly overcome.
Having forcibly restrained his inclination toward desired objects, he acts—that is, performs—just as if he were being directed or employed [by another]. || 36 ||
To this, the Blessed One replied:
"This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of rajas;
it is all-devouring and most sinful—know this to be the enemy here. (37)
That by which this person— rendered subservient by the snares of afflictions such as beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) whose nature has been described—

is impelled to perform evil deeds, is this very desire (*kāma*), a volition (*saṃkalpa*) directed toward sense objects that consist of mere fragments of pleasure which are momentary and ultimately insipid upon transformation.
This very [state], because it is struck down by the counteragent to the nature of the conscious and unconscious, becomes anger (*krodha*);
the cause for the activity of its injury is hatred (*dveṣa*). Thus, this defect consisting of desire and hatred arises from the quality of passion (*rajas*), from the quality of passion.
It arises from the natural quality (*prakṛti-dharma*) which has as its cause attachment and aversion consisting of the desire for sensory pleasures;

therefore, it is "one who eats much" (*mahāśana*), meaning one whose consumption— characterized by the seizing of sense objects— is great and insatiable due to the ever-increasing nature of its pride.

Likewise; and therefore, because that entire enjoyment has exclusively the ripening of suffering as its result, it consists of the maturation of great sin, being the cause of miserable rebirths (*durgati*). Know—that is, understand—such a thing here in *saṃsāra* to be an enemy, an assassin (*ātatāyin*), because it bestows terrible suffering that is difficult to overcome. By that...
This person, being instigated, commits a sin. || 37 ||
Then Arjuna, desiring to know its true nature in detail, said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, how does this [ignorance] arise, and how does it increase?
What is its essence, and what is its conduct? Tell me, who am asking you. (38)
This defect consisting of desire and the like, which has been presented as an enemy— how does it exist,
by what manner does it experience its being characterized by persistence, and by what manner does it increase and expand? What is its self, its essential nature, and what is its conduct?
"What is he practicing? Tell all of that to me, who asks with doubt. (38)
To these four questions, the Blessed One gave the answer in sequence:
"O Pārtha, this subtle and supreme enemy of embodied beings, dwelling as if under the control of pleasure along with the senses, remains deluding them. (39)
Consisting of desire and anger, terrible, arising from arrogance and joy, egoism is essentially self-conceit; it is difficult to cross for those of sinful deeds. (40)
Turning away his joy, this [mind] bestows sorrow upon him;
and deluding him again and again, it produces fear for him as well. (41)

This defect, originating from the quality of *rajas* and manifesting in the form of desire and anger, is the supreme and subtle enemy of embodied beings; for although it is extremely close at hand, it is difficult to perceive.
And this defect culminates in nothing other than egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), because:

By the passage beginning with "The senses, they say, are superior" (3.47), he will demonstrate that very [Self] to be supremely subtle. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he now declares its very nature; and such is it.
This enemy, accompanied by his retinue of the sense-faculties—
which wield weapons consisting of mastery over desire, anger, and the like— slaughters all living beings with those very faculties. In order to demonstrate his invincibility:
He describes the state that is distinct from all enemies: while being the cause of all suffering (p.

87), he sits—meaning he is seated—as if in a category consisting of pleasure and governed by pleasure; for this very reason, he remains deluding, superimposing the erroneous cognition characterized by the notion of the body and so forth as being the self.
This explains the answer to the question, "How does he come to exist by experiencing stability?";

now, the explanation for the question, "How does he increase? is given: "consisting of desire and anger" (*kāmakrodhamayaḥ*) means that whose nature (*prakṛti*) consists of desire and anger as previously described; such is he. [He increases] through rigidity (*stambha*), which is pride (*garva*).
Likewise, it is the source—the place of origin—of joy (*harṣa*), which transforms into despondency (*viṣāda*) and gives rise to exultation (*pramoda*);

for this very reason, it is said that it increases and attains height precisely as something terrible and cruel, through its nature as the defects of lust, anger, arrogance, joy, and so forth. Now, what is its essential nature?
The question and answer are now explained: this enemy of all embodied beings is known as *ahaṃkāra* (egoism), whose nature is self-conceit (*abhimāna*).

Self-conceit consists in the notion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth—which are subject to limitations such as caste and the like, which are composed of the three *guṇas*, and which are the sole locus of defects such as impermanence.

"I am a Brahmin," "I am Devadatta," "I am of noble birth," "I am handsome," "I am clever," "I am wealthy"—such false cognitions, which are based on the apprehension of the self in what is not the self, constitute its nature; such is that [ego]. For this very reason:

Those whose actions are difficult to overcome due to evil deeds— because, in the absence of right knowledge, they are devoid of the discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and whose conduct consists of terrible, sinful, and demeritorious karma that serves as the cause for falling into the hells of saṃsāra.
The creation of the Asuras is difficult to overcome for men who resort to such [qualities].

Now, the answer to the question "What is his conduct? is explained: this enemy of the *kṣetrajña* called egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) [seizes] joy—the bliss experienced through the realization of the true Self.

Having turned back and removed sorrow— that is, the act of grieving— it bestows [peace], for it is by this enemy that one is deluded; thus, one grieves over the body and so forth, which are perceived as the self and are being struck down by afflictions such as disease and separation from loved ones, thinking, "Alas!"

"I am ruined," he thus laments. For this very reason, this enemy causes him fear and produces terror from the causes that destroy his desired objects. What does it do while acting in this way? It deludes him at every moment.
Bringing about a state of mental derangement characterized by the opposites of what has been explained;
by this enemy called egoism (ahaṃkāra), which is accompanied by a retinue of the senses and established like a king.

Driven by the self that is increasing through defects such as desire, anger, arrogance, and joy, and which performs acts such as the robbing of another's happiness, the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field) commits sin.
Having resolved Arjuna’s question, [the Lord] now elaborates upon the true nature of that very egoism.
To explain this, he said:
"This is that turbid, base one who watches for flaws, O Dhanañjaya;
impelled by passion, deluded in nature, it is the affliction of human beings. (42)

This very egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), whose nature has been explained as such, is a source of affliction for all mortals because it is the cause of *saṃsāra*, which is the repository of all defects; since it consists of the three *guṇas*, it is turbid and eternally impure, and for that very reason, due to its impermanence, it is base.
Likewise, it is fragile, seeking out vulnerabilities, and ever-watchful for opportunities to cause harm; the rest is clear in meaning. || 42 ||
He states what has been done to this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) by that [ignorance]:
"Just as fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so too is this [knower] covered by this [ignorance]. (43)
By this ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the self (ātman) of these transmigrating beings is thus enveloped and its power rendered obstructed. He makes this clear through a simile. How is it enveloped?
Just as fire is [obstructed] by a stain called smoke, which arises from defects such as the dampness of fuel.
Just as fire, its radiant power obstructed, is rendered covered, even so this Self,
by this very defect consisting of egoism produced by Māyā, has its own power— which consists of the reflective awareness of its true nature— obstructed. And just as...

A mirror or a looking-glass is covered by impurity produced through contact with dust, breath, and so forth; its own power, characterized by the manifestation of things as they truly are, is obstructed. Just so, a mirror or a looking-glass is covered by impurity produced through contact with dust, breath, and so forth.

Just as its own power, characterized by the manifestation of the state of cessation and the non-existence of things as they appear, is produced, in that very same way this Self is veiled by this [ignorance], and its capacity for the manifestation of the ultimate reality of the world’s objects— which had been ceased— is rendered inactive. Just as...
Just as the embryo residing within the mother’s womb is covered by the *ulba*— the fetal bed—
and its power for the movement of all the senses is obstructed, even so this Self has its own power characterized by universal agency obstructed by this [body]. By this...

By means of these three similes, it has been demonstrated that ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) obstructs the three intrinsic qualities of the Self (*ātman*), characterized by its being essentially omniscient, omnipotent, and [the locus of] all agency. || 43 ||

Although this defect of the self known as egoism (ahaṃkāra) is the obstructer of all powers, nevertheless, with the intention of emphasizing the primacy of knowledge, he says: "Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the wise."
O son of Kuntī, by means of that which takes any form at will and by that fire which is difficult to satiate.
By this aforementioned enemy, characterized by the notion of the body and so forth as the Self,
the primary knowledge— consisting of the self-realization of the conscious knower—
is veiled and obstructed; for because of that [enemy], desire [arises].

That whose nature is desire based upon external objects is, for that very reason, difficult to satisfy; it cannot be filled by any object once obtained. For the objects being brought to it only increase passion and [the power] of the senses.

Nurturing the capacity to savor objects that become increasingly superior one after another, they bring about detachment from those [previous] objects. For this very reason, it is "anala," meaning there is no "alam-bhāva"—that is, no prevention—of this [consciousness] regarding sense objects. By such a [consciousness], the characteristic of self-awareness (svabhāvasaṃvedana) [is established].
The primary knowledge is veiled; and when that is veiled, all its powers are likewise veiled—this is the intended meaning. || 44 ||
Now, with reference to what does this [passion] veil his knowledge? He says:
"The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat;
through these it deludes the embodied soul by veiling its knowledge. (45)

The sense organs— beginning with the eyes and speech— and likewise the mind, which consists of volition, as well as the intellect, are the instruments of this ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which is characterized by the fourfold functions of manifestation, maintenance, growth, and activity.

The substratum is that which consists of determination (*adhyavasāya*). For, having established itself upon these [faculties], this aforementioned ignorance (*avidyā*), by means of delusion (*moha*)—which causes the embodied being, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), to be ignorant of its own true nature and to possess only limited knowledge and limited agency—deludes him. (p. 90)
One is joined with ignorance. || 45 ||
Therefore, he says how this kind of enemy is to be overcome:
"Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restrain your senses and abandon this evil which destroys knowledge and realization. (46)

Since he is of such a nature, therefore, having first restrained all his faculties— the organs of perception and the organs of action, together with the mind and the intellect— which serve as his substrates,
by means of the conviction that the Self is established in the nature of the True Self as previously described;

Having restrained this evil one— consisting of ignorance and possessing the form of a great sin— by prohibiting the manifestation of defects such as passion and hatred, [one should suppress it] through knowledge (*jñāna*) attained by means of the scriptures and so forth,
which is the awakening to ultimate reality, as well as through realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), characterized by the direct realization of one's own self.
Abandon—that is, cast aside—the destroyer of distinguished knowledge, its obscurer, its supreme enemy. || 46 ||
And since this enemy is to be conquered by supreme effort, such as vigilance and the like, because of its extreme subtlety, he says the following to demonstrate that subtlety:
"They say the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses."
The intellect is superior to the mind, but that which is beyond the intellect is He.

Objects such as sound and the rest first become perceivable to anyone through the medium of the senses; therefore, with respect to those objects, the knowers of reality say that the senses are "higher," meaning they are subtler than them. For the senses [do not perceive themselves].
Like sound and other objects, these are directly perceivable by someone.
From those subtle sense organs, the mind is subtler still, being the cause of their engagement and withdrawal.
Just as the sense organs are perceived in some way, the mind—which is exceedingly fickle—is not perceived in that same manner.

Furthermore, the meaning is that intellect (*buddhi*) is subtler than the unmanifest mind (*manas*). For while the mind is somehow apprehended, intellect—which consists of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) occurring in the moment of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*)—is not apprehended in that same way. And of that [intellect]...
That which exists beyond such a level of intellect as being supremely subtle—(p.

91)—is that previously mentioned enemy called *ahaṃkāra*. For just as the intellect is somehow understood by those who apply themselves to it, this [enemy], the first sprout of ignorance, is not so understood.
It can be perceived even by someone whose eye of knowledge has been produced by the grace of the Supreme Lord, which has been opened.
Therefore,
having thus understood what transcends the intellect and having steadied yourself by means of the self,
slay the enemy in the form of desire, O mighty-armed one, who is difficult to overcome. 48.
Thus, having recognized this enemy as superior to the intellect in the manner described,

and considering him supremely invincible because he is so difficult to perceive, one should therefore steady oneself by means of the self alone— maintaining fortitude— and [conquer] that which is difficult to approach, being hard to reach.

"You can overcome him; slay him, destroy him! Of what nature is he? He is 'kāmarūpa,' one whose form (*rūpa*) is desire (*kāma*), that is, longing for sense objects. For it was previously stated that his existence consists of desire, anger, and so forth. Therefore, although he..."

Because it is extremely subtle, it is difficult to conquer; nevertheless, by destroying its state consisting of desire through the method previously described, you will indeed become capable of overcoming it—this is the meaning. Thus, the Blessed One has spoken in a manner appropriate for a Kṣatriya.

Arjuna was encouraged to destroy the egoism that stands as an obstacle to attaining the fruit of the instruction set forth. For you, even by Mahendra, have many times struck down numerous enemies who were difficult to conquer, without depending on any allies; therefore, with yourself alone as your companion, [overcome] this enemy as well.
"You ought to strike it down," he said. "Om. 48.
The application of one's own karma is the sole touchstone for proclaiming the excellence of the qualities of the refined gold of the reality of consciousness;
it has been manifested for human beings in this world for the sake of attaining the supreme goal.
Thus, this third chapter has been duly explained.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Sarvatobhadra*, a commentary on the meaning of the sentences of the *Bhagavadgītā*, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Thus, the subject matter of this treatise— which contains within it the essence of the entire science of spiritual self-knowledge— is characterized by the synthesis of knowledge and action.
Having established the purpose characterized by the attainment of the Supreme Self, [the Lord] now,

by means of establishing the relationship and the subject matter, reveals His state as the Supreme Cause in order to remove Arjuna’s delusion regarding the mere perception of His own self as being merely a person.
The Blessed One said: Thus I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat declared it to Manu, and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
Thus this [yoga] was handed down in succession; the royal sages knew it.
Over a long period of time, O scorcher of foes, that yoga was lost.
This very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today;
for you are My devotee and My friend, and this is indeed the most supreme secret.
In this very manner, just as this yoga has been declared to you,
so too at a certain time did I, the Supreme Lord, declare this yoga to Vivasvat, the great lord of yogis.

He, whose body consists of unsurpassed splendor fashioned by the sovereign power of his own yoga, spoke—that is, taught—what kind of yoga? It is imperishable (*avyaya*), like the supreme cause, which never decays or diminishes; for even while performing the work characterized by the creation of the world and so forth, it remains unchanged.
The Supreme Lord,
by virtue of being solely established in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose essential nature is characterized exclusively by non-dual pure consciousness as previously explained,
[is the goal] of this yoga, which consists in the practice of the integration of knowledge and action.
Having thus stated the primary connection of Yoga as being that of the first practitioner,
he now explains that very same connection through the lineage of its practice in sequence,
saying, "Vivasvān spoke it to Manu. That Vivasvān [spoke it] to his son, known as Manu, the first king.

"He said" (*prāha*) means he spoke. In the word *prāha*, the substitution of *āha* for the *liṭ* (perfect tense) suffix is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. He, Manu, likewise spoke to his son named Ikṣvāku.
Thus, [the teaching has been transmitted] through a lineage starting from the Supreme Lord himself.
Renowned and celebrated in the world through the continuity of a lineage consisting of worthy sons and disciples,
Janaka and other royal sages (*rājarṣis*), though performing the duties characteristic of kingship,
