were seers (*ṛṣis*) and sages (*munis*) because they were established in the aforementioned knowledge; they knew this as it has been described.
The expression "vidāṃcakruḥ" is a Vedic usage in this sense. Over a long period of time,

numbering thousands of yugas and so forth, because all qualities such as wisdom have gradually declined among people in the world, and because there was no longer a fit recipient [for the teaching], [the knowledge] was lost.
The meaning is that he has attained invisibility and remains established in the Supreme Cause itself. That very same one,
whose essential nature is unimpaired, today— at this time— by me, the Supreme Lord who have descended into the Yadava clan for the benefit of the world, [bestows] upon you that ancient, eternal Yoga.
Since you have been declared to me as a devotee, one who is desirous of hearing [the truth], and likewise a friend and a well-wisher,
therefore this has been taught by me to you, who are endowed with the primary qualities of a disciple characterized by devotion and affection; for this is the most excellent secret among all secrets.
In this way, he has also established the connection and the subject matter of this treatise for Arjuna,
whose ultimate nature is about to be made directly perceptible by the gift of the divine eye consisting of unsurpassed knowledge.
The Blessed One has begun to declare His own supreme sovereignty by means of dispelling Arjuna’s perception of Him as a mere human being born in the lineage of Yadu within His own self; therefore,
Arjuna, having become filled with doubt, spoke:
Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier;
how then am I to understand this, that you spoke [this teaching] in the beginning?

Since your birth—your origin—was in this junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages, it was inferior (apara) and later; whereas the birth of Vivasvat, established from the beginning of creation, was superior (para) and earlier.
How then am I to understand this, you who possess a birth belonging to this present age?
He taught this yoga even to this Sūrya, whose birth occurred a very long time ago. || 4 ||
(94) Here the Blessed One spoke this reply:
"Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe. (5)
It is true that my births and yours have been innumerable, having passed away and gone by through the assumption of various bodies; all of those,
both yours and mine, I know and understand, but you do not know mine and your own.
You do not know them. || 5 ||
Therefore, although I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, and although I am the Lord of all beings,
yet by presiding over my own material nature, I manifest myself through my own creative power (māyā).
Though unborn and of undecaying nature, being eternal, He is free from birth and destruction;

yet, because He exercises sovereign control over the maintenance and dissolution of all beings, both stationary and moving, He is the Lord and Master. Nevertheless, even while possessing His own supreme nature...
Abiding in and remaining within that very nature characterized as non-dual pure consciousness,

I manifest from that nature without ever falling away from it, by means of my own *māyā*— a specific power dependent upon my own self— which has as its sole life-force the appearance of duality and serves as the cause [of manifestation].

I assume the existence of birth and other states; therefore, by virtue of my eternity, my lordship, and my acting according to my own will, I bring about the manifestations of myself— as well as the past, future, and present modifications such as birth and so forth— for all embodied beings like you.
I alone know [all], for my power of omniscience is eternally unimpaired. || 6 ||
Thus he states the purpose for assuming his own birth: "Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata, and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest my own portion. (7)
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the evil-doers,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.

Whenever and wherever, at whatever time, there occurs a decline or decay of Dharma— which is distinguished by the regulations of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) and consists of righteous conduct— and consequently [there arises] that which is its opposite;
When there arises— the emergence or manifestation— of unrighteous conduct, which is the cause for the subversion of the established order of castes and other social divisions,
then, at those various times, I [manifest] some particular portion, some small measure of power, of the Self who is the supreme cause.
For the sake of protecting the play of the world imagined by my own will, I create— that is, I bring forth— from which,

in this world manifested by itself through the distinction between the creation of gods and asuras, there arise the virtuous who partake of the divine creation and who are the objects of instruction in the scriptures.

For the sake of protecting those whose wisdom is stainless due to the excellence of their virtuous qualities from obstacles that cause the obstruction of righteous deeds, and likewise for the sake of guarding the wicked— those evildoers who violate scriptural injunctions and perform corrupt acts that disrupt the stability of the world— from such evils.

For the sake of destruction— that is, for total annihilation— and for the sake of establishing, that is, for the perfect planting of dharma, which consists of the conduct of the virtuous distinguished by its specificities of caste, place, time, and so forth,
I manifest in each age in various forms.
I manifest the state of having an origin, yet in reality I do not experience even the slightest touch of the stains of the modifications of existence, such as birth, destruction, and the like.
Therefore,
O Arjuna, he who knows in truth thus my divine birth and action, having abandoned the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to Me.

In the manner thus described, he who is awakened knows my birth and action in their true nature and ultimate reality— that is, how even while possessing a body there is no deviation from the aforementioned supreme nature, and how there is no contact with the fruits of various actions; for this very reason, it is divine.

The light is universal; he whose mind is perfected by the aforementioned knowledge, having abandoned the body and relinquished the notion of "I" with respect to the body, does not undergo rebirth. He abandons the delusion of being subject to birth and destruction regarding that which is manifested as eternal by nature, and thus he attains Me—he reaches My own essential nature.
For by this [knowledge],
many who have become free from passion, fear, and anger, who are absorbed in Me and take refuge in Me, being purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained My state of being.

(96) Purified— that is, made holy— by this specific vow, which has the characteristic of the aforementioned knowledge and is the cause of unsurpassed purity, many yogis have attained my state (*madbhāvam*), meaning they have reached my own being (*māmikāṃ sattām*) or achieved non-difference from me; for [this occurs] through the constant cultivation of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
"Free from passion, fear, and anger": passion (*rāga*) is the longing for sense objects;

likewise, fear (*bhaya*) or terror is the dread arising from causes that obstruct those [objects] and are impossible to counteract; and similarly, anger (*krodha*) is directed toward those [obstacles] that can be counteracted. These constitute the shackles of the difficult-to-break prison of *saṃsāra*.

Those whose defects have been removed, gone away, and shattered—they are therefore "consisting of Me" (manmayāḥ), meaning they have My alone as their essential nature and take refuge in Me. I alone am their refuge because I am free from all danger; they are such that I am their distinguished shelter and the cause of their stability. || 10 ||

But surely, throughout his treatise, the Blessed One has established that there is only one single reality, characterized by the specific attributes as they have been set forth, as existing in the ultimate sense;
and it is precisely this that is now designated by the term "I. So how is it that some [claim otherwise]?
Anticipating Arjuna’s doubt— that he might think it is merely said that they have "attained my state" because his understanding of the Supreme Lord's playful sport was not yet perfect— the Lord says:
"In whatever way people surrender unto me, in that same way do I reward them."
O Pārtha, human beings follow my path in every respect.

It is indeed true that, like the ocean which is the sole locus of the rising and setting of the entire mass of foam, bubbles, and waves— each distinct from one another in their various forms— I alone am the single abode of all things.

And by me, in such a manner, through my own power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), those various individual knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) who have been manifested as having diverse forms— by virtue of being established in ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) within bodies and so forth delimited by their respective fixed capacities— among them, in whatever way, by whichever...

By whatever manner of resolve whosoever seek me— that is, pray to me— they at that moment become absorbed in me; them I cherish, I take as my refuge, by that very same manner of bestowing fruits appropriate to their respective resolves.

For all human beings, at the time they desire to accomplish their respective purposeful actions, follow and emulate my path— characterized by unwavering enthusiasm— which is the cause for attaining the way of the unique wish-fulfilling gem that grants all desires to everyone. Just as I do...
(97) With supreme enthusiasm, I alone perform everything and am aware of it; yet you,
while performing and knowing your respective tasks,
think "I do" and "I know," because you lack the power to experience my meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
They imagine suchness—[the Self] which is a doer of little and a knower of little—to possess agency and other such qualities.

What is meant by this? Just as animals, children, and others, whose vision is assisted by the light of the sun, perceive their respective objects, being intent upon their various practical activities; |||
And they do not consider sunlight to be the cause there because of their ignorance,
since they are habituated to such a conventional usage; likewise, all individual subjects (*kṣetrajña*), seeking their respective purposeful actions,
are endowed with consciousness illuminated by my own self-luminosity at that very moment.
Whether it be for a visible purpose or an invisible one, they perform and know all things;
yet, being deluded by Māyā, they consider themselves to be the cause therein, and they do not consider Me to be the cause therein. || 11 ||
For this very reason, he says:
"Desiring the success of their actions, they worship the deities here in this world;
for in the human realm, success born of action is swift. (12)

Seeking the fruit of action— namely, success characterized by the attainment of their respective desired objects through actions with visible purposes; and likewise, desiring results characterized by the attainment of pleasures to be enjoyed in various other worlds through sacrifices and the like with invisible purposes.

The virtuous worship—that is, they honor by means of offerings and so forth—the deities in the form of Indra and others. What is the purport here? From Brahmā down to a mere insect, whoever, with whatever intention, desires to do or seeks to know anything whatsoever—

Because in this human world, which is perceptible to all, every accomplishment born of action arises from activities rooted in various volitions, my own unperceived meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) is the sole cause for the attainment of each respective fruit that necessarily occurs at that time.

The attainment of the fruit is accomplished swiftly, at that very moment, solely through the power of my meditative absorption (samāpatti); for in the ultimate sense, no other agent or knower is possible. || 12 ||

(98) Now, if you alone are the sole agent, then you yourself would be connected with the fruits of actions performed through the state of being a *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field); consequently, it would follow that you, like the *kṣetrajña*, would also be subject to the connection with pleasure and so forth. Desiring to dispel this doubt of Arjuna, [the Lord] says:
The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the division of qualities and actions;
know me to be its creator as well, yet the non-creator and the immutable.

It is true that, according to the differentiation of qualities— namely, in the form "this one is sāttvika, this one is rājasa, and this one is tāmasa," which is rooted in the diversity of creation— and likewise according to the differentiation of duties— such as "the Brāhmaṇa must study, must sacrifice, and must give," and so forth— it has been taught by me.

By a single creator, possessing the nature described above, the fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*) was created— the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, were fashioned. One should know him to be the creator of such a fourfold system, which consists of those who partake in various fruits corresponding to their respective actions, in accordance with the division of their own qualities and duties.

Know that even the creator is likewise a non-doer, because he lacks connection with the fruits of such actions and is devoid of the attributes of an agent. Why? He provides a qualifying description containing the reason: know him as a non-doer while being what? As the imperishable (*avyaya*), which is eternal, since I do not deviate from my single essential nature.
I do not depart; I do not go away; I do not abandon my very nature as non-dual pure consciousness.

And thus, know me to be imperishable and a non-agent. For the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) are composed of the three *guṇas* and consist of the ego-identification with the transient body and so forth, which are manifested by my *māyā*.
Those who act with volitional intent are joined with fruits such as pleasure and the like; however, I, whose nature transcends the qualities, am never joined with them. || 13 ||
And therefore, actions do not taint me, nor do I have desire for their fruits.
He who understands me thus is not bound by actions. 14.
Actions— those activities characterized as meritorious or non-meritorious— do not smear me;
they do not defile me with the stain of their own fruits in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth,
because I am eternally satisfied by my own innate bliss regarding the results of actions.

Even toward those forms that become increasingly sublime in successive stages, there is neither desire nor longing for one who perceives all this as consisting solely of the nature already described; and he who, by means of the aforementioned torrent of the nectar of knowledge—

Because all stains of conceptual construction have been washed away, the yogi of stainless wisdom "thus," that is, in the manner described, "fully knows me" and realizes me; consequently, he is "not bound by actions performed like me," meaning he is not constrained by the fetters of the afflictions such as attachment and the rest. || 14 ||
Furthermore,
having understood this, even the seekers of liberation of old performed action;
therefore, you too perform action alone, as it was performed by those of old in times even more ancient.
Thus, even though action has been explained in this way, because it ultimately results in non-action,

having known and realized that truth, even the ancients such as Manu and others who were seekers of liberation performed and practiced the actions enjoined by the scriptures; therefore, you too [should do so].

Being established in the knowledge as previously described, perform only action— specifically the activity of battle and so forth— as prescribed for your own class; it was performed even earlier, from the very beginning, by those various ancestors born in times long past.
But even the wise are deluded as to what is action and what is inaction;
therefore, I shall declare that action to you, by knowing which you will be liberated from evil. 16.
Regarding the knowledge of the distinction as to what action is to be performed and what inaction is to be avoided, even the seers and sages are deluded;
they too do not correctly understand the division between these two. Therefore, by means of that [knowledge], through the avoidance of inaction—

I shall now explain to you in detail the action that ought to be performed, by knowing which you will be liberated— freed— from the inauspicious and evil nature of the bondage of saṃsāra, from which [bondage] it arises.
For one must understand action, and one must understand improper action;
and one must understand inaction as well—the course of action is profound.

There exists a specific reality to be understood regarding action that has been taught as something to be performed in a general sense; and there also exists a specific reality to be understood regarding non-action, which is the avoidance of action.

And it should be understood that the same applies even to prohibited action (*vikarman*) and contrary action (*viruddhakarma*); for the course (*gati*), meaning the pervasive reach (*vyāpti*), of this threefold established action is profound and its true nature is difficult to ascertain. || 17 ||

And in order to demonstrate how that [action] is to be understood, he says: "He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction—he among men is wise, and he is called a performer of all actions. (18)

When one who knows reality performs the duties enjoined by the scriptures with steadfastness in the aforementioned knowledge, he perceives non-action (*akarma*)— the absence of action— in that very activity, because he does not perform the effects of action characterized by worldly bondage; thus, even regarding his son, he views him as being without a son [in terms of the cycle of rebirth].

Likewise, regarding non-action— that is, the prohibition of action as prescribed— he perceives through the vision of knowledge that it possesses the nature of *karma* (action), because, according to the reasoning stated previously, the attachment to defects such as passion is difficult to sever, and thus it performs the function of *karma* characterized by bondage.
He who determines thus is endowed with praiseworthy intelligence among men;

and he alone is called the performer and executor of "complete" action—that is, action that is unimpaired—because he accomplishes the entirety of the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*). For action that results merely in worldly enjoyment, even if it is complete and lacks no part, [is not considered such].
Because that which has been performed is not a cause for the fruit characterized as liberation (*apavarga*), it is not "complete" (*kṛtsna*);

therefore, the meaning is that its performer is not a "doer of complete action" (*kṛtsnakarmakṛt*). Thus, by this verse, that which is to be understood regarding both action (*karman*) and inaction (*akarman*) has been explained. || 18 ||
Now, in order to reinforce the firm conviction regarding what was previously stated— that action itself becomes inaction— the Lord explains by way of recollection:
"He whose undertakings are all devoid of desire and purposeful resolve..."
The wise call him a learned man whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. || 19 ||

"Desires" (kāmāḥ) are so called because they are desired; they are those various enjoyments sought as the fruits of action. One who is devoid of "volition" (saṃkalpa)—that is, desire—for them, and whose "all undertakings" (samārambhāḥ), meaning all activities or engagements with objects seen or revealed in scripture, are free from such [desire], is that person.

As it has been stated, he is one by whom karma has been burnt— that is, whose seeds have been reduced to ashes— by the fire consisting of the knowledge of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) as previously described; [this is] because the capacity for the production of the sprouts of saṃsāra has been removed.

Those who know the ultimate truth call such a person a wise scholar; for true scholarship culminates in the fulfillment of all purposes through every means, and that is possible only for one possessing the aforementioned knowledge. || 19 ||

Thus it has been explained that the wise man perceives non-action even in action itself; he specifies this very point: "For, having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent."
Even though he is fully engaged in action, he does not do anything at all.
Such a yogi,
whose intellect is firmly established in the supreme nature consisting of ultimate bliss, is eternally satisfied;
his desire for all external objects has utterly perished, and for that very reason, he is without any further support.
Having withdrawn from external objects of support distinct from one's own true nature, one should abandon attachment to the fruits of actions—
namely, the results of sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and so forth,
characterized by enjoyments such as heaven— and regard that very [renunciation] as the supreme fruit.

Having abandoned the state of a dejected mind and being fully engaged in innate action, such a yogi— though intent upon its performance— does nothing at all, because every action lacks the capacity to produce its own effect characterized by bondage. || 20 ||
For the very purpose of praising the aforementioned yogin, he says:
"Free from desires, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions, performing action merely for the sake of the body, he incurs no sin. (21)
Content with whatever is obtained by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, and free from envy—
one who is the same in success and failure is not bound even while acting.

This has already been explained previously. Although the object to be understood regarding both action (*karman*) and inaction (*akarma*) has been explained, nevertheless, the fact that the object to be understood regarding wrong action (*vikarman*) must also be understood is explained by this very exposition; for [wrong action] is simply the avoidance of action.

Regarding that which was stated to be a cause of bondage for one who possesses knowledge yet is devoid of [right conduct], what delusion could there be concerning the binding nature of action that contradicts the rules of caste and stage of life? Therefore, it too must be abandoned in its entirety; this is the defining characteristic [of the teaching].
The object to be understood has indeed been explained. || 22 ||
Previously, it was taught in general that action alone is to be performed, stating: "Now, action must be performed in every way;
apart from action for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action" (3.9).

Introducing, by means of establishing the true nature of the yogi, the fact that he possesses the specific form characterized by sacrifice as indicated by this [verse], and that his sole fruit is liberation, [the Lord] says:
"For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge..."
For one who undertakes action for the sake of sacrifice, all action is entirely dissolved.

For one whose mind is established in the knowledge as described, who has attained firm wisdom, and for that very reason whose attachment to the practice of sense-objects has ceased— and who is consequently liberated through the attainment of success in the samādhi of discriminating between the Self and the non-Self— from the [cessation] of the notion of the body and so forth as being the Self...

For one who has emerged from great bondage and is undertaking— indeed, performing— the action prescribed by the scriptures for the sake of sacrifice (*yajña*), that is, for the purpose of the sacrifice whose distinctions will be described hereafter,
[this occurs] through the inclusion of all [actions] divided into bodily, vocal, and mental types.

However, with its threefold internal distinctions, it becomes uncountable; it dissolves and melts away, meaning that its essential nature—characterized by being the cause for attaining Brahman and by initiating perishable results—perishes. || 23 ||
"How is it that very action, while being performed, is dissolved?"—

with this in mind, he speaks in order to establish the non-duality of Brahman, which is inseparable from the attainment of discriminative concentration (*vivekasamādhi*) and serves as the cause for the dissolution of action.
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is absorbed in the yoga of Brahman-action, Brahman alone is to be attained. 24.
The connection is as follows: by that yogin, who is distinguished by such qualifiers as "free from attachment," Brahman alone is to be reached;
therefore, his entire karma is dissolved. This is now explained:
by that yogin, [that which is] denoted by the word "Brahman" is [reached], because of its association with attributes such as vastness (*bṛhatva*).

(p. 103) Only the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*), manifesting in a non-conceptual manner by virtue of its inherent fitness (*yogyatā*), is to be approached as the recipient (*sampradāna*) to whom one should present [the offering]. For such a yogi does not [approach] various other deities with a view toward specific fruits.
It deserves to be understood as the recipient [of the action], that is, as the goal to be reached. By what means is that Brahman to be reached?

It is by "concentration on the work of Brahman" (*brahmakarmasamādhi*). When the divine eye, whose nature is higher knowledge, has opened, the "work of Brahman" is the activity manifesting as non-different from the aforementioned Brahman; that very thing is [the means].

By such a person, whose yoga is unsurpassed samādhi— by what kind of [person] is Brahman to be reached? By a sacrificer who, considering himself non-different in essence from Brahman, has offered oblations— that is, has gratified— the Jātavedas fire, which is realized as being of the nature of Brahman.

Furthermore, what is the nature of Brahman? It is that in which the act of offering (*brahmārpaṇam*)—that is, the ladle, the clarified butter, the milk, the soma, and other sacrificial materials and implements such as the hands—is perceived solely as being of the nature of Brahman; likewise, the oblation (*brahmahaviḥ*) is [perceived] as being Brahman itself.
That [place] where the oblation being offered—such as the substance of clarified butter (ājya) and so forth—is presented; such is that [place].

By this, the following is established: whatever object manifests in whatever manner, because it is manifesting, its essential nature is non-different from the light of consciousness (prakāśa); therefore...

Although it has been established by those who know reality— through a sequence of demonstrations based on unshakable reasoning and perception— that, from the perspective of ultimate truth, no collection of entities whatsoever exists apart from the Supreme Self, as this is to be known through one's own direct experience;
This non-dual system of the self’s sovereignty does not fall within the range of comprehension for just anyone, because it has been established by the Supreme Lord as a specific restriction.
Thus, this divine restriction [applies] even to those whose essential natures appear mutually distinct through the manifestation of His own will.
Among innumerable subjects, he favors only a certain one by virtue of his own will;
and for that person who has merely been favored,
[his grace] is a stream of thunderbolts for shattering the great mountain-king of doubt, which obstructs the vision of reality.

Devotion awakens; and by its power, the aforementioned knowledge of reality, consisting of the scriptures, arrives through the instruction of a reliable authority and other means. And in that [knowledge], by means of the supreme [devotion]—which has washed away all stains of conceptual construction in the ocean of perfected, pure faith—
When this is continuously cultivated through wisdom,
the gate to the city of non-duality— characterized by the knowledge that discriminates between the body and the embodied self— is thrown open. Having gained entry there, in this [state]...

(104) A yogi becomes qualified for the method of offering to Brahman; therefore it has been said: "For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, and who undertakes action for the sake of sacrifice, that action dissolves in its entirety" (4.23).

And by that [path], Brahman alone is to be reached. Here, it should be understood that the term "sacrifice" (yajña) is used as a designation for ritual action in its primary sense, while also serving to indicate all actions pertaining to both the seen and the unseen realms;
for this reason—
"Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling," and so forth—
in these and all other activities, he will indeed teach this contemplation of the non-duality of Brahman;
now, however, [he speaks] regarding those various [states] distinguished by caste, stage of life, qualification, condition, and so on.
Among the various types of sacrifice, this meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) must be performed by the yogi through the agency of the practitioner;
explaining that [cultivation], he first presents its two modes according to the predominance of external and internal means,
together with the two modes that constitute the cause of that very sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*).
With three verses he said:
"Some yogis worship sacrifice as the divine alone;
others offer sacrifice by means of sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman. (25)
Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses. (26)
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of self-restraint, which is kindled by knowledge.
Certain other yogins, because they have not yet produced the aforementioned knowledge of reality,
are absorbed solely in ritual action and worship sacrifice as the gods—
primarily the deities Agni, Soma, Prajāpati, Indra, Āditya, and so forth.

Because they are being sacrificed to, they partake in the sacrifice related to the gods through its performance; they do not partake in any other [sacrifice] wherein external substances—whether conscious or unconscious, such as the officiating priests, clarified butter, milk, Soma, and so forth—are the instruments.
Others, distinct even from those, who are knowers of reality, [partake] by that very same sacrifice.

With the self consisting of those various implements existing as such, they offer the sacrifice—that is, they gratify—the Self alone. Where? In the fire of Brahman; "Brahman" here is the knowledge of reality, for it is of the nature of supreme illumination and is the cause of burning away the fruits of all auspicious and inauspicious karma.
"Agni is in that. (p.

105) This is what is meant: those who know the injunction regarding the offering to Brahman transform even the sacrifice to the gods into the nature of a sacrifice of knowledge. Now, there are some others...

Yogins, established in samādhi characterized by the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, perform a sacrifice that is not accomplished through external means; they offer their senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the very fires of the restraints (saṃyamas) which consist of samādhi upon their respective objects of meditation.

The meaning is that those who withdraw their senses from sense-objects and cause them to be absorbed in various meditative concentrations (samādhis) consider themselves to have achieved the perfection of sacrifice. Others, however, yogis, by avoiding sense-objects such as sound and the rest, offer them into the senses, such as the ear, which have their outward expansion restrained.

The meaning is that others— certain individuals— perform such a sacrifice, considering the very non-perception of sound and other objects to be the oblation into the senses which are like fires, once the mind has attained self-restraint within the functions of the senses. Others, some, [perform] this kind of yoga-sacrifice.

For the sake of attaining the state of the sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña), all actions without exception— both external and internal— of the senses, as well as all the various functions of the single vital breath (prāṇa) in its general form, proceeding through the distinctions of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, and so forth.

They offer those [senses] into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint within the Self—that supreme Cause whose characteristics have been set forth. That which is restraint (*saṃyama*) is the firm binding of the mind; that which consists of such restraint is yoga, which is *samādhi*. Into that very fire they cause them to dissolve. Of what kind is it? It is "illumined by knowledge" (*jñānadīpite*).
It is illuminated—that is, made manifest—by the knowledge and awakening characterized by non-duality with the Self. What is meant?

Those who cast the activities of the mind and vital breath, like sacrificial oblations, into the fire of samādhi established in the Self amidst those various diverse yogas, [attain] such knowledge born of yoga.
The meaning is that they bring about the state of being a sacrifice of knowledge. || 27 ||
Having thus established the fourfold nature of sacrifices according to the distinction of their functions,
he now speaks two and a half verses to establish the different types of sacrifice by means of explaining the different stages of life (āśramas).
Some perform sacrifices with material offerings, some with austerity, and others with yoga;
likewise, there are ascetics of rigid vows who offer sacrifice through self-study and knowledge.
(106) Others offer the prāṇa into the apāna and the apāna into the prāṇa;
having restrained the movements of both prāṇa and apāna, they are devoted to prāṇāyāma. || 29 ||
Others, restricted in their food, offer life-breaths into the life-breaths.
Those for whom sacrifice consists of material substances such as clarified butter and the like— namely, the ritual procedures of the *pākayajña* and other offerings—
are "sacrificers of material substances" (*dravyayajña*), who perform the execution of sacrificial rites primarily dedicated to the worship of various deities.

The word "arise" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Furthermore, those residing in the householder stage of life (*gārhasthya-āśrama*) are primarily intended here, because only householders possess the primary qualification for the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), which is accomplished through material wealth.
Among those, the *pākayajñas* are common to all social classes (*varṇa*), since even a *śūdra* [is entitled to them].
"He should himself perform sacrifices with *pākayajñas*.
Thus,
the *namaskāra* formula is prescribed for him as the sacrificial mantra.

By such statements, their qualification for these [duties] is ordained. Likewise, "other sacrifices of austerity" refers primarily to those belonging to the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage of life, whose sacrifice—the ritual procedure of worship—is performed through that specific austerity distinguished by the regulations pertaining to each particular caste; for they alone are principally devoted to austerity.

Since all stages of life (*āśrama*) have been prescribed—with the exception of the one who is free from desire (*nirāśiṣ*), as stated in such passages—a Śūdra also possesses the qualification for these [acts], namely for asceticism and sacrifices. Likewise, there are other "sacrifices of yoga" (*yogayajña*), which are accomplished through yoga consisting of the limbs such as restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*), in both its forms: with seed (*sabīja*) and without seed (*nirbīja*).
Those for whom sacrifice consists of *samādhi*, characterized solely by the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, are the "sacrificers of yoga";
they are primarily those belonging to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśramin*), because it is primarily they who are devoted to yoga.
Here too, the eligibility of the *śūdra* is ordained, since it was stated by the venerable sage Vyāsa himself:
While teaching the duties common to the four castes, self-knowledge was mentioned among them.
Likewise, in the dialogue between Janaka and Parāśara, [Janaka said]:
"O Blessed One, tell me the specific duties of the castes."
Likewise, you are indeed skilled in all universal dharmas everywhere.
Having thus asked this question and explained the specific duties, the Blessed Parāśara said:
"Compassion, non-violence, vigilance, sharing with others, performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), hospitality toward guests, truthfulness, and freedom from anger."
Contentment with one's own wife, purity, constant freedom from malice,
self-knowledge, and forbearance— these, O King, are the common duties for all.
In this very matter, elsewhere it is also determined that a Śūdra does not fall [from his status],
nor is he eligible for the sacraments (saṃskāra) here.
He does not enjoy the dharma set forth in the Vedas,
nor has there been any prohibition of dharma made for him.
In this very place, and elsewhere as well,
O King, all social classes, having duly performed their religious duties and having spoken words of truth, [attain their goals].
"Having abandoned cruel unrighteousness in the world of the living, they go to heaven; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan, Chapter 302).
Others perform the sacrifice of self-study and knowledge; as for self-study—

The study of each respective scripture— be it the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Smṛtis, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, logic (tarka), statecraft (daṇḍanīti), or economics (vārtā)— is [the duty]. In this regard, those in the stage of the religious student (brahmacarya-āśrama) are primarily authorized, since they are the principal [subjects] therein.
Devotion to the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) is firmly established; and in that regard,

there is some degree of eligibility for a *śūdra* as well, since his eligibility for *pākayajña* sacrifices is admitted by the injunction "he himself should sacrifice," which necessitates some knowledge of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for those rites.

The study of some portion of the scripture necessarily follows in one way or another; likewise, there are those for whom the sacrifice of knowledge is a sacrificial rite consisting of knowledge, which is the realization of the non-duality of the Self as propounded in the treatise.

In that context, all castes and all stages of life (āśrama) are included; therefore, even a Śūdra has the qualification [for this practice]. And so it has been stated right here by the Blessed One, while designating the Self as the nature of the Supreme Brahman:

"For even those who may be of low birth— women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras— even they, O Pārtha, attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in Me" (9.33). Nor is this merely hyperbole, since the Sage himself [states so] in the Mokṣadharma:

Women such as Piṅgalā and Sulabhā, Vaiśyas such as Tulādhara, and Śūdras such as Dharmavyādha, having manifested the knowledge of reality, have been cited in various places. Therefore, by means of this sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña), the previously mentioned varieties of sacrifice—

It is thus stated that they attain the state of the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*). The qualification "of firm vows" (*saṃśitavratāḥ*) should be understood as applying to those for whom the sacrifice of self-study (*svādhyāyayajña*) is characterized by extreme discipline, and to those for whom the sacrifice of knowledge is characterized by devotion to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because of their possession of the defining characteristics of a true ascetic (*yatī*). Now, [regarding]...

In order to demonstrate the distinct nature of the sacrifice of breath control (prāṇāyāma-yajña), which is common [to many], he says: "Others—certain yogins—offer the prāṇa, the air established in the function of exhalation (recaka), into the apāna, the bodily wind established in the function of inhalation (pūraka). This is the prāṇa-sacrifice.

The meaning is that they perform the ritual procedure of sacrifice by conceiving the *vāyu* as the oblation (*havis*) and the *apāna* as the fire. When the exhaled *prāṇa*, turning back through the function of the *apāna*, abandons its own form, then— considering that it has been offered into the *apāna*— it becomes sacrificed.

It has been stated: "They offer the prāṇa into the apāna. By this very sequence, when the prāṇa is conceived as the fire, others offer the apāna, which has become the oblation. This occurs by way of resting in the function of inhalation (pūraka) preceded by the function of exhalation (recaka), and by way of being preceded by the function of inhalation.

Having explained the two-fold sequence of prāṇāyāma consisting of the state of rest in the functions of exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), he speaks in order to explain the sequence consisting of the function of retention (kumbhaka): "Others," meaning different [practitioners],
having blocked— that is, having restrained— the two movements, that is, the activities, of both prāṇa and apāna.

"Devoted to breath control according to their capacity": those for whom the *parāyaṇa*—the final goal or culmination—is the lengthening of the restrained breaths (*prāṇa*) through their maintenance for a long duration; such are those "devoted to breath control. By this...

It should be understood that the regulation (*āyāma*) of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is stated even with respect to the functions of exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*). And being such, they— having restricted their food and consuming what is beneficial and pure within the limits of measure and time— [control] the vital breaths.

They offer the winds, which flow through various channels and serve as the clarified butter (ājya), into the central vital breaths that have become fire; they cause them to dissolve therein and remain supported by the function of the central breath. This is the sequence of the sacrifice of the vital breaths (prāṇayajña).
This has been established: even this [practice], when performed with steadfastness in the previously mentioned knowledge,

attains the status of a "sacrifice of knowledge" (jñānayajña), because in the two preceding modes it is characterized by being absorbed in the juncture of the rising and setting of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The state of being a sacrifice of consciousness (*vijñānayajñatā*) arises for those two [breaths] as they attain the nature of causes for absorption into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Furthermore, in the third sequence, that [state] arises through the mind being transformed by the central vital breath (*madhyamaprāṇa*). And although this sequence of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), established as a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*), has already been mentioned, it is stated once again.
This should be understood as being for the purpose of explaining a specific sacrifice belonging to Kevala alone. || 29 ||

Having thus established the different types of sacrifice according to the differences among their performers, [the Lord] says the following in order to demonstrate how all of them result in the fruit of liberation:
"All these are knowers of sacrifice, whose sins have been destroyed by sacrifice. (30)
"Eating the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice, they go to the eternal Brahman.
All these performers of the various sacrifices as described,
without exception, go to the eternal, constant, and imperishable Brahman— the reality of the Supreme Self— without distinction.

They go; that is to say, they become that very [Brahman]. Of what sort are they? Being knowers of sacrifice (*yajñavidas*), if they know the sacrifice—that is, the various forms of ritual worship—as described according to the sequence of the method of offering to Brahman as previously set forth, and realize it through non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatayā*).

Then, having had their impurities destroyed by such a sacrificial rite, and having eliminated the primary great sins characterized by ignorance, they— being thus purified— [attained] that very [state] which remains from the sacrifice performed in that manner, namely,
that which is to be acquired immediately following such a sacrificial procedure.
Those who, through the vision of the ritual of offering to Brahman,

partake of the nectar-essence— which, being composed of Brahman, is beautiful with the taste of the unsurpassed bliss of immortality— and who, for the sake of nourishing their own self consisting of supreme consciousness, chew it; such are they.

The meaning is that the virtuous attain the state characterized as Brahman, as previously described (p. 110). Apart from the knowledge of the offering to Brahman, those who perform these specific sacrifices obtain from them various limited fruits of diverse forms.
It is established by implication that they attain [it].
But for him who does not perform any sacrifice whatsoever— neither by mere action alone, nor by the combination of knowledge and action, nor even by one of these two methods—
for that non-sacrificer, O best of the Kurus, this world does not exist; how then could another?
For one who performs no sacrifice, even though possessing both [this world and the next], this world—which is visible—does not exist for him because he is devoid of sacrifice;
being an atheist, he is hated by all people. As it has been said:
"From a man who has fallen from truth and dharma, one should flee as from an enraged venomous serpent."
For even an atheist trembles with fear; how much more so, then, a believer?

Thus, for such a person of evil character, what other [cause] exists besides this [world] that could be designated as the "unseen" (adṛṣṭa), serving as the locus for the enjoyment of fruits consisting of heaven and liberation in the world beyond? || 31 ||
Now, in order to demonstrate that all these sacrifices result in the nature of the sacrifice of knowledge by establishing their origin in action, he says:
"In this way, many kinds of sacrifices are spread out at the mouth of Brahman."
Know them all to be born of karma; knowing this, you shall be liberated.
In this manner, according to the method described, manifold sacrifices have been spread out at the "mouth" of the Veda— that is, through the gateway of the scripture—
expanded by way of the sequential exposition of their specific results; and all of those are born of action (karmaja).

Know that these arise from action because they are accomplished through the operations of speech, mind, and body; determine that there is no other way for them to attain their own existence. For even those sacrifices which have the intellect alone as their means—

The non-deviation of such subtle intellectual activity remains established. Therefore, because they are co-emergent and unavoidable, the accomplishment of liberation consists in the performance of sacrifices—which are of the nature of action—by means of steadfastness in the aforementioned knowledge. Having understood this thus:

"By practicing correctly, you will be liberated by yourself alone; you will become a solitary one (kevalin) and will not depend on any other cause"— this is said to demonstrate the ease with which liberation is attained through the knowledge of synthesis (*samuccaya-jñāna*).
"You shall be liberated"—this is a construction where the agent and the object of the action are identical (karmakartṛ). || 32 ||
Now, for the purpose of praising this knowledge, He says:
"O scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects;
O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge. (23)

The phrase "from sacrifice consisting of material substances" (*dravyamayād yajñāt*) should be understood as an illustration for all sacrifices of the types explained and set forth above. Therefore, the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*), which consists of knowledge, is superior—that is, more praiseworthy—than all other sacrifices. It is composed of knowledge.
For this [knowledge] accomplishes all sacrifices, beginning with the sacrifice of material objects (*dravyayajña*), such that they result in liberation;

thus it is said that when knowledge exists, all sacrifices become [knowledge-sacrifices]. Indeed, knowledge is called the "sacrifice of knowledge" because it consists in devotion to all sacrifices, and its fruit is liberation, not something separate from it.

In the knowledge described above, all action in its entirety—whether classified as the sacrifice of material substances and so forth—is completely subsumed within that knowledge; it reaches dissolution and, like a burnt seed, no longer possesses the capacity to produce its own fruit, even though it has been performed. (33)
Know that such [knowledge] is obtained by prostration, by inquiry, and by service.
The wise who perceive the truth will instruct you in that knowledge.

That knowledge, which consists of the awakening that serves as the means for attaining the unsurpassed fruit characterized by absorption into the Supreme Self, will be taught—that is, imparted—to you by gurus who possess it. Are they merely those who know the scriptures? No; he says:

Those who perceive reality are the seers of the ultimate truth as it has been explained through their own direct experience. For what reason will they teach it? By means of prostration—preceded by bowing at their feet and with total self-surrender—as well as by means of inquiry.

By means of that inquiry— which is a repeated questioning preceded by a request for the sake of cutting through all doubts on every side and in every respect— and likewise by that service, because of the offering of oneself in its entirety,
in all things.

(112) Know for certain—that is, understand with conviction—that it is the gurus alone, propitiated by sincere devotion and faith through non-conceptual service, who instruct one in such a matter of great exaltation. || 34 ||
"What is that knowledge like? He says:
"O Pāṇḍava, having known which, you will not again fall into such delusion;
by means of which you shall see all beings without exception in yourself, and then in Me. (35)

Having known this and having practiced it correctly, thereafter, regarding your own duty— which consists of the slaughter of enemies and must necessarily be performed— you shall not incur delusion, which is characterized by error and ignorance, in the form of practicing what is unrighteous; and by which...
By means of knowledge acting as the instrument, you shall see all beings—the living entities moving and unmoving—situated in Me, the supreme cause, and likewise in the Self. What is this meant?
That all beings [are seen] from one's own Self, which is non-different from the supreme cause.

"By this knowledge, you will directly realize the actual non-difference. Regarding what the Blessed One said— namely, that even while He Himself is imparting knowledge, "the knowers [of truth] shall impart knowledge to you"— therein lies Arjuna's lack of specific knowledge concerning direct experience of reality, which is characterized by the realization of the true nature of things.

The purpose is the generation of longing; for, by means of this, the Blessed One will indeed cause [the disciple] to realize the truth through an intensification of the desire to know the specific knowledge that arises in successive stages. || 35 ||
When one's own duty, characterized by battle, is being performed, how could there be any connection with sin for you? For this is the power of this knowledge:
"Even if you are the most sinful among all sinners..."
By means of the boat of knowledge alone, you shall cross over all evil.

Moreover, even if you are the most sinful of all sinners— exceedingly an evildoer compared to others because of having committed such evil deeds as the killing of kinsmen, gurus, and so forth— nevertheless, regarding this [sin] characterized by the killing of kinsmen and the like:

Since action is your own duty, you shall cross over the entire ocean of sin born from it— which is as difficult to traverse as the sea— by means of the boat characterized by the knowledge previously described. || 36 ||
For,
O Arjuna, just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. (37)
Just as a most blazing fire reduces pieces of wood to mere ashes,
so too does knowledge burn away all actions without exception by exhausting their capacity to yield fruit again; this occurs through its own inherent nature.

It has been stated that this knowledge is capable of bringing to fruition even all those extremely terrible actions that have already become established, but not those [actions] prescribed by the scriptures.
As was said previously:
"One's own duty, though deficient, is better"—and so forth [from Gītā 3.35]. (37)

Furthermore, there exists no purifier in this world equal to this knowledge, which brings to its conclusion even the most terrible deed by leading to the attainment of the supreme fruit characterized by liberation.
One who is perfected in yoga finds that very thing within oneself in due course of time. || 38 ||
Because no other purifying entity exists in the world equal to knowledge,
and its purifying power is fully perfected through the practice of yoga— that is, through the aforementioned meditative absorption in action refined by knowledge.

Having attained the supreme fruit characterized by absorption into the Supreme Self, the yogi— whether quickly or after a long time, according to the intensity or mildness of his practice— obtains and takes possession of it by himself, by his own self. || 38 ||
And he describes the sequence for attaining that knowledge of such power:
"The person of faith, devoted to it and with senses restrained, attains knowledge;
having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace without delay. (39)
Faith (*śraddhā*) is the conviction regarding the fruit that is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) in an object taught by a trustworthy person (*āpta*);

by virtue of which, a serene clarity (*saṃprasāda*) arises in the mind that has already attained its fruit. And that [faith] is the first blossom of the celestial tree of the grace of the Supreme Lord.
It arises together with devotion. One who possesses that [devotion] is endowed with it;

through the destruction of terrible obstacles consisting of doubt, he is intent upon that, meaning his mind is not directed elsewhere, and likewise his senses are restrained—having brought the entire collection of his faculties under control by means of the sequence previously explained.

The seeker, through diligent application, obtains from someone who has realized the supreme truth— impelled by the will of the Supreme Lord— the knowledge that is supremely purifying. Having attained that and having accepted it with firm conviction through constant practice and cultivation, he reaches the supreme state in a very short time, within a mere few moments.

He attains, that is, reaches, unsurpassed peace—the unwavering tranquility resulting from the destruction of all disturbances caused by conceptual construction—and the bliss born from the realization of one's own true nature. || 39 ||
But one who is devoid of these qualities, being ignorant, lacking faith, and possessed of a doubting mind, perishes.
For the doubting soul, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. (40)

The ignorant one, devoid of knowledge, perishes because he lacks the attainment of the fruits of both the higher and the lower; he sinks indeed into *saṃsāra*. Of what nature is he who perishes? He is one lacking faith (*aśraddadhāna*), who, without the grace of the Supreme Lord, has no faith whatsoever nor conceives of anything, because—

Due to the absence of faith, one whose nature is characterized by doubt lacks the realization of certainty in all matters; thus, his intellect is permeated by uncertainty. Consequently, for such a person whose mind is everywhere suspicious, neither this visible world exists, nor does the other, invisible world characterized by heaven and liberation.

Consequently, he possesses not even happiness; for one who is beset by doubt, when a trustworthy person such as a physician prescribes a remedy such as medicine as the cause for alleviating a disease, his mind remains wavering, and since the disease is not thereby destroyed, he thinks, "This very world does not exist— how then could there be another?"
Or else, there will be another [birth], or happiness, or the attainment of desired fruits to be enjoyed in both worlds. || 40 ||
But those whose characteristics are distinct from these—
him who has renounced actions through yoga, whose doubts have been rent asunder by knowledge,
and who is self-possessed— actions do not bind, O Dhanañjaya. (41)

By means of the yoga as previously described— that is, by the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consisting of action purified by knowledge— one is such that actions being performed are renounced (*saṃnyasta*), meaning they are abandoned because of being free from attachment to fruits characterized by impermanence, pleasure, and selfhood; thus, those actions are cast aside through knowledge.

He by whom doubt— consisting of uncertainty regarding the determination of the categories of existence and non-existence— has been severed and its root cut away by the aforementioned awakening; for that very reason,
being possessed of the Self through the realization of the true Self, actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious, do not bind him.
They bind [beings] by bestowing fruits characterized as pleasure and pain, but they do not themselves take possession of them. || 41 ||
Since this is so, therefore, having cut through this doubt residing in the heart—which has arisen from ignorance—with the sword of knowledge of the Self, take refuge in yoga; arise, O Bhārata! (42)

Therefore, for the reason established by the preceding discourse, practice—that is, perform—the yoga, which is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as prescribed for actions enjoined by the scriptures and refined by the aforementioned knowledge; here, arise and be intensely diligent. Having done what? Thus...

Having cut through doubt—the sole cause of all defects—with the sword of knowledge as previously described, having severed it right from its root—what kind of doubt? That which resides in the heart, situated within the chest, born of ignorance, and arising from delusion. By this [description], its location in the heart is indicated.

And it has been stated that because [ignorance] originates from delusion (*moha*), it is not distant and is rooted in what is insubstantial, for the purpose of demonstrating its ease of eradication. Thus ends [the section]. 42.

In this [work], the Blessed One himself narrated to Pārtha the origin of this Dharma— which is the sole abode of all that is auspicious, the destroyer of the world’s terrible sins, and whose essence is Brahman, like the water of the celestial river— and which transcends all things.
The fourth chapter has thus been explained in sequence, indicating his greatness.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meaning of the statements, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.

Now, having heard at the conclusion of the second chapter the statements praising the intellect (*buddhi*) and the preceding discourses on the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), [one perceives] their mutual contradiction.

Although the question that was posed by Arjuna— who, thinking thus, said, "O Janārdana, if you consider knowledge to be superior to action" (3.1), and so forth— has indeed been resolved by the Blessed One in the third chapter;

Nevertheless, at the conclusion of the fourth chapter, having heard the words "one who has renounced action through yoga" (*yogasaṃnyastakarmā*) and "one whose doubts are rent asunder by knowledge" (*jñānasaṃcchinnasaṃśayam*) in verse 4.41, one might consider the term *yogasaṃnyāsa* to mean *saṃnyāsa*, that is, renunciation [in the sense of abandonment].
Arjuna, whose doubt had arisen once more, said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you praise both the renunciation of actions and yoga.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is superior. (1)
You praise the renunciation of black actions and you likewise praise their performance through practice; therefore, regarding these two contradictory acts—
the abandonment and the acceptance of action— expressed by the terms *saṃnyāsa* and *yoga*, [how can they exist] simultaneously?
Since the practice of both together is not possible, tell me without any doubt which one between these two—renunciation or yoga—is superior and more praiseworthy. (1)
Then, in order to dispel Arjuna’s doubt arising from the mere difference in words,
the Blessed One said:
"Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good."
But of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
It is true that both these— the renunciation of actions and their performance— when practiced by different individuals, serve to accomplish liberation and worldly prosperity respectively. Just as:

(p. 117) Those who advocate for exclusive knowledge (kevalajñāna) desire liberation through the total renunciation of all actions, whereas those who advocate for their combination (samuccaya) desire it through the performance of actions without renouncing them;
yet, although there is a scriptural promise of the fruit for both of these—renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and yoga—between these two:
Compared to renunciation—that is, abandonment—karmayoga, the performance of prescribed duties, is superior; it excels when one considers the reasons already stated and those yet to be stated. || 2 ||
To explain how he is distinguished, He says:
"He who neither hates nor desires should be known as a perpetual renunciant;
for, O mighty-armed one, being free from the pairs of opposites, he is easily liberated from bondage. (3)

One who practices the combined path (samuccaya), even while performing actions, should be understood as a perpetual renunciant (saṃnyāsī) who has always abandoned action—provided he is one who hates nothing and desires nothing. Why is he a perpetual renunciant? Because he is free from the pairs of opposites (nirdvandva).

Having emerged from the duality characterized by aversion and attachment, which is expressed by the word "desire" (*ākāṅkṣā*), even while performing actions, he is liberated from bondage—that is, from the miserable pit of *saṃsāra*—easily and without affliction; he attains liberation by himself. This is what is meant here.

The intended meaning is as follows: for those dwelling in the dungeon of the prison of saṃsāra, attachment and aversion alone are the two bonds that are difficult to sever; he by whom these very two have been cut with the sword of the aforementioned knowledge of the Self, his actions—even while being performed—are as if unperformed, and thus he is called a "perpetual renunciant" (nityasaṃnyāsī).
But he who, even while abandoning actions, is not able to sever passion and hatred—
even though he has renounced action, he is as one still seeing action, because the bondage produced by that [action] and its fruit does not cease.
And just as the renunciation of all actions is impossible, so too is it impossible to renounce some of them.
The non-cessation of passion and aversion, which serve as the cause for bondage, has already been established previously, and will be further demonstrated hereafter. || 3 ||

And thus, knowledge and action, which were previously set forth by the terms "number" (saṅkhyā) and "yoga," are here expressed by the terms "renunciation" (saṃnyāsa) and "yoga. Therefore, he asks: what is the cause of your doubt regarding them? He says:
(118) The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
one who is properly established in even one of them obtains the fruit of both. 4.
Sāṅkhya is the knowledge of the reality of the self as it has been explained.
Yoga is the performance of prescribed actions whose power to bind has been neutralized by the practice of remaining inseparable from that [knowledge]. These two—

They are non-different because they possess a complete nature attained through eternal mutual non-separation. However, the ignorant—being childish due to their lack of proficiency in the conventional usage of the knowledge of reality—proclaim and explain them as existing in separate states, as if they were distinct persons to be pursued individually; but this is not so.

The wise are those who know the ultimate truth. For, by properly relying upon—even just one—either Sāṃkhya or Yoga in the form as it has been explained, one attains and obtains the fruit of both, namely liberation (kaivalya). What is meant?

It is as follows: just as the form of consciousness, which has the aforementioned Sāṅkhya as its other designation, does not culminate in its fruit without yoga, so too yoga, when devoid of Sāṅkhya, is exactly the same. || 4 ||
To confirm this very point here, he says: "The state which is attained by the followers of Sāṅkhya is reached by those of Yoga as well;
he who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one truly sees. (5)

Persons who are connected with the knowledge of Sāṅkhya are called "Sāṅkhyas" by way of metaphorical designation; likewise, they are called "Yogins" because of their connection with Yoga. By such Sāṅkhyas—those possessing the aforementioned knowledge—that state which is the locus of rest is attained.
It should be resorted to as the unsurpassed goal; that very [goal] is subsequently pursued through yogic practices and accepted.

It has been stated that because practice is preceded by knowledge, that which is attained by the Sāṃkhyas is pursued by the Yogins; however, this does not mean [they differ] in the accomplishment of the fruit characterized by liberation (kaivalya).
Because their causes are identical, there is no difference between the two; therefore, he alone truly sees who perceives—that is, knows—Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one.
Only for him does the power of vision consist of true knowledge, but not for one who perceives that liberation comes through knowledge alone, while bondage results from every form of action-yoga.
Regarding this, it is said:
"But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
the sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman before long. (6)

The meaning is that, through lack of yoga—that is, without the application of action and mental composure according to the method already described—renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which has as its fruit the absence of connection with rebirth, is difficult to attain; it is acquired only with great hardship. For this reason:

One who is disciplined in yoga— being constantly engaged in the meditative concentration on action through single-minded devotion to the knowledge as previously described— and having become a sage, very quickly attains Brahman, the supreme reality characterized as the Supreme Self, reaching it as one's own self.

What is meant is this: the performance of one's own duty with steadfastness in knowledge is the cause of being a sage (*muni*), because it serves as an unfailing and non-contradictory means for attaining the fruit characterized by the realization of Brahman; however, mere knowledge alone is not.
Because the abandonment of action in its entirety is impossible, and because that [abandonment] is not the means [to liberation]. || 6 ||
Why is it that Brahman is easily attained only by one who is disciplined in yoga? He says:
"One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, whose mind is conquered, whose senses are subdued, and whose self has become the self of all beings—even while acting, he is not tainted. (7)
The connection is as follows: because one who is engaged in yoga is not tainted even while performing actions, he therefore attains Brahman before long. This is explained:
"in yoga"—that is, in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consisting of the practice of the combination of knowledge and action—one is "engaged" by being devoted to it.

The yogi, who is eternally composed, even while acting like an ordinary transmigrating person, is not tainted by his own karma—which is the cause of bondage—nor by its fruit, which consists of pleasure and so forth; he is not led to a state of impurity. For he is the pure Self, whose sole defining characteristic is the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya).

The Self is by nature pure, consisting of consciousness alone; its impurity consists in this: that, due to beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), it identifies itself solely with the limited body—which is essentially an object of cognition, subject to various delimitations such as caste and so forth, and is strictly determined.

The purity of this [self] consists solely in the absence of that [duality]; he whose self is thus purified is one who, by means of the sense of "I" established in the true nature of reality, has attained natural clarity— this is the meaning.

(p. 120) And thus, one who has conquered the self (*vijitātmā*) and conquered the senses (*jitendriya*). Here, by the words "self" (*ātman*) and "senses" (*indriya*), the expansion of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-prapañca*) is intended. He by whom both of these have been conquered—that is, brought under control as his own powers because their engagement and withdrawal are subject to his own will—is described by those two terms in that manner.

For thus the practitioner of action (*karmayogin*), disciplined in yoga and being of purified soul, even while engaging in activities, reflects: "That power of mine which is non-different from me— whose sole nature is the awareness of the essence of uncreated light— that very [power is this]."
Flowing forth in order to manifest the objects that constitute its own nature— the knowable and the effects produced by its own will—

it appears in two modes through the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*). Of these, the aspect consisting of knowledge is the group of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and that which consists of action is the group of external organs (*bahiṣkaraṇa*).
Just as the power of the sun, whose nature is light, manifests through the form of the wheel of instruments (*karaṇacakra*),
even so this very power of mine unfolds itself in the form of the internal and external organs. And it is not [an object] by virtue of its being manifest.
This [consciousness] can be defiled by objects that are connected to it through internal and external forms;

for the rays of the sun cannot be colored by their own appearance by the various objects to be illuminated, such as blue or yellow, but rather illuminate them while remaining entirely independent. In the same way, these [faculties] also [behave].
"The various powers consisting of the internal and external organs are mine"— thus one whose self is conquered and whose senses are subdued. But even so,
it may be objected that the state of being characterized by the previously explained attributes such as "purity of self" (viśuddhātmatā) and the rest is not established.

[This concerns] the practitioners of action (*karmayogin*). Since engagement with sense objects and withdrawal from them are not possible without [determining their] worthiness of acceptance or rejection, and when that occurs, the stain of attachment and aversion is difficult to avoid; and when that exists, how can there be purity of self and so forth? To resolve this point:
He states a qualification containing the reason: "whose self has become the self of all beings.

All beings—meaning all things, both stationary and moving, without exception, which have come to the state of being objects—are "his own self," meaning his essential nature (ātman) has attained their very form.

He who is such is "of that kind. What is the purport here? It is this: regarding those objects toward which a practitioner of action (*karmayogin*) engages in activity or cessation by means of the functions of the internal and external senses, for him, because his wisdom is perfected through the aforementioned knowledge, such [states] arise.

(121) Firm conviction regarding what is above [the world] is as follows: these objects, whether sentient or insentient in form, which have attained the state of being sense-objects, do not acquire their respective natures apart from being perceived. Therefore, it is self-consciousness itself that appears in those various forms; in reality, they do not [exist independently].

This notion that "this is some other distinct entity" is removed by the grace of the Supreme Lord through the dispelling of the darkness of *māyā*; thus, when the one ultimately real essence of the Self has been realized, the delusion of the appearance of duality ceases for one who possesses right vision.
Perceiving the entire multitude of objects— consisting of internal and external organs and their respective domains—
as being absolutely non-different from the nature of the Supreme Self, one who is disciplined in yoga proceeds with innate activities prescribed by the scriptures.
It incurs the fallacy of deviation regarding the qualifiers such as "being of pure self" and so forth. || 7 ||

This very state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the practitioner of action (*karmayogin*)— which is independent of preparatory disciplines such as the practice of postures (*āsana*), mastery of breath (*prāṇajaya*), and withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*)— is characterized by unimpaired supreme dispassion at all times and in every way, even upon contact with objects as they arise.

In order to explain in detail the unsurpassed fruit, characterized by the attainment of the easily accessible foundation in the Supreme Self for everyone, he says: "He who, being a knower of reality, thinks 'I do nothing at all'— "
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, breathing, and sleeping; || 8 ||
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, and even closing them—
he should maintain the awareness that it is merely the senses operating upon their respective objects.

Therefore, he who is thus disciplined, whose true nature has been explained, and who is absorbed in *karmayoga*, is not tainted even while acting; for, thinking "I do nothing at all" in all activities, even while conducting himself like an ordinary person in the world, he attains the very fruit of *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action)—this is the connection [of the verses]. Why?

Acting thus, he thinks: "Even while seeing," and so forth, meaning even while setting in motion the functions of all the sense organs and the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Thus maintaining" means carrying out such a form of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) which serves as the means for attaining the aforementioned fruit of this yoga of action (*karmayoga*). How does he maintain it?

Even though the senses and the vital breaths are engaged in activities such as seeing and so forth, they abide within their respective objects— the domains of the senses— and experience them merely through contact; however,
[this does not affect] that which is of the nature of eternal, unsurpassed, conscious luminosity with respect to those objects connected to its own domain.

(On page 122: "It may be thought that, like worldly beings, I am subject to the internal touch of the stain of passion and so forth. By the passage beginning with "paśyan" (seeing) and ending with "nimiṣan" (winking), all the functions of the senses and the vital breaths (*prāṇavṛtti*) are subsumed. Likewise, the functions of the cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya-vṛtti*) [are included].

The five forms of the sense organs— namely hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell— are presented by the five words beginning with "seeing" (*paśyan*) and ending with "eating" (*aśnan*), without regard for their sequential order. In the same way, the functions of the organs of action— namely speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and procreation— are [presented] by the word "prattling" (*pralapan*).

These are established by the four terms: "grasping," "going," "releasing," and [the implied "sleeping"]. For, by the term "releasing" (*visṛjan*), two functions—excretion and procreation—are indicated; and by the term "sleeping" (*svapan*), the function of the mind is indicated, since in the state of sleep it is the mind alone that experiences its own activity.
These are not the sense organs; rather, by the two words "opening" (*unmiṣat*) and "closing" (*nimiṣat*), the activity of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) is indicated.

Since the activity of the intellect consists of determination, when it functions with respect to existence (*bhāva*), it is expressed by the word "opening," and when it functions with respect to non-existence (*abhāva*), it is expressed by the word "closing."

For existence and non-existence are determined solely by the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). However, the modification in the form of the ego (*ahaṃkāra-vṛtti*) resides in the Puruṣa alone, who is designated as the agent in such expressions as "seeing" and "hearing. These are the modifications of the internal and external organs. By the word "breathing," the modification of the vital breath (*prāṇa-vṛtti*) is indicated.
For the maintenance of life is indeed the act of breathing. This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of this statement: "In whom all... [and so forth].
Thus, it refers to the Supreme Reality, the Self, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), whose essential nature has been explained.

That very power, which is non-different [from the Lord] and consists solely of the reflective awareness of such a nature, flows forth as the object of His play— the world consisting of knowable effects manifested by His will—
and [thus serves] for transmigrating beings who perceive through the distortions produced by that Māyā.

In brief, although they consist of the forms of knowledge and action, they result in being the cause of bondage to saṃsāra, as they manifest by spreading through fourteen paths due to the distinctions between the functions of the internal and external organs and the vital breath (prāṇa).

(p. 123) However, it is solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord that those whose own eye of knowledge has been opened and purified of the stain of duality— even while engaged in all worldly activities— [perceive reality].
Because it consists solely in the reflective awareness of the nature [of reality] as previously described,
it manifests to those engaged in the aforementioned practice of action precisely for the sake of attaining the fruit of liberation, characterized by absorption into the Supreme Self; therefore—
It has been stated [in the Gītā]: "The one who is disciplined thinks, 'I do nothing at all,'" and so forth. || 9 ||
