Now, in order to reveal this very point, he says:
"He who performs actions by placing them in Brahman, having abandoned attachment, is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (10)
Having placed all actions being performed upon Brahman, the Supreme Self,

and having established them as His power, one should likewise abandon worldly attachment— that state of the mind being immersed in objects appearing as distinct from one's own nature— and [act] according to what has been stated.

He who, having entered into the state of the Supreme Lord through the vision of knowledge, performs all actions and conducts himself like an ordinary worldly person, is not smeared— nor defiled— by sin in the form of the fruits of action consisting of pleasure and so forth, just as one is not affected by water due to the absence of any intervening barrier.
Though closely joined, it is like a lotus petal. || 10 ||
Therefore, for this reason:
"Having abandoned attachment, yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, for the sake of self-perfection. (11)

By the mention of "the body," the organs of action are included; by the mention of "mind and intellect," the organs of perception are included here. By these alone—being pure because they do not grasp the ego and so forth, which are their objects, or being separate from them—[one attains liberation].

Those established in the yoga of action perform and indeed carry out their respective duties as prescribed by the scriptures, which are difficult to abandon because they are inseparable from the body and other such factors; however,
for the sake of attaining the aforementioned True Self— that is, for the realization of the sense of "I"— they must abandon attachment.
Having abandoned [attachment], they perform [actions]. What is meant by this? Renunciation is indeed the abandonment of attachment, not the abandonment of action. || 11 ||
And that abandonment of attachment arises from the renunciation of the fruits of action as set forth in the preceding discourse; thus he says:
"The disciplined one, having renounced the fruit of action, attains the peace of final liberation."
One who acts improperly, impelled by desire and attached to the fruit, becomes bound.

He who, being engaged in action through steadfastness in knowledge, having abandoned the fruit of action by way of non-attachment, attains the peace that is final— situated in the ultimate limit of the highest state.

He attains tranquility, which consists in resting in the true nature of the Self that is free from the agitation characterized by the cognition of duality; however, he who is always engaged in action— which is by nature difficult to abandon— and thus is not disciplined, being not concentrated according to the aforementioned method, will inevitably...
Because of attachment to the fruits [of action], one is bound and constrained within saṃsāra. || 12 ||

Now, at the conclusion of this chapter where these two— karma-yoga and saṃnyāsa— have been explained in detail, [the Lord] speaks as follows, first restating their essential natures and then clarifying the attainment of the final fruit for the one who practices them:
Having mentally renounced all actions, the self-controlled embodied being dwells in happiness within the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action to be done.
Here, by the word "mind" (*manas*), it is precisely the intellect (*buddhi*) that is intended. That mind is of two kinds: worldly and related to yoga.
Among these, [the worldly mind] consists of the darkness of dualistic cognition arising through the power of the inconceivable *māyā* of the Lord.

The worldly [cognition] is that by which the world conceives of the single ultimate reality as having manifoldness; whereas the cognition belonging to the yogi is that by which the yogi— purified by the power of knowledge manifested through the grace of the Blessed One— [perceives] all entities.
They consider [the mind] to have the singular nature of the aforementioned Supreme Self.

Thus, this twofold nature of the mind has been demonstrated by the Sage himself in the *Anugītā* through the very words of the Blessed One, by means of a narrative sequence for the sake of Arjuna’s enlightenment.
As it is said:
"Both Speech and Mind, having approached the Inner Self (Bhūtātman), asked:
'Tell us which of us is superior; O Lord, resolve our doubt.'"
(125) Then the Blessed One said to Sarasvatī, "Mama.
Thereupon Vāk said to him, "I am the cow of plenty for you."
He said to her:
"Know that both the immobile and the mobile are my two minds:
the immobile is indeed in my presence, while the mobile is within your domain."

Thus, because of being solely intent on contemplating the nature of the perfectly stable Supreme Self, with a mind— that is, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)— which dwells in the proximity of the Supreme Lord and is described by the word "stable" (sthāvara) due to its steadiness, one [should perform] all actions: all activities performed by the mind, speech, and body that are enjoined by the scriptures.

Having renounced those actions inseparable from the body by abandoning the various intentions for fruits which are causes of bondage, and having deposited them in Brahman alone, the yogi of action— being self-controlled, having conquered his mind, and having realized his true nature— abides in happiness through that very process.

The meaning is that he remains in a state of composure, resting within his own Self, which consists of unsurpassed bliss due to the natural cessation of all contact with afflictions (*kleśa*). Being of what nature does he abide? In this very city—the body—which is designated as a "house" by virtue of its general characteristic of being a dwelling place; for this reason, of what kind is it? It is the "nine-gated" one.

In that [body] which possesses nine gates— the six openings of the eyes, ears, and nostrils, which are the pathways for the engagement of the activities of seeing, hearing, and smelling; and likewise the three, namely the mouth, anus, and genitals, which are the pathways for the engagement of the activities of tasting and excretion.

Because he rests in the nature of the Supreme Self, which is non-dual pure consciousness, he realizes all actions and all effects as being nothing but his own essential nature; thus, unlike other embodied beings, he does not act and does not experience the conceit of agency. For some indeed maintain that there are distinct embodied selves for each body.

They consider [the self] to be endowed with an inherent and specific agency, such that it neither acts itself nor instigates others. For some others, however, consider the self to be the instigator of the activity of inert *prakṛti* merely by its presence; but for this [self], it is both ways.
Agency is negated; for, being absorbed in the Supreme Self, he neither acts nor causes others to act. || 13 ||

(p. 126) For this very reason, reminding [the seeker] of the nature of the Supreme Self, He says: "The Lord creates neither the agency nor the actions of the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is inherent nature that operates. (14)
Because he is established in the single nature of non-dual consciousness alone, the Lord, the Sovereign,
or the Supreme Self, does not, in his real form, possess agency over the world or over the multitude of individual souls (*jīva*) whose mutual distinctions are manifested by the power of his *māyā*.
Among those actions, which are determined and have determined fruits, it does not create the state of being an agent, nor does it create actions characterized by merit or demerit for anyone,
nor does it create a connection with their fruits consisting of pleasure and so forth; therefore, it is identical in nature with that [action].

The connection with the preceding verse is that the practitioner of action (*karmayogin*) becomes exactly like that. Now, an objection may be raised: "If, as you say, the Lord does not act nor cause others to act because he is established solely in his own essential nature as described, then from where does this worldly activity arise? To this, he replies: "But it is nature (*svabhāva*) that acts."

By the word *svabhāva*, that very power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), whose nature is inconceivable, is denoted as a synonym for *prakṛti*; it proceeds and expands forth in order to manifest the city of the Gandharvas— the variegated world— arising from the differentiation of infinite entities.
For she, whose very life consists solely in the non-apprehension of the non-difference between all real entities, manifests all this through the necessity previously explained. || 14 ||
Even though it appears in this manner, when examined through the vision of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it does not differ from the aforementioned nature of the Supreme Self.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord’s agency over specific effects and so forth is not an inherent, real attribute. Consequently:
To demonstrate that this delusion of bondage and liberation is indeed created by māyā, he says:
"The All-pervading Lord does not take on the sin or even the merit of anyone;
knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that, living beings are deluded. (15)
But for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge,
that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun.

The omnipresent Lord, whose nature has been explained as it truly is, does not, in the ultimate sense, take upon Himself the sin or defilement that constitutes the cause of bondage for any living being, such that by its removal that being would attain the highest good characterized by liberation. Nor...

One might take upon oneself the merit that is the cause of liberation for someone else, by which, through that taking, one attains misfortune characterized by bondage to saṃsāra. Then what, indeed, is the cause of bondage and the cause of liberation for living beings? To this he says: "Through ignorance."

By means of the absence of knowledge— which consists merely in the non-manifestation of the non-difference between the ultimate reality and the supreme Self— just as by dense darkness, the nature of objects is obscured; that is,
the awakening whose essence is the manifestation of the principles as they have been explained is now covered and eclipsed.
For that reason, all living beings are deluded;

they experience bondage through views consisting of erroneous knowledge characterized by the grasping of the notion of a self with respect to the body and so forth. However, for those whose ignorance has been eliminated as it has been explained, [bondage does not occur].

That [ignorance] has been destroyed— that is, utterly eradicated— by the knowledge of the reality of the self as the object of knowledge, according to what was stated, for those yogins who, through the grace of the Supreme Lord,
are qualified for the practice of the renunciation of action (karmayoga) as previously described.

Supreme knowledge, which is the highest goal, illuminates—that is, makes manifest—the reality characterized by the nature of the Supreme Self. How? Like the sun; just as the Lord Sun, having risen at dawn, dispels even the dense darkness that is difficult to overcome by its mere radiance.

Just as a lamp, having cast aside all visible objects, makes them manifest beyond doubt, even so knowledge—having arisen at the opportune moment through the grace and will of the Lord—dispels ignorance, which is the cause of the concealment of one's true nature; such is the meaning of the simile. (15, 16)
Thus, in order to demonstrate the fruit of practicing that very knowledge— which illuminates the supreme reality and destroys ignorance—
it is said: "Those whose intellect is absorbed in That, whose self is That, who are established in That, and for whom That is the supreme goal."
Those whose impurities have been washed away by knowledge go to the state from which there is no return. || 17 ||
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the primary cause that serves as the means for realizing the various objects to be known;
by it,
the entire aggregate of instruments (*karaṇavarga*) is to be understood as being implied, as is the case with the word "Self" (*ātman*).

"One who understands is called a person. In this context, those whose intellect (*buddhi*) is fully established in that aforementioned knowledge are "those whose intellect is that" (*tad-buddhayaḥ*); likewise, those whose self (*ātman*) is in that very knowledge are "those whose self is that" (*tad-ātmānaḥ*), meaning their sense of "I" is fixed in the aforementioned knowledge.

Those for whom the two— characterized by the nature of intellect and the basis of all worldly transactions— are composed of non-dual knowledge, are such [as described]. Furthermore, by the word *niṣṭhā*, the limit of the supreme goal (*upeya*) is expressed here, and by the word *parāyaṇa* as well.

That which is intended as the means for attaining that [knowledge] is called "that-para" (tat-para), meaning that by which one is carried beyond. Those for whom that aforementioned knowledge is the culmination (*niṣṭhā*) are "those devoted to that" (*tanniṣṭhāḥ*); those for whom that very [knowledge] is the ultimate goal (*parāyaṇa*) are "those for whom that is the supreme resort" (*tatparāyaṇāḥ*).
Thus, these two characteristics—namely, the goal (*upeya*) and the means (*upāya*)—constitute the domain of the practitioner's discourse.

Those for whom [the self] consists precisely of the knowledge as previously described are such that they possess the objects of all things pertaining to both saṃsāra and liberation, which are based upon the knowledge of reality; therefore,
by means of such knowledge, [the mind] is washed clean without remainder.
Those yogis whose stains of ignorance in the form of sin have been washed away reach the state of non-return; that is to say, they attain liberation from which there is no further rebirth. || 17 ||
Now, in order to demonstrate the mental state of such yogis, which is distinct from that of all the world, he says:
"In a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant..."
The wise see with an equal eye both a dog and an outcaste. || 18 ||
In that [Brahmin] who is endowed with— that is, connected to— the science of knowledge (*vidyā-śāstra*) and discipline (*vinaya*), which is a specific rule concerning the practice of its meaning;
and likewise in cows and other animals whose entire conduct is restricted solely to fear, food, and sexual intercourse.
Even in the case of an outcaste (śvapāka), though existing in human form yet largely like an animal, those who are wise—

awakened by the knowledge of reality as it has been described— are seers of equality; they perceive that which is equal, common, one, whose nature is untouched by all particularities, and which is pure consciousness alone.
Those whose nature it is to see and to realize are such [as described]. What is meant by this?
Those for whom the divine eye of primordial wisdom has fully blossomed do not perceive [reality] as a multiplicity through eyes impaired by illusion.

(129) They constantly perceive the entire range of manifest phenomena as having the single form of Brahman. Nor should it be thought that they apply to outcastes (śvapacas) and the like the same conduct prescribed for Brahmins and others, or [apply to Brahmins] that which is prescribed for outcastes and the like.

Regarding the phrase "among Brahmins and others," those who persist in improper actions (vikarman) subvert the world-order established by the Supreme Lord. For they perceive the expansion of worldly existence exactly as it stands, as being of the nature of Brahman, and do not practice its subversion.
He explains that very state of equanimity:
"Having obtained what is pleasant, he should not rejoice; having obtained what is unpleasant, he should not be agitated.
Steadfast in intellect and undeluded, the knower of Brahman is established in Brahman. (19)

He who knows Brahman through scripture— that is, one who knows the reality of Brahman as it has been described, whose intellect is firm and therefore unshakable even by powerful doubts, and who is consequently undeluded, his mind being free from uncertainty regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted— [abides] in that Brahman attained through the scriptures.

One who is rested in the Supreme Self through constant cultivation does not experience the joy and agitation caused by the attainment of the pleasant and unpleasant—qualities indicative of partiality that are characteristic of worldly persons. Therefore, it is said that the wise possess equal vision toward Brahmins, cows, and others. || 19 ||

Furthermore, the position of those who advocate for absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) is that stability in such Brahman occurs only through the total abandonment of external objects; however, this is not possible according to the reasoning previously stated,
or even if it were possible in some way, it would be as painful as a thorn.

In order to establish that the state of being established in Brahman is indeed unshakable precisely because its object is prescribed by the scriptures, he says, adopting the position of their combination (samuccaya):
"He whose self is unattached to external contacts finds happiness in the Self."
With his self united in yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable bliss. || 20 ||
That happiness which is established by its own nature in the Self, the supreme reality—

the attribute characterized by eternal bliss— one whose mind is unattached to external contacts such as sound and so forth, which are determined as "this" and are not contradictory [to liberation], remains firmly fixed in the Self alone through the power of right knowledge.

The yogi whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is immersed in *sattva* perceives—that is, attains—bliss without effort, being one whose self is disciplined in yoga; that is, one whose self is disciplined in the meditative concentration on action (*karmasamādhi*), having an internal organ that is constantly attentive through steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*). (p. 130) Bliss without affliction.
Having rendered the imperishable Brahman, the supreme cause, free from interruption, one enjoys it—that is, one pervades it—as one's own self. || 20 ||
To demonstrate how a yogi does not find happiness residing in the self within external contacts, he says:
"For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of suffering."
They have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī; the wise man does not delight in them.

The word "hi" indicates the reason. Because those enjoyments—desires born of contact, arising from contact with objects such as sound and so forth—are impermanent due to being characterized by birth and destruction; and while they are present, [the suffering] born of separation from them...

Because suffering is invariable, and because there is an invariable suffering consisting of longing for things not yet attained, these very sources of suffering produce nothing but suffering. Therefore, the wise person—one who possesses knowledge—does not delight in those enjoyments; he does not experience pleasure. What has been stated by this?

It is so. The practitioner of action (karmayogin), though truly engaging with sense objects through the senses like an ordinary worldly person, does not become happy by means of the pleasure produced thereby; for he experiences the innate happiness that resides within the Self. || 21 ||
In order to demonstrate that such a wise one possesses both the state of a yogi and happiness, he says:
"He who is able here, even before the release from the body..."
That yogi who [subdues] the impulse arising from desire and anger is considered happy.

He who, while remaining right here in this very body, by virtue of his connection with objects that are invariably present, is able— through abiding solely in the Self— to endure and maintain composure against the agitation born of passion, hatred, and the like.
Even before casting off the body, that concentrated yogin becomes capable and empowered;
he is happy, possessing the fruit of samādhi characterized by unsurpassed bliss. For others who know the reality, being proponents of mere knowledge, practice yoga while fleeing from sense objects.

While those enemies are seeking an opportunity against them, yoga and its fruit are difficult to attain even in this very body; therefore, they will obtain them only upon the abandonment of the body. But he who is a practitioner of *karmayoga*, whose self-abidance remains undisturbed even amidst sense objects—he is liberated while still living. Thus it is said:
Thus it has been said: "He alone is the yogi; he alone is happy. || 22 ||
For this very reason, he describes its essential nature:
"O Pārtha, he who is happy within, who rejoices within, and who likewise has light only within, having become Brahman, attains the supreme Yoga. (2.54)

Bliss (*sukha*) is the tranquility (*nirvṛti*) resulting from various specific actions; a pleasure-garden (*ārāma*) is that in which one takes delight, being the locus for the experience of bliss; light (*jyotis*) is the illumination that causes the manifestation of both of those. He in whom even this triad exists within the inner self (*antarātman*) alone—he is such a person everywhere.

When the object is being experienced, the notion of a non-self dissolves; for that very reason, having become Brahman—having attained the nature of Brahman, the Supreme Self—he reaches and attains supreme yoga, the unsurpassed meditative absorption (samādhi). || 23 ||
For this reason:
"The seers, whose taints are exhausted, who have severed all doubts, who are self-controlled, and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the Brahman-nirvana. (24)
Those great souls who have severed their dualities,

whose shackles of worldly bondage consisting of the notion of duality have been snapped, who are therefore cleansed of all taint and have destroyed the great sin of all ignorance— these are the sages.

Those who possess right vision, and for that very reason do not perceive any collection of objects as distinct from their own true nature, are devoted to— that is, firmly intent upon— the welfare and well-being of all beings as if it were their own;
they [attain] Nirvāṇa, which is the supreme reality of Brahman, tranquil because it is untouched by the threefold suffering.
They obtain and attain [the goal], but not those who, perceiving objects as distinct [from themselves], flee from them; for the latter remain indeed unliberated from the bondage of duality. || 24 ||
He specifies this very point:
"For ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained, and who have realized the Self, the extinction into Brahman exists on every side. (25)
(132) Those whose minds are restrained— that is, whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are controlled by being free from defects such as passion and hatred,
and not merely by being separated from sense objects— who have known the Self,
who have realized the nature of the supreme cause, and who possess the primary characteristics [of the liberated].
For ascetics who are supreme yogis, the aforementioned Nirvāṇa, which is Brahman, exists directly before them, face to face. || 25 ||
Then, in order to demonstrate the distinction of the practitioner of action (karmayogin) from the practitioner of dispassionate yoga (naiṣkarmyayogin), he says:
"Having placed the external objects of touch outside, and the eyes between the eyebrows..."
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal, moving within the nostrils.
The sage whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained, who is devoted to liberation, and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed—he is indeed always liberated. (27)

A sage (*muni*) of this kind, being an ascetic (*yati*) devoted to liberation (*mokṣaparāyaṇa*), attains the supreme liberation because he desires its attainment; however, he is not yet liberated [in the absolute sense], for his mind still rests upon objects to be rejected or accepted, and he is not yet free from defects such as attachment and aversion. But for one in whom desire, fear, and anger [have ceased]—
The mental defects previously explained, which were difficult to restrain,

have been especially gone beyond— that is, utterly destroyed— by virtue of his being established solely in his own Self, which is by nature free from defect, characterized by non-return. Such a practitioner of karma-yoga is indeed liberated, because of this [realization] regarding the Self.

When that power, whose characteristic is universal consciousness and which is pure by nature, through the influence of *māyā* fails to reflect upon its own true nature, becomes obstructed by the notion of "I" regarding the body and so forth, and assumes the state of being a subject following after objects to be rejected or accepted, then—

It is said that the mind is "stained" by defects such as passion and the like; however, when it is separated from those defects through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), then, attaining its own nature—which is characterized solely by eternal, infinite, and incomparable purity—it remains as nothing but pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*). Thus it has been said:
The mind itself, when defiled by the afflictions such as passion and the like, is indeed saṃsāra;
that very same mind, when liberated from them, is called the end of existence.
Thus, in this way, because he is free from the manifestation of defects such as passion even while objects are present,
the practitioner of action (*karmayogin*), having attained identity with the Supreme Self, is liberated even while living. But he who possesses characteristics other than these—
A yogī of this kind, even if he is solely intent upon supreme liberation, is not yet liberated.

Of what nature is he? He is one by whom the senses—the instruments—and the mind (*manas*), which consists of volition (*saṃkalpa*), and the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of determination (*adhyavasāya*), have been restrained and controlled.

Of such a kind. Having done what is he thus? Having cast out externally the external objects—sound and so forth—which, because they are touched by the senses, are designated by the word "touch" (*sparśa*), and which are distinct as objects of apprehension; that is, by not being grasped by the senses, he has separated them from the mind. By this [it is meant]:

By this qualification, the limb of yoga characterized as the withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) of the senses from their objects is set forth; and by that, the preceding limbs such as posture (*āsana*) and mastery of breath (*prāṇajaya*) are implied. Having done what else? [Having fixed] the eye between the two eyebrows, in the space between the brows.
By the phrase "having made [the mind] the power of vision," the yoga-aṅga characterized as *dhāraṇā* (concentration) is also stated.

For by this, the binding of the mind is described as being fixed upon the region characterized by the space between the eyebrows, with the subtle element of light (*tejomātra*) as its object. Furthermore, [it refers to] those two which move within the nose.

Having brought into equilibrium— that is, made equal through simultaneous flow in an identical manner— the two bodily winds known as *prāṇa* and *apāna*, which have the habit of moving within the mouth-like cavity consisting of the pair of right and left channels (*nāḍī*).
The characteristic of meditation (*dhyāna*), which is an auxiliary of yoga (*yogāṅga*) to be accomplished by one-pointed intelligence, has been described.

For when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has a single object as its support, meditation is perfected; by the power of that, the prāṇa and apāna take recourse to the equinoctial course (*viṣuvadgati*). Thus, [this is established] through threefold action.

The yogi whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained has attained the stages of yoga up to the limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and meditation (*dhyāna*); however, because there is no absolute concealment of the intellect, he has not yet ascended to *samādhi*. For that [samādhi] is not accomplished for him without liberation from the body.
This is because the existence of one whose residual impressions of mental modifications persist until the dissolution of the body is admitted.

Thus, it has been established that the practitioner of Karma-yoga, whose consciousness is always established in its own true nature, is superior to the yogi who is devoted to the practice of Yoga characterized by the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. || 27 ||
For he, knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, attains peace. (28)
Having known me— Nirvāṇa, expressed by the word Brahman, the unsurpassed goal, the Supreme Self— and having realized me as one's own self, one attains peace,
which is characterized by the cessation of all disturbances of conceptual construction and the attainment of final bliss.

The meaning is that one is liberated simply by knowing my true nature. Having known me as what? As the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities—here, various acts such as sacrifice and austerity are enjoined by the scripture as things to be performed; yet their performers, deluded by ignorance, [do not know this].
Ordinary people consider themselves to be distinct from one another as the enjoyers of their respective fruits;

however, those who know the ultimate truth, because there is no difference among agents, hold that "I alone am the single agent and enjoyer of all actions and their fruits," and thus [the Lord] is the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities. Likewise:

The Great Lord of all the world, who, for the sole purpose of sport, manifests himself in manifold forms by his mere will to any and every class of living beings; the Supreme Master, because he alone is the single director of those various activities. Thus...

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no distinction among all beings, and because I am always a friend to all, established solely in my own nature which is by nature free from defect, I am neither hostile toward anyone nor attached to anyone. Knowing me to be such, one should engage in actions just as I do.
Thus, it has been established that this practitioner of action (karmayogin) is indeed superior to the aforementioned yogin, because he attains peace and liberation. || 28 ||
Where the mind of renunciation has attained oneness with the intellect of yoga, like the celestial river [Ganges] uniting with the Yamunā—
approach this chapter, which is a supreme sacred ford.
It is the essence for the realization of the Self, like Prayāga as the fifth [tīrtha].

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meaning of the statements, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter.

By means of the first chapter, [the author has established] the fundamental tenet of the entire treatise, which consists in the performance of the combination of self-knowledge and prescribed ritual action.

The introduction has been commenced; by the second [chapter], the essential nature of knowledge and action has been demonstrated; by the third, the misconception that knowledge and action have different practitioners as their respective objects has been dispelled; and by the fourth—

Thus, the engagement in yoga, which consists of the performance of such a synthesis, has been shown to proceed from a supreme cause, and the manifold nature of action has been demonstrated; furthermore, by the fifth [chapter], it was shown that those very two—knowledge and action—are renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and yoga (*yoga*). Now, [the sixth chapter begins].

Regarding those two— knowledge and action— which have been taught as to be practiced in combination, is everyone belonging to all castes and stages of life entitled [to them], or are only certain restricted persons so entitled? It is for the purpose of dispelling this doubt that the universal applicability of this [teaching] is established.
In order to explain this through another chapter,
the Blessed Lord said:
"He who performs the action that must be done without depending on the fruit of action..."
He is both a renunciant and a yogi; he is neither one who maintains no sacred fires nor one who performs no actions.

The fruit of that specific action— such as a sacrifice or other rite being performed— is the experience of heaven and so forth; he who, being unattached— that is, not supported by it due to the absence of any desire for reward—
performs the duty enjoined by the scripture according to the regulations of caste and stage of life.
One who performs and carries out action is called a renunciant, one who has abandoned [worldly ties], a yogi, and one who is concentrated;
by this it is stated that all social classes (varṇas) and all stages of life (āśramas) are qualified for the performance of the combined practice that results in liberation.

The definition of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is merely the absence of attachment to the fruits of action, and likewise, the performance of prescribed duties is yoga; thus, the subject matter expounded throughout the entire treatise has been established in its essential form. And therefore—
Because his internal organ is solely intent upon the knowledge of the Self as it has been explained,
he is free from longing for any separate fruit consisting of pleasure;
and because his nature is liberated from defects such as passion, [he remains so] from the time of his qualification.

p. 136) Whoever performs the practice introduced from that point onward—be he a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra; whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic—he alone becomes a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogin; it is not, however, one who is merely without sacrificial fires or merely inactive.

By the words "without sacrificial fires" (niragni) and "without ritual action" (akriya), the student (brahmacārī) and the ascetic (yati) are indicated; for some, considering only these two stages of life, imagine that because they have not reflected upon the supreme reality, they possess the conceit of being free from action (naiṣkarmya),
and thus believe that only the student and the ascetic possess the state of renunciation (saṃnyāsitā) and the state of yoga (yogitā).

They maintain this: for he who, from the very beginning of his life as a student (*brahmacarya*), has taken recourse to the duty of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), being one who has not taken a wife and thus has not established the sacred fires, is considered by them to be, from the very root, one who has abandoned sacrificial rites and other such activities—a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who is simultaneously a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi; or else, he who...

Having abandoned all activities— such as Vedic study, sacrifice, giving, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts— which are performed in the three stages of life (āśramas), and having taken refuge in the stage of life that is free from desire, he is the second type of renunciant (saṃnyāsī), a yogi who is a wandering ascetic (yati).

And this is the opinion of those [who hold both views], because when there is the abandonment of these very two types of activities which are the causes of bondage, one partakes in the fruit of liberation. || 1 ||
To demonstrate that this doctrine of the proponents of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) is indeed untenable, he says:
"Know that which they call renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava;
for no one becomes a yogi who has not renounced his mental resolves (*saṃkalpa*). (2)

You should understand that what these proponents of "knowledge alone" (jñānamātravādins) describe as the goal characterized by actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) under the name of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is actually yoga, which is the very performance of action;
for without renunciation, there is no yoga among them, yet that renunciation [is present].

This [result] arises only from *saṃkalpa*, that is, from the desire for fruit, and not from ritual action (*karman*), because there is an absence of ritual action among all castes and all stages of life. For those two who are considered renunciants— the ascetic (*yati*) and the student (*brahmacārin*)— they abandon the ritual actions appropriate to the householder and the forest-dweller respectively, by virtue of their renunciation of action.
But for oneself, renunciation is established only for one who performs certain specific duties that are the cause for attaining perfection through effort and so forth;

for if one acts according to one's own whims, those two states ultimately result in nothing but the state of being established in forbidden action (*vikarma*). Therefore, because he has renounced by mere intention (*saṃkalpa*), his status as a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) is established—this refers to the yogi who is always [thus].

In every way, having renounced the intention for the fruits of action through the state of a firmly rooted *ahaṃpratyaya* (I-consciousness) in Brahman— whose characteristic is the Supreme Self eternally satisfied by the nectar of its own bliss— that yogi becomes one possessed of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in action; he does not [otherwise].
"Another," it says.

By this verse, it is established that all social classes (*varṇas*) and all stages of life (*āśramas*) are qualified for the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and yoga as previously described, which are to be practiced by a single person; however,
since the state of desiring to ascend (*ārurukṣā*) regarding the aforementioned yoga is possible for the practitioner, [the following is] based on that.
To explain its distinction, he says:
"For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means. (3)

For the sage who has attained knowledge instantaneously, for the practitioner established in reflection, and for the one desiring to ascend the aforementioned yoga— wishing to attain an unimpeded firm footing therein— action consists of those various rites that have descended according to the sequence of caste and stage of life.
The cause is the basis for ascending to yoga. Beholding, hearing, touching, smelling, and [tasting] that very same kind of object which has become the cause, while not abandoning it— (5.8)

By such statements as these, [it is shown that] for one who has ascended to yoga (*yogārūḍha*)— whose mind has attained stability in yoga through the power of constant practice without interruption as previously instructed— and who has merged with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), tranquility (*śama*),
which is the cessation of the agitation caused by volitional constructions and conceptual fluctuations (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*), is the cause, the motivator, and the instrumental condition.

What is meant by this? For a beginner yogin who has received instruction based on scripture alone and is eager to attain stability in yoga, it is indeed karma that serves as the means (*upeya*) for attaining that [stability]. And when that [karma] is properly performed with faith and reverence, [it leads to the goal].

And when knowledge has reached the pinnacle of clarity, even while that [previous] karma is not yet abandoned, tranquility becomes the cause [of liberation], because it is the supreme goal to be attained. || 3 ||
Therefore, He states the characteristic of one who is tranquil and has ascended to yoga:
"When indeed one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all volitions, then he is said to have ascended to yoga. (4)

For when, in that very state, even while the sense organs are being contacted by non-contradictory objects among the sense-objects, or while engaged in actions such as sacrifice and austerity which are the causes for attaining them—
Even while actions are being performed, he does not become attached because he is satisfied by innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); he does not indulge in clinging.
Like the wind, even while touching the multitude of objects, he remains established solely in the space of his own nature (*svabhāvavyoma*). At that time, of all volitions (*saṃkalpa*)—

Because he has renounced and abandoned all intentions for fruits, he is said to be "one who has ascended to yoga"— that is, one who has ascended to yoga, which is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in action, and has attained firm stability therein. Thus, for such a person,
who possesses this state of having ascended to yoga— the cause for attaining the supremely tranquil Brahman— there is no [further need].
Apart from the self, no external thing can exist as a means of proof.
Therefore:
One should uplift oneself by means of oneself; one should not let oneself sink down.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. (5)
The self is the kinsman of that person by whom the self has been conquered by the self;
but for one who has not conquered the self, the self itself would behave as an enemy toward the state of enmity.
For one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the mind is equal toward others and oneself,
as well as toward cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and likewise honor and dishonor.

One should, by one's own self and with enthusiasm aroused by the instruction of the aforementioned knowledge, rescue oneself from being submerged in the deep ocean of worldly existence— which is crowded with thousands of terrifying waves of conceptual construction tossed about by the wind of the irresistible cognition of duality— and restore that very nature of the self.

One should cause [the practitioner] to reach the shore characterized by the yoga as previously described; one must not, through neglecting him due to forgetting his own strength, allow him to sink or drown right there. For it is the self alone—not anyone else—that is both the benefactor and the adversary in the matter of his rescue or his downfall.

To the question "How so?", he says: For that person, the self alone—indeed its very own nature—is its kinsman, acting as a relative who provides a remedy for all calamities. As it has been said: "If the self itself does not restrain the self from harmful things..."
Who else is more beneficial than he who will restrain him?

Thus [it is asked]: for whom is the Self alone the kinsman? For that person by whom that Self—his own essential nature (svasvabhāva)—has been conquered through the power obtained by the practice of consuming the nectar of knowledge (*jñānāmṛta*), and has been brought under control by being made the object of perfect reflective awareness (*pravimarśa*). But for him by whom that Self...

Being disregarded by one who is intent upon the Supreme Knower (*pramātṛ*), it is neither conquered nor brought under control; for such a person, this [mind] persists in the state of enmity, obstructing all desires. And thus it has been said:
"One should not do that which even a sharp sword or a serpent with virulent poison might not do."
Or rather, when one's own self is ill-governed, it is like an enemy who is perpetually enraged.

Thus [it is said]. He states the fruit of the aforementioned conquest of the self (ātmajaya): for one who has conquered the self—that is, one by whom the self has been brought under control in the manner described—and who is therefore tranquil, because of the attainment of the Supreme Self which is free from the defects of one's own nature, and whose disturbances of conceptual construction have ceased.
When other embodied beings are perceived as distinct from oneself,
there nevertheless arises an equal cognition that grasps a single common nature regarding both the self— as experienced through the notion of "I"—
and others; likewise, this occurs with respect to cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and so forth, whether produced by external or internal causes.

In the face of the afflictions of dualities— likewise when honor and worship are bestowed by another, as well as in dishonor and defeat— the mind remains exactly the same; for it does not deviate from that single, all-pervading nature which is free from modification.

The sense of "I" regarding the Supreme Self is distinct; even when various causes of modification are present, his contemplation upon his own true Self is not interrupted, unlike that of worldly people—this is the meaning. || 7 ||
And such a person as this is called one who has ascended to yoga; thus he says:

"The yogi whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realized wisdom, who is steadfast and has conquered his senses, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same—he is said to be 'steadfast' (yukta)."

*Jñāna* is the mere comprehension of the essential nature [of reality] through the scriptures; *vijñāna* is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that reality as understood from the scriptures. One whose self—meaning whose very nature—is satisfied by these two and free from further longing is such [a person]; for this very reason, he is immovable (*kūṭastha*).
Because he has attained the realization of the supreme reality as the eternal Self, he is immovable like a mountain,
free from trembling; for he has conquered his senses and brought both the external and internal organs under control,
rather than being subject to them, since he is thus devoid of defects such as greed and the like.
He for whom a clod of earth and a stone, as well as gold, are equal—that one is called "yoked," one who has ascended to yoga. || 8 ||
One who possesses an equal mind toward well-wishers, friends, enemies, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen— and even toward the virtuous and the sinful— is preeminent.

He whose intellect is uniform— due to perceiving the single reality that is non-different from Brahman and characterized by suchness— in all beings, whether they be friends, enemies, or others, who are of various kinds and mutually distinct in form on account of being causes for attachment or aversion; he is distinguished.

He attains superiority over the yogin of action-inaction (*naiṣkarmya-yogin*). For whatever object he avoids because it is an obstacle to *samādhi*, and whatever he accepts because it is conducive to it—by those two, namely aversion and affection, the defects of hatred and passion are revealed. But he who...

It has been stated that one who has attained complete equanimity is distinguished as being "already become Brahman" because of his even-mindedness, even while engaged in activities. Now, the distinction between friends and others is explained:
a *suhṛt* is one whose heart is naturally auspicious; a *mitra*...

One whose friendship has been established through the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); an enemy (*ari*) is a foe who hates by virtue of some cause; a hateful person (*dveṣya*) is one who is unpleasant even without a cause; a neutral person (*udāsīna*) is neither a friend nor an enemy;
and a mediator (*madhyastha*) is one who may, in some way, be regarded as either a friend or an enemy.
Relatives are kinsmen; the virtuous are those disciplined by the right conduct prescribed in the scriptures;

the wicked are their opposites, characterized by evil conduct and intentions. It is to be understood that equanimity toward all of these belongs only to this practitioner of *karmayoga*—that which [regards] the state of being an enemy...

Even when engaged in actions such as lawful killing as enjoined by the scriptures, there remains steadfastness in the one Self which is changeless; however, there is no improper hostility toward an enemy because it is not so enjoined by the scriptures. If it were otherwise, then Arjuna would have possessed self-knowledge in that situation.
If it were intended [otherwise], he would have stated at the conclusion, "Therefore, fight. Therefore,

for the practitioner of action (karmayogin), what is intended here is the cultivation of equanimity toward all states of being, precisely while not transgressing those various actions enjoined by the scriptures that have come down through the sequence of his particular caste and stage of life.
Therefore he said:
"In this very world, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity;
for Brahman is faultless and equal, therefore they are established in Brahman. (10)

p. 141) Right here, in this very body performing such actions, rebirth—that is, renewed existence—has been conquered and cast down by those whose mind and consciousness (*citta*) are established and have attained firm footing in the equanimity and non-differentiation of all things as they have been explained; for Brahman is indeed one.

Because it is free from passion and other factors that cause inequality, it is faultless; therefore, it alone is equal—entirely, always, and everywhere—having as its sole nature pure consciousness alone. Thus it has been said: "Those who abide in equanimity abide in Brahman itself. (10)

With six verses, [the Lord] describes yoga— characterized by the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind for one who is concentrated and does not deviate from the aforementioned equanimity— as being similar to other ritual acts in its timing of practice established within the day and night, and as being accompanied by specific procedures, for the sake of the practitioner of karma-yoga.
Granting permission, he said:
"The yogi, staying in solitude, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from desire and possessions, should constantly apply himself to yoga. (11)
Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place— neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass, one over the other— 12.
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained, one should sit upon a seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self. (13)
Holding the body, head, and neck erect and motionless, steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around at the quarters. 14.
With a tranquil self, free from fear, established in the vow of celibacy, having restrained the mind and fixing it on Me, let him sit disciplined, intent on Me as the Supreme Goal. 15.
Thus constantly disciplining the self, my devotee with undivided mind attains the peace that culminates in liberation and abides in me. 16.

This will be explained in sequence: the yogin, by means of the preparatory purification— which is distinct from other methods of exposition presented or yet to be presented in this continuous treatise— [proceeds] with the nature of that which is being set forth.

The practitioner of yoga, by means of *karmayoga*—which is not inconsistent with time and place, independent of specific meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and characterized by an unrestrained flow even within all internal and external faculties and the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*)—is so called because it is prescribed by the scriptures. (p. 142)

Remaining alone and solitary in a secluded place free from distractions to one-pointedness, he should constantly—every day—at fixed times established by his own discipline, sit with his mind and self (ātman) restrained, that is, fully controlled. Here, "self" (ātman) refers either to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) or the individual soul (jīvātman). "Alone" means being by himself, and "with mind and self restrained" means the mind (citta), which is the intellect (manas), has been thoroughly subdued.

The meaning is that one who possesses such a self as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), being of that nature, should concentrate upon the Supreme Self and practice yoga, characterized by the cessation of mental fluctuations; however,
he is "irāśīḥ," meaning he has departed from *āśiṣaḥ*, which is the desire for fruits, even regarding the fruit characterized by liberation.

One should practice this yoga with vigilance through the concentration of *karmayoga*, being free from wretchedness in one's prayers, likewise free from the conceit of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) regarding everything due to non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*), and endowed with the qualities to be described hereafter, such as having the mind fixed on Me (*mac-cittatva*). Thus, one should practice this yoga without negligence.
Thus it has been said. Now, its preliminary purification (*parikarma*) is being described. Having done what should one apply [the practice]?

One should prepare a seat in a pure place for oneself—such as the vicinity of a sacred river, a mountain cave, and so forth, depending on whether one is an ascetic (*yati*) or the like; or, for a householder, in a well-smeared and secluded dwelling—in a purified location.

Having established the seat of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and brought it to a state of stability—of what kind? Firm and motionless, as well as devoid of excessive elevation or depression for the sake of comfort—and likewise having spread out cloth (*cela*), deerskin (*ajina*), and *kuśa* grass (*darbha*) upon that; thereafter...
That is the primary requirement. Therefore, for a householder, [the seat] is cloth over a deerskin; for an ascetic and others, it is kusha grass over [the skin].

Having sat upon such a firm and comfortable seat, one should make the mind—the internal organ—single-pointed, fixed upon a single object chosen as the object of meditation; and for this very reason, one whose activities of the mind and senses are restrained.

Having restrained the activities of the mind, the senses, and the organs— their functions consisting of volition, doubt, and the perception of sound and other objects— so that they do not extend outward, one should practice yoga, which consists of the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, and thus attain composure.

For what purpose? For the purification of the self—that is, for the washing away of the impurity characterized by external attachment of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), or for the wiping away of the stain consisting of the notion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). Thus...

Having explained the concentration of the mind (*cittasamādhāna*), [the author] states the bodily posture (*kāyasaṃsthāna*) which serves as its means of accomplishment: "The body (*kāya*) is the part of the physical frame below the throat;
the head (*śiras*) is the crown; the neck (*grīvā*) is the nape; 'body-head-neck' (*kāyaśirogrīvam*) refers to those [parts taken together]; that [posture] is 'even' (*samam*)."
Holding [the body] straight and without bending the face, maintaining that posture, yet remaining immovable and unshaking—

free from causes of mental distraction such as bodily trembling— and steady, likewise beholding the tip of his own nose, that is, the end of the nostrils, and for that very reason not looking toward the cardinal directions (kāṣṭhā).

"Not looking about" means not glancing around; the instruction to fix the gaze on the tip of the nose is for the purpose of avoiding the casting of the eyes in various directions, but the intention is that this [tip] itself is not to be made the object of focus.
For one who has thus prepared all the requisites for meditative concentration (samādhi):
In order to establish a qualification that serves as the cause for attaining liberation, characterized by absorption into the Supreme Self (paramātman), he says:
"one whose self is tranquil" (praśāntātmā)—that is, one whose internal organ (ātman) is tranquil, being free from the agitation of doubts and other such conceptual constructions (vikalpa). Thus.

Having realized the self-nature of all things, he is free from fear and devoid of trepidation toward the entire range of beings, both moving and stationary; likewise, he remains established in the vow of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*),
meaning he abides in that discipline which consists of the renunciation of desire and volitional intent.
By this qualification, the state of being devoid of longing for the objects of all goals is expressed.

Having thus restrained the mind and withdrawn the consciousness from everything, one whose consciousness—that is, perception—is fixed solely upon Me, the Supreme Self, the One Reality, is "yukta," meaning concentrated; being thus, he is "mat-para" (devoted to Me).

With his mind focused on no other object due to such yoga, he should sit— that is, remain— thus characterized by these qualifications. Constantly, day after day, yoking— that is, concentrating— the self,
which is the internal organ, my devotee, having taken refuge in me alone as the Self, for that very reason...

"With mind not on anything else" means one whose mind is not directed toward another object; however, according to the reading *mayi yuktaḥ*, it means being "joined to me alone," having realized my very attainment as the fruit of meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
[one attains] the peace residing in me.

He attains—that is, accepts—tranquility, characterized by being naturally devoid of all modifications. What kind of peace? "Supreme Nirvana": *nirvāṇa* is the cessation of the agitation caused by the notion of a self and so forth with respect to what is not-self, such as the body; it is "supreme" (*parama*) because it is the most excellent fruit.
That in which it is situated is so described; [he entered] that [city]. || 16 ||

(144) Thus, in order to set forth another preparatory practice for this yoga— which arises from the Great Yoga characterized by action and meditative absorption (*karmasamādhi*), which is to be performed as a commitment to the aforementioned knowledge of the non-dual Self, and which is authorized [by scripture]— he says:
Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all;
nor for him who is habitually addicted to excessive sleep, O Arjuna, nor for him who is ever awake.
For one who is disciplined in diet and conduct, disciplined in actions,
and disciplined in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.

This aforementioned yoga does not exist, nor is it possible, for one who practices in such a manner. For what kind of person? For one who eats excessively—that is, eating to the point of complete satiation—and likewise for one who does not eat at all, in every respect; for such a person, it does not exist.
For one who habitually sleeps excessively and is constantly devoted to sleep, as well as for one who is perpetually awake and sleepless,

there arise defects such as heaviness of the body, pain, and congestion due to overeating, which render the mind unfit for action; and from extreme fasting, there arises the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and other ailments.
They bring about a loss of capacity; from excessive sleep, laziness and other such states arise;
and from the total removal of sleep, indigestion and other ailments produce dejection and so forth. Therefore, it is proper for one’s food and conduct to be moderate.
Of one for whom food, eating, and recreation— such as walking and so forth— are appropriate because they are restricted to the time when it is beneficial; and likewise,
who is disciplined in activities (vyāpāra) concerning both seen and unseen matters.

For such a yogi— whose activity culminates in the non-exhaustion of the body of consciousness (*cittaśarīra*), whose mental and physical functions are thus engaged, and for whom sleep and waking are appropriate because they occur at their proper times— this yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
The meaning is that when practiced, it destroys affliction and one attains happiness with ease. || 18 ||
Having thus described the rules for diet and conduct, he speaks of the yoga characterized by perfection:
"When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone, free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be 'yoked' (yukta). (19)
When the mind of this yogi, having reached the pinnacle of the practice of samādhi, is restrained and controlled,
it becomes established on the level of *samprajñāta-samādhi*.

Accompanied by initial thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*), [the yogi], having attained mastery (*saṃyama*) over gross and subtle objects of meditation, transcends them;
leaving those behind, he abides in one object of meditation—the Self alone, in its very essence. When he attains stability, a firm foundation, and mastery therein, then—

In that state, because he finds delight in the Self alone, being free from longing and desire for all external enjoyments, he is said to be "yoked," having attained seedless (nirbīja) samādhi. || 19 ||
He provides an analogy for that yogic mind, which is established in self-meditation and is denoted by the word "yoga":
"As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile taught."
For the yogi whose mind is restrained, as he practices yoga within the self.

For the yogin who is engaged in yoga—that is, meditative absorption (samādhi)—upon the self as the object of meditation, which is most excellent, his mind is restrained (*yata*) because it has been withdrawn from all [external objects]; such a state is remembered by those who know reality as being "like that" (*tad-upamāna*). Just as a lamp is an illuminator...

Remaining in a place where the wind has ceased, it does not move or tremble; likewise, one must supply the sentence of the object of comparison: "the yogi’s mind, established in the concentration that takes the Self as its support, does not tremble. By means of this simile of the lamp—
Because its powerful adversaries are close at hand, it has been demonstrated that the mind of a yogi must be protected with effort. || 20 ||
Now he states the definition of this supreme yoga:
"Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest;
and where, seeing the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction in the Self. (21)
Where there is absolute bliss, which is beyond the senses and perceivable by the intellect, where one knows it and, being established therein, does not fall away from reality. || 22 ||
Having gained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering. (23)
One should know that disjunction from the union with suffering is designated as yoga. That yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency. (24)

One should know—that is, understand—that object designated as "yoga" and called "samādhi. What is it? That in which the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga—that is, by the cultivation of yoga, which is samādhi, or by the cultivation of another means to be attained—is stilled, having its outward activity ceased.

Through service, through taking refuge, and because it has realized the supreme goal to be attained, the mind comes to rest in that very state and abandons effort directed toward other forms of yoga, for that yoga alone is unsurpassed. Therefore, in that state, the yogi, seeing the Self by means of the Self alone—

Experiencing its own nature through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it finds satisfaction within itself—that is, within its own essential being (*svabhāva*) which serves as the substratum—and attains supreme delight; one should know that state to be *yoga*.
For at that time, all external taints have ceased.

The mind, having attained identity with the Self, abides as that very nature characterized by pure consciousness. Likewise, therein lies the innate (*sahaja*) bliss, which consists of the wondrous experience of an absolute, infinite, and incomparable essential form.

Bliss is manifested. Of what nature is that happiness? It is beyond the senses—that is, it transcends the external senses such as the ear and so forth; for this very reason, it is graspable by the intellect, meaning it is to be perceived and experienced by the intellect characterized by immediate awareness, through the self’s own power alone.

This yogi knows and understands that yoga; he should know it as such. Likewise, established therein—having found rest in that—he does not fall away from, nor is he separated from, the ultimate reality (paramārtha) which is in truth the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman). Furthermore, having attained that yoga, there is nothing superior to it.

Therefore, the yogin does not consider, nor perceive, any other superior gain or attainment of the desired; for this very reason it was stated previously that "where he stands, from there he does not fall away in reality. For this very reason, established in that state, with all other activities ceased, the yogin, even by his teacher—
One should know that object designated as "yoga" to be that which is neither shaken nor displaced by any powerful mental or physical suffering. Of what nature is it?
It is the disjunction from the conjunction with suffering; "suffering" here refers to that produced by the engagement of the senses with sense-objects.
*Rājasa* is affliction; *saṃyoga* with that is the connection during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

From that, *viyoga* is separation—the meaning of which is precisely the absence of connection with the suffering born from the longing for objects to be abandoned (*heyavastu*). Yoga characterized in this way is the supreme.
Concentration (samādhi) is the cause of great power, characterized by the attainment of unsurpassed bliss;

it must be applied and cultivated with certainty, free from doubt, with a mind undiscouraged and a heart unperturbed. For a yogi who has not yet attained the stage [of realization], doubt arises first.
And since it is certain that suffering may arise for one who desires to ascend during the stage of practice, it has been stated that he must apply himself with a mind free from despondency. (21–24)

Having thus described the attainment of *samādhi*, characterized by the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*), through the process of abandoning external objects, he speaks again— relying precisely on the sequence of the previously mentioned *karmayoga*— in order to demonstrate its attainment:
Having abandoned all desires arising from volitional thought without exception, and having restrained the entire collection of senses on all sides by means of the mind alone; || 25 ||
One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness;
having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone.
For supreme happiness comes to this yogin whose mind is tranquil, whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from taint. 28.
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi of restrained mind easily attains the ultimate union with Brahman. (29)
This is explained in sequence:

by gradually ascending through ever-higher distinctions, one should not cease all at once from attachment to external objects, nor should one turn away from the conceit of selfhood regarding the body and so forth. By what means?

By means of the *sādhana*—that is, by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) or right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Of what kind? "Seized by fortitude" (*dhṛtigṛhītayā*): fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the steadfastness characterized by the support of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) within the Supreme Self; [the intellect] is seized, that is, accepted, by that.
By that kind of intellect— namely, that sattvic fortitude which sustains the intellect—
is what is worthy of being the means in this yoga, the characteristic of which fortitude he will state:
"That fortitude by which one sustains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses."
"O Pārtha, that fortitude which, through yoga, is unswerving—that is sattvic. (18.33).

Having previously done what, should one desist? One should do so with the mind alone—the supreme consciousness directed solely toward liberation—which was previously described by the term "stationary."

Having abandoned all desires— those arising from volitional construction, produced by the mind which is restless in grasping sense objects, whether they be all of them collectively or each individually, whether pertaining to what is seen or what is heard, and which consist of nothing but non-existent mental impressions; and having abandoned all enjoyments, he...

Having thus withdrawn by that very mind— and not by means of the objects of the senses— the entire collection of organs (the group of instruments), having restrained them from all sides even from those sounds and other objects that are permitted, and having specifically subdued them through the abandonment of defects such as passion; by this [it is meant].

He recalls the previously stated sequence of abandoning desire and restraining the senses, which pertains to the yoga of action (karmayoga) to be accomplished through the performance of the practice of "collecting" (samuccaya) that has been introduced. In this manner, by this sequence,
[the mind] becomes established in the Self— that is, properly situated in the primary Self, which is another name for Brahman.

Having attained rest—that is, having brought the mind, the internal organ, to a state of repose—one should not meditate upon any other object whatsoever apart from that. For at that time, everything indeed shines forth as being of the very nature of Brahman. By such a sequence of practice, from whatever [object], from whichever [source]...

From whatever internal or external source it may be that acts as a bond, the mind—the consciousness—emerges and goes forth; therefore, having restrained and prohibited it from each and every such source, one should bring it under control within the Self alone, the Supreme Cause, and bind it right there. For this is its nature.

Because it is flickering and restless, it does not remain long even when directed toward an object; therefore, when that [mind] has been brought under one's own control, this yogin— whose mind is tranquil, whose heart is satisfied by the cessation of the agitation of longing for sensory pleasures, and who is at peace— becomes supreme of his own accord.

Because its nature is eternally irreproachable, it attains—that is, reaches—the supreme bliss, which is innate joy (*sahajānanda*). What kind of yogi? One whose *rajas*—the quality that causes engagement with sense objects—is stilled, meaning dissolved; for this very reason, one who has become Brahman (*brahmabhūta*).

Because he has attained the Supreme Self, he is stainless— meaning he is free from the blemish of the stain characterized by ignorance. Thus, by this aforementioned sequence previously established in the treatise, his mind is firmly composed.

With his internal organ fully restrained, the yogi— constantly, in all states such as those described by the verse beginning "seeing, hearing" (5.8)— yokes and composes himself upon the Self, with ease,
due to the absence of the hardships associated with posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, concentration, and so forth.
He does not attain—that is, he does not reach—the ultimate, eternal, and absolute union with Brahman, the Supreme Self, which is non-difference. || 25–29 ||
Thus, in order to explain the supramundane conduct of the practitioner of action (*karmayogin*) who has attained the unsurpassed perfected samādhi, [the Lord] says:
"The Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self..."
One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives with equal vision everywhere.
He who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me—for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to me. || 31 ||
He who worships me as abiding in all beings, established in the state of oneness—
even while acting in every way— that yogi dwells in me.
He who, by comparison with himself, sees everywhere the same—whether it be pleasure or pain—he, O Arjuna, is considered the supreme yogi. 33.

In this aforementioned yoga of action (*karmayoga*), the yogi— whose self is disciplined, who is composed, and whose mind is attentive everywhere, at all times, and in every way— perceives the Self, whose nature has been described as consisting solely of non-dual pure consciousness,
within all beings, both moving and stationary, which exist in mutual distinction from one another.

He perceives that which resides within all living beings; the meaning is that he beholds all beings as being of the very same nature as his own single form, which is pure consciousness in its universal aspect. Thus, within his own self, whose nature has been described as such, he perceives all beings as having their mutual distinctions dissolved. This is the nature of the Self.
Furthermore, the vision of non-difference among all beings has already been established;
this [text] is primarily intended to demonstrate that vision of non-difference. And how this is possible, in that manner...

This has indeed been established previously; nevertheless, it is stated again for the sake of recollection. This so-called Self is characterized solely by the light of pure consciousness, which is devoid of all conceptual constructions such as pleasure and pain, the grasped and the grasper, delusion, emptiness, and so forth. Its nature as the cognizer is invariable.

This is the quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, whatever it perceives, that very thing, while being perceived, acquires its own nature through each respective form. And this state of being perceived is preceded by a non-conceptual state (*nirvikalpa-avasthā*).
Consequently, whenever, wherever, and by whichever perceiver (*pramātṛ*) anything whatsoever is perceived, [it does so as such].

Thus, the essential nature of everything is non-dual, infinite pure consciousness; consequently, there is no real distinction whatsoever between the self who perceives and all beings who are perceived.
The conceptualization of "object" and "subject" is merely produced by the inconceivable *māyā* of the Supreme Lord.
All this appears as mutually distinct;
yet when that [distinction] dissolves— being perceived as such by those who know reality through the divine vision called *vidyā*, which has been opened by the grace of the Supreme Lord— then:
All this appears as a unity through its nature as the Self, like the waters of the ocean when the barriers have been broken.

And in this Great Yoga, which consists in the practice of the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*), only one whose power of wisdom has arisen is qualified. Thus, the practitioner of action (*karmayogin*) [is qualified] everywhere, whether in the stationary or the moving.
And he is said to have equal vision toward the multitude of beings, seeing the non-dual reality of the Self alone.

To demonstrate the non-difference—that "whatever is the Self, that indeed am I"—the Blessed One says: the yogi who, everywhere among the collection of entities, perceives Me as having the single form of the aforementioned reality of the Self, according to the reasoning already stated...

He sees everything in Me, and likewise, he who perceives reality sees Me as well; for him, I do not perish nor do I become invisible, and because He has become my very own nature, He too does not perish nor does He attain invisibility— thus it is for the yogin perfected in the yoga of action.

Furthermore, this word of the Blessed One is intended to establish the non-difference of [all things] from one's own self. Moreover, that yogi who, everywhere— in all things beginning with the body— regards pleasure, pain, or any other attribute of living beings as being identical with himself...

(p. 151) By means of reasoning, he sees—that is, he understands—that which is being experienced as having the nature of consciousness, as being identical with it, as having the single nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) alone. How?
"By way of analogy with oneself" (*ātmaupamyena*), meaning by taking oneself as the standard of comparison, just as in one's own experience. He...
Even while existing in every way, in every respect, and by whatever common mode [of being], he exists within me;
the meaning is that he is non-different from me, he is indeed myself. Such a yogi, in all states, remains untainted, relishing the fruit of unsurpassed samādhi.

The meaning is that he is "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*) because he has ascended to a state of total equanimity like that of the Lord (*īśvara*), being endowed with a supreme, unsurpassed excellence compared to the previously mentioned yogin; this state is attainable through steadfast devotion to the practice of the limbs of yoga, which is otherwise difficult to accomplish due to the persistence of hosts of obstacles that are hard to restrain. (30–33)
Then, Arjuna, considering the impossibility of this samādhi— the fruit of which is the realization of universal equality— because it has not yet been experienced,
said: "O Madhusūdana, this yoga which has been taught by You through [the principle of] equality..."
Because of its flickering nature, I do not perceive its supreme stability.
For the mind is restless, O Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. (35)
O Kṛṣṇa,

regarding this yoga characterized by the practice of action (karmayoga), which you have described as distinct from other forms of yoga— I do not perceive, nor can I conceive, its supreme and excellent final state, because of the mind's restlessness.
Because it is unstable. Since that means of accomplishment, the mind, is flickering and by nature restless, it is therefore "disturbing," having the habit of agitating;
for, due to its tendency toward wrong paths, it quickly destroys even a stage attained with great difficulty. Nor can it be turned back...
For it is possible [to restrain] his force, which is difficult to hold back like a mass of water shattered against the peak of a king of mountains as he rushes toward sense objects;
for it is firm because of his firm attachment to the flavors of sense objects practiced throughout thousands of births. Of that [force...].

I consider the restraint of such a mind— the prevention of it from the wrong path— to be exceedingly difficult and hard to accomplish; for this mind is like the wind, which, spreading freely through the directions, is impossible to restrain.
Then, anticipating this very admission, the Blessed One spoke this reply:
"Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain;
but by practice and dispassion, O son of Kuntī, it is brought under control. (36)

There is no doubt in this matter: this mind, which is restless and fickle by nature, can be restrained through suffering; however, it is captured and controlled by means of two methods—practice and dispassion. And here, practice refers to the yoga of action (karmayoga).
