By means of the previously mentioned sequence beginning with "seeing" and "hearing" (5.8), while all the functions of the sense organs proceed toward their prescribed objects and all the functions of the vital breaths likewise proceed— since they are inseparable from the body— the practitioner who follows the instruction [should remain established].
The effort directed toward attaining the state of abiding, which consists of gradually establishing oneself within one's own self as previously described,
and detachment— which is non-attachment resulting from not forgetting the incomparable taste of innate bliss experienced when touching upon unforbidden objects— by means of these two, thus...

By means of these two methods— practice and dispassion, which pertain exclusively to the person authorized for the yoga of action— it is indeed possible to restrain this extremely fickle mind. || 36 ||
Therefore:
"Yoga is difficult to attain by one whose self is uncontrolled;
but it can be attained through the proper means by one who strives with a self-subdued mind. (37)

Since it lacks the means characterized by the practice of what has been explained, this yoga is difficult to attain— that is, hard to reach— for a person of uncontrolled self, whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is not restrained;
however, for a person with a self-controlled self, whose internal organ is submissive, it is [attainable] through striving— that is, through making effort.

By one who exerts effort through constant and uninterrupted enthusiasm, it is indeed possible to appropriate [the goal] by means of the method—that is, by the method characterized as the aforementioned knowledge. || 37 ||
Now, since the means, which consists of knowledge, is understood through mere hearing,
and because both practice and dispassion are extremely difficult to accomplish, and because the transmigratory attributes of the self do not cease;

Considering yoga to be difficult to attain and doubting whether faith alone could be a means toward yoga or not, Arjuna said: "One who is endowed with faith but lacks self-restraint, whose mind has strayed from yoga— "
Desiring the path of the virtuous, he was utterly bewildered on the way to Brahman.
With a distracted mind, wandering and fallen under the very sway of delusion, having failed to attain perfection in yoga, what goal does he reach, O Kṛṣṇa? (39)

Faith (*śraddhā*) is said to be the conviction regarding the attainment of the fruit through the means taught by a reliable authority (*āpta*), due to the absence of doubt; one endowed with that is "possessed of faith" (*śraddhāvan*). For this very reason, he follows the path—the way—of the virtuous (*satām*), that is, of excellent persons (*satpuruṣa*) who seek the supreme fruit.

Even one who is preparing [for it], if through yoga— meaning samādhi characterized as previously described— their mind has wavered and their mental fluctuations have lapsed, and for that very reason they are "unrestrained" (ayataḥ), being devoid of effort; and consequently, they are utterly bewildered on the path to the supreme Brahman, the reality to be attained, which consists of the means for reaching it.

The deluded one is devoid of right knowledge; and because of this lack of certainty regarding the means, he possesses a distracted mind due to being agitated by conceptual constructions and being restless at every moment. Consequently, his mental activity is manifold and he is utterly bewildered, finding no stability anywhere, as he has fallen under the sway of delusion itself—that is, ignorance.

He would become subject [to rebirth]. Not having attained the perfection of yoga— that is, the attainment of meditative absorption (samādhi)— due to that very collection of defects, what destination does such a person go to after death, he who has faith as his sole support and is devoid of the remaining means?
The meaning is: into what kind of other womb does one go? || 38-39 ||
He asks about that very point:
"Does he not perish like a scattered cloud through the loss of both, O mighty-armed one? Being without support, does he rather meet with destruction? (40)
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely;
for no one other than you is capable of being the dispeller of this doubt.

The word *kaccit* is used in an inquiry regarding what is desired. Indeed, if a person who possesses such faith were to lose both goals— namely, heaven and liberation (*apavarga*)— and yet have hope for one of the two goals, he would perish like a cloud scattered by the wind, its form dissolved like a severed fragment of a cloud.

Does he then undergo reintegration in that same way? Or, due to the absence of certainty regarding the means for either of the two destinies, being without support and without refuge, does he meet with absolute destruction and fall into the abyss of *saṃsāra* so as never to rise again? Such is this very doubt.

You ought to destroy my [doubt], because other than you— who know the destinies of all transmigrating beings and are omniscient— no one else can be conceived as a remover of this aforementioned doubt. For it has been said by the Blessed One:
In this verse beginning with "Many births of mine have passed" (4.5), [the Lord] teaches that all living beings possess the knowledge of their various future destinies. || 40 || 41 ||
Then, in order to sever such doubts, the Blessed One said:
"O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him;
for no one who performs auspicious deeds, my dear, ever goes to a miserable state. (42)
For such a person—
one whose mind has been refined by the quality of faith, which serves as the seed for the accomplishments characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation—
destruction regarding any object whatsoever is the cause of all miserable states of existence.
There is no disappearance characterized by the loss of knowledge. Where is it not found? Neither "here" nor "there.

"Here" means in this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is the locus of perceived and scripturally revealed enjoyments; "there" means elsewhere than this, namely in liberation (*apavarga*), which is the cause for being established in one's own Self. For:

One who performs wholesome deeds and is intent upon what is virtuous does not fall into an evil destiny or reach a corrupt state of birth, because they are not defiled by ignorance. Furthermore, for one possessed of faith, the performance of wholesome deeds is necessarily established; for faith, indeed, is...

The seed-germ of the wish-fulfilling tree of the Supreme Lord’s grace does not cease until it has brought about the abundant perfection of the fruits characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation; it merely requires a specific period of time according to the gradations of [the devotee's] mild, middling, or superior capacity.
It accomplishes its own function. || 42 ||
Since this is so, therefore:

"Having attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for countless years, he who has fallen from yoga is born again in the house of the pure and the prosperous. (43)
Or else, it arises only in the families of illustrious yogins;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in the world. (44)
There he regains that same mental disposition belonging to his previous body;
from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more for perfection.
For by that very same prior practice, one is carried forward even against one's will;
even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Brahman of sound.
But the yogi who strives with diligence, having his impurities completely purified and perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal. (47)

One fallen from yoga— fallen from the meditative absorption characterized by the performance of one's own duties as prescribed in the scriptures through steadfastness in the knowledge previously described— and having thus failed to attain the fruit characterized by absorption into the Supreme Lord, being cast down; |||
Even though the seed of faith exists, because at present there is an absence of intense spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) due solely to the power of the Lord’s will,
it possesses a fruit that depends upon other factors— namely, the totality of auxiliary conditions such as effort—
and thus pertains to those who perform meritorious deeds, such as the most excellent sacrifices, gifts, and ascetic practices.

Having reached and attained the worlds of their relatives— those realms that serve as the basis for the experience of fruits appropriate to their karma— and having dwelt there for eternal years, numbering in the thousands, experiencing their residence in accordance with that karma.

Then, at the conclusion of experiencing the fruits of such karma, he is born— that is, he attains birth— in a family and lineage of those who are pure, illustrious, of noble descent and conduct, and possessed of fortune, on this land of action (karmabhūmi); because his mind is tainted by even a trace of longing for yoga.

This destination has been specified for one who has met with failure due to the improper performance of *karmayoga*. However, even though one’s inclination is toward liberation, if for some reason the *karmayoga* was not properly accomplished, such a person attains this destination.
Having set aside the other alternative, he says on page 156: "Or rather, 'fallen from yoga' refers to those among the yogins—
who are established in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on the aforementioned actions and are for that very reason wise."
Because he is endowed with preeminent knowledge, he is born— that is, he arises— in a lineage, a family, of those possessed of praiseworthy intelligence;
such a birth in the family of yogins of this kind is even more difficult to obtain than falling away from karma-yoga, and cannot be attained by anyone except through that.

And in that birth, he regains that same connection with intelligence—that link with the intellect refined by knowledge. What is it? It is that which pertained to his previous body, wherein there was the performance of the combined practice of knowledge and action.

Having resorted to yoga, he did not carry it through to completion. In that regard, it is said that he indeed possessed a connection with a mind refined by the knowledge that serves as the cause for resorting to such yoga;
and that [connection] does not occur without the grace of the Supreme Lord. And that—
The grace of the Supreme Lord does not cease without having bestowed its fruit; therefore, after being delayed for some time due to some slight obstacle, it certainly manifests once again, and then,
through the greatness of that application of intelligence, he begins to strive yet again.

For the sake of perfect accomplishment and for the purpose of attaining the fruit of yoga, one is drawn toward it— made one's own— even against one's will and without desire, by that very practice related to a previous birth, which, though slight, persists in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the subject of yoga.

Why is he surpassed by that practice? He says: because even one who merely desires to know—that is, wishes to understand the essential nature of yoga characterized by the concentration on action—transcends, or goes beyond, the *śabdabrahman*, which is the reality consisting of the scriptures.

In the absence of certainty, activity directed toward yoga is not even possible; yet, for one who is in doubt, the scripture is beneficial. Therefore, it was said that "the seeker of yoga transcends the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*). Furthermore, that yogi, striving through effort and exertion, is *yatamāna*.
Practicing yoga and, by virtue of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from that practice, having his sins completely purified—

meaning the stain of ignorance consisting of sin has been washed away— he, through many births, ascends to the supreme pinnacle of such knowledge; immediately thereafter, he becomes fully perfected (*saṃsiddha*).
Having attained what was to be attained— the supreme goal characterized by absorption into the Supreme Self—
he reaches the highest stage, beyond which no further state to be reached exists.
(42) To praise such a practitioner of *karmayoga*, he says:
The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge;
and the yogi is superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi. (48)

Because even the most intense austerity alone yields finite results, the yogi— who possesses a samādhi consisting of eternal, unsurpassed bliss— is superior and more excellent than those who practice austerity; likewise, he is superior to those who possess knowledge,
who rely solely on mere knowledge, as well as to those who perform ritual actions.
Since [this] is superior to those who perform mere rituals such as sacrifices, therefore, having accepted the yoga as it has been taught, become a yogi preeminent among all. || 48 ||

Since there exist various types of yogis due to differences in their philosophical views, the Lord concludes this chapter by demonstrating that among them all, this kind of yogi is the most excellent:
"Of all yogis as well, he who with his inner self absorbed in Me..."
He who, endowed with faith, worships Me, is considered by Me to be the most disciplined of all. || 49 ||

Among all yogis, that yogi is considered by Me to be the most disciplined— that is, pre-eminently disciplined and composed— who, being endowed with faith consisting of all perfections, has his inner self absorbed in Me, as follows:
By means of the internal organ (the mind), having approached me— the Supreme Self, the Lord, the one Reality— as the supreme goal through the path of the knowledge already taught,
and by worshipping with speech, mind, and body while performing only activities directed toward me, one becomes my devotee.
He who worships Me alone, preceded by the realization of My true nature according to the method of knowledge as described, he indeed is the most perfectly concentrated. || 49 ||
If other forms of yoga can at most attain the status of being limbs to that [true] yoga—
which is accessible through dispassion born from the practice of the easy integration of knowledge and action—
then those who truly desire to attain it must worship the Supreme Guru with faith.
This sixth chapter [should be studied] by the noble ones with attentive minds, having abandoned all other activities.

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meanings of the statements, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 6 ||
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Thus, regarding that unsurpassed [yoga] consisting of the combination of knowledge and action, for which the status of being yoga is established through other yogas that have attained the state of being its auxiliary limbs—

The Blessed One spoke in order to clearly set forth another object of knowledge— primarily indicated previously such as His own nature as the cause of the universe— for you, even though you are a practitioner of Karma-yoga and My devotee, there still remains something further to be known. He said:
With your mind attached to Me, O Pārtha, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me, listen to how you shall know Me fully and without doubt. 1.

That which was stated at the conclusion of the sixth chapter—that he who worships me with his inner self absorbed in me is the most disciplined yogi—is here reiterated by these two lines: "with the mind attached to Me" and "having taken refuge in Me. Furthermore, having known My true nature, [he worships] Me...
Listen now to that by which, and in what manner, you— having rendered yourself free from doubt— will know Me in My entirety, that is, in My complete nature.
For some [hold] that this phenomenal world is a transformation of the eternally established *pradhāna*.
Some maintain that [the world] arises from the heating of atoms;

others that it is produced by the delusion of a momentary stream of consciousness; and still others that it is otherwise. Since there is thus room for doubt as to what the truth in this matter might be, this [treatise] is composed for the sake of its ascertainment.
"Pay close attention to what is about to be said; for by that very attentiveness, the complete knowledge of my true nature will arise. || 1 ||
He says that very thing:
"I shall declare to you this knowledge together with realized wisdom (vijñāna) in its entirety;
having known which, nothing further remains to be known. (2)

This knowledge, which has just been introduced, concerns the realization of the ultimate truth regarding the phenomenal world and the complete realization of my own true nature; it is presented in the form of logical arguments.

I shall explain this treatise in its entirety, accompanied by a distinguished knowledge that is the cause for the direct realization of both; having understood which, there remains no other further reality to be known.
The meaning is: something remains, through the comprehension of which you will have known everything that is to be known and thus become one who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 2 ||
And as for these two—knowledge (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*)—their fruit culminates in direct experience alone;
and because that is the supreme secret, it is not easily accessible to everyone, for: "Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection."
Even among those who strive and have attained perfection, only some know me in truth.

In this boundless expanse of the creation of living beings, human birth alone is indeed difficult to obtain. For those humans, having attained birth in the land of action (*karmabhūmi*), are the ones authorized for the accomplishment of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*). Of them—
Among thousands of human beings, only a rare few—
having developed disenchantment with cyclic existence through the ripening of such karma—
strive for success, which is characterized by the attainment of non-rebirth, and are intent on the effort of adopting various means to that end.

It occurs; however, one does not yet attain perfection. Even among those striving ones who have attained perfection—having reached the state of perfection characterized by liberation as determined through their respective philosophical views—only some indeed [attain it].

By the power of the discriminative knowledge born of discernment— which has been purified by faith and devotion toward the unsurpassed [truth] as previously described, manifested through my grace, and attained by virtue of the maturation of preeminent merit—
he knows Me according to My explained nature and realizes Me as his own Self. || 3 ||
Having first set forth the true nature of that world, He speaks to instruct [the disciples]:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—this is My material nature (prakṛti) divided eightfold. (4)
But know that there is another, higher nature of Mine,
O mighty-armed one, which is the life-force by which this entire world is sustained.

I, who— though never deviating from my own nature as pure, eternal consciousness— manifest as if having two forms through the division of the insentient and the sentient due to the majesty of the power of my own inconceivable *māyā*, and thus carry out this play of the world; of me, that very one...

That insentient *prakṛti*, which consists of the three qualities (*guṇa*)— *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— and which pervades all existents by virtue of being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is this [eightfold nature] divided into eight ways, having attained distinction. What are those eight?

The modes are "earth" and so forth. In this context, it should be understood that by means of the five modes beginning with earth—which are specified according to the sequence of dissolution—the subtle causal elements are indicated; and by means of those, the five gross divisions beginning with earth, which are the effects, are indicated.
The fivefold groups, beginning with the five objects of the senses, are each comprised of five; the group of the organs of cognition and action is ten in number.
Thus, by means of the five elements beginning with earth, the twenty principles are implied.
Furthermore, the mind is the leader of all the senses, the intellect (buddhi) is of the nature of determination, and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) [functions] with respect to the body and so forth.

The notion of a self with respect to that which is not-self constitutes the internal organ; thus, there are three types of internal organs, making twenty-three in the category of effects and causes. Corresponding to these, the Pradhāna, whose nature consists of the three guṇas, is the cause; thus, the reality is composed of twenty-four principles.
Prakṛti appears as insentient;
and she is gross in comparison to the living prakṛti that will be described later as the supreme (parā), because this [former] is insentient,
an object of cognition, dependent, and non-divine, whereas the latter is sentient, the cognizer, independent, and eternal.

She is distinct from the principle of the individual soul (jīva-tattva); therefore, he says: "Know that other than this aforementioned Prakṛti, there is another, distinct, supreme, and preeminent one who has become the individual soul (jīvabhūta), having attained the state of being a kṣetrajña appearing as mutually differentiated through the power of Māyā. Know this; understand this.

Of what nature is it? It is that which, acting as the agent, sustains this world consisting of the multitude of principles as previously described; for the stability of the objects of the world is bound to the supreme *prakṛti*, characterized by the living soul (*jīva*).
Thus, there are two *prakṛtis*: the insentient and the sentient, manifested through the distinction between the supreme and the subordinate by means of *māyā*. (4–5)
Understand that all beings have this as their source;
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world.

Thus, understand with certainty— that is, realize through your intellect— that all beings have as their source (yoni), or cause of origin, my two natures (prakṛti) whose essential character has been explained in this way. For nature, being the individual soul (jīva), does not deviate from its nature as consciousness.
In reality (p. 161),
although she is non-different from me— the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self who is the ultimate cause—
she has, through the power of my *māyā*, as it were, attained a state of difference due to her association with insentient *prakṛti* since beginningless time.

Being bound, she— identifying that very *prakṛti*, which consists of the *guṇas* and has evolved into the form of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, as her own self— requires objects consisting of various conscious and unconscious states in the form of the means for pleasure and the like; thus, this bondage is beginningless.

The relationship between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is the cause of the world; thus it has been stated that these two *prakṛtis* are the source (*yoni*) of all beings. And so he will say: "Whatever exists that comes into being, whether stationary or moving..."
"Know that, O bull among the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field" (3.29).
Thus, he says "I" to show that my own *māyā* is the cause for the manifestation of these two *prakṛtis*, which are related to me and constitute the cause of the world. Of the entire...

I am the origin and the dissolution of the entire universe, consisting of the infinite variety of moving and non-moving beings; the meaning is that this world proceeds from me alone and dissolves back into me alone.
These two natures, the insentient and the sentient, are manifested solely through my *māyā*, which is brought forth by my mere volition (*saṅkalpa*).
These two are manifested, and creation and dissolution are based upon them; thus, the meaning is that I alone am the fundamental cause of this world's origin and its destruction. || 6 ||

For this very reason—because I alone am the supreme cause—I have no dependence on any other cause for the attainment of my own nature; thus he says: "O Dhanañjaya, there is nothing whatsoever higher than Me."
All this is strung upon me like clusters of gems on a thread.
Nature (prakṛti), being insentient, is called the lower; in relation to that, the individual soul (jīva) is the higher.
But I am the cause of these two and am therefore the highest. There exists no other entity whatsoever apart from me that could be more supreme by virtue of having me as its cause; I alone am so.

The meaning is that the cause is unsurpassed. For all this multitude of beings is woven upon me, who am the universal substratum; how so? Just as, for example, clusters of jewels, though distinct from one another, maintain their positions when strung upon a single thread, so too [is this world].
The meaning is that all beings, moving and unmoving, whose mutual distinctions are manifested by my *māyā*, abide within me alone as their single substratum. || 7 ||
Now, one might object: "Both of these, the insentient and the sentient, are my two *prakṛtis* (natures), and *prakṛti* is said to be *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature).

Therefore, how can it be logically possible for that which is essentially non-dual pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) to possess an intrinsic nature of manifold forms through mutual delimitation—given that the insentient aspect is perishable and the sentient aspect is eternal? This is the [objection].
In order to establish the non-duality of the knower (pramātṛ-advaita), he says:
"I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun;
I am the sacred syllable *praṇava* in all the Vedas; I am the sound in space; and I am the virility in men. (8)
I am the pure fragrance on the earth, and I am the radiance in the fire;
I am the life in all beings, and I am the austerity in ascetics.
Know Me, O Pārtha, as the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid.
And among the powerful, I am the strength that is free from the passion of desire;
I am the desire for beings that is not opposed to righteousness, O bull of the Bharatas. 11.

All entities, while being experienced, attain their respective natures; for there is no perception of anything whatsoever in any state through a mode other than being experienced. Thus, the one truly real cognizer is none other than consciousness itself as it cognizes.

It creates entities (*bhāva*). Therefore, it is the power of the perceiver alone that unfolds in the form of entities; there is nothing else whatsoever apart from that. Thus, having internalized the non-duality of the subject—which is self-established by the fact that "my two natures, the supreme and the inferior, are essentially one"—that which was stated at the very beginning [is confirmed].

He establishes this through four verses beginning with "I am the essence" (*raso 'ham*). In that context, whatever quality exists as the predominant factor for something is its very self (*ātman*); thus, the essence (*rasa*) of the waters is their self, and that is I, because—according to the reasoning already stated—I exist as that which is tasted.

The waters, being perceived, attain their own nature as taste; therefore, the power consisting of taste belongs to the taster alone. And because my own essential nature, characterized by the state of being an experiencer, is never absent, I am the taster; thus, I am in the waters.

It has been stated that [the essence is] *rasa*. Just as *rasa* is established as the essential nature (*ātmatva*) in water, so too is *gandha* (smell) established as the essential nature in earth; and in the various elemental forms characterized by fire—namely the moon, the sun, and fire—the quality of form (*rūpa*), denoted by the word "light" (*tejas*), is established as their essential nature. Likewise, in the sky (*kha*), which is space (*nabhas*).
Sound is its quality; likewise, touch is also to be enumerated here as the quality of air.
Thus, by the previously stated principle, I am established within the five elements as the nature of their predominant qualities, such as smell and the rest, according to the aforementioned division.

It has been established that my nature consists in the differentiation of the insentient primordial matter (*prakṛti*), which takes the form of the twenty principles (*tattva*) comprised within the five elements (*bhūta*). Furthermore, in this context, the word "meritorious" (*puṇya*) should be understood as qualifying all qualities by virtue of their predominance. Thus it is with respect to the elements and living beings.

Desire that is not contrary to Dharma is I; volition and the mind are I. Likewise, among men and living beings, the state of being a person—consisting of egoism—is I alone. Similarly, among the intelligent, intelligence is I alone. Thus, the internal organ characterized by mind, egoism, and intellect is I.

The three primary attributes (guṇas) of persons, along with the aforementioned principle "I alone" (ahaṃkāra), constitute a group of twenty-three categories consisting of causes and effects; by means of these three, they become the cause of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra)—but this is not the case for the yogin who perceives the equality of all things. This is the meaning.

Likewise, my devotion— characterized by knowledge, which is the supreme culmination, the unsurpassed fourth stage, and my own essential nature— is followed by the twenty-fourfold expansion of insentient *prakṛti*, which is my very own nature. Thus [it is said].

This has been established by means of separated words: likewise, among all beings, life—the vital breath—is primary, and that too is indeed I. Similarly, among all the Vedas, the Praṇava, the syllable Om, which consists of its own uttered, unmodified sound, is indeed I; for it is He.
Because it is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it is the primary among all the Vedas;

for all the Vedas are indeed its modifications (*vikāra*). Likewise, among all ritual actions (*kriyā*), the action consisting of austerity (*tapas*) is the primary; therefore, the austerity existing in those who practice austerity is none other than myself.

The strength that is free from sensual desire is the foremost among the strengths of the powerful, and that too is none other than I. Likewise, among those who possess splendor—that is, those endowed with an excellence of power—splendor or power is the primary quality, and that too is none other than I. In this manner, [I am] the essence of all beings.

"I alone am the seed and the cause"— in this manner, it has been established through words that convey a remote connection (*viprakṛṣṭasamanvaya*) that *prakṛti*, which is of two kinds according to the distinction between the insentient and the sentient, is my very own nature (*svabhāva*). Likewise, "I am *rasa*" and so forth are stated with the intention of emphasizing predominance (*prādhānyavivakṣayā*).
This has been presented merely as an illustration. || 8-11 ||
But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), according to the reasoning previously stated, not even the slightest collection of objective entities exists;
in order to demonstrate that there is nothing which is not "I," he says:
"And whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*), passion (*rājasa*), or darkness (*tāmasa*)..."
Know that they are from Me alone here; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.

In the infinite proliferation of entities, since every entity consists of the transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), all things are established within the three *guṇas*. Among them, some have *sattva* predominant with *rajas* and *tamas* subordinate; others likewise have *rajas* predominant; and some [have *tamas* predominant].

Those characterized by *tamas* as predominant are subsumed under the number three— without regard for their infinite variety due to differences in degree— so that whatever states of being (*bhāva*) there may be, whether *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*,
they all arise from Me alone, the Supreme Cause, according to the principle previously stated.

Know that they have arisen from the nature of light; however, while those entities exist— having acquired their own being as objects of knowledge produced by me— I do not exist [as a separate entity], for my existence does not depend upon their existence.

[The Self] exists as one whose sole characteristic is that of being an eternally perceiving subject established by its own nature. However, those [objects] of such a form exist when I exist; the meaning is that all entities whatsoever have their existence dependent upon my existence, according to the reasoning already stated. || 12 ||

(p. 165) But if this self is indeed the Supreme Lord alone, who is the sole agent of all things by virtue of being the material cause consisting solely of His own power, then from where does this delusion of living beings arise,
such that they perceive only some limited object within their own sphere as having its nature derived from another cause?
And they act. Here, having internalized the majesty of His own power of *māyā* which is about to be described, He gives the subsequent answer:
"By these three states consisting of the qualities (*guṇas*), this entire world..."
Deluded, he does not recognize me, who am beyond these and imperishable.

The entire world, the whole realm of living beings, is pervaded by these aforementioned states consisting of the *guṇas*— such as the *sāttvika* and others— which result in experiences culminating in pleasure, pain, and delusion, and which are objects of perception.

Deluded by these categories of objects— which, by obstructing the reflective awareness of things as they truly are, produce the darkness of ignorance characterized by the false notion of a self distinct from one another in the body and so forth—
one [realizes] that which is superior to all these phenomena, because they are of the nature of being solely objects of cognition and are therefore impermanent.

He does not recognize— that is, he does not realize— Me, the Supreme Reality, whose nature is distinct [from all else], and for that very reason immutable, meaning devoid of any decay characterized by the loss of the essential nature as it has been described. || 13 ||

But surely, according to the manner established throughout this treatise, you alone, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, manifest as the one reality; so what are these so-called "qualities" (guṇas) by which the world is deluded with material states and does not know me, as was stated? To this, he says:
This divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the three gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross beyond this illusion. 14.

As for what you ask, "What are these so-called *guṇas*?"—this is indeed my divine *māyā*, composed of the *guṇas*. Because it causes the Divine One, who is myself, to play (*devana*) or sport, it is related to me; though non-existent, it appears as if real. It is my power, which is indeed my supreme, ultimate reality.

Power (*śakti*) is indeed one; when it perceives my aforementioned essential nature as "I," it is called *vidyā* (knowledge). However, when it perceives it as "this" (*idam*), it is conventionally designated as my *māyā* (illusion).
Indeed, the perception of "this" acquires its own form by bringing forth an object of knowledge that is distinct [from the self].
Furthermore, that object of cognition (vedya) is, in brief, of only two types based on the distinction between the insentient and the sentient;

yet, although it is infinite through the conceptualization of intermediate subdivisions, it ultimately results in being an object of cognition by way of the threefold nature of its cognitions, namely the distinctions of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Everything is subsumed within the nature of the three qualities (guṇas), beginning with sattva; therefore, it is said that my Māyā consists of the universal manifestation and is composed of the qualities. Consequently, even for me, whose sole purpose is sport, my own will alone—expanding through the state of being composed of the qualities—cannot be overstepped by any other superior power.

It has been said that [this] is difficult to transcend. Now, if this is so, and it cannot be made otherwise by anyone, then since the delusion of saṃsāra would necessarily never cease, this instruction on the means for attaining the path to liberation (apavarga) would be entirely useless. To this, he says: "Only unto Me alone."

Those who, having been awakened by the desire for My grace, take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, whose nature is as described— that is, they resort to Him through the aforementioned knowledge which culminates in non-difference from Me— they transcend this [world]; indeed, it is I alone [who am that world].

The one whose nature is eternal, blossoming light— like the sun, he can never be touched by this darkness; therefore, because I have attained my true nature, having dissolved the ego-notion (*ahaṃpratyaya*) regarding the body and so forth, I myself have become that [light] and [thus overcome] this [darkness].

One is able to transcend the illusion that consists of the dense darkness of the appearance of distinctions between phenomena which are ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature; however, others—whose own defects are blinded by the sleep of delusion—are not capable of even perceiving its true nature. || 14 ||
Now, as to why not everyone seeks refuge in you, he says:
(p. 167) "The foolish evildoers, the lowest of men, do not seek refuge in me;
their wisdom has been carried away by illusion, and they have taken recourse to a demonic nature. (15)

By my will alone, they have resorted to—that is, fallen into—an Asuric state of being, which is abundant in *rajas* and *tamas*; for this very reason, their knowledge has been stolen away by *māyā*—that is, by ignorance (*avidyā*) as previously described—and their realization of the supreme truth has been eclipsed; and consequently, they are doers of evil.

Possessing knowledge that results in falling into the abyss of saṃsāra and characterized by wicked actions, they are therefore deluded, senseless, the lowest of men, and the most base among persons; they do not take refuge in, nor do they resort to, Me, the Supreme Self. || 15 ||

But those who, by the very power of my will, partake of the divine creation, whose awakening of the power of knowledge is manifested through my desire to bestow grace, and who are engaged in meritorious actions that have the attainment of liberation as their fruit— they are the awakened ones.
O bull among the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people always worship Me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom. 16.

Even though there is equality in the reality of the benefactor, people—divided into four types according to the present classification—worship me and become my devotees due to the gradations of intensity in their desire for grace and so forth; for this very reason, they are the performers of meritorious deeds. He now describes their fourfold nature:

By the words "the distressed" and so forth: therein, the distressed person worships me— he whose mind is tormented by the experience of the threefold suffering, which has long been manifest as a result of the morbid fever of worldly delusion being shattered by the most gentle medicinal herb of my grace.
Desiring the cessation of that [bondage], my devotee resorts to gross means such as the various well-known worldly names and forms;
then, by virtue of the gradually increasing slight degree of immersion (samāveśa), he becomes my devotee. From that, through the power of the progressively increasing slight degree of immersion...

The seeker (jijñāsuḥ), who is engaged in deliberating upon what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted regarding the nature of the world as it arises—thinking, "Who am I? What is this great web of delusion consisting of the body, senses, objects, and so forth? How [did it come to be] from this?"—(p. 168) [is the one who seeks knowledge].
Desiring to know the truth— that "I might be completely liberated from bondage"— and with a mind intent upon the study and hearing of various scriptures,
one who is beset by doubt becomes devoted to my worship. For this very reason:
Due to the intensity of his resolve to investigate reality, the light of the latent impression of discrimination arises; as the dense darkness of erroneous cognitions dissolves by that light,
there occurs for the first time the discernment of objects to be abandoned and to be adopted as they truly are, and thus the seeker of the goal resorts to [the teacher].

He who, having attained certainty through the power of repeated study of the scriptures, seeks— that is, longs for— the reality characterized as the nature of the Self as the supreme fruit because of its worthiness to be attained;
thereafter, that wise one worships Me, his mind confident that all medical treatment has been brought to an end.
Having adopted the supreme means characterized by the aforementioned knowledge, he worships Me alone, whose nature has been described, without any mediation. || 16 ||
In order to demonstrate the superiority of the man of knowledge among these four, He says:
"Among them, the man of knowledge, who is ever-disciplined and devoted to the One alone, is distinguished;
for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me. (17)

Among those such as the afflicted (ārta) and others, the man of knowledge (jñānī)—who possesses the aforementioned awakening—is distinguished because he has desisted from everything, both gross and subtle, and has attained the realization of what is to be accepted;
for this very reason, he has ascended to the supreme pinnacle of means and possesses the singular nature of being solely the knower (vedaka). In that [state],...

Because he possesses devotion toward Me, the Supreme Reality, and for that very reason is ever-disciplined— meaning his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) remains uninterrupted in all circumstances— I am exceedingly dear to such a knower, being the cause of his love by setting aside the entire multitude of objects in the world; and he likewise is dear to Me in the same way.
"This is dear to me" is intended to establish non-difference. || 17 ||
(p. 169) But if it is only the man of knowledge (*jñānin*) who is preeminent, why have the distressed (*ārta*) and the others been excluded?
To this he says:
"All these are indeed noble, but the man of knowledge is, in my view, My very Self."
For he, with his self disciplined, is established in me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
Although these types, beginning with the *ārta*, are distinct from one another in that each subsequent one is superior to the preceding, nevertheless,
being presided over by my single supreme power which has arisen in the form of devotion (*bhakti*),
they are all equally noble, possessing elevated minds through the single quality characterized by magnanimity (*audārya*).

This is logical; however, those who exist in states characterized by affliction, the desire to know, purpose, or seeking, take hold of objects distinct [from the Self]. But I, being possessed of knowledge, take hold of my own nature alone through non-difference, thinking "I am. Therefore, it is the Self alone that is intended by me. This very point—

Since that wise one reveals [this], he belongs to Me alone, not to any other separate entity; for he has taken his stand upon, that is, resorted to, the path characterized by the knowledge of non-difference, which is the cause for attaining the unsurpassed, peerless goal, because his self is disciplined in Me alone.
This person has a concentrated internal organ. || 18 ||
Therefore:
"At the end of many births, the man of knowledge attains Me, realizing 'Vāsudeva is everything. Such a great-souled person is very rare. (19)

At the end— the exhaustion— of the majority of births and the assumption of bodies experienced in states such as affliction, all this collection of moving and unmoving beings [is absorbed] because the Blessed One, whose nature is the ultimate, eternally changeless universal consciousness, dwells everywhere.
Or, because He dwells within all, He is called Vāsudeva; through the certainty that He is non-different from all, one attains Me, the Supreme Cause.
And such a person, whose nature is the most exalted of all, is extremely difficult to find—most difficult to encounter and hard to reach—even among millions of human beings. Such a one as this...
Is great power obtained or not? || 19 ||
(170) To demonstrate that the sole cause for why such a person is so extremely difficult to find is simply one's own will (*svecchāmātra*), he says:
Those whose knowledge has been carried away by various desires resort to other deities,
adhering to their respective rules of discipline, constrained by their own innate natures.
Whatever form of deity a devotee desires to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his firm and unwavering. (21)
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that [deity];
and from that, he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone as beneficial.
But for those of small intelligence, their fruit is finite;
the worshippers of the gods go to the gods, while My devotees come to Me as well. (23)
In this world, according to the manner already explained,
persons— who are composed of my own nature as the manifold individual souls (jīva)—
[are bound] by their own *prakṛti*, which consists of the *guṇas* and manifests the relationship of cause and effect brought forth by my will.

Being restricted by their mutual distinctions— each having attained its own individuality through the nature of specific cause and effect according to the differences between various persons— and being constrained by their distinct forms consisting of body, senses, objects, and so forth, they [experience] that which consists of pleasure and the like, which is of the nature of *prakṛti*.

They have understood form itself as the self; for this very reason, their knowledge has been stolen away by various desires— objects of enjoyment to be experienced in various other worlds— which they long for as things to be attained as the fruits of action, being suited to their respective natures and having become their own property.
Being those whose awakening regarding the single reality characterized by the ultimate truth has been stolen away, they regard other deities—

those such as Hari, Hara, Hiranyagarbha, Āditya, and others, who are distinct from the supreme divinity characterized as the Self— as having various scriptural powers that bestow their respective desired fruits, [all] because of their mutually distinct natures.
Being understood, they attain and resort to [their respective goals]. How?

By adopting—that is, by relying upon and taking hold of—each specific rule (niyama) well-known in its respective system of philosophy, which consists of a particular form of ritual procedure (itikartavyatā). This being the case, whichever individual knower of the field (kṣetrajña) there may be...

In accordance with his desire for specific fruits, whatever particular form or body— distinguished by features such as having four arms or three eyes— the devotee resorts to with faith, directed toward a distinct deity that bestows only that much fruit;

To him who desires to worship— that is, to honor— in order to attain various specific fruits, I grant that very same unwavering devotion directed toward a distinct deity capable of bestowing only those particular fruits; I do not grant any other higher devotion directed toward the single Supreme Reality, though such devotion remains established as its object.

Since it has already been established that the arising of all states of being, such as the *sāttvika* and others, proceeds from Me alone, he—endowed with that faith bestowed by Me—strives toward the propitiation and worship of that particular deity in whatever form it may appear;
that is, he exerts himself through mind, speech, and body. And from that:

From a specific deity who has been propitiated, one obtains desired objects— enjoyments that are beneficial and favorable— which have been ordained and released by me alone as the ultimate agent, according to the reasoning previously stated; however, [one should seek] me alone, the Lord, the granter of all desires.
Precisely because they lack right knowledge and thus do not understand, those of limited wisdom obtain a limited result characterized by enjoyment that is finite and impermanent.
For, being deluded by ignorance, they perceive the Self, the deity, and the fruit as distinct entities.
They proceed accordingly. And thus, those who worship and gratify the gods—who they have perceived as manifold—by means of finite specific rites such as sacrifices, go to the gods;
that is, they go to those respective worlds of the gods which serve as the abodes for those particular deities. But those who [worship] me...

The single reality, whose nature has been described, is resorted to by devotees who, impelled solely by My will according to the sequence already explained, gradually ascend through the stages up to the state of a knower; they attain Me alone, the supreme cause, in non-difference as "I am."
They enter [into meditative absorption]. || 23 ||
"Those of small intellect think of Me, the unmanifest, as having come into manifestation,
not knowing My supreme nature, which is imperishable and unsurpassed.
(24) Thus, in this manner, the world— consisting of both the demoniac and the divine creation— has been brought about by Me alone through My own will.

To demonstrate in summary that one, being directed toward the two dharmas of engagement and withdrawal by means of the power of knowledge called *māyā*, attains the fruits characterized as saṃsāra and apavarga, he says:
Enveloped by my yoga-māyā, I am not manifest to everyone;
deluded, this world does not recognize me, the unborn and immutable.

Even amidst manifold diversity (*vaiśvarūpya*), the state of divine absorption (*aiśvarasamādhi*)— characterized by not deviating from abiding in the nature of non-dual pure consciousness— is expressed by the word "Yoga. Enveloped by that power of Māyā produced through the majesty of such Yoga, which is the cause for the erroneous perception of my true nature as something other than it;

Being concealed, I am not manifest as the Self to every person of demoniac nature who is deluded by my own Prakṛti, and thus cannot recognize Me. Consequently, this entire deluded world does not know Me— the unborn and immutable, who, by virtue of My eternity, am devoid of birth and destruction.
One does not reflect upon it as being the self. || 25 ||
For it is said:
"I know the beings that have passed away and those that are present, O Arjuna, as well as those that will be; but no one knows Me. (26)
Bodies, because they consist of the "I-notion" which culminates in the transformation of an impermanent nature,
have attained a state of being perceived that is limited in every respect;
therefore, I am all embodied beings— beings who are the subjects characterized by the past, present, and future states.

"I alone, whose nature is the knower of the ultimate reality, know [it]. But no embodied being knows me, whose majesty—due to my eternity—is devoid of limitations such as the measurement of time. By this, [the author] establishes that the Supreme Cause possesses a unique nature as the sole knower, which is not shared by anything else.
Furthermore, it has been established that the world, which is its effect, possesses a nature distinct from it, precisely because it is an object of cognition. || 26 ||
To the question "Why does no one know you?", he says:
"O Bhārata, O scorcher of foes, all beings fall into delusion at the time of birth due to the confusion caused by the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion. (27)
Since all these beings, by virtue of my *māyā*, are mutually distinct,
possess impermanent bodies as their essence, and undergo birth and destruction when creation occurs,
they fall into delusion— that is, they attain ignorance consisting in the failure to discern their own true nature. By what means?
By reason of the delusion caused by dualities. "Dualities" refers to things consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth;

"delusion" is the very failure to perceive reality, and it is by that [delusion]. Of what kind? Arising from desire and aversion—that is, produced by passion and hatred. The intended meaning here is as follows:

Deluded by the creation of the *prakṛti* composed of the qualities (*guṇa*) manifested through my *māyā*, all living beings— perceiving this world as consisting solely of the transformations of mutually distinct and impermanent qualities—
become attached to some things and feel aversion toward others, thereby experiencing the revolution of the wheel of *saṃsāra*. Therefore...
They do not worship Me, the Supreme Self, whose nature is as described—eternal, changeless, and of the singular essence of consciousness. || 27 ||
To the question "Who, then, worship you?", he says:
"Those people of meritorious deeds whose sin has come to an end—they, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites and firm in their vows, worship me. (28)

But for those people whose power of knowledge has arisen solely through my grace— and who are therefore meritorious doers of virtuous deeds— their sin, characterized by ignorance, has reached its end, having attained destruction; they [attain the goal] as previously described.

Freed from the delusion of dualities, firm in their vows and steady in their observances, the virtuous worship Me alone as the Supreme Deity; they take refuge in Me through a service that culminates in the realization of my non-difference [from all beings].
And thus:
"Those who, taking refuge in me, strive for liberation from old age and death..."
They know that Brahman in its entirety, as well as the entire inner self and all action.
They know me as being with the elemental beings and the divine, and likewise as being with the sacrifice;
even at the time of departure, they know me, their minds being disciplined.

Those who, having taken refuge in Me whose nature has been described, and having made Me their objective support through the fourfold devotion, strive constantly with undiminished effort for liberation from the defects of dualities such as old age and death— they are the ones of disciplined mind, whose minds are, as described, perpetually concentrated.

They know me—that is, they understand me—through the sevenfold vision of consciousness that will be explained in the immediately following chapter by way of distinctions such as the nature of Brahman; thus ends the section. 30.
In this world, there are certain virtuous ones who have reached their station in the seventh chapter of the Gītā, which is the nature of Truth; having fully reaped the fruits of their good deeds,
they remain free from doubt regarding the arrangement of all the regions throughout the expanse of the universe.
May they behold it clearly, like an amalaka fruit held in the palm of the hand.

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* named *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meaning of the commentary, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.

Now, regarding what was stated by the Blessed One— that those who possess the knowledge expounded in the seventh chapter and are proficient in the discernment of the characteristics of devotion know the various modes beginning with Brahmā— concerning those modes:
Arjuna, having developed a desire to know their true nature, said:
"What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action (karman), O Supreme Person? And what is declared to be the elemental (adhibhūta)? What is called the divine (adhidaiva)? (1)
Who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, O Madhusūdana?
And how are You to be known at the time of death by those of self-restraint?

These interrogative sentences have their meaning already understood; however, regarding the word "tat" (that), this is the intended sense: among those modes which have been mostly stated by the Blessed One, what is that Brahman? Which mode is the nature of Brahman? And what is adhyātma, and who is it?

"Regarding the inner nature" refers to the desire for a detailed classification. "How are You to be known at the time of departure? is a separate question concerning a matter not previously mentioned. (1-2)
In order to answer the question as it was stated, the Blessed One spoke this reply: "The supreme Brahman is the Imperishable; its own nature is called the Adhyātma (the Inner Self).
That which brings about the origin of the existence of beings is the Visarga (emission), known as Karma (action). (3)
The perishable state is the object of experience (adhibhūta), and the Puruṣa is the presiding deity (adhidaivata);
I alone am the sacrifice (adhiyajña) here in this body, O best among the embodied.
Even at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone, attains My state; there is no doubt about this.

Regarding the question, "What is called Brahman there?", the answer is as follows: the supreme imperishable (akṣara) is Brahman; it is called "imperishable" because it does not decay, does not fluctuate, and does not deviate from its own nature, being of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa).

And that [nature] occurs in two ways: as the form of Brahman and as the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). That which is the form of Brahman is the supreme; it never undergoes any deviation from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), because its essential nature is continuous.
It is characterized as pure consciousness alone, unconditioned by the modifications of existence such as birth and destruction;

its sole attribute is innate, eternal bliss. Although it is the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) because it illumines all phenomenal states of the universe, it is in no way connected with them as something delimited, like the objects of the universe themselves.

That which is distinct from them has indeed been explained. However, the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), while being immutable (*kūṭastha*) and imperishable (*akṣara*), does not abide as supreme like the Supreme Brahman,
because it is under the influence of *māyā*.
When there is an objective support for the notion of "I" consisting of perishable,

natural states, then— just like the natural states of the body and so forth— for one who conforms to their nature, there occurs the dissolution and emergence [of those states], or birth, death, and so on, upon the occurrence of a connection with the loss of one's true nature.
The state of being the supreme imperishable (aparamakṣaratva). As he will say:
"There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak (kūṭastha) is called the imperishable."
"Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). (15.18).
Thus, although the individual souls are eternal in comparison to Brahman, [the Lord remains supreme].
The answer to the first question—that the imperishable (*akṣara*) which has been explained through reasoning is the inferior one, whereas the supreme imperishable is Brahman—is as follows:
regarding the question "What is called the internal self (*adhyātma*)?", the answer is that "one's own nature (*svabhāva*) is the internal self. By the word "own nature,"...
"Earth, water, fire, [air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego]—by these, this world is sustained. (7.4) and so forth. (7.5)
By this passage, the lower (*aparā*) and higher (*parā*) *prakṛti* previously taught by the Blessed One (p.

177) is here described. Thus, the nature consisting of *prakṛti* is called "internal" (*adhyātma*) because its various selves—which are of the nature of the ultimate cause and manifest as the essence of reality—are dependent [upon it].

It has been said: for the Self, which is the Supreme Lord, manifests itself alone through its own will by means of the division into the insentient and the sentient; as it is said: "The divine Self, by its own power of illusion (māyā), fashions itself from itself."
"He alone creates the distinctions; such is the conclusion of the Vedānta" (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 2.12).

Thus, because its nature, characterized by the two kinds of *prakṛti*, is dependent upon the Self (*ātman*), it is called "internal" (*adhyātma*); this is the answer to the second question. Now, what [is the third]?

Regarding the term "karma" here, the answer is: "The *visarga* (emission) is designated as *karma*. *Visarga* refers to a specific creation distinct from the Supreme Brahman, and it is designated as *karma*. He provides a qualifying description of it that contains its own cause: "the cause of the arising of the existence of beings," meaning [of] beings...
The existence (*bhāva*), which is the being (*sattā*) of those things consisting of both insentient and sentient natures—
the former being eternal by way of a continuous flow, and the latter being eternally immutable despite their mutual differentiation— the arising of that existence...

He who effects a manifestation whose nature is such an appearance is so described. That creation consisting of one's own objective world, produced by the conjunction of the two natures— the insentient and the sentient— through the beginningless continuity of the Lord’s will, is called their "action" (karman), as was stated previously.
"Understand that all beings have this as their source" (7.6).

Thus, there is the manifold creation of insentient *prakṛti*, characterized by the expansion beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the earth; and likewise, that which is characterized by the fourteenfold expansion of living beings.

The manifold creation belongs to *prakṛti*, which has become the individual soul (*jīva*); because it arises from the union of those two, it is described as their "emission" (*visarga*) by virtue of being their activity—this is the answer to the third question. Now, regarding the question "What is called *adhibhūta*?", the answer is: "*Adhibhūta* is the perishable state (*kṣaro bhāvaḥ*). The perishable...

That entity which, by its nature of undergoing transformation, is intent on the movement of its own form, and which— constituted by a collection of diverse causes and effects for each individual person—
is the category of "adhibhūta," because it is dependent upon the elements (*bhūta*).

The answer to the fourth question—that "the mutable entity (kṣara-bhāva) as the material principle (adhibhūta) undergoes transformation through the nature of cause and effect, being the primordial matter (prakṛti) in its elemental form"—is as follows: Now, regarding the question "What is called the divine (adhidaiva)?", the answer is "The Person (puruṣa) is the divine. Here, "Person" refers to the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

The singular number is used to denote the class. Therefore, those various persons, abiding as presiding deities over objects that consist of perishable states—the differentiated effects and causes transformed according to their respective latent impressions (vāsanās)—possess the nature of *adhidaivata*. Thus it is said.

"Person (puruṣa) is the presiding deity (adhidaivata)" is the answer to the fifth question. Now, regarding the question, "In this body, how, by what manner, and who is the presiding sacrifice (adhiyajña)?", he gives the answer: "I alone am the presiding sacrifice here. In this [body], which is presided over by various individual souls (kṣetrajña) who are possessed of mutually distinct notions of agency and egoism—

Although within the body only the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) deserve to be the performers of sacrifice, as they carry out various sacrificial injunctions with the intention of attaining specific results, they nevertheless identify such a limited self as the agent; yet, [this is not] the ultimately real agency.

Because it is not shared by any other, I alone am the primary agent of all sacrifices; thus, I alone am the *adhiyajña* (the presiding deity of sacrifice), and no other. To the question "In what way?"—even regarding this inquiry into the manner—the answer is this very same thing:
"I alone. By the very term "I," I am the *adhiyajña*. This is the essential meaning here: even he who...
The egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) of the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), which has the body and so forth as its objective support and cause,
and that which is established in the supreme nature as "mine"— between these two, there is no difference whatsoever in their being egoism;
it is only due to the power of *māyā* that, because it is established in an objective support that delimits the knowers of the field, it appears as if delimited.

"But He," however, "is I alone"—unconditioned because He is established in His own nature—and none other, being established in the primary ego-consciousness as the Adhiyajña (the Lord of Sacrifice), and not in any other manner;
thus, I alone am the authorized master over all sacrifices. As he will say:

"For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices" (9.24)—this is the answer to the sixth question. By this same principle, it should be understood that "I alone am the adhidaivata"; for in reality, through the state of being the elements (*bhūta*), I alone am [the adhibhūta].

The meaning is that he is "established. In the same way, regarding the mode described as being designated as the *puruṣa* by virtue of his status as the presiding deity (*adhidaivatatva*), one should understand that the brief explanation of the six questions is simply this: "I alone am authorized therein"—namely, that which is known as Brahma, the Self, and Karma.

In the seventh chapter, the triad of principles consisting of the Supreme Self, the Knower of the Field, and the transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) was determined; therein, it was established that I alone exist in reality in the form of the sacrificial, the divine, and the elemental, and that nothing whatsoever exists apart from Me.
The intended meaning is as follows:
having thus stated these three principles in the passage beginning with "In that way, they know that Brahman in its entirety" (7.29), etc., [the Lord proceeds].
"They know Me as that which includes the elemental beings and the divine, and as that which includes the sacrifice" (7.30).
Thus, the Blessed One has pointed out Himself as the all-pervading Self. Now, at the time of departure—the moment of transition from one body to another—
To the question, "How are You to be known by those of self-restrained nature who have controlled their internal organs? the answer is given here:

"Even at the time of death, [think of] Me alone," and so forth. Even at the time of death—that is, at the moment of the dissolution of each respective body due to the exhaustion of its various karmas—one should think of Me, the Supreme Self, endowed with the aforementioned attributes.

Having remembered and reflected—preceded by the discernment of my own true nature—one who departs, having abandoned the physical body (kalevara) through his own autonomy and liberated himself from it, goes forth;
he attains my state (madbhāva), that is, my own existence (maddīyāṃ sattām), and becomes none other than I. In this regard, there is no...
There is no doubt; there is no uncertainty. || 3-5 ||
To demonstrate this reasoning, he says:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when one finally leaves the body, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state. (6)

Whatever state of being— whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)— a person remembers as a mental object, and whatever they contemplate with a mind of that same quality at the end,
at the time of leaving the body, into that very state they enter their next body. In this regard:

He states a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbha*): "always permeated by that state" means always, at all times, because he has been permeated—that is, his disposition has arisen—toward such a state, whether it be *sāttvika* or otherwise. What has been said?

It happens as follows: whatever object—be it characterized by *sattva* or otherwise—a person contemplates through practice while in the present body, that very object he necessarily remembers at the end, due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) instilled by the excellence of that practice of contemplation. And whatever he remembers as he departs from that body, that very [object] he attains.
Immediately thereafter, one attains another body, as it will be said:
"But when the [quality of] sattva has increased, the embodied soul meets its dissolution;
then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Supreme."
"Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action;
likewise, dissolved in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
Since this is so: "Therefore, at all times, remember Me and fight;
with mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt. (7)
Therefore, from the moment of attaining the instruction of the authoritative teacher— the aforementioned cause—
at all times (the word "time" being used here figuratively to mean at all places,
in all forms, and in all states), [know] Me, the Supreme Self, whose nature has been explained as it is.

"Remember the Supreme Lord"— contemplate Him; remain with dense concentration that does not cease from meditation on My true nature, and "fight"— perform your own duty, so that your internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is eternally established in Me in the manner described.
Without doubt you shall come to Me; you shall attain non-difference from Me, meaning that you shall become My very self. || 7 ||
In order to strengthen practice, he speaks again to explain this very same point:
"By means of a mind disciplined through the yoga of constant practice and not wandering elsewhere, O Pārtha, one who meditates upon the supreme divine Person goes to Him. (8)
By one who is joined— that is, bound— to the concentration characterized by the effort of constant recollection; for this very reason,
by one who does not go elsewhere, meaning whose movement has ceased toward any other object apart from the reality as it has been described.

Constantly reflecting with his internal organ and meditating through the power of latent impressions, he goes to— that is, attains— the supreme Person, who is superior to all individual souls (kṣetrajñas), the one divine Self existing in the heaven of the highest ether, which consists of His own essential nature.
It attains identity with that. || 8 ||

Having thus established the supreme method of *utkrānti*, which is the means for achieving the previously explained supreme non-dual gnosis (*anuttarajñāna*) preceded by the presentation of uncontradicted logical arguments,
[the author now] explains that other [method], the practice of yoga to be accomplished through the conquest of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
To explain this, he says:

"One should meditate upon the Poet, the Ancient, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle, the Sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, who has the luster of the sun, and who stands beyond darkness. (9)
At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga,
having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows, he attains that supreme, divine Person.

Such a yogi attains—that is, reaches—that divine Being who exists in the "divine" (divi), namely the supreme void (paramavyoman), and for that very reason, the Supreme Person, the Lord, the Self. Who is He?
He who, through devotion, is reached by the dawn-twilight of the day of the Lord’s grace.
Being endowed with that power of samādhi which defines his present nature— the seed for the accomplishment of all human goals—
he, in that state, [perceives] with a mind that is unshakable and firmly concentrated, that is, with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
One should remember the Destroyer of all, the Supreme Cause; at the time of death, one should contemplate Him.
How? Of what nature? Having properly caused the internal vital air—the breath made independent through practice—to enter and be fixed within the central path between the eyebrows.

One should meditate upon Him who is sun-colored, whose form is a light distinct from all other splendors, and for that very reason exists beyond darkness—that is, as something separate from ignorance. Of what nature is He? One should remember Him as the Destroyer of all, because in His supreme state He is characterized by such attributes as "the Seer" (kavi) and so forth.
It is inconceivable because its nature is that of ultimate knowledge; it cannot be made the object of the act of thinking, since it is the ancient seer, without beginning, the beholder,
and likewise the instructor of the entire creation of the moving and the unmoving, the controller by means of various regulations.

Therefore, it is stated that [the Lord] is omniscient and the creator of all; likewise, although the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and so forth are minute and subtle by their very nature, [the Lord is] even more minute than them—exceedingly subtle.
The intended meaning here is this: because in His supreme state He is the sole object of non-dual knowledge...

When that [object] has become an object of the function of recollection—that is, in its subsequent state consisting of conjunction with it—the yogi, by means of the aforementioned sequence, remembers it as having a restricted location and a restricted form;
he approaches that very person, meaning he goes into his presence. || 10 ||
He promises to explain correctly how the very sequence of yoga results in the attainment of the supreme state:
"That imperishable syllable which those who know the Vedas proclaim, and into which the ascetics free from passion enter..."
I shall declare to you in brief that goal, desiring which they lead the life of celibacy (brahmacarya). || 11 ||

I shall describe—that is, I will tell you—in brief, that is, in summary, that state which is to be attained by yogis; what is that state? That which the knowers of the Vedas—those learned in the meaning of the Vedas—call the Imperishable (*akṣara*), the eternal, through their teaching.
They explain: that which ascetics, solely devoted to knowledge, enter— that is, attain—

and that which those desiring it— those wishing to obtain it— practice as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), meaning they follow the conduct consisting of the study and hearing of the Veda (*brahman*), and thus take refuge in it.
Some, reading the variant *vidanti* (they know), explain it as follows: by the mention of "those who know the Vedas" (*vedavit*), householders and forest-dwellers are indicated, because,
being proficient in the performance of the rites prescribed in the scriptures, they know— that is, they realize— that state.

[Ordinary people] determine [the Self] as something to be attained; the ascetics (yati), however, because they have accomplished what was to be done, enter into it and attain identity with it; whereas the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), desiring to attain that, devote themselves to specific vows, being established in the study of the Vedas, the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures, and so forth. || 11 ||

To state what was promised, he says: "Having restrained all the gates [of the senses] and having confined the mind within the heart, placing his own life-breath in the head, he remained established in the practice of yoga-concentration (yogadhāraṇā). (12)
Uttering the single syllable "Om," which is Brahman, and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal. (13)

The yogi attains—that is, reaches—the supreme goal, the excellent state previously mentioned. Who is he? He who, while abandoning—relinquishing—the body, the physical frame, thus departs—that is, ascends. Of what nature is he? One who, remembering Me and established in the concentration of yoga, [remembers] Me.

Meditating upon the reality of Brahman— the supreme cause whose nature has been described as denoted by the syllable *oṃ*— he stands established in, or relies upon, the stage of *dhāraṇā*, which consists of the restraint of the mind upon an object that serves as the support for a certain yoga or meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

How is he established? First of all, having restrained all the gates— the eyes and so forth, which are the pathways for the flow of mental fluctuations— and having withdrawn them from their respective objects,
he fixes the mind in the heart, that single region of the body which is the locus of all consciousness and is known through instruction.

Having restrained [the senses] and brought to a halt the movement of the objects of the senses, and likewise having caused the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the internal wind, to find its path by piercing the knot located between the eyebrows—which serves as the bolt of the city of Brahman—at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) in the crown of the head; [he should contemplate: *tatra*... [there... (Note: The provided fragment ends with "labdhamārgaṃ santam" [having found its path], and the subsequent portion beginning with "*tatra*" appears to be the start of the next section of the source text.)

Having placed [the breath] there, and likewise uttering— that is, pronouncing— the Brahman which is the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*) in the form of the well-known single syllable *om*, one should thus perform the impelling of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to the crown of the head,
the recitation of the *praṇava*, and the remembrance of my own nature, which is signified by the *praṇava*.

And thus, the essential meaning is that the yogi who, preceded by the restraint of all the senses and the mind, brings about this triad simultaneously and effects the abandonment of the body, attains the supreme state. || 13 ||

Regarding how a yogi, whose mind is agitated by the circumstances of that moment at the time of departure, might achieve meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in this situation, he states the previously mentioned reason:
"He who, with a mind focused on no other, constantly remembers Me always..."
I am easily attained, O Pārtha, by that yogin who is constantly disciplined.

For that yogi who is ever-disciplined and whose concentration is uninterrupted, I am always easily attained and readily accessible in all conditions, whether they be of the nature of pleasure or of the nature of pain. For whom? For him who constantly and without interruption [remembers] Me in the form of the practice of yoga as described.
With a mind not directed elsewhere—having withdrawn the internal organ from any object other than Me—one remembers the single reality, the Supreme Self, and reflects upon It as one's own self.
