Whatever state of being one remembers when departing... (8.6)
By such reasoning as stated above,

for the yogi whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been made firm through the repeated contemplation (*pratyavamarśa*) of my own nature— which is the self of all— how could that state be difficult to attain, since in that state he has become my very self?
This is the intended meaning. || 14 ||
And those who have taken refuge in me by this path—
having come to me, these great-souled ones do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering; they have attained the supreme perfection.

The "Great-Souled Ones" (mahātmānaḥ) are those whose very self (ātmā) is the Great Lord (maheśvara)— the one who transcends all— due to their cultivation of the knowledge as it has been described; therefore, having approached and taken refuge in Me with the aforementioned devotion, they attain supreme perfection.

Having gone from this saṃsāra to the supreme perfection of the fruit, which is characterized by non-dual absorption (*abhedasamāpatti*), they do not— indeed, they no longer— obtain or undergo birth, that is, the acquisition of another body.

What kind of birth? It is an abode, a locus, for the three types of sufferings—internal and so forth—which, in their detailed expansion, possess infinite varieties; likewise, it is impermanent, necessarily involving the destruction of everything including the body, the sense faculties, and all possessions. [It occurs] in what is not-self.

The connection with all suffering and the bondage to transformations such as birth and destruction belong to living beings who have failed to realize the one Self— the common, supreme cause— through the sense of "I. For those who have realized it, however, these do not exist.
The intended meaning is that it arises. || 15 ||
And thus, according to the method described, he says that apart from the single means of taking refuge in Me, no other cause for non-return [to worldly existence] is possible:
"O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return."
But having attained Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist.

The world of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, is the world of Brahmā, which is attainable through meritorious deeds such as supreme and most excellent austerity, sacrifice, and charity; taking that as the limit, whatever other worlds exist that are attainable through meritorious deeds— among those worlds, [those which...]

Because they are performers of those respective rituals, these people have attained rebirth; yet, due to being devoid of the aforementioned knowledge, when those performed rituals come to an end, they are subject to return—they reappear once more on the path of saṃsāra. [But not so] me.
Furthermore, having approached the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman and who is accessible solely through the means of devotion purified by the aforementioned knowledge,
and having relied upon Him until the attainment of identity with Him, there is no more rebirth— that is, no further arising on the plane of saṃsāra.

It does not exist at all. Regarding the statement "having come to Me, they are not born again," it should be understood here that the agent of both the action of attaining [Me] and the action of being born is one and the same. || 16 ||
Now, as to how even those dwelling in the world of Brahmā return again, whereas those who have taken refuge in Me do not— He states the reason for this in sequence:
"Those who know that the day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas..."
Those people who know day and night understand that the night ends after a thousand yugas. || 17 ||

Those who consider only that specific portion of time characterized by the rising and setting of the sun— which serves as the cause for states such as waking and dreaming— to be day and night, do not truly know the essential nature of day and night.

But those who know that the day of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, has as its limit and boundary a thousand cycles of four yugas according to divine reckoning, and who likewise know the night to be of that same measure— they are called knowers of reality and knowers of day and night.

What is meant by this? Just as for mortals a period of time delimited by sixty *nālikās* constitutes a day and night (*ahorātra*), so too for those dwelling in the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), a period of time delimited by two thousand sets of four *yugas* constitutes a day and night. And therefore, just as mortals...

The established rule here is that after having passed a human lifespan of a hundred years— calculated by the reckoning of their own days and nights— they again assume another body; likewise, even for those dwelling in the world of Brahmā,
[the same applies] through the calculation of days and nights delimited by the aforementioned measure, for a hundred years.

Having passed through a full human lifespan, they again assume another body; thus, there is a distinction based on the shortening or lengthening of time— from a single day and night up to a full human lifespan— among mortals dwelling in the land of action (karmabhūmi) and those of meritorious deeds residing in the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), but not [otherwise].
In their state of being subject to saṃsāra, there is no distinction among them; therefore, just as mortals return again,
so too those dwelling in the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), having passed their human lifespan according to its own temporal measure, return once more.
It has been stated: "All worlds, up to the world of Brahmā, are subject to return" (8.16). Therefore, the intended meaning here is as follows:
[this applies] to that which is obtainable through the performance of specific meritorious deeds devoid of the aforementioned knowledge.

A person of discrimination should not be deceived by a false sense of stability regarding the world of Brahmā and other such realms, which are merely substrates for experiences that are empty and limited by time; for even those realms remain within the cycle of saṃsāra due to their connection with specific birth, lifespan, and experience.

Even a duration of time as long as a thousand yugas does not exceed the length of a day and night for mortals, because it is finite; thus it has been said that those who consider the period measured by two thousand yugas to be a single day and night are "knowers of the day and night. || 17 ||
Now, however, by means of explaining the nature of that Brahma-day and night,
[the text] intends to demonstrate its similarity to the cycle of mortal days and nights for the sake of purifying the discernment of those to be instructed.
To provide instruction, he says:
"At the arrival of the day, all manifest beings arise from the Unmanifest;
at the arrival of the night, they dissolve back into that very same thing called the Unmanifest. (18)
This very same multitude of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves helplessly at the arrival of night, O Pārtha, and comes forth again at the arrival of day. (19)
From the Unmanifest— the substance known by the name Pradhāna, whose nature is the equilibrium of the *guṇas* and which has been manifested as the cause of the world by Īśvara—
when the day of Brahmā, measured by a thousand *yugas*, has dawned, all manifest entities [come into being].
All the specific qualities of all things arise and manifest; just as all the various activities of all living beings arise when the day begins with the rising of the sun,
so too do they arise at the onset of the night of Brahmā, which lasts for a thousand yugas.

In the aforementioned principle known as the Unmanifest (avyakta), all things dissolve, abandoning their manifest form and remaining as mere potentiality (śakti-mātra), just as here, for all living beings,
when night falls following the setting of the sun, the activities of all the senses cease within.

They dissolve. What is the intended meaning here? There is no difference whatsoever between rising and setting, or between creation and dissolution, as these two proceed in alternation; it is merely that [the former] is associated with the notion of non-existence, which is subject to destruction like a physical body, whereas [the latter] is the naturally uninterrupted consciousness.

This specific delusion regarding distinctions—produced by the conceptualization of shortness and length—is for those who are deluded by the power of *māyā*; it does not exist then when, through proficiency in the aforementioned knowledge, the discerning ones have firmly established the realization of "I" within their own true Self, which is unconditioned by time. He concludes this very point:

"This very same collection of beings" means that this very same collection of beings— the multitude of living creatures, both moving and unmoving— is divided by the fourteenfold manifoldness (prapañca), having come into existence at the beginning of creation according to the sequence already described.

Having come into being again and again by attaining manifestation, it dissolves—that is, becomes latent—at the arrival of night, at the time of dissolution known as the "night of Brahmā"; and it originates—that is, attains manifestation—at the arrival of day, at the beginning of creation. || 19 ||

Having thus established the nature of creation and dissolution in connection with the demonstration of the meaning that "thus all worlds, up to the world of Brahmā, return again," [the Lord now explains] the reason why those who have attained Me do not return.
To demonstrate this, he says:
"But beyond that is another eternal entity, both manifest and unmanifest, which does not perish even when all beings perish. (20)
He is called the unmanifest and the imperishable; they say he is the supreme goal, reaching which they do not return—that is my supreme abode.

Therefore, beyond—that is, other than and distinct from—the entity called *pradhāna*, which is designated as the "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and appears as the cause of the world, there exists another reality (*bhāva*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the truly existent entity; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Of what nature is it? It is both manifest (*vyakta*) and unmanifest (*avyakta*). Manifest...
Because the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which has attained primacy as the causal principle, is a reality whose essence is the primary cause (*pradhāna*);

it is of such a nature that, by virtue of its intended characteristic as the Lord (*īśvara*), this conventional designation "unmanifest" is indeed understood; or alternatively, [it refers to] both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

This word is to be explained by resorting to a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). For that reality (*bhāva*), while manifesting all this [universe] precisely as its eternally arisen nature of light, is indeed manifest;
yet, due to the power of *māyā*, it is unmanifest because there is no such realization for everyone. Likewise...

He is called *sanātana* because he exists eternally at all times; thus, he is the eternal (*nitya*). Of what nature is he? He is such that, while all beings—living creatures within the infinite manifold (*prapañca*) consisting of the two broad categories of insentient and sentient, with their endless internal subdivisions—are perishing as described above, [he remains].

While the primary cause (pradhāna) undergoes dissolution through various modes, [the Self] does not perish, because its nature consists of the eternally manifest light of non-dual consciousness; thus, it does not even admit such designations as "dissolved," let alone "absolute non-existence. To the question, "Why then is it not perceived? he says:

Because it does not manifest in its actual, eternal form to those deluded by the power of its own inconceivable *māyā*, it is unmanifest from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); furthermore, it is imperishable (*akṣara*), for it does not decay nor does it deviate from its own essential nature. And that entity which is of such a kind—him...
Those who know reality say that it is the supreme goal, the attainment of the unsurpassed. For this very reason, what is it like?
Having reached it, having attained it, and having realized it as one's own self, the aforementioned yogis—whose longing for other attainments has been completely stilled—do not return.

Because they do not descend into the path of saṃsāra, that state which is of such a nature is my abode—the supreme cause, the Supreme Lord, the Brahman; it is the eternally manifest light or the unsurpassed station. Those who have taken refuge in Me, who am of such a nature, they [do not descend].
Thus, the cause for the non-return of such yogins has been established, in contrast to those who return again. || 21 ||
Concluding the essential nature of that very state as previously described and reminding [the disciple] of the means for its attainment, He says:
"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone."
Having attained which, O Arjuna, yogis do not undergo rebirth.
Within whom all beings reside, in whom everything is established—
that reality whose nature has been explained as it is— is the Supreme,
called by the term *puruṣa*, because its power transcends all *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field) and is unsurpassed.
The Puruṣa is the Supreme Self because He dwells within the interior of all bodies. Of what nature is He?

Having attained Him—that is, having realized Him as one's own self—in the manner already described and to be described hereafter, yogins who have mastered various types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) do not undergo birth again, that is, they do not return to the state of transmigratory existence.

They do not attain, that is, they do not obtain, their own arising; for thus, within the heart characterized by universal consciousness, all moving and non-moving beings abide as one. Indeed, they do not exist in such a way as to have mutually distinct forms.
Without entering into non-dual pure consciousness alone, existence is impossible;
therefore, in that [Reality] which is the common substratum for the entire multitude of objects in the world, all this is established and finds its fixed position. Furthermore, such is He:

He is to be attained—that is, reached—through service consisting of the four stages beginning with the state of being most excellent and culminating in the knowledge of the realized soul (jñānin), which are offered with devotion; [and] of what kind? With that which is "ananya" (non-dual), meaning without deviation from His true nature.
By that [wisdom] which is of such a nature, having no other object of focus whatsoever in any state.
Now, introducing another instruction on yoga concerning the subject of departure [from the body], he says: "But at what time yogis [attain] non-return and indeed return... (23).

I shall describe that time, O bull of the Bharatas, at which those who have departed— namely, the yogis who have cast off their bodies— attain either non-return or return. At whichever time hereafter I shall describe, they attain these states.

They attain—that is, they enjoy independently—a connection with a body and so forth that is fit as a basis for distinguished enjoyments; I shall teach that such time, which is easily accessible only to yogins according to the sequence to be described. || 23 ||
He said to him: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern course [of the sun]. (24)
Departing from there, people who know Brahman go to Brahman;
[so too do those who travel by way of] smoke, the dark fortnight, the night, and the six months of the sun’s southern course. (25)
And there, having reached the lunar light, the yogi returns.
Here, Agni and Soma are light and darkness, which characterize day and night; the two fortnights, the bright and the dark; and likewise the northern and southern solstices, each measuring six months.

From a coarse perspective, they describe the divisions of time according to their respective domains of gods, ancestors, and mortals, as well as their superior, middling, and inferior durations. This being the case, fire is light, which is the solar radiance; that which is characterized by it is the day, measured by a duration of thirty *nālikās*.

A portion of time called a day; fifteen days and nights, characterized by the waxing moon, constitute the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), which is indicated here by the word "bright" (*śukla*). Likewise...

The six months characterized by the movement of the sun as it traverses the six zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn are known as the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*); these are the well-known specific periods of time. In such a collection of specific temporal conditions, those knowers of Brahman who have realized the nature of the supreme cause—

They go forth, they depart, they cast off the body; they go to Brahman, the supreme reality, meaning they attain the state of liberation from which there is no return. Likewise, smoke is Soma because it consists of water; similarly, the night is well known as being indicated by that [Soma]. [And] the dark fortnight...
The dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) consists of fifteen days and nights characterized by the waning moon;

it has not been explained according to its textual order because of its sequential nature. Likewise, the six months of the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) are characterized by the sun moving through the six zodiac signs beginning with Cancer.

In that very circumstance, having reached the lunar light— the radiance (*tejas*) that serves as the cause for rebirth— within such a temporal conjunction (*kāla-sāmagrī*), the yogi possessed of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) returns once more and enters the path of *saṃsāra*. Regarding this, certain discerning individuals initiate the following reflection:
In this regard, there are two ways of knowing the aforementioned Brahman, the supreme cause:

direct realization through self-awareness, or merely the comprehension of its essential nature as taught by a qualified authority. Among these, for those who know Brahman by means of the former method, [the result is as follows].
Since that which is to be attained has already been attained, the aforementioned collection of conditions cannot be the cause for the attainment of Brahman;
even in the second view, those who are knowers of Brahman merely through the comprehension of its essential nature have not yet directly realized that reality.

It cannot be said that the mere attainment of the specific time mentioned is the cause for attaining Brahman, which is the cause of non-return; likewise, even for those knowers of Brahman who possess both [types of] natures, the attainment of Brahman at the time of death is dependent upon the attainment of the aforementioned time.
This is consistent with reason. Furthermore, for a yogi who has attained a specific meditative absorption,
it is illogical that he would return [to cyclic existence] merely by reaching the aforementioned specific time, without the removal of the power of that [absorption].

"Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end," (8.6)— by the reasoning established by such passages, because there is no deviation from a state that has been cultivated through very firm contemplation, even if that which was cultivated slowly is not remembered at that moment;
Reversion remains a certainty; what, then, will the aforementioned time accomplish? Thus, the claim that the yogin returns again upon reaching the specific time as described is also not convincing.
Furthermore, as for the argument: "If this aforementioned time were not the cause for attaining Brahman and so forth..."
How is it that even for Śāntanava, a knower of Brahman, we hear of an expectation for the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) for the purpose of relinquishing the body? It is true that this is heard;
however, he did not wait for that time as a means for attaining Brahman. For if he [had done so]...

If it were the cause for attaining Brahman, then all knowers of Brahman would wait for that very time at the casting off of the body, and all those who cast off their bodies at that time would attain the state of non-return. But this is not the case; nor is an injunction such as "one should die at such a time" tenable, given that death occurs for everyone [at its own appointed time].
Because he lacks independence; however, since Bhīṣma possesses independent control over his death, another cause must be inferred for his waiting for such a time. And that is this:
from the perspective of the gross view, the aforementioned time has indeed arrived at the moment for the casting off of the body.

His effort to await such a time was for the purpose of validating the scriptural statement that [the Lord] is the cause of bestowing a specific state of rebirth; therefore, the aforementioned time is not primarily of the nature of days and nights. Consequently, for the knowers of Brahman and for yogins, [it is otherwise].

Regarding these two courses of time which have been described as the causes, respectively, for attaining Brahman and for returning again, there must necessarily exist some distinction therein that is to be understood.
For [the author] will say:
"Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded" (8.27).
And it is not merely the names "Devayāna" and "Pitṛyāna" applied to these two paths, which consist of specific external times, that is meant here.

Knowledge shall be the cause for attaining [the state of] Brahmā and the other [deities]. Therefore, they declare that some specific factor must be inferred here as the cause for the connection with the aforementioned meaning. For in the secret scriptures (rahasya-śāstra), time is established as being of two kinds, through the distinction between external and internal. Among these—

The external mode is characterized by the movement of the well-known sun and moon, whereas the internal mode is characterized by the movement of the sun and moon in the form of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Among these,
because the existence of refutations has been established for the primary external mode, the internal mode is secondary.
It is relied upon; therefore, words such as "fire" (*agni*) up to "northern course" (*uttarāyaṇa*) are employed here because they signify the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),

since it is precisely the movement of the vital breath that is described in various secret scriptures (*rahasya-śāstra*) as consisting of the temporal divisions beginning with the day and ending with the northern course.
This [notion] is well-known in relation to various specific bodies and so forth. Such being the case,

for those who are knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) established in the aforementioned knowledge, at the time of death, their vital breath (*prāṇa*) is naturally restrained within the flow through the aperture of the head known as the "gate of Brahman" (*brahmadvāra*).

At the moment when the flow of consciousness ceases through the pacification of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one enters the great ocean of universal consciousness— which is inherently pure and free from all waves— and attains a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*); for them, the attainment of Brahman is established as being immediate and without interval.

For that is indeed the path of the gods (*devayāna*) for those who know Brahman; this is the one eternal goal pertaining to that [knowledge]. However, as for the yogin who, apart from the aforementioned knowledge of reality, has adopted yoga through practice alone, his stream of consciousness—even though regulated by the aforementioned movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—[is different].
At the moment when the vital breath is stilled, because the state of being a knower of Brahman has not yet arisen,
[the mind], its flow obstructed by the mountain of the ego-notion regarding the body and so forth, turns back;
and as it is turning back, it...

Having relied upon the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa), which is characterized by the downward movement of the vital breath (apāna) as described by the sequence beginning with smoke and ending with the term "southern solstice" (dakṣiṇāyana), he enters another distinguished body appropriate to the excellence of his practice of yoga, wherein— due to the mind being restrained by prior practice— [he attains his goal].
It has been stated that one who strives with most excellent enthusiasm will attain supreme perfection.
Therefore, this is the summary of the meaning here: those who, being knowers of Brahman through their state of wisdom, at the time of death [follow] the sequence as it has been explained...

Those whose mental fluctuations take the vital force (*prāṇa-śakti*) as their support cast off the body even at the moment that [force] is stilled, provided their memory of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) remains undisturbed;
by virtue of attaining Brahman without interruption, they do not return. As for those who are merely practitioners of yoga (*kevala-yogin*):

The *santaḥ* (the tranquil ones), having relied solely upon the function of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) while abandoning the body, depart because, due to the absence of realized knowledge (*jñānitva*), there is an absence of recollection of the supreme reality (*paratattvasmṛti*).
Because their sense of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) has not ceased with respect to the body and other such things, they [assume] the function of the downward breath (*apānavṛtti*).

Relying upon the path of *saṃsāra*, they attain a distinct other body; for, having departed from the body of any embodied being— which exists by relying on the vital function (*prāṇavṛtti*) common to all transmigrating beings— they [proceed] by relying on the function of *apāna*.
The transition to a future body occurs; however, in this context, the specific distinction regarding those who know Brahman and yogis is precisely what has been set forth. || 25 ||

For this very reason, he says the following in order to subsume these two paths, which are distinguished by the internal characteristics of the prāṇa and apāna: "These two paths of the world, white and black, are considered eternal."
Of these two, by one there is no return, while by the other one returns.

These two aforementioned paths, consisting of the movements of prāṇa and apāna and designated as the path of the gods (devayāna) and the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa), are the two eternal and constant ways for the entire world of living beings; therefore,
not every person [attains liberation] by resorting to the path of the vital breaths.
It departs from the body, but it migrates to another body by resorting to the path of the *apāna* breath.
This is the distinction between the knower of Brahman and the yogi: that between these two paths, one proceeds by the upward-flowing *prāṇa*, which is white, in the manner already explained.

At the time of death, the knower of Brahman, by relying upon that [path], attains non-return—that is, he reaches Brahman. But the yogi, departing by that same path—or rather, by another path in the form of the downward breath (apāna), which is dark—returns for the reason stated [above] and transmigrates into a specific other body. || 26 ||
For this reason:
"Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogi whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna. (27)
Knowing these two paths— the movements consisting of *prāṇa* and *apāna*— as they have been explained,

and proceeding by means of the aforementioned greatness, the yogi who has accepted the primary yoga previously described does not become deluded; rather, everyone who knows those paths becomes such a one.

By resorting to the path that is the cause for attaining Brahman, one attains Brahman itself, and not transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), because of the avoidance of other paths. Those who know reality declare that such greatness belongs to these two paths, which exist as objects of knowledge for the knowers of Brahman. [The mind...]
This flow of the vital breath (prāṇa) arises from that which accompanies its expansion, and therein it sets;

that is the state of realizing the reality of Brahman, which is devoid of all phenomenal proliferation such as the calculation of time. Consequently, the entire [phenomenal world] of time and so forth is bound to this aforementioned flow of the vital breath.

The conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) dissolves for those knowers of Brahman whose consciousness is capable of discerning the states of its arising and subsiding. And that supreme yogi who, having attained such a state, casts off the body while knowing Brahman, becomes merged in Brahman itself and does not return again. As for the one who is merely a yogi...

He is not capable of disregarding that state; rather, resorting to the lunar light in the form of the expansion of the *apāna* breath, he departs and migrates into another body, where he will gradually attain perfection. Thus is the knowledge of the distinction between the causes of perfection regarding these two paths.
Therefore it has been said:
"Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, the yogin is not deluded," and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore at all times, from the perspective of external vision—

Become engaged in yoga— that is, become attentive and absorbed in the meditative concentration (samādhi) consisting of the knowledge of the movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths— in the manner already described, among the many divisions such as the northern and southern solstices (uttarāyaṇa and dakṣiṇāyana). || 27 ||
For this is the power of this yoga:
whatever meritorious fruit is declared in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities, and in acts of charity;
Having understood all this, the yogin transcends it all and attains the supreme, primordial state. || 28 ||
Having understood and known this matter, which consists of the exposition of the seven questions,

the yogi— possessing the aforementioned samādhi— transcends and surpasses all that, namely the fruit of meritorious actions such as the study of the Vedas, sacrifice, austerity, and charity; for it is the primordial, unsurpassed, and therefore supreme state.
Because it consists of infinite bliss, he approaches— that is, attains— the most exalted station, the *dhāman*,
and obtains his natural foundation in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Although this meaning has been explained by some in this very manner, through such an interpretation...

Those who know Brahman, having departed by means of the totality of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), go to Brahman by way of ascending through the intermediate worlds known as "light" (arciḥ) and so forth;
and for this very reason, the yogis are designated by the term "yogin" when they depart during the totality of the time of the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
Having departed, they reach the lunar light and,
by means of the sequence of ascending through other worlds designated as smoke and so forth, they return to the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, this interpretation is also inconsistent with the reasoning previously stated, according to the logic already explained.
Moreover, some maintain that this sequence as well is included within these two very destinies; in this matter, those who know the ultimate truth are the authority. Om. 28.

May a person easily grasp this extensive commentary on the eighth chapter, which— like the great ocean— is filled with the seven topics beginning with Brahman, which are profound, vast, pure by nature, and radiant with the splendor of their glorious meanings.
Only he who is capable of accepting it deserves the sole sovereignty of the learned.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meaning of the statements, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.

At the conclusion of the eighth chapter, in the determination of the seventh question, knowledge of the two paths— the bright and the dark— at the time of death was taught as the means for attaining Brahman.
Therefore, lest you think that the means for attaining Brahman is merely that much,
the Blessed One, reminding Arjuna of the very instruction already set forth in the eighth chapter, spoke in summary:
But this most secret knowledge, together with realized wisdom, I shall declare to you, who are free from malice; having known it, you shall be liberated from evil.

The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. Apart from the means characterized as described in the eighth chapter, this knowledge—which is eternally present within one's own intellect—is the means for attaining Brahman; it is distinguished by "vijñāna," that is, by a specific knowledge or awakening culminating in the direct realization of one's own consciousness (*svasaṃvit*).

I shall speak—that is, I will declare—to you this [teaching] which is connected with the highest excellence, presented in brief by way of establishing the essential core; and to what kind of person? To one who is free from envy, because his intellect is supremely pure, since he does not feel envy toward this knowledge.
Because you cannot conceive of the result as it has been described, like one who is ignorant, you do not begin to censure it.
What kind of knowledge shall I speak? Among the previous chapters, certain knowledges were taught that are secret, more secret, and most secret; but this [knowledge] is even more secret than those.
It remains in the cave of the heart, situated on a path far away for those whose knowledge born of discrimination has not yet manifested;

or it is "secret" (guhya) because of its hidden nature. Therefore, by knowing that [Self], you shall be liberated from the impure and the non-beneficial, which is characterized by the revolving wheel of birth, old age, and death.
You shall attain liberation by yourself alone. || 1 ||

Since it has already been indicated that one who is devoted to the means of knowledge to be described hereafter attains Brahman even at the time of death— apart from the two aforementioned paths of departure— it is for the sake of praising this knowledge that he says:
This is the royal science, the royal secret, this supreme purifier; it is directly perceivable, consistent with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable. (2)

This knowledge about to be declared is supreme, unique, and purifying—that is, a cause for washing away the mud of all sins and blemishes. For there are indeed purifiers such as sacred fords, mantras, austerities, sacrifices, gifts, and so forth; yet these are finite because they are devoid of knowledge.

Furthermore, those who are refined by this knowledge shall attain infinite fruit; for this very reason, it is called the "supreme purifier. Since this is the "royal science" (rājavidyā), it belongs even to kings such as Janaka and Aśvapati, who were performing their own rigorous duties.

Knowledge is heard of as having liberation as its fruit; therefore, this is the secret, the hidden mystery of those kings, because it is characterized by direct comprehension— that is, a realization whose understanding is perceptible and known through one's own self-awareness— whereas for others...

The realization of the fruits of purifying acts will occur at another time, in another body, and in another world; likewise, that which is righteous— consistent with dharma as declared in the scriptures, divided according to the order of castes and stages of life, and not departing from the conduct of the virtuous— is therefore very easy to perform and accomplish.

It brings about ultimate happiness because it is accomplished solely through the practice of the innate nature (*sahajasvabhāva*); and although it is of such a kind, it is imperishable (*avyaya*), meaning it is without decay, because the fruit to be attained—characterized by union with me—is eternal. || 2 ||
And this is easily attainable only through the perfection of qualities such as devotion and faith arising from my grace; for:
"O scorcher of foes, those persons who lack faith in this dharma..."
Failing to reach Me, they return to the path of the cycle of death and worldly existence.

Those persons who lack faith in this dharma— which consists of knowledge already described and that which is yet to be described— and who are intent on the impossibility of the aforementioned results, shall fail to reach Me,
the Supreme Brahman whose nature has been described, and shall not attain union with Me.
They turn back— that is, they repeatedly fall back— into the path of death and birth, which are constantly revolving among living beings.
What is meant by this?

This knowledge is easily accessible only to those by whom it is worshipped—that which is the sole cause for the production of all accomplishments, and which is like a cluster of blossoms on the celestial tree of faith that has emerged from the nectar-ocean of my grace; it is not so for others. || 3 ||
To demonstrate that very knowledge now, he says:
"By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded;
all beings dwell in Me, yet I do not abide in them. (4)
Yet beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga!
My Self, the source of all beings, sustains beings but does not dwell within them.
Behold—that is, attain—the yoga existing in me, who am related to you as the Sovereign Lord, the one absolute Master; a yoga that has no other locus, which is meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
For this [Self] is everything for all subjects insofar as it is the object of knowledge.

In brief, the object— which consists of all moving and unmoving entities and is limitless through the conceptualization of its intermediate subdivisions— is, by me, [perceived] as independent of other causes such as material and auxiliary causes,
and as never deviating from its own nature, which is eternal, changeless, universal, and pure consciousness alone.

The world— the entire universe— has been thus expanded and spread out by a single Creator, whose sole purpose is His own unsurpassed play that cannot be imitated by others, and whose sole instrument is His own will. It exists in the form of an infinite manifestation of wonders.

"By him whose form is unmanifest" (*avyaktamūrtinā*): because it is impossible for all subjects (*pramātṛ*) produced by my *māyā* to delimit it as "this," his form—meaning his configuration or essential nature—is unmanifest; that is, it is devoid of any definable individuality (*vyapadeśyavyaktivirahita*). Such is he, by whom [the world is perceived] in that manner. What is being said? [The answer follows: It is said that although the entire universe is indeed manifest within the Lord, who is the supreme subject, it is nevertheless unmanifest with respect to those subjects who are produced by His *māyā*. This is because they are unable to perceive it as "this," due to its extreme proximity. For example, just as the light of a lamp, though clearly manifest to one standing nearby, is not perceived as such by another person situated at a great distance, so too is this universe. Thus, while the universe is manifest to the Lord, it is unmanifest to those other subjects. Therefore, it is called "unmanifest. This is the meaning. Whatever object is to be known by every subject— from Brahmā down to the most minute insect—
in whatever manner, at whatever time, and in whatever place it may manifest, that object obtains its very self only while being known; and this state of being known is [the essence of manifestation].

The transition of the experiencer into the state of being an object of experience implies that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the experiencer must always remain one and the same—
being that which never, in any way, at any time, or in any place, admits of contact with the qualifying attribute of "being an object of experience. Therefore...
All beings— both stationary and moving, all things to be perceived— reside within me alone, the perceiver. Thus, I am the creator of all and the cause of all power,
yet I do not abide within those beings, just as [the space within a jar does not abide in the space outside].

The meaning is this: my own established state—which does not deviate from the essential nature of being the eternally conscious perceiver—is the cause for the establishment of all beings who are objects of perception; it is not the case, however, that the establishment of all beings is the cause for my own establishment. For indeed, all beings...

Precisely because they are objects of cognition, they are impermanent due to their connection with attributes such as arising and destruction; for me, however, the sole characteristic is that of being the cognizer—how then could my own existence be dependent on the persistence of the elements? Thus, although the elements have their existence dependent on me, they do not abide in me.
They do not abide as my very nature within the cognizer, because they manifest as objects of cognition (*vedyatayā*);

for while I, the cause of the existence of all beings, eternally manifest solely as the cognizer, other beings do not do so, since they are perceived only through their state of being objects of cognition. Thus, according to what has been stated:

In this manner, my self—my essential nature—is the sustainer of beings; it supports and maintains the elements, establishing them in their respective forms. Yet, as has already been stated, it does not abide in the elements, nor is its own existence dependent upon the stability of the elements. And for this reason, by this sequence, it is the "originator of beings," for it causes the elements to come into being.
The meaning is "she creates. || 5 ||

In this regard, He provides an illustration by means of a certain point of similarity: "Just as the great wind, omnipresent and eternal, resides in space, so do all beings reside in Me; understand this. (6)

In this manner, understand—that is, realize—that all subtle and gross beings situated in various places exist within me, whose majesty is unlimited, having attained the state of being supported [by me]. How? Just as [all things] eternally [exist] in space, which possesses an uninterrupted pervasion.

The wind is always present. Of what nature? It is all-pervading (*sarvatraga*), having gone to and occupied various places; it is great (*mahān*) and, in comparison to others, all-encompassing (*vyāpaka*). In this way, understand that "all beings abide in Me. Herein lies the essential meaning (*tātparya*): just as [it is with] the wind...

In every respect, qualities such as omnipresence and greatness have their sole basis in the infinite space of the ether; likewise, all the qualities of all beings have their sole basis in the penetration of my own nature. || 6 ||
To conclude this point, he says:
"In this way, indeed, I move among all beings unobserved, abiding in the very nature of beings, both together with them and apart from them. (7)

Thus, in this manner, comparable to the relationship between wind and space, I move through all beings—that is, I pervade them—unobserved, my true nature not determined as "this" by anyone. Having done what do I move? [I move] through the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) of beings.

Relying upon—that is, presiding over—the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), whose characteristics as the conscious self of the elements have been previously explained; how do I move? "Together" (*saha*) and "even without" (*vinā*):
because they are eternally interconnected, and because there is no difference in their essential nature characterized as the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*).
Indeed, even without any mutual separateness: for one is my own nature, which is the essence of the knower, and the other is the essence of the known, manifested by my will. (7)

To demonstrate that these [beings] are brought forth by my will, he says: "O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature; again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth. (8)

All these beings, whether conscious or unconscious, at the conclusion of a great aeon (mahākalpa), go to my own nature (prakṛti), which is my very essence; the meaning is that by my will alone they are dissolved into me.
And at the beginning of the aeon, at the commencement of another aeon, I myself emit them again in their fourteenfold variety.
I illuminate; the meaning here is not that I create again those very same things that have dissolved.
Because the will of the Lord is beyond questioning, even in His absolute sovereignty, He withdraws and emits the fourteenfold creation of beings during the states of dissolution and production.
And the intended meaning is that [He] is the Supreme Lord. || 8 ||
He concludes this very point: "Underlying my own nature, I project again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature. (9)

Without relying upon or depending on anything else as a cause, but solely upon its own *prakṛti*— its own inherent nature— it repeatedly, again and again, through the conceptualization of time such as the beginning of a *kalpa* proceeding in an endless succession, brings forth this entire multitude of beings, this collection of living creatures.

"I create" means I manifest [the world] solely by the power of primordial nature (prakṛti), being "unwilling" and "not independent" precisely because of my dependence on my own inherent nature (matsvabhāva). And at the end of the eon, I likewise withdraw [it]; this is to be understood as following from the context. || 9 ||
Furthermore:
"And those actions do not bind Me, O Dhanañjaya, for I remain as if indifferent, unattached to those actions. (10)

Those actions, consisting of the forms of creation, destruction, and so forth, do not bind me again, as they do the various individual souls (kṣetrajña) manifested by my māyā; for, by determining the commencement of their fruition and so on, they do not make me subject to their control, unlike the case of the actions of those individual souls.

The meaning is that [the fruits of action] become causes for bondage in *saṃsāra* by initiating the ripening (*vipāka*) characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience; it is not so with my actions at the beginning of creation and so forth.
In what state am I such that they do not bind me? This is the sense of the underlying reason (*hetugarbha*).

He states the qualification: because of non-attachment to those actions, due to the absence of grasping such as the sense of "mine," he remains—meaning stays—as one whose mind is not submerged, like one who is indifferent, like a bystander. Just as, regarding the actions of another, that other person thinks, "These are not mine; they do not yield their respective fruits for me."

Considering himself as a bystander and experiencing through those various actions such as being the enjoyer of their fruits and so forth, he is not constrained by them; likewise, he is not bound by the acts of creation and so on,
because those acts of creation and the rest [are performed by another].

With respect to the individual knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), whose mutual distinctions are manifested by my own inconceivable power of self-illusion (*svamāyā*), my agency consists solely in making them appear in such a manner through my mere will. For it is the knowers of the field themselves who are deluded by my *māyā*.

The wise perceive that entities appearing as distinct from one another possess connection with states such as creation and so forth; however, for me, all these entities, even while partaking in their respective states of creation and so forth, [remain] within my own nature, which is characterized solely by non-dual consciousness.

"They are not divided"—by this it is said that these actions do not bind Me, who remains among those works as if indifferent. And thus is the meaning: even though I am their agent, know Me to be the non-agent, the immutable, as has been stated again and again previously [in verse 4.13].
This has been established by such passages as "Actions do not taint me, nor do I have desire for their fruits" (4.14),
and so forth. || 10 ||

If, according to the actual state of things, the Supreme Lord is not thus [directly involved], and yet He appoints this world to its tasks such as creation and so forth, then by whom is this world created? To this He says:
"Under Me as supervisor, Nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving."
By this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.

By me, the Supreme Lord, who am eternally established as pure being alone, acting as the presiding witness and the underlying cause, Nature— whose higher and lower forms have been explained in the seventh chapter through the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious— is indeed nothing but the activity of its own inherent nature.

It gives birth to, that is, it generates, the world consisting of infinite distinctions between the stationary and the moving; for this reason and by this cause, this world revolves, circling within the wheel of the continuous succession of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. || 11 ||
Thus, the foolish disregard me, who have assumed a human form, because they do not know my supreme, imperishable, and unsurpassed nature— me, the sole abode of such wondrous sovereignty.
The deluded— whose knowledge of reality has been stolen away by *māyā*— disregard me, whose essential nature has been explained as such:
though my very nature is illuminated by a perpetually arisen, unsurpassed radiance of light, they treat me with contempt.
Due to the severance of the power and enthusiasm of delusion, they resort to contempt even when desiring to know Me.

In what state do they despise Me? They despise Me while I have assumed a human body; the mention of "human" is for the sake of illustration, [meaning] by way of the distinctions of humans and so forth.
They have resorted to that which consists of the forms of infinite, mutually distinct particularities—a veil that conceals their ultimate essential nature. For this very reason, they are deluded.
Being such as they are, how can they disregard me? By my *māyā* of this kind, my...
But beyond this phenomenal world (prapañca), which is characterized by various conscious and unconscious states, there is something else that is distinct and of a different nature;
likewise, it is imperishable and indestructible, and for that very reason, it is unsurpassed—
meaning that when one investigates further and further for excellence, no other superior or more excellent thing exists.
Because, being ignorant of that such state—that ultimate reality—and thus failing to understand Me due to a lack of such inquiry... || 12 ||
For those fools— whose hopes are vain, whose actions are vain, whose knowledge is vain, and who are devoid of discernment—
have resorted to a delusive nature that is demonic and even fiendish. (13)

They have resorted to *prakṛti*, which by its very nature causes ignorance and is composed of the *guṇas*; their existence is bound by the ego-identification with the body. For this very reason, what kind of *prakṛti* is it? It is *āsuri*, characterized primarily by *tamas* accompanied by a trace of *rajas*. Furthermore—

A *rākṣasī* is one in whom darkness (*tamas*) alone predominates, whose nature was previously explained in the introduction through the classification of the creation of Asuras into superior and inferior types. Since they have resorted to such a nature, they are "those whose hopes are vain"— that is, those whose hopes are fruitless and devoid of result.
Such persons, being of the nature of Asuras and Rākṣasas, and being composed of rajas and tamas,
are possessed by desire; they form only a resolve directed toward objects of enjoyment, but not that which is prescribed in the scriptures as the cause for attaining its fruit.

(p. 205) They undertake actions; therefore, they are called "those whose hopes are vain. Likewise, those whose actions are vain (*moghakarmāṇaḥ*) are such that whatever action they undertake becomes vain—that is, fruitless—due to the absence of the restrictive rules regarding scriptural means (*śāstrīyopāyaniyama*). For he will say later concerning the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* types: [text follows]
The definition of action (karman) is as follows:
"That action which is performed by one desiring objects of desire, or again, by one possessed of egoism (ahaṅkāra),
and which abounds in afflictions (kleśa), is declared to be rājasa."
"Action that is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for consequences, loss, injury, or one's own capacity— that is said to be tāmasa. (18.25) Likewise,
such is also the definition of the agent characterized by tamas.
"One who is full of attachment, who desires the fruits of action, who is greedy, violent by nature, impure,
and possessed by joy and sorrow— such an agent is proclaimed to be rajasic. (18.27) Likewise:
"One who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent, and procrastinating is said to be a doer of tamasic nature" (Gītā 18.28).
Likewise, those whose knowledge is fruitless [are so called] because it lacks the cause for the accomplishment of the action they intend to perform.
Those for whom even the knowledge that precedes the commencement of action is vain and fruitless are described as such; for action is preceded by knowledge, and it is precisely this knowledge—
belonging to a knower who relies on an asuric or other such nature— that is meant.

Because it is connected with the fault of practicing erroneously and because it is inconsistent with the fruit of action, its fruitlessness is indeed established. And so, he will describe even the definition of such knowledge as follows:
"But that knowledge which [perceives] various entities as distinct and of different kinds..."

That which perceives [only] among all beings is remembered as being of the nature of passion (rājasa). Likewise, that which knows nothing fully, which is attached to a single task, and which is without cause— (18.21).

"That which is devoid of the true meaning and meager is declared to be tāmasa" (18.22). Because their knowledge is fruitless, they are "devoid of discernment"; because they lack abidance in the true meaning, even though [the truth] exists, it has departed from them. Since it fails to perform its own function, characterized by right knowledge, it is as if non-existent.
Those whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the mind (cetas) are such [as described]. || 13 ||

Having thus explained the conduct of those who are entirely embraced by illusion and rely upon an asuric nature, [he now describes] those who are favored by knowledge and have become fit vessels for the instruction of the scriptures concerning the spheres of engagement and withdrawal.
Desiring to explain those who rely on the divine nature, [the Lord] first speaks in order to establish those who rely on the supreme divine nature:
"But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, relying on the divine nature..."
They worship with undivided minds, knowing him as the immutable source of all beings.
Therefore, let them take refuge in the divine nature (prakṛti) of the Supreme Goddess— which consists of the higher and lower forms explained in the introduction—

and which is related to those denoted by the word "deva" because it possesses the quality of illuminating perfect knowledge and discernment; that is, let them take refuge in her essential nature (svabhāva).
Thus, these great-souled ones, who are of exalted nature, worship me— the Supreme Self—
with fourfold service, being single-minded because their realization is firmly rooted in the absence of any other object apart from me, in me alone as the sole reality.

Since it is established that "those whose minds [are fixed on Me] are such [devotees]," and that "knowing [Me], they practice," in what manner do they worship Me after having known Me? They worship Me as the *bhūtādi*— the beginning (*ādi*) among all beings, both sentient and insentient— and likewise as the *avyaya*, because of My eternity.
The meaning is that destruction does not exist for me. The purport here is that all beings have a beginning and an end, whereas I am only the beginning and do not have an end. || 14 ||
Moreover:
"Constantly glorifying me, striving with firm vows, and bowing down to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined. (15)

Thus, relying on divine nature, awakened and constantly proclaiming me without interruption through the recitation of mantras, prayers, and hymns; likewise striving through meditation and other means, and bowing down with devotion, they become my devotees.
Being ever united with that which has become the cause, they worship; the meaning is that they attend upon Me by performing activities of speech, mind, and body, making Me their sole object. || 15 ||
Furthermore:
"Others also, sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me—as one, as distinct, and manifoldly as the one whose face is everywhere. (16)

Others, distinct from those previously mentioned who are intent on sacrifice by resorting to well-known modes of devotion, worship and serve Me by means of a sacrifice characterized solely by the meditation upon My own nature as pure consciousness through knowledge.

How do they worship me with the sacrifice of knowledge? By means of oneness—that is, by my own nature as non-dual pure consciousness alone through the abandonment of the entire phenomenal world—and likewise by means of difference, that is, multiplicity; and for this very reason, in many ways, through manifold knowledge.
In terms of its diverse forms such as ritual actions and other attributes that are metaphorically attributed to it, what is its nature in reality?

It is "facing in all directions" (*viśvatomukham*); that is, it is such that every single thing is its "face"—meaning its point of recognition—because there is no difference between it and all that is to be worshipped. This is the intended meaning here.
The ultimate method of worshiping my own nature is twofold:

one has as its means only the knowledge whose object is the single reality that is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*); the other, because that very same reality possesses a multitude of powers for manifesting the various worlds, proceeds by way of those [powers] toward each [particular manifestation].
"Upāsana" (meditative worship). || 16 ||
To demonstrate that very same omnipotence of the one Reality, He says:
"I am the sacrifice, I am the offering, I am the ancestral oblation, and I am the medicinal herb;
I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation. (17)
Although the terms *kratu* and *yajña* are used interchangeably, nevertheless,
in the presence of the word *yajña*, it is specifically the sacrifice characterized by means such as animals and Soma that is denoted here by the word *kratu*.

(p. 208) It has been stated that by the word *yajña* (sacrifice), the *pākayajñas* (domestic sacrifices) are included; therefore, according to the established state of the non-duality of Brahman as explained above, every ritual procedure of sacrifice involving offerings to various deities is indeed myself alone. Likewise, *svadhā*...

I alone am also the mantra for the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*). Likewise, I alone am the medicinal substance consisting of various modifications of herbs, which serves as the material for the sacrificial implements. Similarly, I am the various words denoting diverse objects, such as the invocation of the deities who are the recipients of the offering.

I am the specific form of the mantra, as well as the specific implements of sacrifice; likewise, I am the clarified butter (ājya), the substance for libation; likewise, I am the fire, such as the Āhavanīya, which is the locus for the sacrificial rite;
and likewise, I am the offering, the act of pouring oblations—thus, in the form of sacrifice and so forth.
The intended meaning here is that, according to the principle of the "offering to Brahman" (brahmārpaṇa), I alone remain present. || 17 ||
Furthermore:
"I am the father of this world, the mother, the supporter, and the grandfather;
I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, and also the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus. (18)
He is the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend;
He is the source, the dissolution, the foundation, the treasure-store, and the imperishable seed. (19)

Because I am the fundamental cause of the origin of this entire universe, including all things moving and unmoving, I am both the father and the mother; or rather, just as parents are ever-vigilant in providing for the total welfare and security of their offspring, so am I toward this world.

Likewise, He is the Ordainer (Dhātā), the Sustainer (Dhartā), and the cause of stability. Similarly, He is the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) because, as the creator of the world beginning with Brahmā, He is the progenitor of those who exist. He is the Supreme Purifier (Pavitram Paramam), the object to be known (Vedyam) and realized (Jñeyam). Likewise, He is the syllable Om (Oṃkāra), the designator of the Supreme Brahman.

The *praṇava* is the specific sound that is the beginning of the Vedas, and from it the *ṛc*, *sāman*, and *yajus* mantras originate. Likewise, it is the "going" (*gati*), meaning the means by which the supreme reality is reached or known. Likewise, it is the "supporter" (*bhartṛ*), meaning the nourisher. Likewise, it is the "lord" (*prabhu*), meaning the sole master who has the power to employ [it] as he desires. Likewise, it is the "witness" (*sākṣin*).
He is the presiding witness over auspicious and inauspicious karma; likewise, he is the dwelling place for all beings, the sole abode;
likewise, he is the refuge and the support for the pacification of all calamities; likewise, he is the true friend.

He is the benefactor through his entire being. Likewise, because he is the cause of birth, destruction, and maintenance, he is the source, the dissolution, and the abode. Furthermore, that wherein the dissolved remains—that which consists of the Pradhāna—is the repository. Likewise, that from which [the world] originates is also of the nature of the Pradhāna.
"Imperishable, undecaying seed, cause"—the meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever which I am not of this world. || 19 ||
And so it is said:
"I heat; I withhold and I send forth the rain;
I am both immortality and death, as well as being and non-being, O Arjuna. (20)
Having become the sun at the beginning of summer, I scorch because I then withdraw the moisture;

indeed, it is I who withhold and restrain the rain. And in the rainy season, having become Parjanya, I myself release it through the acts of heating and raining, thereby producing food and other sustenance.

The meaning is: "I alone set the world in motion. Likewise, that which is immortal and indestructible, and even death, the cause of destruction—I alone am that. What is the use of saying more? Whatever exists in the world, whether it be real or beautiful, or whatever is unreal, the opposite of that—[all is I].
All that is my power alone, appearing as a single unity through the state of both being and non-being. || 20 ||
Thus, having briefly described the nature of Brahman in the context of explaining the various types of creation based on the higher divine nature (*paradaivaprakṛti*),
[the author] now [explains] the activity of persons who rely upon the lower divine nature (*aparadaivaprakṛti*).
To explain this, he says:
"The knowers of the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven."
Having attained merit, they enjoy divine celestial pleasures in heaven within the realm of the lord of the gods. || 21 ||
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world,
they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted;
thus do those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas.
Those who desire objects of desire obtain only coming and going. || 22 ||

Those who study or know the three branches of knowledge characterized as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas— the purpose of which culminates in the instruction of mere ritual action devoid of [transcendental] knowledge—
are called *traividyas*. Primarily, these are the members of the three higher castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, whose sins have been purified from the time of conception (*āniṣeka*).

Because they are endowed with the purificatory rites prescribed by the scriptures, their impurities have been destroyed; likewise, being those who have fulfilled the rules of the stages of life (āśrama) such as studentship (brahmacarya) as previously described, they are "drinkers of Soma" (somapāḥ), which means they are devoted to the performance of their own obligatory and occasional duties (nitya-naimittika-svakarma). Being of such a nature, they—

Even though they do not know Me, yet— by means of those various sacrifices prescribed in the scriptures, which take the form of rituals for worshipping other deities— they, being full of desire, worship and honor Me alone, and thereby attain the heavenly state, that is, reaching the world of the gods.
They pray and entreat, for by means of various sacrificial rites they worship those various specific deities;
thus, they worship Me alone, the one Reality whose face is turned everywhere. It is only that, at present, not being favored by the power of knowledge, they do not recognize My supreme nature.

Considering the fruit of rituals such as sacrifices to be mere enjoyment, they long for heaven; such persons, possessing the three Vedas, having gone at the end of their bodies to the vast and extensive world of the gods— the heavenly realm brought about by their own actions— and having experienced the enjoyments found there, [fall].
Having enjoyed [the fruits] in that merit acquired through their own actions, and when that merit is exhausted by the passing of time corresponding to it, they reach the end;
having reached the mortal world, this land of action, they enter—that is, they attain it—by resorting to specific births according to their own karma. Thus, by this...
Gradually, having resorted to and followed their respective duties as prescribed by the three Vedas and their own specific conduct,
even those belonging to the four castes, desiring objects of desire and longing for enjoyments such as heaven, have gone to the state of "gone and come" (repeated birth and death).

They obtain—that is, they attain—the going to realms such as heaven, and their subsequent return from there to the land of action (*karmabhūmi*); the meaning is that, being subject to the bonds of *saṃsāra*, they come into existence again and again. || 21 || 22 ||
Having explained *jñāna* with the preceding portion of the text, He now speaks of *vijñāna*:
"Those people who, thinking of no other, worship Me alone—for those who are ever-devoted, I provide both acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*). (23)

Those persons who have taken refuge in the supreme divine nature, having become dispassionate toward enjoyments consisting of qualities perceived through sight or heard through scripture, which are fraught with defects such as impurity, excess, and decay;

Those who, while not abandoning their own duties, worship me—the Supreme Cause, the Reality of Brahman, which is an ocean of eternal, stainless, unsurpassed, and infinite bliss—serve me from all sides by being established in the knowledge as it has been set forth. Being of what nature? They are *ananya* (non-dual).
The meaning is that those for whom no other object exists apart from Me experience all this as consisting of Me alone; such are they—
those who are eternally devoted, being constantly engaged through the one-pointedness of the aforementioned knowledge.
The meaning is: for those who, in all circumstances, are solely intent on remembering my true nature as it has been described;

I, the Supreme Lord, carry out their *yogakṣema*—*yoga*, which is the connection with the fruit consisting of the realization of my own nature not previously attained, and *kṣema*, the preservation of what has already been attained.

Furthermore, I maintain that the characteristic is non-loss; the meaning is that for those who are eternally absorbed in Me, how could there be any loss of their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*)? Thus, by virtue of having established the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the state of being free from the defects of the aforementioned means.
The essential meaning is that devotion itself, having ascended to the supreme pinnacle consisting of the experience of my own true nature, is what constitutes realized knowledge (vijñāna). || 23 ||

But surely, since you alone are the one Reality whose face is turned everywhere, even those who worship other deities are in fact non-different [from you]. Why, then, was it said: "I carry the acquisition and preservation of those who worship Me with no other [thought]"?
To this, he says:
Even those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith, they too, O son of Kuntī, worship me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.

It is true that even those people who, as devotees of other deities, worship various specific gods such as the Sun, Indra, and others— though they appear distinct from one another— they too, in the ultimate sense, worship Me alone with faith, because there exists no second reality apart from Me.

They sacrifice and worship with the expectation of various distinct fruits, but not according to the prescribed rule. Such a rule for sacrifice has already been stated and will be further explained; namely, that one should remain established in the knowledge as described regarding all the specific deities to be worshipped, the various sacrificial acts, and the sacrificer himself.

The experience of one's own true nature, characterized as non-dual pure consciousness within oneself, is not possible as a prescribed injunction for those who rely solely on mere ritual action devoid of knowledge;
therefore, it is said that they sacrifice without being preceded by such an injunction. || 24 ||
To reveal this very point, he says:
"For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall. (25)

Of all sacrifices, of the various types of rituals, I alone am the Supreme Lord, the sole enjoyer and the one who accepts the fruit. Likewise, I am the Master, presiding over the action of the substratum. All sacrifices are indeed I; it is not otherwise.
They do not recognize Me in truth, in the ultimate sense, as described; they do not realize Me as one.
For this reason, such performers fall away—they become separated from Me—meaning that they perceive everything through the lens of manifoldness. || 25 ||
And so, those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors;
those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me go to me.

Those for whom the vow—the discipline—is for the sake of the gods, they are the worshippers of Śakra and other deities; being "devavrata," they go to the gods themselves upon the successful completion of that service, meaning they become partakers of those worlds. Likewise, those who are "pitṛvrata" go to the ancestors. Similarly...
Those for whom sacrifice (ijyā)— that is, ritual offering— is intended for beings such as yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas,
go to those very [beings] as before. Those who sacrifice to the gods and ancestors are characterized by sattva.

But those who sacrifice to the elemental spirits (bhūtas) are characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa). As it has been said: "Those of goodness (sāttvika) worship the gods; those of passion (rājasa) worship the yakṣas and rākṣasas;
and those people of darkness (tāmasa) worship the departed spirits (pretas), the bhūtas, and the piśācas" (17.4).

Thus: those who are free from the three qualities (guṇas) are "worshippers of Me" (madyājinaḥ)—those whose nature it is to worship Me alone, whose essential form transcends the three qualities; they go to, that is, attain, My very own nature as the Supreme Brahman. || 26 ||
And that sacrifice of intoxicants is not at all like the sacrifices of Devavrata and others, which require the collection of various specific materials; thus he says:
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water..."
Therefore, I eat what is offered with devotion by one whose self is disciplined.

Devotion (*bhakti*) is the worship of one's own self, or of various specific deities, through the contemplation of the reality of Brahman, whose nature is non-dual pure consciousness. By means of that devotion as a spiritual practice,
whatever— even a mere leaf or something small— a knower of reality offers to me, that belongs to him.

I eat—that is, I enjoy—what is offered by one whose self is thus purified and whose internal organ is concentrated in such non-dual knowledge; the meaning is that I accept it exactly as it is offered with whatever particular state of contemplation. || 27 ||
Therefore, whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away,
and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me. (28)

Whatever you do— that action which you perform out of a desire for its fruit— and whatever you eat— that which you enjoy as the result of that action— all that you must offer unto Me; that is, an offering made unto Me, whose nature is Brahman, by means of the realization that I am your very self.

(214) Perform—that is, accomplish—that task. He explains that such a task is established as having various fruits for those devoid of knowledge: "that which you offer" (*juhoṣi*)—meaning that which you cast into the fire by means of the act of oblation (*havana*) in various sacrifices for the purpose of satiating the respective deities—and that which...

Whatever austerity or specific observance you perform when giving to worthy recipients at the sacrificial altar and other such occasions— that entire practice, you must offer unto Me. In all necessary actions characterized by sacrifice, charity, and austerity,
do this by abandoning the wretchedness of desiring their respective fruits.
The meaning is: "Take as your sole fruit the very experience of my true nature. || 28 ||
He states the fruit of this meditation:
"In this way, you shall be released from the bonds of karma through their very fruits, both auspicious and inauspicious.
With your self united in the yoga of renunciation, liberated, you shall come to Me. (29)
In this manner, even while performing your own rites such as sacrifices and the like,
you shall be liberated from the fruits of those actions— whether auspicious, consisting of happiness, or inauspicious, consisting of suffering— and they shall not lead to your bondage.

The meaning is that they will conceptualize. By what means? By the bonds of karma (*karmabandhana*). Karma refers to those actions devoid of knowledge; "bond" refers to that which is the cause of restriction. It is by such [actions] that the fruits, being bound by karma, bind one who is devoid of knowledge, but not otherwise.

Endowed with the knowledge as described, you— therefore, with your self joined through the yoga of renunciation, that is, through the meditative absorption of non-attachment to fruits, and thus being liberated, having emerged from all bonds— [attain] Me alone, the supreme cause.
"You shall attain" means "you yourself shall become [that]. || 29 ||

Now, one might object: "Since you become a cause of bondage for some who serve you through sacrificial rites and the like, yet a cause of liberation for others who offer leaves and such, does this not imply that even you are subject to attachment and aversion? To this, he replies:
I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear.
But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I also am in them.
Since, in all beings who have spread forth through the fourteenfold manifestation (*prapañca*),

the ultimate reality (*tattva*) is in fact one, I am identical with the supreme reality (*paratattva*), equal, and of undifferentiated function; therefore, because there is no existence apart from me, nothing whatsoever is hateful to me.

Neither is one who is dear a cause for the fault of passion; these two are attached only to those who perceive duality. Therefore, those great souls who, by my will alone, through the grace of the power of knowledge, become seers of the single reality and [perceive] me as I have described my true nature—
Those who worship and serve with the devotion described above, and who meditate with the realization described above, abide in Me;

and I likewise abide in them in a state of absolute non-duality. This is because, through Me, the bridge of the perception of insurmountable difference between them and Me has been shattered, and they have become of one identical flavor within the ocean of the nectar of Brahman.
Of each respective distinction. || 30 ||

Thus, by means of the aforementioned meditation, He speaks a praise of devotion to the Blessed One: "Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved. (31)

Even though, according to the view propounded by you, he may be one whose conduct is exceedingly wicked due to the performance of terrible deeds such as war, if he is a devotee of no other— having Me alone as his support— and worships Me,
such a person should be considered and understood as a truly virtuous man of good conduct; for:

Because his knowledge is correct and free from error, he is devoted accordingly, being thus resolute and having firmly adopted that resolve. This alone is the defining characteristic of right conduct (*sadācāra*) and misconduct (*durācāra*): he who is my devotee with undivided devotion is one of right conduct; anyone other than that is of misconduct.

This much is the essential point here: for the power of the Blessed One, whose will is beyond questioning, has descended upon some recipient to be graced, and all wickedness has been utterly and root-and-branch destroyed.
To reveal this very point, he says:
"He quickly becomes righteous in soul and attains eternal peace;
O son of Kuntī, I promise you: my devotee does not perish. (32)
Immediately, at the very moment of receiving grace, he becomes one whose self is Dharma— that is,

he becomes such that his supreme self-nature (ātman-svabhāva) is characterized by the yoga of knowledge as it has been taught. As soon as he has become thus endowed, [he remains] forever, at all times.

He attains peace— that is, the cessation of the agitation characterized by the mental state of knowing objects of knowledge such as the self and non-self as they have been explained— specifically, the profound tranquility consisting of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) upon the reality (*tattva*) as it has been described.

He attains it. In the reading "niyacchati" (he restrains), he restrains it within himself, making it fixed and unfailing. And for that reason, I make a promise to you: that my devotee—one who worships me in the manner described—does not perish.
