It does not undergo destruction characterized by the realization of its distinction from my own nature. || 32 ||
Therefore, He said:
"For even those who may be of low birth—women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—even they, O Pārtha, attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in Me. (33)
How much more so, then, O meritorious brahmins and royal sages who are my devotees!
Having reached this world which is impermanent and full of suffering, worship me. (34)
Those who are born into a sinful womb— that is, those for whom the cause of their birth is the ripening of evil karma—
whether they be women, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, or anyone else whatsoever, by taking refuge in Me and becoming as described my sole resort, shall attain the supreme, unsurpassed goal.

They attain the state from which there is no return. And it has already been explained previously that this is not merely a figure of speech (atiśayokti). What more need be said here? Those who are meritorious, performers of virtuous deeds, and who have attained superior births as Brahmins through the ripening of their meritorious karma—[they attain this state].
And the royal sages (*rājarṣi*), being in the state of kingship,

because they partake in liberation, are the primary sages— seers and devotees— who shall attain the supreme goal. Thus, by this, the universality of self-knowledge for all the worlds [is established].

The Blessed One has taught this: since my devotion yields such an exalted fruit, therefore, having reached this world—meaning, having obtained birth here in this realm characterized as the land of action (*karmabhūmi*)—worship me. Of what kind is this world? It is impermanent, [being the locus] of the body and the instruments of enjoyment.

Furthermore, because enjoyments are finite, they are unstable and unhappy. Even that which is grasped here through the delusion of happiness, when examined with a discerning intellect, is nothing but suffering. As it has been said:

To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the guṇas. (Yoga Sūtra 2.15)
"And because of the conflict between the functions of the qualities (guṇas), everything is suffering for the discerning person.

Just as the acquisition of a supreme jewel by one fallen into the midst of the ocean might somehow be possible, so too is the acquisition of devotion to Me possible for one fallen into the land of karma, which has nothing but suffering as its cause.
The meaning is that this is indeed possible in this world. || 34 ||
Having obtained this world of such a nature, He says: "Devote yourself to Me, the cause of unsurpassed happiness:
'Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.'"
Thus, having disciplined yourself and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone.

Being such as this, become My devotee. Of what nature? One whose mind is fixed on Me (*manmanāḥ*), who sacrifices to Me (*madyājī*), and likewise one who is intent on saluting Me (*mannamaskāraparaḥ*). By these three qualifications, there is the characteristic of the unity of the single reality defined by the Lord's own nature within the activities of the mind, body, and speech.

The primary mode of devotion has been set forth. For by the words "bow down to me," prostration toward the Blessed One in the form of mantra-recitation, salutation, praise, and so forth, is expressed. In this manner, by this method—

Having yoked the self—that is, having concentrated the internal organ—and being devoted to Me, having become one whose sole support is Me, you shall come to Me alone; you shall attain non-difference from Me. Om. 35.

In that [state], where the mass of objects shines forth with extreme clarity, preceded by knowledge and realization, its own stainless serenity blossoms twofold— like the host of luminaries in the sky when it has become clear through the subsiding of thick darkness, and like the sun, moon, and others.
In this ninth chapter, may the goddess of speech move like a royal swan.

Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* named *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meanings of the statements, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Thus,
[the subject] has been explained through various types of lucid yet profound expressions woven together in the concluding portion of the ninth chapter.

Having observed that Arjuna’s heart was filled with a particular satisfaction arising from hearing the meaning of the supreme secret concerning knowledge, discernment, and so forth, yet was simultaneously dissatisfied because this matter is the ultimate reality that is exceedingly difficult to comprehend;

Approaching with exceptional serenity and compassion, the Blessed One spoke these words, which manifested his desire to bestow unsurpassed grace— the very cause for the direct realization of the supreme reality as described in various places:
Listen once more, O mighty-armed one, to my supreme word, which I shall speak to you, who are pleased with me, out of a desire for your welfare. (1)

Although the subject matter to be taught has for the most part been explained in detail and without remainder, nevertheless, because of its extreme subtlety, it does not immediately find a firm footing in the hearts even of those possessed of the highest intelligence; therefore, I shall once again elaborate further upon that which was previously stated by me.
Listen to this most excellent speech, for it is preeminent because it establishes the supreme goal.

He states the reason for speaking so many words: "That speech which brings satisfaction to you, who are being pleased, I [shall speak] to you out of a desire for your welfare—that is, with the wish to bring about ultimate well-being."

Now I shall speak. What is meant by this? [It is that which]—by the touch of a mere fraction of the supreme nectar of the ultimate meaning of the subject matter presented, which removes the sorrow of the poison of delusion so difficult to extract through other means—[brings about liberation].

If the heart is not gladdened, how can there be joy? Therefore, for one in such a state, there would be only agitation from the repetition of what has already been said. Consequently, [the author], whose heart is permeated with compassion and who desires to act for the benefit of that disciple whose specific qualities have been revealed through his state of joy, [proceeds].

The Blessed One’s intention is that the supreme guide should instruct by means of various modes of expression until the disciple, having properly grasped the meaning, reaches a state of being free from further inquiry; thus, you should not be distressed by the repetition of words. Alternatively:

When the words of the Blessed One— which suddenly dispel the sleep of delusion, bestow the splendor of inner awakening upon seekers whose efforts toward their desired goals have become fruitful, and which ever renew themselves— have come forth, what conscious person would not be moved?
It will incur a sense of agitation born from redundancy, as if among the rays of the sun.

In this context, the goal—which consists precisely in the realization of my own nature—has been stated and will be further explained. Since that nature of mine is most secret, it cannot be understood or taught with little effort; therefore, be attentive to hearing these many words. || 1 ||
For this reason: "Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin;
for I am, in every respect, the source of the gods and the great seers. (2)

The hosts of gods—the multitudes of deities such as Brahmā, Indra, Sūrya, and others—do not know, that is, they do not understand, the origin or production (*prabhava*) of my single, eternal reality from the perspective of ultimate truth; or, if the reading is *prabhāva*, [they do not know] its majesty. [Nor do] the great seers (*maharṣayaḥ*).
Bhṛgu and the others are likewise; for they,
having their respective forms, powers, and so forth manifested by the power of my *māyā*, perform their various offices in every *kalpa*.
I, however, am their first and foremost because of my eternity, as they partake in states associated with impermanent conditions such as creation and dissolution. Thus, by way of this excellence,
even gods and others who endure for long periods such as a kalpa are, in comparison to my supreme existence, [merely temporary].

They are finite; and being deluded by my illusory power (māyā), their capacity is sufficient only for the fulfillment of their own specific offices, so that they do not know me in reality at this time. || 2 ||
Then:
"He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—he, undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins. (3)

(p. 221) Whoever is a rare great soul, whose power of right knowledge has arisen solely through my grace—he [perceives] the Unborn, who is devoid of birth because of his eternity, and for that very reason beginningless (*anādi*), meaning there is no other preceding person; likewise, he perceives the Great Lord of the worlds (*lokamaheśvara*) of all worlds.

The "Lord" (svāmin) is the supreme master of those people denoted by the word *loka*— meaning those who are seen, perceived, and known, beginning with Brahmā— because He possesses the independent power to ordain their great states of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth.

For even for those beginning with Brahmā, their sovereignty extends only as far as their own respective domains; in that regard, I am the cause—this is the meaning. He who knows Me in this way, who recognizes Me as the Self among mortals—that is, among gods and others who are subject to death because they are encompassed by Māyā—[attains immortality].

The meaning is that among all living beings, he is undeluded; because his conviction regarding the Self has taken firm root in Me alone—the True Self—there exists in him no delusion characterized by error, which is ignorance. For this very reason, [he is free] from all [actions] performed without remainder by means of mind, speech, and body.
One is liberated from, or completely freed from, sins—the various impurities that serve as the causes for rebirth in different species.

For the mere egoism established upon impermanent things such as the body is indeed the cause of the arising of all sins; however, for one who possesses right knowledge, that [egoism] does not exist. Thus it is said:
"He is called 'unconfused'. || 3 ||
Explaining further that very state of being the Great Lord of the world, which was described as being the cause of all conditions for all beings,
he says: "Intellect, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, and tranquility..."
Happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence, fear and fearlessness as well. || 4 ||
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—these various states of beings arise from Me alone. (5)
In this regard, it has already been demonstrated many times that I alone am the one reality, existing as the ultimate truth (*paramārthasat*).

Furthermore, this multitude of fields (*kṣetra*), divided into the two classes of gods and asuras, has been manifested in this manner solely by my *māyā*. Thus, it is also the case for this multitude of knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Proceeding by taking recourse to that *ahaṅkāra*,
the various and manifold states such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth arise— that is, they are produced— from me alone, the single cause. For these diverse [states]...

When the various states of existence are examined by the awakened through the vision of the knowledge of reality, they do not differ even slightly from my supreme nature. Therefore, this appearance of things as distinct is merely *māyā*; and since that is indeed my own power, it proceeds from me.

It has been stated that "these are the states (bhāvas) [of the Self]. What are those states? Intellect (*buddhi*) is the primary internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by which the object to be known is perceived—that is, determined through non-conceptualization. Knowledge (*jñāna*), however, is the specific internal organ designated as the mind (*manas*), by which...

The object to be known is conceptualized. These two states, designated as intellect (*buddhi*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), are common to all cognizers. Non-delusion is knowledge established in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
All other knowledge, having different objects, is associated with defects such as error (*viparyaya*) and the like.
It consists of the nature of non-delusion. And that state characterized by non-delusion belongs only to those seeking liberation.
Forbearance is the absence of transformation through speech, mind, or action;
it is the capacity to endure the offenses of others with one's whole being, even when one possesses the power [to retaliate]. This too [is required] in the stage of the ascetic (yati) and others.

Dharma is the means to liberation for those seeking release (*mumukṣu*). For in another stage [of life], since the non-abandonment of one's own duties—by virtue of being established in knowledge—is a means to liberation, even that which is "incompetent" (i.e., incapable of producing immediate results) becomes a means to liberation when enjoined by the scriptures. This is true.
The definitive statement of things as they have been perceived, culminating in the ultimate welfare of living beings,

is common to those who seek the fruits of heaven and liberation. Self-restraint (*dama*) follows from the striking of the bridle— namely, the cultivation of dispassion and so forth— upon all the horses of the senses that have strayed onto wrong paths.

Refraining is tranquility (*śama*), which is the state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) remaining unchanged whether success or failure occurs. These two pertain to the domain of the yogi. Pleasure (*sukha*) is the state of a contented mind resulting from the cessation of longing upon obtaining various desired objects. Pain (*duḥkha*) is the opposite of that. Existence and non-existence (*bhavābhāvau*) refer to birth and death.

Fear is the dread arising from the cause of suffering due to the difficulty of its remedy; fearlessness is the absence of that, which is a state of mind free from apprehension. These qualities, such as happiness and the rest, are states common to all living beings.
Non-violence consists in the absence of malice toward all creatures.

(223) Complete abstention from malice is [the means]. And that [abstention] is a means to liberation only in states such as that of an ascetic (*yati*), because, like the non-endurance of injury, it serves as a means to liberation in other states.
For instance, killing and the like enjoined by the scriptures in sacrifice, or the slaying of enemies in battle [do not constitute malice in those specific contexts].

Furthermore, the restraint of the wicked, although it consists of violence, is a means to liberation for virtuous people who are devoted to their own specific duties. Equanimity toward enemies, friends, noble ones, and neutrals— [is likewise a means to liberation]. (6.9)

By such statements as these, it is shown that the vision of the single reality whose nature was previously explained is the duty (*dharma*) of those alone who seek liberation (*mumukṣu*). Contentment directed toward all beings is a state of mind pertaining specifically to those seeking liberation, because happiness has been established as being common to all. As for austerity (*tapas*):

It is a specific restraint brought about by speech, mind, and body. Giving (*dāna*) consists of transferring one's own property into the state of another's property, distinguished as *iṣṭa* (sacrificial rites) and *pūrta* (charitable works); however, in the case of knowledge and so forth, giving is their transmission to another without the cessation of one's own ownership. This [is for] those who seek the fruits of heaven and liberation.

Common [to all]. Fame is the praise directed toward all people resulting from the performance of auspicious actions enjoined by the scriptures with a *sāttvika* intellect. Infamy is the lack of praise resulting from conduct contrary to that. (4–5)
He says that the substrata (dharmin) which serve as the locus for such phenomena (dharma) originate from me alone, even up to the Prajāpatis:
"The seven great sages of old, as well as the four Manus."
Those who were born from my mind through my own nature became these progeny in the world.

Because they existed during the prior period consisting of the Manvantara of Svāyambhuva at the commencement of the previous Kalpa, the seven great sages (maharṣis) beginning with Marīci, who were previously declared to be the ancient Prajāpatis, are [referred to] as the first.

Some, however, speak of seven great seers (*maharṣis*), namely intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), and the five great elements (*mahābhūta*); they say that these too are "lords of creatures" (*prajāpatis*) because they are the causes of the creation of beings.
(p. 224) There are four Manus: Brahmasāvarṇa, Rudrasāvarṇa, Dakṣasāvarṇa, and [Dharmasāvarṇa].
Born from the daughter of Dakṣa at the beginning of the creation of beings, these were the first men for each of the four castes;
because they were the cause of the origin of the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, they possess the status of Manu and Prajāpati.
These are "of my nature," meaning that their existence and origin proceed from me alone, the supreme cause.

"Of such a kind": being what sort? "Possessing my nature," meaning born from my mind, that is, produced from volition (*saṃkalpa*). These creatures in the worlds—the various realms—are connected to those Prajāpatis who are heard of as the creators of progeny at the beginning of the Kalpa.
The meaning is that they possess the state of being creators manifested by the mere measure of my will. || 6 ||
He states the fruit of such knowledge of His sovereignty:
"He who knows this glory and yoga of Mine in truth, he is joined by unshakable yoga; there is no doubt in this. (7)

This aforementioned majesty (*vibhūti*)— the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consisting of being the creator of the world and so forth— and likewise this Yoga, characterized by the non-deviation from the nature of non-dual pure consciousness even while connected with agency and the manifestation of the manifold variety of existents, is most wonderful and unparalleled.
He who knows and understands my *raṇa* (battle) in its true and ultimate sense— that person is joined with, or connected to, my very own unshakable yoga, which is at all times free from affliction;
there can be no doubt whatsoever regarding this matter, because:
He who correctly contemplates the manifestation (*vibhava*) of the world as the nature of my very self— the single reality that has appeared through the perfect knowledge born of my grace—
becomes connected with my meditative absorption (*samādhi*) because he is absorbed into my own essential nature; what more is there to say?
There is room for doubt. || 7 ||
Because He is of such a nature—thinking, "He is the source of all; from Him everything proceeds"—the wise worship Me with devoted hearts. (8)
The wise worship me by my will alone, because they possess a state of being whose creation rests upon divine nature;
having become vessels for my grace, their awakening has manifested,
and as preeminent scholars, they worship me in the form described, but not others.

Those whose dispositions belong to the demonic creation are then joined with my meditative absorption (*samādhi*). And having done what do they worship? Thinking thus, that is, having ascertained my true nature in this way—how so?—[they realize]:
"This Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, is the source of the entire multitude of beings."
Since the cause of origination has been demonstrated many times through the force of logical arguments, and because there is no other cause apart from this,
it is for this very reason that all this proceeds and expands. This is the intended meaning here.
Knowledge is twofold:
one is that which generates a firm conviction based on the instruction of the treatises that demonstrate the non-conceptual ultimate reality;
and another, arising from that [first], is the direct realization of reality produced through a gradual process. Those who possess these are the wise.
They are also of two kinds. Therefore, as has been stated, those who possess knowledge of the yoga of My twofold majesty are united with My samādhi;
thus there is no doubt in this matter—so it was said. || 8 ||
But as for those who worship me, their conduct is of this kind; thus he says:
"With their minds fixed on me, their lives surrendered to me, enlightening one another and constantly speaking of me, they are contented and they rejoice. (9)

With their minds fixed on Me— those whose internal organ (citta) is directed toward Me, such that the expansion of their knowledge and action is centered solely on Me— they inform one another, making it known through the corroboration of their own experience, and likewise speak of it.

Proclaiming according to their understanding through the words of the scriptures, they are satisfied by the correspondence [with truth], they themselves rejoice, they delight with one another, and they experience pleasure. || 9 ||
And to those such as these—
who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love— I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me. (10)
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.
To those wise ones who, by virtue of their very wisdom,

serve [Me] with affection— preceded by the satisfaction born from the knowledge of reality— and who are for that very reason ever-striving, I grant the yoga of the intellect, that is, the connection with higher wisdom (prajñā), by which...
"By being the cause, the wise come to me and attain my yoga"—
thus has the cause for the devotees' attainment of His own yoga been established beyond doubt;
for it is for the sake of compassion toward them alone, who partake of the divine creation, that [He acts] by severing the afflictions of saṃsāra.

Out of compassion, I shall destroy and utterly eliminate the darkness born of ignorance, arisen from delusion, consisting of the failure to realize reality— by means of the radiant lamp of knowledge, endowed with the light of supreme consciousness.
By means of the lamp of awakening as described. Being of what nature? Abiding in one's own being (*ātmabhāvastha*).

"Being" (*bhāva*) refers to the state of self (*ātmatva*), that is, the nature of the self who experiences; thus, he abides by that. Although the single Self, "I," is all-pervading, nevertheless, by its own will, it [resides] only in those whom it favors.

The meaning is that I abide as the Self, whereas others have the notion of the Self in the body and so forth. Thus, those whom I favor— being knowers of the truth regarding My manifestations (*vibhūti*) and Yoga— they worship Me in the manner described, [realizing] My very Yoga.
They enter [into that state], which means they attain liberation characterized by the destruction of intoxication.
As the knowers of Brahman have said:
"This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing."
He alone whom this Self chooses can obtain Him; to him this Self reveals its own form.
(Maṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 3.2.3; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.23).
Then, having understood the true nature of the Blessed One directly from the Blessed One’s own mouth— due to his distinguished qualities such as faith resulting from the Blessed One’s words—
Arjuna spoke in order to inquire about the specific details of His manifestations (vibhūtis): [Arjuna said:]
You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and the highest purity; you are the eternal, divine Puruṣa, the primordial God, unborn and all-pervading.
All the sages, as well as the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa, have told you this; and you yourself are telling it to me. (13)
In the ultimate sense, you alone, O Blessed One, are that reality which is supreme, unsurpassed, characterized as the Supreme Self, and endowed with such qualities as incomparable greatness;
for there exists no other entity apart from Brahman, other than that which is manifested through *māyā*.

Because even the gross objects of knowledge, such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the rest, are designated by the word "Brahman," Brahman is here specified as being "supreme" (*para*). As he will state later, and as it has been said:
"Of those [energies], the Great Brahman is the source" (14.4).

Thus, in this context, the term *brahman* is used as a designation for *prakṛti*; likewise, in the passage "he transcends the word-Brahman" (6.46), it refers to the creation consisting of the forms of words such as the scriptures and so forth. Similarly, [in the case of] the supreme...
You are the light, the unsurpassed abode whose nature is universal consciousness.

The qualification "abode" is further specified as being supreme even in comparison to the consciousness associated with the field (*kṣetra*) that has differentiation as its object. Likewise, you are the highest, the most excellent, the pure, and the purifier.

The characteristic of delusion is its being the cause for the destruction of great sins. To demonstrate that the means for understanding the aforementioned meaning is scripture (*āgama*) and the words of the Blessed One (*bhagavad-vacana*), he says: "Because all the sages (*ṛṣi*), the seers of the higher and the lower, [perceive] the eternal, perpetual Puruṣa..."
They call You the Supreme Self; they describe You as such. Of what nature? Divine, residing in the supreme ether. Likewise, the Origin, prior to all.
A God, whose nature is to shine by virtue of being the light of the highest reality, and therefore unborn, devoid of birth. All-pervading.
It is all-pervasive. Not only all the sages, but even the great seers named Nārada, Asita, and Devala speak of You in this very way; and You Yourself speak directly to me.
I consider all this that you tell me, O Keśava, to be true;
for even the gods and the great seers do not know your manifestation, O Blessed One.
(228) O Supreme Person, O Source of all beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Master of the universe, you alone know yourself by yourself. 15.

I consider all this—which you speak of directly as the nature of your own manifested power (*vibhūti*), yoga, and so forth—to be *ṛta*, that is, the truth; for even the gods do not know your ultimate manifestation, nor do the great seers (*maharṣis*) likewise know it. Therefore...

"Previously, when I heard this from the great sages, I had no conviction; but now, by the word of the Blessed One, my understanding of this matter is free from doubt. As for the reason why the gods and sages do not know you, he himself states it in the words beginning with 'svayam' (by himself), etc.: O Lord of the world, O Sovereign of the universe, O Creator of all beings."

He is the creator merely by bringing about the state of being perceivable through meditation for all beings, both moving and unmoving; likewise, he is the Lord (īśa), the Master (svāmin), who is himself, by his own self, solely independent in the exercise of their disposal according to his will.

You know yourself as your own true nature because your sole essential being is that of the knower; how then could you descend into the state of being an object of knowledge for another, such as a god? For everything is the object of knowledge for you alone, the omniscient one, but you are not the object of knowledge for anyone. (14–15)
Therefore, for that reason,
you ought to describe in their entirety your auspicious manifestations (vibhūtis),
by which manifestations you abide pervading these worlds.

"You ought to speak—that is, be gracious enough to tell—your own manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*), which are the expansions of your sovereignty, in their entirety and without omission. Of what kind are these manifestations? They are "auspicious" (*śubhāḥ*), pertaining to everything that exists as established through the distinction between the real and the unreal, and manifested by *māyā*.
The meaning is: since the multitude of objects in the world consists of both auspicious and inauspicious, command whatever auspicious manifestation exists in whichever creation;
that is, ordain each such auspicious form. What are those manifestations?
They are those by which you exist, pervading and encompassing these seven worlds. In this regard—

Some read the text as "divyā ātmavibhūtayaḥ" with the nominative case ending; they justify this either by supplying the correlative pronouns *yat* and *tat*, or by treating it as a Vedic usage. || 16 ||
He states the purpose for hearing of His manifestations:
"O Great Yogi, how may I contemplate You, knowing Your true nature? And in what various forms, O Blessed One, are You to be meditated upon by me? (17)
O Janārdana, speak again in detail of Your own yoga and majesty; for there is no satiety for me as I drink this nectar.
O Blessed One, sole refuge of qualities such as omniscience, great yogin,

uniquely established in a samādhi not shared by others— how and in what manner may I come to know the vidyā by reflecting upon and recollecting You who possess such a form? And in which various [contexts]?

Among all existing things and objects, you are to be contemplated— that is, you are to be meditated upon— by me. Therefore, this aforementioned sovereignty, meditative absorption, and manifestation of power,
characterized by the appearance of the world, has been described in detail, that is, with full expansion, as the unfolding of my own sovereign majesty.

Tell me more, speak further; for as I listen to this nectar—the essence of ambrosia characterized by the exposition of Your true nature—drinking it with my two ears, there is no satiety or contentment. (17–18)
Thus requested, the Blessed One said:
"Very well, O best of the Kurus, I shall describe to you my auspicious manifestations according to their principal ones; there is no end to my full extent."
Very well, since you have agreed, I shall indeed describe to you my auspicious manifestations exactly as you desire to hear them. However, among the conscious and unconscious entities—
which are divided into an infinite variety of classes— whatever specific manifestation exists within whichever particular class;
Because it is preeminent, I shall describe each of those superlative manifestations (vibhūti), since there is no end— that is, no final limit— to the expansion and vastness of my manifestations. (19)

Now, at the conclusion of this introduction concerning the description of various manifestations (*vibhūti*), [the author] speaks first in order to establish the supreme manifestation characterized by the nature of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svarūpa-lakṣaṇā parā vibhūtiḥ*), which will be described later:
I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings;
I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.
The Self, I, am established and firmly rooted in the heart—the seat of consciousness—of all sentient beings.

In the ultimate sense, the Self is one alone, whose nature is universal consciousness manifested within the hearts of all knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*). That indeed is the supreme manifestation (*parā vibhūti*), for this [universe] is dependent upon it alone.

I am the manifold expansion of various manifestations whose nature consists of the entire universe revealed by my own power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*). When meditated upon as being of that very nature, I become known as the sole cause of the vast extension of infinite manifestations; for I am the beginning—the prior state consisting of creation—of all beings, and also their end.

The state of destruction is the middle, and the state of persistence is "I alone. For, by the power of my *māyā*, I alone—whose nature is eternally and undifferentiated pure consciousness—abide within all beings who appear to one another as being joined with the states of creation, persistence, and destruction. By those [who perceive otherwise]...
By such a great pervasiveness, I am impossible to conceive; therefore,

for the sake of practicing the realization of that [pervasiveness], wherever in whatever group there is anything superior, those who consider each of those things as a portion of my own glory shall attain a state that is unsurpassed and all-pervading.
My supreme manifestation, whose nature is universal consciousness, can be realized even at the conclusion of the section explaining various manifestations,
as that which is distinct from the inert portion consisting of the general form.
"I pervading this entire world stand with but one part" (10.42)— thus he will say later. Therefore, in such an expansion of the creation of beings consisting of fourteen kinds,
within the eightfold divine origins among the creations of gods and others beginning with the Ādityas, and within the sixfold...
In the wombs of humans and other beings, and within the creations of humans and others, whatever is most excellent—

that should be contemplated as a mere fragment of my supreme light. Thus, [the Goddess] is the Supreme (Parā), consisting of the manifestation of an unsurpassed, preeminent, and extraordinary consciousness.
The purport of this chapter is that My divine manifestation (vibhūti) is to be realized. || 20 ||
Now, in order to demonstrate those various portions of His own glory through the sense of "I," He says:
"Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among luminaries I am the radiant Sun."
Among the Maruts I am Marīci; among the stars I am the Moon.

Since all gods are sons of Āditya, they would all technically qualify as Ādityas; however, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the name "Āditya" is well-established for a specific group of deities mentioned in the Purāṇas—namely Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, and so forth—who are delimited by the number twelve. Among these, [the following occurs]:

I am the Sun-god named Viṣṇu, who is recited among that group [of Ādityas]. Because of my possession of the excellence of power characterized by the maintenance and protection of the world, I possess a portion of my own sovereign majesty.
Likewise, among the luminaries shining in the sky, I am Ravi (the Sun), the source of all splendors.

I am the Sun. Of what nature? He is "possessing rays" (*aṃśumān*), meaning that while possessing rays for the purpose of illuminating the entire world, he is endowed with preeminent rays; for this very reason, he is a partial manifestation (*vibhūty-aṃśa*) of my power. Likewise, [I am] of the winds...

Among the forty-nine specific classes of gods, I consider myself to be the wind-god named Marīci. Because he possesses the power characterized by being the creator of the progeny within that group, he is a portion of my own manifestation. Likewise, among the twenty-eight constellations—

In the middle is the moon, Śaśin; I am that moon. Because the moon is the lord of the constellations (nakṣatras), it is counted among them; and because it possesses the power of being the cause of nourishment and so forth, it is a portion of my own manifestation. || 21 ||
With that same vision, He spoke of others as well:
"Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods I am Vāsava;
among the senses I am the mind; and among beings I am consciousness. (22)
Among the three or four Vedas that are well-known,
I am the Sāmaveda; its preeminence was revealed by the Blessed One himself when the Vedas had been lost.
Having uttered the *udgītha* as the person with the face of a horse (*vājivadanapuruṣa*), he himself was previously withdrawn [into me];
therefore, he is a portion of my own manifestation. Among the gods enumerated in the Purāṇas according to the divisions of the thirty-three groups, I am Vāsava, Indra. Of him—
Because He is the Lord, the mind is a portion of My manifestation (*vibhūti*). Among the eleven senses, the mind is "I" because it is predominant as the cause of their engagement and withdrawal;
thus, being predominant, it is a portion of My manifestation. Beings are of two kinds: moving and stationary.

For both of these [classes], consciousness is primary, because the existence of moving beings is well known to be characterized by consciousness; and even the arrangement of stationary beings is based on consciousness, since they are capable of volition when favored by it. Therefore:
I am the consciousness established as the preeminence among all beings; though undivided, I am the power of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).

By virtue of its primacy, it constitutes a portion of my manifestation. Some, however, designate consciousness as the intellect (*buddhi*); and of that [intellect], there are those which have emanated through the distinction between cause and effect.

They say that among insentient beings alone she possesses preeminence; for she causes all those [beings] to perceive by means of the state of consciousness arising from the proximity of the Puruṣa. || 22 ||
Furthermore:
Among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas I am the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
among the Vasus I am Pāvaka (Fire); and among the peaked mountains I am Meru. (23)

Among the eleven Rudras, who are well-known by names such as Aṅgāraka and others mentioned in the Purāṇas, I am Śaṅkara; and among them, because of his preeminent sovereignty, he is a portion of my own glory. Likewise, among the Yakṣas...

Because of his association with the Guhyakas, as well as the Rākṣasas and Piśitāśins, [he is included among] the Piśācas who are seen even within the divine births; there, I am the Lord of Wealth (Vitteśa), the Master of Riches, for he is appointed over that class [of beings], and thus he possesses a portion of my own majesty. Likewise:
Among the eight Vasus, well-known by names such as Dhara and others,
I am the Vasu named Pāvaka;
for he holds preeminence by virtue of being the locus for various sacrificial rites and other such functions.

This refers to being a portion of My glory (*madvibhūtyaṃśatva*). Likewise, among the *śikhariṇaḥ*, that is, the mountains, I am Meru, the Golden Mountain; its preeminence is due to its being the abode of the gods and the cause of the sun's rising, and thus it is a portion of My glory. This is to be understood in all subsequent cases. || 23 ||
Furthermore:
"And know me, O Pārtha, to be Bṛhaspati, the chief among domestic priests;
among army commanders I am Skanda, and among bodies of water I am the ocean. (24)
Know me to be Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the king of the gods, the foremost and principal among the domestic priests and royal preceptors, because of my preeminence among them;
and know Skanda Kumāra to be the leader of the army among the commanders of hosts.
Among those, I am the preeminent one due to my possession of extraordinary heroism. Among lakes—that is, reservoirs of water—I am the ocean;
among them, the ocean is preeminent because it is the source of various jewels and for other such reasons. || 24 ||
Furthermore:
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words, I am the single syllable Om;
among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña); and among immovable things, I am the Himalaya. (25)

Among the great and eminent sages, such as Marīci, Aṅgiras, and others— distinguished by their status as Ṛṣis, Maharṣis, and Prajāpatis— I am Bhṛgu; my preeminence is due to the fact that, in comparison with them, I am heard to possess a superior excellence in knowledge and other qualities.

Likewise, because it is that which brings speech to completion, among those things denoted by the word "speech" (gīḥ), I am the single syllable known as the *praṇava*; for that [syllable], being the very word (*pada*),
possesses primacy because it denotes the nature of the Supreme Lord, who transcends the universal form.

Among the sacrifices (*yajña*) previously mentioned—those specific types of ritual offerings accomplished through material substances—*japa* (the silent recitation) of the *praṇava* and other purifying mantras is itself the sacrifice; I am that sacrificial rite. As it is said:

The gods are propitiated through the recitation of mantras (*mantra-japa*), not in the same way through sacrifices involving material offerings (*dravya-yajña*) and the like; therefore, the former holds primacy. For, compared to the fruit that is to be attained by one devoted to the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*) without aiming for any result, even the attainment of various other worlds is regarded as a state of hellish rebirth.
It is established in the *Mokṣadharma* sections; and thus it is said there:
[This applies] to the four world-protectors, to Śakra, to Bṛhaspati, to the Maruts, to the Viśvedevas, to the Sādhyas, and even to the two Aśvins.
O dear one, these indeed are the hells for the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and other celestial dwellers, in comparison to the abode of the Supreme Self.

(Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 196.6), meaning "of that which is to be attained by the primary reciter. Likewise, among stationary beings—those characterized by qualities distinct from mobility—I am the Himālaya. Of that...

The preeminence of [the Himalaya] among all stationary beings has been stated by way of its being the source of various gems and medicinal herbs; since the distinction of Meru among mountains was previously mentioned, while that of the Himalaya among stationary beings is now stated, there is no tautology. || 25 ||
Furthermore: "Among all trees, the Aśvattha; among the divine sages (devarṣis), Nārada;
among the Gandharvas, Citraratha; and among the Siddhas, the sage Kapila. (26)
Know me as Uccaiḥśravas among horses, born from the nectar;
as Airāvata among lordly elephants, and as the king among men. (27)
Of weapons I am the thunderbolt; of cows I am the wish-fulfilling cow;
I am Kandarpa, the progenitor; and of serpents I am Vāsuki. || 28 ||
Among the Nāgas I am Ananta; among the aquatic creatures I am Varuṇa;
among the ancestors I am Aryaman; and among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama. (29)
Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon time, I am Time;
among beasts I am the king of beasts; and among birds I am Vainateya. (30)
Among purifiers I am the wind; among those who bear weapons, I am Rāma;
among fish I am the makara; and among flowing rivers I am the Ganges.
I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations, O Arjuna;
among sciences, I am the science of the Self (adhyātmavidyā), and I am the debate of those who debate.
Among letters I am the letter *a*; among compounds I am the copulative (*dvandva*) compound.
I alone am inexhaustible Time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned in every direction.
I am death, the destroyer of all, and the source of those who are to come into being;
among women, I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness.
Likewise, among the Sāmans I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among the meters (chandas) I am the Gāyatrī;
among the months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; and among the seasons I am the flower-bearing spring. || 35 ||
Of deceivers, I am gambling; of the radiant, I am splendor;
I am victory, I am resolve, and of those possessed of goodness, I am goodness.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages I am Vyāsa; among the poets, the poet Uśanas.
I am the rod for those who seek to subdue; I am statesmanship for those who desire victory;
I am silence among secrets, and I am knowledge for the wise. (38)
Since it is well known that among the categories of objects beginning with trees— namely those consisting of thirteen verses—

the preeminence of specific varieties such as the *aśvattha* tree and others is established by their respective qualities, such as being fit for sacrifice (*yajñiya*), the entire [text] has not been explained here according to its literal subject matter; rather, [only the essential points are addressed].
In some places (p.

336), a certain word is explained: therein, *prajanaḥ* refers to the agent of the act of procreation; it is used in the singular to denote the class (*jātāv ekavacanam*), meaning "among those who procreate" with respect to the act of procreation.

Because he is the primary cause, I am Kandarpa, Kāma; for it is well known that when he exists, others possess the power of procreation. By the word *yādas*, they mean the water-deities (*abdevatā*); among them, Varuṇa is the principal. Likewise, Yama Vaivasvata is a specific deity from whom [all things] proceed.

Wherever that womb may be, in that or another womb, it subjects all the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*). Among all those who possess mastery—that is, those capable of the act of restraint—it holds preeminence.
The form *saṃyamatām* is a Vedic usage (archaic) where the substitution of *ya* for *ya* has not occurred. Some [commentators] are skillful in this regard.
Regarding the reading "saṃyacchatām" (let them restrain) instead of "kalayatām" (let them reckon) in this context: here,

since there exists as ultimate reality a single, eternal principle called Īśvara, whose majesty is entirely unconditioned, there is no such thing as "time" that is a distinct entity separate from Him.
This may be so; however, in this world which consists of both insentient and sentient entities manifested through that Māyā,

when there exists for the sentient being characterized as the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) a state of subjectivity toward mutually distinct objects, [this occurs] by virtue of having impermanent things as its domain.

Time manifests as having mere mental construction (*kalpanā*) as its sole cause. For entities are indeed impermanent, possessing the characteristics of arising, persistence, and cessation; because they participate in the states of past, present, and future, they undergo the state of being calculable and delimited by this or that form. And of these...
The subjects belonging to the realm of Māyā are indeed the limiters (kalayitāraḥ). Therefore, time is precisely the act of limitation (kalanakriyā).

Consequently, among the limiters, this time possesses primacy within the very act of limitation, which serves as the primary instrument for the conventional usage of the objects to be limited; thus, regarding time conceived here as an action (kriyātvena), [it is the foremost].
Its essential nature has been established. Furthermore, its status as a distinct substance is also determined;
this he will explain later. Because the phonemes of the *mātṛkā*—which constitute the parts of words—are the very life-force of all living beings, the letter *a* holds primacy. For it is...
Like the individual soul (jīva) among bodies, he exists as one who pervades those phonemes (varṇas).

For those who know reality say that his form— which exists while not having attained modifications such as the long vowel 'ā' and so forth— is the supreme essence of sound (śabdatattva), consisting of resonance (nādātmaka).

Likewise, among the collection of compounds— such as *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and so forth— the *dvandva* is predominant by virtue of the primacy of all its constituent members and because it expresses multiple substrates simultaneously (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatva*). Similarly, when time (*kāla*) is regarded as a substance (*dravya*), as in the expression "imperishable time" (*akṣayaḥ kālaḥ*).
If it is postulated that [the world] is eternal, then, just as the eternality of the creations and so forth— which are in constant operation— would apply, so too, given its eternality,

there would be inexhaustibility and infinity among its own constituent parts, which are impermanent and range from moments (*kṣaṇa*) up to the limit of a kalpa (*kalpānta*), such as the closing of an eye (*nimeṣa*) and so on.

Its primacy is established solely in relation to its own constituent parts; however, the mention of those parts must be inferred here by implication. Such an inference is indeed possible, since time can be understood in both ways—as action and as substance. And it is precisely with this possibility in mind that the Blessed One [stated]:

Furthermore, a specification of time is made: "Or rather, that which is I—the inexhaustible ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), indestructible due to its eternity—that very thing is Time; I alone manifest myself as Time. This refers to the previously mentioned Time.

The repetition is for the purpose of demonstrating that its essential nature is fashioned by my mere will; or else, because the Blessed One perceives time as having the nature of action in some instances and the nature of substance in others due to differences in perspective, he has made this twofold designation. Likewise, that which is constant...
Death, which simultaneously seizes the life-faculty, the body, the objects of the senses,
and so forth— that death, as the cause of dying existing at that very moment— is preeminent among other killers; likewise, gambling is preeminent among those who deceive and those who defraud.

Even though it is deceptive in nature, it possesses primacy because it does not deviate from dharma. Likewise, wealth acquired through gambling in accordance with dharma is commended for rites such as *śrāddha* and the like.
Because its root lies in the intention to deceive others, its deceptive character remains established; yet, for those possessed of *sattva*, [it serves a higher purpose].

Among the qualities characterized as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, the quality of *sattva* holds primacy because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*). Likewise, that by which kings subdue the ill-behaved—namely, punishment (*daṇḍa*) as a specific form of restraint prescribed by the scriptures—is the primary means; thus, it alone is the subduer (*damayitṛ*). By that [means]...

Among those who seek to subdue others, punishment (*daṇḍa*) is paramount. Likewise, for those desiring victory— those wishing to conquer adversaries— it is policy (*nīti*) alone that constitutes the method,
consisting of the five constituent parts beginning with the initiation of action and ending with the accomplishment of the task.

According to the principle that "the primary means [is the most effective]," those who desire victory hold preeminence among their peers. Likewise, among secret methods (*guhyopāya*), I am Mauna—established as silence in the form of restraint of speech—wherein even the conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) regarding various objects does not arise. For he...

It is the supreme concentration (*parama-samādhi*); and when that exists, there is the accomplishment of *mauna* (silence), which consists in the restraint of speech that has volition as its root. That very thing is said to be the "supreme secret. Likewise, by the inclusion of the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*), various distinct cognitions having manifold objects are understood.

Among those, the preeminence belongs to non-dual knowledge whose object is the single reality characterized solely by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, by this [verse], the preeminence of that aforementioned single knowledge among the various types of knowledge is established. (26–38)
Concluding the demonstration of his manifestations, he says:
"Moreover, O Arjuna, I am the seed of all beings;
there exists no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me. (39)

What is the use of this extensive description of my manifold manifestations? This supreme manifestation of mine is summarized as follows: I am that which is the seed—the cause of origin—for all beings who have emanated through the previously explained distinction between the higher and lower natures (*prakṛti*). Indeed, there is no external cause.

The meaning is that nothing whatsoever in the worlds comes into being except for my own power of *māyā* alone; because there exists here no object—whether conscious or unconscious—that possesses existence and yet arises without me. Therefore, apart from all apparent causes...
"In the ultimate sense, I alone am the cause of all beings. || 39 ||
And by me, who am the Supreme Cause, there exist various manifestations based on the distinctions of diverse entities brought forth through the power of my own *māyā*; of these—
O scorcher of the foe, there is no end to my divine manifestations;
this detailed account of my manifestations has been declared by me only in brief. (40)

There is no end to my glories— which are related to me, which have arisen from the sky of my heart, which are situated as all infinite objects, and which manifest through the expansion of my own power. But this...
In this section, because a certain dharma has been mentioned by way of brief enumeration, the expansion—the extensive manifestation—of its own power (vibhūti) has been described. || 40 ||
To summarize, however, I speak this so that you may recognize my own manifestation: whatever being possesses power, or is endowed with splendor, or is even majestic,
know that each of them has arisen from a fragment of my splendor.

In all these worlds, whatever being there may be— whatever collection of things, whether sentient or insentient, possessed of power (vibhūtimat), endowed with majesty (vibhūtiyuktam), and for that very reason glorious (śrīmat) as being perfected with supreme beauty, and vigorous (ūrjita) as being endowed with the capacity for various purposeful actions— that very thing [is He].
"You should understand— that is, you should disregard— that everything related to me has arisen from, and is produced by, that mere fraction, a tiny portion, of my supreme light. || 41 ||
In order to demonstrate that his state of perfection does not depend on any other means, he says:
"Or rather, what is the use of many words, O Arjuna?
Sustaining this entire world with but a single fraction of myself, I remain. (42)

Now, what is the purpose for you in understanding that each respective object within each respective category exists as a manifestation of My power— by means of this aforementioned extensive knowledge set forth in many books, even when it has been thus comprehended? There is no task [to be accomplished].
For this entire, complete world— consisting of all things of infinite variety,

extending throughout the seven worlds— is always and everywhere [perceived] by means of a single part or portion, which is the nature of consciousness containing diverse universals and is distinct from the objective aspect of what is known.
"Having seized, having stepped upon, and having pervaded, I remain. By this, the following is stated:

in various philosophical systems (*darśana*), regarding this world which is explained through various distinct modes, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is, in brief, twofold. One part is the cognizer (*vedaka*), whose nature is singular and who exists at all times and in every respect.
The first is the nature of pure consciousness, free from modification; the other, although possessing manifold forms, has as its sole essential nature the object of knowledge (*vedya*).

Therein, by means of a consciousness that has attained rest in the subjective aspect (*vedakāṃśa*)—which is the sole cause of the manifestation of that [object] through the exclusion of the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*)—the practitioner [attains realization].
It must be so, by which my supreme majesty is attained; thus, Om. 42.
For those who are resolved to fully attain the sovereign power of the Supreme Brahman— extending here to all the manifestations of Viṣṇu that transcend the entire creation—
it is this very devotion alone that becomes truly pure for the wise.
The commentary on the tenth chapter should always be kept in mind.

Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the sequential connection of the meanings of the statements, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Then, through the ten chapters, preceded by the knowledge and realized wisdom taught by the Blessed One,

from the mere hearing of all the subject matter, there arises an understanding of the Blessed One’s status as the Supreme Lord; thus, regarding His being the ultimate cause, in the words spoken by Him—

Arjuna, having communicated his own state of mind— free from doubt regarding the excellence of the means due to its non-contradiction with the aforementioned results— and impelled by a desire for direct perception of that [reality] which he had previously understood through scripture alone, spoke as follows:
By those words which you have spoken for my benefit— the supreme secret known as the inner self— this delusion of mine has vanished.

For the sake of favoring me— to show me grace and to awaken me by means of your own supreme power— you, the Supreme Lord whose nature is self-manifested, have yourself imparted this speech, this discourse consisting of ten chapters known as the *Adhyātma*.

Consisting of knowledge whose object is the Self, it is for this very reason the supreme secret, the most excellent mystery, which has been spoken—that is, taught. By means of that [teaching] as a cause, this delusion—which consists of a perception contrary to the realization of the ultimate truth thus established—subsists by encompassing all people; such is ignorance (*ajñāna*).
"My [defilement] has ceased and departed. || 1 ||
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"For the origin and dissolution of beings have been heard by me in detail from you, O lotus-eyed one, as well as your imperishable majesty. (2)

For from you alone, the single supreme cause, the origin and dissolution—the birth and absorption—of all beings, both stationary and moving, have been heard by me in detail and at length; however, they were presented merely as heard and not yet fully comprehended. Moreover:
I have heard of your imperishable and eternal majesty, characterized by unsurpassed sovereignty and greatness:
"I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe."
"Nothing whatsoever exists that is higher than me" (7.7)—

from such non-contradictory words of the Blessed One himself, it is evident that the Blessed One alone is the sole cause of the existence and non-existence of all beings, even while remaining in that state [of transcendence].
The meaning is: "And it has been understood by me that [He] is the sole abode of wondrous sovereignty, due to His non-deviation from the nature of pure, luminous consciousness alone. || 2 ||
Thinking, "I have understood this merely by hearing it, but not through direct experience," he says for that purpose:
"It is exactly so, just as you describe yourself, the Supreme Lord."
O Supreme Person, I desire to see your divine form.

In whatever manner and by whichever means you have previously stated that you are the Self, whose essential nature is the Supreme Lord— being the sovereign even over lords such as Brahmā and others— and thus the most excellent Master; this matter exists in this very way, and there is no doubt for me in this regard.
The meaning is that it is an illusion. Therefore, I desire—that is, I long for—the opportunity to see and directly perceive Your divine form, Your sovereign body belonging to You, the Lord.
For by means of this present form in human shape which is being seen now, that supreme form [cannot be perceived].
This which was previously described by me through mere words as being situated entirely within that One—
this I have now accepted as truly existing in such a manner, based on my conviction in the words of the Blessed One. Therefore, O Supreme Person, by your grace, [I shall see it] directly.
"I desire to see him," [he said]. || 3 ||
But if you think, O Lord, that it is possible for me to see it,
then, O Lord of Yoga, show me your imperishable self.

O Lord, Supreme God, if You think— that is, if You know— that such a true form, whose very sight is prayed for even by the highest yogis, can be seen and directly beheld by me, a mere mortal, and is bearable; if...

Since you regard my competence as being so great, therefore, O Lord of Yogins, because of your possession of innate, perfected, and unsurpassed yoga, you are the master of all other practitioners of yoga whose practice is achieved through effort. (p. 243) My [master].
"Show me—make manifest before my eyes—your own nature, the immutable Self that is without beginning or end. || 4 ||
Thus entreated, the Blessed One, becoming inclined toward grace,
said: "Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and by the thousands—
divine, of various kinds, and of diverse colors and shapes."
Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
behold many wonders never seen before, O Pāṇḍava!
Behold today, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe with its moving and unmoving beings gathered together here in one place within my body, as well as whatever else you desire to see.

O Pārtha, behold—look upon—the innumerable forms, consisting of specific configurations, which, through the excellence of my own sovereignty, are connected as my own powers to me alone, the Supreme Reality, the Supreme Self. Of what kind are they? They are of various sorts.
"Variegated" means precisely for that reason having various colors and forms, and possessing diverse appearances and configurations;
likewise, "divine" means superhuman. Having thus introduced the subject in general terms, he speaks in order to specify the particular ones:
"the twelve Ādityas," who are specific classes of deities; likewise, "the Vasus."

Having mentioned the forms of the deities by way of enumeration according to their prominence— namely, the eight Rudras, the eleven Aśvins (the Dasras), and the forty-nine Maruts, who are specific classes of gods—
he said in brief: "These, for now, have been described by you."
Behold all those many immeasurable wonders, never before seen and never before observed, which were witnessed by me while dwelling in the celestial realm;
what need is there for more? Behold them all here, within this single form that is my own body.

Behold all things in their entirety, without exception, existing together in one place; for, in brief, they consist of two types— the mobile and the immobile— and whatever else you desire to see according to your wish, that too you shall see as gathered in one single place.

The intended meaning here is this: behold this most wonderful phenomenon—that which is the single, ultimately real, supreme cause possesses the nature of infinite entities mutually distinct from one another, manifested by its own power of *māyā*. || 7 ||
Precisely because this matter is so exceedingly wonderful:
"But you are not able to see Me with these very eyes of yours;
I shall give you a divine eye; behold My sovereign yoga. (8)

By this very eye of yours, which perceives only limited objects due to its mortal nature and is based upon the physical orb of the eyeball, you will not be able— nor indeed can you— to see or behold Me in the wondrous form that I am about to reveal.

You shall become patient. Then, by virtue of the power of all-seeing divinity, I shall grant you the eye—the vision consisting of supreme knowledge—which arises from the supreme space that is the nature of the Supreme Self; I give it to you through my own sovereign power, even while you remain effortless.
"I shall manifest it; therefore, behold my divine form—belonging to the Lord—which is about to be revealed; perceive it directly. || 8 ||

Now, just as Arjuna was favored by the Blessed One through the highest meditative absorption (*samādhi*) so that he might be granted the fitness for the vision of his own unsurpassed form, in the same manner,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra had previously obtained divine vision through the grace of the sage Vyāsa, the Blessed One.
In order to explain this, Sañjaya said: "O King, having spoken thus, Hari, the great lord of yogis, then— "
He revealed to Pārtha his supreme, sovereign form.
He possessed many mouths and eyes, displaying many wonders;
he was adorned with many divine ornaments and held many uplifted divine weapons.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
that god is composed of all wonders, infinite, and facing in every direction.

p. 245) These three verses have their meaning already explained. However, that single supreme form of the Lord—which pertains to the Blessed One and consists essentially of pure consciousness alone—is what appears, by means of His very power of *māyā*, as the manifold diversity of forms belonging to the entire world of living beings. Therefore...

One should understand that these specific forms have as their sole purport the fact that the entire universe is indeed the form of the Blessed Lord; for it is by way of this grammatical coreferentiality with "form" (*rūpa*) that the text connects with the passage: "the infinite God whose faces are on all sides. || 11 ||

Therefore, in order to establish the true nature of that one whose essence is the light of consciousness— non-dual in the ultimate sense— which appears in manifold forms, he says: "In the sky, the light of a thousand suns rising simultaneously..."
If that light were similar to the light of that Great-souled One, it would be so. || 12 ||
If the light and radiance that should arise simultaneously from a thousand suns risen together in the sky were ever to exist,
it might be similar to the splendor of that one Great Soul, the Supreme Person, whose very nature is supreme illumination.
It should be explained by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) as "it might be equal," so that it results in the sense: "by which [means] it would not be similar.
For [it is impossible for anything else to be equal] to Him, whose nature is unsurpassed light, who illuminates all things that are themselves not illuminated by another.
Even the radiance of ten million suns rising simultaneously would not be able to attain even a resemblance to a mere fraction of its light. || 12 ||
Thus, within that Supreme Light,
the son of Pāṇḍu then beheld the entire universe, though divided manifoldly, situated as one within the body of the God of gods. (13)
Then, at that time—

characterized by supreme grace consisting in the gift of the divine eye, which is the nature of transcendent knowledge and serves as the cause for beholding such a universal form (vaiśvarūpya) of the Blessed One— in that state which consists of the supreme light;
It exists as a single entity within the very body of the God of gods, the Lord of all, residing in one and the same substratum;
yet it is also manifoldly divided, scattered throughout the forms of all cosmic beings, in its entirety and without exception.
(246) Sañjaya said this because, having seen with his divine eye the grace of the Supreme Lord upon Arjuna, he stated that Arjuna had directly perceived the universe by means of that vision. || 13 ||
Now, the text describes what Arjuna did after having beheld the universal form of the Supreme Lord:
"Then Dhananjaya, overcome with wonder and his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the God and spoke with palms joined in reverence. (14)

Then, immediately after that moment of direct perception of such an utterly wondrous form of the Lord, even upon the re-manifestation of his human state, he was possessed— his mental faculties overwhelmed— by wonder born from the recollection of the supreme reality he had experienced; for this very reason, his hair stood on end.

With his hair standing on end from joy, Dhanañjaya— having directly perceived the Son of Devakī standing before him and having developed an intense devotion toward Him due to His manifest, unsurpassed majesty— bowed his head, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke these words that are about to be related.
"abhāṣata" means "he said. || 14 ||
He says:
"O Lord, I behold all the gods within your body, as well as the hosts of various classes of beings."
[He saw] Brahmā, the Lord seated upon the lotus-throne, as well as all the Ṛṣis and the radiant serpents. || 15 ||
O God, Supreme Lord, within this body of yours—
which is the sole locus for the existence of the entire universe— reside the gods who dwell in heaven,
as well as others among the various classes of beings, both moving and stationary, including those that are internal.

Having first established that the instantaneous vision of the entire universe occurs within the body of the Blessed One— expressed as "I see thousands of assemblies" by way of the preeminence of the gods and others— he now speaks of the sequential vision of its specific details, beginning with Brahmā, Prajāpati, and Īśa.

By the statement, "I see the Lord seated on the lotus-throne, resting upon a bed of white lotuses," he has described the vision of the upper worlds up to the realm of Brahmā (brahmaloka). And by the statement, "I see all the sages," he refers to them according to their preeminence.
He spoke of his vision of the middle world characterized by the sages;
and when he said, "I see radiant serpents," he spoke of his vision of the netherworld (pātāla) characterized by the lords of the snakes, headed by Ananta and Vāsuki.
"In this way, I behold the three worlds dissolved within your body"—thus he expressed his own direct experience. || 15 ||
Thus, even while beholding the three worlds inhabited by various beings such as gods and others,
he says: "I see You alone as the single refuge of all—
possessing manifold arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes."
I behold You on all sides with infinite forms;
I see neither Your end, nor Your middle, nor again Your beginning, O Lord of the Universe, O Universal Form! 16.

The meaning of this verse is clear. However, regarding the various limbs—such as arms, stomachs, mouths, eyes, and so forth—of the beings existing within the three worlds, I perceive them as belonging to you alone, the one whose majesty is everywhere unlimited, as your very own limbs. In this regard:
This is the intended meaning. || 16 ||
And he says: "By Your grace, I behold this very form standing before me, consisting of the supreme splendor of the Lord"—
namely, the one wearing a crown, holding a mace, and bearing a discus.
I behold You as a mass of splendor blazing on all sides, difficult to gaze upon from every direction,
possessing the immeasurable radiance of a flaming fire and the sun.
The intended meaning of this has already been explained by the introductory remarks themselves. || 17 ||
For this very reason, he speaks in order to demonstrate the nature of that [Self] through attributes that establish the Supreme Lord:
"You are the supreme imperishable to be known."
You are the supreme repository of this entire universe;
you are the imperishable protector of the Sāttvata dharma; you are considered by me to be the eternal Puruṣa. (18)

You are that supreme, unsurpassed reality— the imperishable (*akṣara*) which is free from agitation characterized by the loss of its own nature, and which is the object of knowledge and realization; likewise,
this entire universe of infinite manifestation has its highest, most excellent repository in you.

The world enters [into You]. But surely there exists the Pradhāna as the repository of the world, wherein it is deposited at the time of dissolution? True, that Pradhāna exists; yet even that dissolves into the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Cause, and from Him alone it arises. Thus, because the Pradhāna itself has its repository in You, You are the Supreme.

It has been stated that You are the treasure-store of the universe. Likewise, because You are not subject to limitation by time, You are the imperishable (*avyaya*), the undecaying (*akṣaya*) protector of the *sāttvata* dharma. "Sat" is a name for Brahman, as he will say:
"The designation of Brahman is traditionally known to be threefold: Om, Tat, Sat" (17.23).

Thus: that which exists [as the essence] is *sattva*; the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is the Supreme Brahman, is the deity of those who possess it, and they are the *sāttvatāḥ*, the knowers of Brahman. Their *dharma* consists of the practice of the conjunction of knowledge and action as previously explained, which is right conduct (*sadācāra*).
Because you repeatedly bring it forth as it becomes obscured by the power of the decline of time, and because you dispel the obstacles that hinder it, you alone are its protector. || 18 ||
Therefore:
"He who is without beginning, middle, or end, possessed of infinite valor, with infinite arms, and whose eyes are the moon and the sun."
I see you with a mouth like a blazing fire, scorching this entire universe with your own splendor.

Because it is infinite, it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; for only a delimited entity possesses such divisions as beginning and so forth. Thus, the power (*vīrya*) that has the capacity to fashion the manifold expansion of the universe is infinite.

(249) [He is] one from whom [the world] has never ceased. Likewise, since those infinite and numerous [limbs] which serve as the means for the various actions of all *kṣetrajñas* belong to the Supreme Lord alone—the ultimate agent—He possesses infinite arms. Similarly, in the body of the *kṣetrajña*...
Because the illumination of fixed objects is performed by the two eyes, he possesses the eyes of the moon and the sun.

Likewise, because Vaiśvānara— the Supreme Lord himself, whose form is the universe— is alone gratified by various specific sacrificial rites performed by those skilled in ritual action, it is said that his blazing fire is the mouth.
Likewise, the connection is: "I behold You, the Self of the universe, who thus illumines and makes manifest all this by Your own splendor, which is the light of consciousness."

Now, in order to describe the form of the all-powerful Supreme Lord as characterized by ferocity— since He is endowed with the power known as Kāla (Time) which has been unleashed for the destruction of the Kuru army— the author says:
For this entire space between heaven and earth, as well as all the directions, is pervaded by you alone;
having seen this wondrous and fierce form of yours.
The three worlds were deeply distressed, O Great-souled One.

Since the entire expanse between heaven and earth and all the directions have been pervaded and filled by you alone with this great form, the three worlds— the inhabitants of the triple world, including the gods and others who are unfit to behold it— have seen this such terrible form of yours.
"Pravyathitam" means intensely terrified. "O Great-souled One" (*mahātman*) is an address referring to the greatness of his form. || 20 ||
To describe the movements produced by the fear arising from the sight of such a form for those gods and others, he says:
"For these hosts of gods are entering into you."
Some, struck with fear, utter words with palms joined;
and having cried "May it be well!", the hosts of great sages praise you with abundant hymns of praise. (21)
Because these hosts of gods, headed by Śakra, enter you— who have manifested a terrible form for the destruction of the wicked— they dissolve into you alone; and some, being terrified and trembling,
utter praises with palms joined in reverent salutation.

Therefore, the hosts of great sages, who are the foremost among the eminent ascetics, for the sake of the world's welfare, utter the word "svasti" and praise and extol you with abundant, meaningful, and coherent hymns that recount your various deeds. || 21 ||
Furthermore: "The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās— "
The hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas all gaze upon you, filled with wonder. || 22 ||
The specific classes of deities beginning with the Rudras have been explained; the Pitṛs known as the Ūṣmapas [are next];

and the Gandharvas and others are well-known. All these, because they belong to the divine order (*devayoni*), possess the potential for a particular kind of knowledge; yet, due to the unprecedented terror [of what they behold], they gaze upon you—that is, they see you.
They were filled with wonder at his form. || 22 ||
To describe that form which, upon seeing it, they became such as they were, he says:
"Your form is great, with many mouths and eyes."
O mighty-armed one, having seen You with many arms, thighs, and feet; with many bellies and many terrible tusks, the worlds are terrified, and so am I.
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 23 ||
(p. 251) By means of seeing that form, he speaks in order to specifically demonstrate his own state:
"Touching the sky, blazing, multicolored, with a wide-gaping mouth and blazing, wide eyes."
For upon seeing you, O Viṣṇu, my inner soul is deeply distressed; I find neither fortitude nor peace.
This verse also has its meaning already understood; however,
at the moment of the Lord's grace characterized by the granting of divine vision, having seen [Your form] with divine knowledge and experienced it,
now that the mortal nature has returned, one remembers that form of Yours.
Being of a fearful mind, one does not attain steadfastness, which is the state of an unagitated mind;

therefore, it should be understood that fear and the like do not arise even at the very moment of seeing. Furthermore, in other instances as well, when using a verb in the present tense, the recollection of what was previously seen serves as the cause.
"It must be understood," thus [it is said]. || 24 ||
Moreover:
Having merely seen your mouths, which are terrifying with fangs and resemble the fire of cosmic destruction, [the worlds tremble].
I do not know the directions, nor do I find peace; be gracious, O Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe! (25)

This statement is clear in its meaning; however, the Lord’s possession of many mouths with formidable fangs is due to the entry of the Person Kṛtānta, who has assumed many distorted forms for the purpose of universal destruction. || 25 ||
For this very reason, he speaks to describe the conduct of Kuru and the others who have been overtaken by the personification of Fate:
"All these are the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
Together with all the hosts of kings,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer (Karna),
as well as our own foremost warriors, [all stood ready].
(252) Your mouths, terrifying and formidable with tusks, are being entered by those hurrying [toward you];
some are caught between the rows of teeth.
They are seen with their heads crushed to pieces. || 27 ||
Being harassed by men of various forms,
those warriors— the sons of Yudhiṣṭhira and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— enter your inconceivable mouth.
All of them were indeed cut down by various kinds of weapons. || 28 ||
Surely these have been destroyed by your splendor; for thus they have entered your body,
just as the many currents of water from rivers enter the ocean.
They flow directly toward the ocean alone. || 29 ||
Thus these heroes of the world of men enter your mouths blazing on all sides,
just as moths enter a kindled fire.
They enter for their destruction with fully increased momentum. || 30 ||
In that very same way, the worlds enter your mouths for their destruction with great impetuosity. This pentad of verses is mostly explained by the words themselves; however, regarding your mouths—
