By means of the plural form "they enter," having begun with the mouths characterized by such attributes as "terrible with tusks" and so forth, that which was stated— "they enter your mouth of inconceivable form"—
refers to the various powers (śaktis) belonging to the Person of Time (kālapuruṣa), which consist of diverse and terrible forms.

It should be understood that this is intended to demonstrate that the Blessed One is the substratum of all powers, insofar as [all things] transform within His one supreme, universal power (*sāmānya-śakti*),
which is expressed by the term "single face" (*ekavaktra*). For...

Because the general power (*sāmānya-śakti*) is inexpressible, its nature is inconceivable; therefore, it is qualified [by specific instances]. This is made clear by the phrase "these [powers] in your body. Here, within these five and a half verses, from the words "in various forms" up to "have entered into your body," [the meaning is explained].

Some do not recite the one and a half verses for the sake of maintaining the symmetry of the verse count. However, some do not recite the half-verse beginning with "struck down by your splendor" (*tvattejasā nihatāḥ*) for this very reason. In this case, however, because we observe many manuscripts and because the sage Vyāsa composed that half-verse there in the *Mahābhārata*, [it is authentic].
Thus, five and a half verses have been recited. || 30 ||
Then, having seen such a terrible form of the Blessed One’s power, he spoke this for the sake of desiring to know the reality of that [power]: "You lick [the world], devouring it on all sides— "
[He devours] all the worlds with his blazing mouths. || 31 ||
O Viṣṇu, having filled the entire world with your splendors, your fierce rays blaze forth;
tell me, who are you of such terrible form?
Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious!
I desire to know you, the Primordial One, for I do not understand your activity.

Swallowing and devouring these entire worlds on every side with your mouths ablaze— your faces emitting fire— you lick them repeatedly; therefore, your splendors are fierce, your radiances are terrible.
Pervading the entire universe with their splendors, they blaze and shine intensely.

(p. 254) Since I behold such a terrible form of yours, whose nature is the supremely tranquil pure consciousness, therefore, O best of gods, O foremost of all deities, salutations to you; grant me your grace.

And do so! Tell me who you are that has appeared in such a fierce form. Since I do not know, nor do I understand in truth, the reason for your engagement in assuming such a terrible form and its manifestation, I wish to specifically recognize you as the primordial, supreme cause.
"I wish to understand," [he said]. || 32 ||
Being thus questioned— "For what reason, being who you are, do you manifest such a terrible form?"— the Blessed One replied: "I am Time (Kāla), the destroyer of the worlds, now grown great."
He has set out here to destroy the worlds;
even without you, all those warriors who stand in the opposing armies shall cease to exist.

"I am Time" means that this terrible power of mine, called Time, is the manifestation of my entire energy in peaceful, fierce, and terrible forms, while I myself remain unswerving from my own nature which is free from all affliction. And because there is no difference between the power and the possessor of the power, it is said that "I myself am Time."

What kind of time is this? It is one whose sole function is the destruction of the entire world. Now, however, it has begun and spread forth to gather together and lead to destruction these people on this earth who have grown arrogant, intoxicated with pride, and have become a burden to the world. Therefore, even without you—despite being apart from you—[it proceeds].
Because their nature is entirely filled with evil, all these will cease to exist even if you do not fight;
they will surely perish. Who are they? They are the warriors, the combatants who stand arrayed in the opposing armies, the enemy forces.
Since these things thus float away, being overtaken by inevitable destruction,
therefore you should rise up and win glory.
"Having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
(p. 255) These have already been slain by me alone;
be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin!"
"By means of my power in the form of Time, which has already begun to destroy them, you shall become merely the instrumental cause"; thus, the meaning of this verse is quite explicit. || 34 ||
And lest you think that Droṇa and the others are invincible because of their peerless prowess, he says:
"Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Jayadratha..."
Slay Karna and the other world-heroes who have been slain by me; do not be distressed, fight,
and you shall conquer your enemies in battle.

The intended meaning is: "Do not fear, thinking that Droṇa and the others—who were the preeminent heroes of the entire world—were slain by me because Time is invincible; for they were already as good as conquered. || 35 ||

Thus, having heard these words of Keśava, Arjuna, with palms joined in reverence and trembling, spoke his state of mind to Dhṛtarāṣṭra through Saṃjaya: "Having heard this speech of Keśava... [and so forth].
Having bowed down again and having prostrated before Kṛṣṇa, he spoke with a faltering voice, being utterly terrified.
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 36 ||
Asking "What did Arjuna say to Kṛṣṇa?", [the Lord] said: "O Hṛṣīkeśa, it is fitting that the world rejoices and is filled with affection by Your glorification."
The Rākṣasas flee in all directions out of fear, and all the hosts of Siddhas pay him homage. || 37 ||

p. 256) Thus, through the proclamation and praise of you, the omnipotent Lord of all, the entire world experiences great joy; for this very reason, it becomes devoted to you. Likewise, the *rakṣas* and *yātudhāna*s, who pervade that [world], flee here and there out of fear.
The hosts of Siddhas—the entire assemblies of distinguished deities—also bow down; all of that is appropriate and fitting. || 37 ||
Reflecting upon the supreme nature of the Blessed One, which has been directly realized solely through your grace,
he spoke again:
"And why, O Great Soul, should they not bow down to you?"
To the one more venerable than even Brahmā, the primordial creator;
O Infinite One, Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe, You are that Imperishable which is beyond both being and non-being. 38.

Or rather, for what reason and from what cause would these Siddhas and others not bow down to you, O Great-Souled One, Supreme Person? To what kind of you? To one who is greater even than Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures—that is, to the supreme teacher—because he is the original creator, the first progenitor, even of him.

For the sake of [your] birth: O Lord of Devas, whose majesty is infinite and boundless; O Sovereign of all Suras, Abode of the World, Sole Treasure of all realms; since you are that which is beyond the existent—that is, distinct from any object capable of being determined through the range of the senses and so forth—and likewise...

And since even that which is beyond the non-existent— which is of the nature of non-being— is the supreme, imperishable, changeless, unsurpassed, ultimate reality; therefore, how could those perfected ones, who have known what is to be known, not know You, the sole nature of the knower, unknowable by another, the supreme cause?
The intended meaning is that they should pay homage. || 38 ||
Then he recited the qualities of the Blessed One as they had been experienced:
"You are the primordial God, the ancient Puruṣa; you are the supreme repository of this universe."
(257) You are the knower and the object of knowledge, and the supreme abode;
by you, O one of infinite forms, the universe is pervaded. 39.
These words concerning the Blessed One have already been explained many times. || 39 ||
Furthermore:
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Śaśāṅka, Prajāpati, and the Great-Grandfather.
He is beginningless, of incomparable power, the Lord of all, and possessed of all great majesty.

He is indeed such a Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All, whose great and preeminent manifestation of power (*vibhūti*)— the unfolding of His capacity— is endowed with all sovereign qualities; for this very reason, He possesses incomparable majesty, a greatness without equal, and is likewise beginningless (*anādimān*).

That which has a beginning is "ādimān"; that which does not have a beginning is "anādimān," meaning the very first of all. You alone are such [a being], as are the specific deities such as Vāyu and others. Just as Vāyu and the others are non-different from the essential nature of the Lord (Īśvara), so too is everything at the beginning.
It has already been explained. || 40 ||
Reflecting upon the Supreme Lord’s nature as possessing all forms, he says:
"Salutations, salutations be unto You a thousand times; and yet again, once more, salutations, salutations unto You!"
Salutations to you from the front, and then from behind; salutations be to you from every side, O All.
All of this has a clear meaning. || 41 ||
Furthermore:
"O Lord, indeed no one else in these three worlds is seen here who possesses such inconceivable deeds as yours."
(258) You possess infinite vigor and immeasurable prowess; you pervade everything, and therefore you are the All. || 42 ||
Even here, there is nothing that remains unexplained. Since You pervade everything perfectly by Your own power, You alone are the soul of all. *Vīrya* is the power of enthusiasm;
*parākrama* is the power of action. || 42 ||

Then, because he had previously perceived the Blessed One as a mere person and thus considered his transgression against the Blessed One to have been committed, he spoke these four verses for the sake of seeking forgiveness, having now realized that the Blessed One’s true nature is that of a Buddha.
Thinking "He is my friend," whatever was said rashly— such as "O Kṛṣṇa," "O Yādava," or "O friend"—
by me unknowing of this greatness of Yours;
Whether through negligence or even out of affection, [I have done so]. || 43 ||
And whatever disrespect was shown to you for the sake of mockery, O Acyuta, whether while at play, on a bed, on a seat, or at a meal, or even when you were alone or in the presence of the virtuous;
Therefore, I beg forgiveness from you, the immeasurable one.
You are the father of this world of the moving and the unmoving; you are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher.
There is no one equal to you; how then could there be anyone superior?
His power is peerless even throughout the three worlds. || 45 ||
Therefore, bowing down and prostrating my body, I seek to propitiate you, the Lord worthy of praise;
as a father for his son, or a friend for a friend.
O Lord, you, being beloved, ought to endure that which is beloved [of us]. || 46 ||

This is easily understood. However, because you thought, "You are my friend," you addressed me with the word "Yādava" and so forth; as for whatever other transgression was committed, it was all done by me while I was unaware of the greatness of the Blessed One at that time.
The connection is that [this] must be forgiven. "In the presence of the virtuous" means either in an assembly or in the vicinity of the wise.
Even in the three worlds there is no one equal to you; how then could there be anyone superior? || 46 ||
Then, in order to proclaim the greatness of his realized wisdom, he speaks these three verses:
"The ancient seers, too, remember your divine and wondrous deeds of old."
There is no other creator of the universe; you alone are the sustainer, the ordainer, the all-pervading one, and Bhava.
What indeed could be wonderful for you, or what could be unbearable?
Or rather, what could be possible for another that I shall proclaim?
For you yourself are indeed the creator of all this.
O All-pervading One, therefore, you alone are all this.
This most wonderful deed is not difficult for you; no comparison for your deed exists,
nor is there any measure of your virtues.
Neither from splendor, nor from strength, nor from prosperity. || 49 ||

Even the omniscient sages of old remember your deeds; therefore, they too are called "ancient" (*pūrva*) with respect to those [deeds]. This term "ancient" is intended to demonstrate that the Lord’s activities, such as the creation and dissolution of the world, proceed in an eternal, beginningless succession.

This has been largely explained; the rest is easily understood. However, the Creator—the sustainer, ordainer, and fashioner—is your own creation, namely the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). What is this wondrous and marvelous deed that is "unbearable" for you, the sole agent whose only instrument is your own will? Precisely because of this—

Because you are independent of auxiliary causes and so forth, nothing that is to be accomplished can be brought about by anything else—that is, by anything other than your own self; this I shall explain to you. And since, being thus independent of anything else, you are the creator of the entire multitude of things, therefore, due to the absence of any other cause, you alone are all this.

The meaning is that it is Your power alone that shines forth in this manner. Consequently, even an action of such wondrous nature is not difficult for You to perform; thus, the rest is clear. || 49 ||
Then,
having emerged from that samādhi which was inseparable from the nature of the Blessed One as experienced during the moment of his grace,
[he beheld] such an exceedingly formidable form of the Blessed One.
Unable to behold him for long due to his restoration to human nature, and desiring to see him as he was before, he said this:
"I am thrilled to see what I have never seen before."
My mind is distressed with fear;
therefore, show me that very same divine form.
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe! 50.
I wish to see you just as before, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with a discus in hand—
in that very same four-armed form.
O thousand-armed one, O you whose form is the universe! || 51 ||
This is clear in meaning. || 51 ||
Then the Blessed One, being thus addressed, said:
"O Arjuna, by my grace, this supreme form has been shown to you through my own yoga."
This universe is composed of light, infinite and primordial,
which has never before been seen by anyone other than you.
This is easy to understand. However, the statement "it was shown through the union with my own self" (ātmayogāt) should be understood in this way:
when you were led by me, who am intent on bestowing grace, into the yoga—that is, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—within my own supreme nature, then this form of yours [was revealed].
It has been directly perceived, because it is impossible to see this nature of the Supreme Lord as something separate [from Himself]. || 52 ||
For this very reason, he said:
"Neither by the study of the Vedas and sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by fierce austerities [is this state attained]."
"O hero of the Kurus, it is not possible for anyone other than you to behold such a form in the world of men."
Let there be no distress and no confusion in you upon seeing this terrible and fierce form of mine;
free from fear and with a joyful mind, look upon me once again.
Behold this very form of mine.

Due to the multiplicity of the Vedas and sacrifices, there is a multiplicity of "attainments" (*adhigama*); and by the word "attainment," qualities such as study and hearing are indicated. By the words "giving," "action," and "austerity," their performance is meant; and the word "action" (*kriyā*) [is used here].
It denotes specific actions such as the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth; and because even those established in such virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*) are devoid of supreme knowledge,
this supreme form of mine is impossible for them to perceive.
It was seen by you solely through my grace, as your divine eye has been opened;
therefore, what occasion is there for fear, delusion, and the like?
On the contrary, with your mind intent on the constant contemplation of my true nature, you should remember that very [reality].

This is the intended meaning: it is "terrible" (ghora) because of its association with the forms of the Person of Time (Kālapuruṣa) and so forth; it is "fierce" (ugra) because of its activity of destruction and so forth; the rest is clear. || 54 ||
Then Sañjaya said this to Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed his own form once again."
And having assumed a gentle form once more, that Great-Souled One comforted him who was terrified. (55)
This is clear in its meaning. However, the Great-Souled One, having been of universal form, again assumed a gentle body;
the Blessed One, having returned to his previous human form with the appearance of Sudarśana, addressed Arjuna, whose mind was terrified by such a wondrous sight, with what follows:
The intended meaning is that he comforted him. || 55 ||
Having thus returned to his natural state, Arjuna said:
"O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours, I am now restored to my senses and have returned to my normal nature. (56)
This is clear. || 56 ||
To reassure Arjuna, the Blessed One said:
"This form of mine which you have seen is very difficult to behold;
even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form. (57)
Neither by Vedic study, nor by austerity, nor by charity,
nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a manner as you have seen me.
This is almost entirely explained by the preceding statement.

Since even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, whose minds are preoccupied with their respective offices from the time of creation onwards, do not perceive His true nature, they constantly long for the direct realization of this form, yet they do not attain it.
Therefore, it is all the more difficult for anyone whatsoever to behold this which has been seen by you,
through the eye of supreme knowledge manifested by my grace. Thus, just as you have perceived me in reality, so too can others perceive me who are devoted to acts such as giving.
"I am impossible [to overcome]. || 57-58 ||
By what means, then, am I capable of being known? To this He says:
"But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, can I, who am of such a nature, be known in truth, seen, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe. (59)

By devotion— which arises solely through my will and is characterized by service easily accessible to those born into the lineage of the supreme divine creation— and by that very power, because right knowledge has manifested,
[the devotee] knows [me] with undivided devotion (*ananya*), since there exists no object of worship other than me. To know...
To understand through non-contradictory comprehension; likewise, to see—that is, to take as one's cognitive domain—by means of the method characterized by right knowledge;
and likewise, to enter [into it] as one's very self through the excellence of the repeated practice of cultivating such a method.

I can be fathomed only by one such as you who have experienced me as you have; I cannot be reached by other means. And because you have seen this supreme form directly, you have ascended to the highest stage, reaching even unto entry.

"Having crossed over the ocean of the delusion of duality, which is so difficult to traverse, take heart. For how can you now have any connection with defects such as fear and the like, which are appropriate only for those who have not seen the ultimate reality?"—this is the meaning. (59)
Establishing this very point as the final conclusion, he brings the chapter to a close:
"O Pāṇḍava, he who performs actions for Me, who regards Me as the supreme goal, who is My devotee, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity toward all beings—he comes to Me. (60)

Whoever else is endowed with such qualities and is devoted, he comes to me—that is, he attains the perfection characterized by non-difference from me. Of what nature is he? He is a performer of my work;
that is, he performs those various duties enjoined by the scriptures as they pertain to his specific caste and stage of life, yet—

"For my sake" means for the purpose of attaining Me according to one's capacity, and not for the accomplishment of any other fruit; therefore, "having Me as the supreme goal" means that I alone am the most excellent object to be attained by him. Consequently, because his mind is detached from all things—whether to be rejected or accepted—that are distinct from Me, he is "My devotee," belonging to Me alone.
A devotee is one whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is surrendered to Me alone in all circumstances. Likewise, he is free from attachment toward all beings, whether moving or stationary;
he is detached, devoid of passion, and free from enmity, being devoid of hatred—that which, through a lack of true knowledge, becomes an object of passion and hatred.
He who constantly experiences my own nature— which is filled with unsurpassed bliss— within all objects grasped by those in saṃsāra, he comes to me alone;
such a perfected one is called liberated here.
Such is the intended meaning; thus, Om. || 60 ||

"This [Self] does not abandon its nature, for it remains singular and absolutely pure despite the many shifting varieties of phenomenal states"— for those whose delusion has been dispelled by such reflection,
may the Lord's manifold cosmic form be manifested within their own very selves, like reflections in a jeweled mirror.
Through this commentary on the eleventh [chapter], the face of this sacred study has been clearly brought into manifestation.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* named *Sarvatobhadra*, which consists merely of the syntactical connection of the meaning of the words, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

Thus, when the eleventh chapter has been correctly understood from this supreme authority— the ultimate source of validity for all means of knowledge— characterized by the words of the Blessed One, the most trustworthy of beings;

There arises an unshakable realization regarding knowledge (*jñāna*), realized knowledge (*vijñāna*), and so forth— the subject matter of this treatise— because their ultimate purpose culminates in the practice of the synthesis of the individual chapters as explained, and because they are most thoroughly established by the facts set forth in this work; for this very reason:

Thus, through the grace of the Blessed One himself— inspired by his perception that [the king] had become a fit vessel for wisdom— he obtained the supreme favor, which consists of the knowledge of others and serves as the cause for the manifestation of the divine eye, all without any effort of his own.
By the mere power of the supreme grace of the Lord, the Supreme Reality was directly realized for a moment;
now, in order to remember it independently, what accessible path should I adopt? Or rather—

Desiring to know the means for crossing over the dense expanse of one's own and others' welfare— specifically, by what path that Reality is to be attained by a seeker who has secured the supreme favor through my words— Arjuna spoke:
Of those devotees who, being thus constantly disciplined, worship You, and those who worship the imperishable and unmanifest—the former, which group are the best knowers of yoga? (1)
Just as You have been directly realized as the very nature that transcends the universe while simultaneously being its soul,

so too those devotees who are ever-united— in this manner, constantly and at all times, in all states such as waking and the rest— being disciplined, composed, and full of affection toward You; [they likewise realize You].
They worship and serve that which is the syllable (akṣara),
whose sole nature is pure consciousness and which is by its very nature immovable; therefore, it is unmanifest (avyakta) and distinct from this manifest (vyakta) reality,
which is within the range of all the senses and characterized by manifold states of being.
Those whose intellects are perfected in the meditative absorption that negates all objects attend upon you;
among these two groups of yogins,
who are the most excellent knowers of yoga (*yogavittama*), meaning those whose meditative knowledge has the attainment of your own essential nature as its preeminent fruit?
Having been thus informed, the Blessed One spoke in order to demonstrate the preeminence of one particular side:
"Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me, ever disciplined..."
Endowed with supreme faith, they are considered by Me to be the most disciplined.

Such yogins as these, who possess the most perfect yoga and enjoy unsurpassed samādhi, are my opinion—meaning they are intended by me. I consider them to be the supreme yogins, and no others; this is the sense. Who are they?
Those who [meditate] upon Me, whose sole nature is the light of consciousness, which illumines all things and cannot be illumined by anything else.

Having entered the mind— that is, having brought it to a state of complete absorption— and being endowed with supreme faith, which is most excellent because it cuts through all doubts and conceptual fluctuations, and is possessed of the conviction regarding the aforementioned fruit, they remain ever-disciplined.

Constantly established in the aforementioned state of samādhi throughout those various conditions— which consist of the experience of all things, both gross and subtle— they worship and serve [the Lord] with unsurpassed devotion characterized by the constant awareness of their own true nature. || 2 ||
Thus, by this, it is established that superiority belongs specifically to those practitioners of action (*karmayogins*) among the knowers of yoga. For this very reason,
he speaks in order to demonstrate the inferiority of the means of other types of yogis, by first acknowledging their exertion and then establishing their difficulty and so forth:
But those who worship the Imperishable, which is indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, immovable, and eternal; (3)
Having fully restrained the collection of their senses and possessing equal intellect toward all things,
those who delight in the welfare of all beings attain Me alone.
But those yogis, however, who— having fully restrained the collection of senses, that is, having properly controlled with vigilance the aggregate of both external and internal senses,
and having withdrawn them from all objects— worship Me; in what manner?

The syllable (akṣara) and the unmanifest (avyakta) have their essential nature explained previously. For this very reason, it is "indescribable" (anirdeśya), because it is distinct from all objects of cognition that can be determined as "this," and thus it is impossible to describe, being beyond the path of speech.

Likewise, although it exists pervading all things as the omnipresent whole, it is inconceivable, transcending the sphere of the intellect. Likewise, because it is eternal in the ultimate sense, it is immutable (*kūṭastha*), established in a single nature that is undisturbed and indestructible. For this very reason, it is immovable and constant; indeed, it is not otherwise.

This [Self] may at some time be joined with an affliction characterized by motion, like an object situated on a mountain peak, or with destruction characterized by absolute non-existence. Being of what nature do they worship Me in such a way? They are those who possess equal intelligence toward all things. Toward everything—
Those whose intellects are described as such are those for whom the intellect is equal—meaning without distinction—because it perceives only my own nature within the vast reality.

Precisely because of this equanimity of intellect, they are devoted solely to the welfare of all beings; since they realize everything as their own self, they do not experience the defilement of the fault of hatred toward anything whatsoever. By this...

It has been established that this samādhi is not accomplished without these two qualifications; for a yogin who has not ascended to the state of complete equality is not said to be perfected. Those yogins of this kind who worship Me, they truly attain Me alone through the aforementioned method of practice.
For those who have perfected their meditative absorptions, the very attainment of my own nature is the fruit of their concentration, and nothing else. || 4 ||
But—greater is the suffering for those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest; for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by those who bear bodies. (5)
For those yogins who are established in the samādhi that negates all entities,

there is a greater and more intense affliction because of their fixation on all entities; they are superior to the previously described yogins who are intent upon my worship, as the latter are the most disciplined.

Of what kind of virtuous ones? Of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest— those whose internal organ (the mind) is fixed upon Me alone, as its sole object of support, in the Unmanifest, whose nature transcends the range of speech and thought.

In order to demonstrate how a mind attached to the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is a cause of even greater affliction (*kleśa*), he says (p. 268): "Because [of this], by those who bear a body (*dehabhṛt*)," that is, by those who, through the cognition "I am," identify with the body—the physical frame delimited by the conceit (*abhimāna*) of a fixed caste.
By such yogis who maintain [this practice], the unmanifest, entirely non-apparent state—the attainment of *samādhi*—is reached or acquired with difficulty, through great exertion.
This is the intended meaning: while the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) is being established within the body...
The attainment of my own nature, which is distinct from all existing things, is indeed impossible; moreover, attachment to that [nature] is nothing but a very great affliction. || 5 ||

Now, there may be some reasoning by which the body itself can be understood as being my own state; for it has been previously established that the cessation of all activity in every respect is impossible.
Therefore, one should remain engaged precisely in those activities enjoined by the scriptures.

The ultimate nature of the self does not bring such happiness to one who is intent on the prohibition of all difficult practices as it does to this [yogi]. Furthermore, such equanimity of mind toward everything is not possible for that kind of yogi, because aversion and other emotions are manifest in his regard for all objects as things to be prohibited.

But for one whose consciousness, due to being perfectly awakened, always and in every way rests solely in my own nature, and who has ceased the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted, equanimity toward all things is logically established.
This is the primary worship of the Lord’s own nature, the fourth stage of devotion (*bhakti*). As for that which...

To demonstrate that even the performance of daily obligatory rites (nityakriyā), which falls within the scope of various established ritual procedures (itikartavyatā) recognized by diverse philosophical systems, is likewise rendered valid by this very perspective, he says: "But those who, having renounced all actions in Me, are intent on Me..."
Meditating on me with undivided yoga, they worship me.
For those whose minds are absorbed in me, O Pārtha, I become their deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence before long.
But as for those yogis who are distinct from the yogis among the unmanifest devotees—
those yogis [should offer] all actions, whether physical, mental, or vocal, whether scriptural or worldly,
all such activities, unto Me, whose essential nature has been established as the sole agent of everything.

Having renounced—that is, having surrendered—the sense of agency consisting of the ego-identification with the body and so forth; those whose conceit has ceased regarding the agency of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field); who are "devoted to Me" (*matparāḥ*), meaning those for whom I alone am the supreme (*paraḥ*) by virtue of being the preeminent agent and so on; such persons [should act] with undivided devotion (*ananyena*).

Meditating upon me— my nature as it has been described— by means of a yoga consisting of the performance of prescribed duties, which is a form of concentration (samādhi) that does not involve union with any other reality distinct from me, they worship me, serving me with either primary or secondary devotion (bhakti).

For those practitioners of action of such a kind, in a short time— that is, in less time than required for the worshiper of the Unmanifest— I become their deliverer, their perfect savior from the ocean of the cycle of death, that sea of continuous succession of repeated destruction and origination.

Of what kind [of people]? Of those whose minds are absorbed in me, the Supreme Cause, the Supreme Lord—those who have surrendered their inner faculties through the contemplation of non-difference from me. (6–7)
Now, how is this most wonderful thing possible— that even while all worldly activities are being performed,
there is the accomplishment of supreme samādhi, characterized by non-deviation from the nature of the non-dual Supreme Brahman? Regarding this:
Although devotion has already been explained, He speaks again—after having taught it as something difficult to grasp due to its subtlety—in order to ensure firmness in its practice:
"Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me."
Abiding in the supreme yoga, you shall dwell within me alone.
In this world, all cognitions of objects for all knowers of the field (kṣetrajña) are dependent upon the mind and the intellect. For instance, the state of the mind is of two kinds:
that consisting of independent conceptualization, and that consisting of conceptualization in the form of recollection of what was previously experienced. This...

And it is of two kinds, due to the distinction between waking and dreaming; this is the case everywhere. Since the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*), however, consists of determination, it is thus established as being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpā*). In me alone—the one who is ultimately real, whose nature is the eternally arisen, stainless light of consciousness, the Supreme Self—the mind possesses the aforementioned nature.

Place it; settle it. Whatever you conceptualize with the mind, know each of those as being of My own nature. Likewise, fix the intellect—possessing the nature already described—in Me alone, who possesses that very nature.
p. 270) Surrender whatever you determine through your intellect; know that as being of my own nature.
This is the intended meaning here: whatever object is conceptualized or determined, in whatever form it is perceived, that [object], precisely because it is being perceived, [is of my nature].

It is non-different from the light of consciousness (*saṃvitprakāśa*). And this light, which is of the nature of consciousness, is the infallible attribute of my own single, ultimate cognizer. Thus, in their true form, all entities in all states are indeed identical with me; it is only that—
The world, deluded by *māyā*, discriminates those [objects] as being "this" or "that"; but you,
having first had your intellect expanded through the instruction of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and then, due to your superior fitness,
having directly experienced my own nature, perceive all entities in all their states.

From the perspective of ultimate reality, you perceive me solely as my own self-luminous revealer; thus, established in— meaning having resorted to— this supreme yoga, which is preeminent in comparison to other forms of yoga,
you shall dwell in me alone, the Supreme Self, and attain stable abidance therein.

The meaning is that you will attain the dissolution of delusion; for this very yoga of action (karmayoga) has as its sole means the performance of prescribed duties refined by the aforementioned knowledge,
and because it is experienced as being perfectly complete in every way, at all times, and in all places.

Its superiority arises from the yoga of practice, whose essential nature is to be experienced only occasionally and with great difficulty due to its being mastered through a sequence of many kinds of subtle practices cultivated over a long period and without interruption, part by minute part. || 8 ||

Having thus established the primary method of worshiping the essential nature of the Blessed One, and considering that not everyone might possess the fitness for it— as was the case with Arjuna— he declares the permission for other means by way of instruction to Arjuna alone:
If, however, you are unable to fix your mind steadily on me,
then seek to attain me, O Dhanañjaya, by the yoga of practice.
If you are unable even to practice, become intent on performing actions for Me;
by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.
p. 271) But if you are unable even to do this, then, taking refuge in my yoga, renounce the fruits of all actions with self-restraint. (11)

The word "atha" (now/then) is used for the purpose of introducing a specific method. If, in the manner already explained, one is able to cause the mind—the internal organ consisting of the functions of the intellect and the senses—to enter into Me, whose nature is as described, in a steady and firm state through unwavering concentration in all conditions; then...
If you are unable— that is, if you lack the power— to offer [the mind] by contemplating it as non-different from my own nature,
then, through the yoga of practice as a constituent part of the yoga of action,
according to the method indicated in the sixth chapter;

Desire— that is, long for— the attainment of Me, whose nature has been described above, by means of *samādhi* characterized primarily by the effort to restrain the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*), as qualified by the specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed in various Yoga scriptures; that is, desire to realize Me through non-difference.

The meaning is: without abandoning the intention to attain my own nature, you should also practice the yoga of meditation (*abhyāsa-yoga*), which serves as the cause for fitness for the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*). If you are unable or incapable even of such meditation—the yoga of meditation—then, being intent on my work (*mat-karma-paramaḥ*), [perform actions] for my sake.

"Perform actions"— meaning, become one for whom my actions alone are supreme because they are the most excellent means for achieving the desired goal; that is to say, practice the performance of *kriyā-yoga*, known as devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*), which is accepted as a limb of *karma-yoga*.

For from that too, the accomplishment of the fruit of samādhi—characterized by the attainment of My own nature—comes about. Therefore, He said: "Even while performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection. Now, if you are unable—that is, if you are incompetent—to do or accomplish even this as it has been described, then [take] My yoga.
Abiding in the meditative absorption (samādhi) that has me as its object and relying upon it as the fruit,
one performs the renunciation of the fruits of all actions— the fruit of all those previously mentioned actions being performed.

Being self-controlled— that is, possessing a restrained internal organ from all objects of sense— perform, that is, accomplish, renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which consists of the relinquishment without desire for the fruits of those various enjoyments experienced in various other worlds,
having concentrated your mind upon Me.
The meaning is: perform all actions prescribed by the scriptures as a means for accomplishing the aforementioned knowledge, without any desire for other fruits. (9–11)

(p. 272) Regarding these various forms of worship of the Lord thus taught, it has been instructed that when one is unable to perform each preceding one in succession, one should perform each subsequent one; this is not on account of the inferiority [of the former], but rather because of the renunciation appropriate to the qualified practitioner.
To demonstrate that it is indeed easier to understand, he says:

"Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge; the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation; and from renunciation follows peace immediately. (12)

The word "hi" indicates the reason. Since such a sequence of exposition as has been explained is intended here, therefore, for the sake of attaining Me, you should perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions, which— by virtue of your superior fitness— is easier to do.

The connection between the preceding and following statements is as follows: what kind of sequence is it? Here, "knowledge" is the realization that all entities have the nature of the Supreme Brahman through the aforementioned reasoning; that [knowledge] arises from "practice," that is, from the yoga of practice previously mentioned.

The better [path] is more praiseworthy because it is easier to perform. For the yoga of practice (*abhyāsa-yoga*) is the effort toward the cessation of mental fluctuations by means of the successive negation of all objects; and that is the domain of a qualified practitioner whose intellect has attained stability through the aforementioned knowledge. Therefore—

Knowledge whose subject matter concerns those qualified by a firmly established intellect is said to be superior because it is easier to accomplish in relation to that [other path]. For this very reason,
it is said that for those practicing through repeated effort (*abhyāsa-yogins*), there is greater hardship if their minds are attached to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

This has been stated previously. Furthermore, from such knowledge, meditation—which is the contemplation of the object to be attained as determined by knowledge—is superior; it excels because it is easier to perform.
For, in comparison to that knowledge...

The qualified practitioner is one who is engaged in the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), for it is precisely by virtue of that being its object that [the practice] becomes easy for him. And the renunciation of the fruits of action is distinguished from such meditation,
because he is in the state of striving (*ghaṭamāna-avasthā*) within that very definition of such meditation.

The cognition of distinction regarding action indeed manifests. With respect to the qualified person for that [renunciation], renunciation has as its object the state of perfection; for such a person alone is it easily performed.
Thus it has been said that the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation. For this reason, such a form of renunciation does not exist here [in the case of the beginner].
This is what is intended: that its accomplishment occurs through mere verbal assertion— such as "I am not the doer, nor is there for me any connection with the fruit of action"—
but rather it concerns the yogi who has transcended previous stages such as practice and so forth.

Because all entities are eternally experienced as having the nature of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma*), the very non-perception of any result distinct from that is called renunciation (*tyāga*). For this very reason, it is said:
"From renunciation comes immediate peace" (*tyāgācchāntiranantarā*); [this is] peace.

Due to the destruction of the agitation caused by conceptualization and discursive thought, there is the undisturbed repose of consciousness as non-dual with the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure non-dual consciousness, in the realization "I am [He]. Between that [consciousness] and its abandonment, there is no interval or separation; for that which is...

Renunciation is itself peace, characterized by absorption in the Lord (īśvara-samāpatti), which is perfection; thus it is said that "from renunciation, peace follows immediately. If the reading is *anantaram* (immediately), this same meaning should be understood as an adverbial qualification of the action. || 12 ||
Now, he describes the characteristics of such a devotee who is renounced, whose consciousness has attained equanimity toward all, and who has become one with the Self:
"He who is not a hater of any being, but is friendly and compassionate..."
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, equal in pleasure and pain, and patient. || 13 ||
The yogi who is always content, self-controlled, and firm in resolve;
whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me. 14.

One who is distinguished by such qualities as these—which indicate absorption into my own nature, which is the Supreme Brahman—is my devotee; he alone is dear to me, for he is beloved because he has become my very self. Of what sort is he?
Because he has attained equanimity toward all, he is one who feels no hatred toward any living beings, whether moving or stationary.

The meaning is that for one who perceives the entire range of existing things as his own self, being free from the defect characterized by aversion, there is an absence of aversion because there is nothing to be rejected. By this, the previously mentioned severance of the continuity of the defect of aversion within the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consisting of the negation of objective existence is reiterated. For this very reason, he is friendly toward all.

He is possessed of friendliness (*sauhārda*). Likewise, he is compassionate (*karuṇa*), that is, merciful, because he is free from the sense of "mine" (*nirmama*)—having emerged from the notion of possession that thinks "this is mine" based on its capacity for purposeful action.
Similarly, he is free from egoism (*nirahaṅkāra*), having emerged from the notion of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*) which is fixed upon impermanent things such as the body.

p. 274) Likewise, for one to whom pleasure and pain are equal—because they appear merely as objects of cognition (*vedyatva*) and because they consist of transformations (*vikāra*) such as hatred and passion which have just been manifested; likewise, one who is patient (*kṣamī*), that is, possessed of endurance (*titikṣāvān*) toward the causes of transformations such as anger; likewise...

Because he has attained the supreme nectar of knowledge, he is eternally content and always entirely free from desire. Likewise, he is one whose self is restrained (*yatātmā*), meaning he is one by whom the self has been established within his own Self alone. For all the unawakened are likewise those whose mental conviction of the self is restricted to non-self objects such as wealth and the like.

One who possesses firm resolve— that is, one whose determination is steadfast and well-established because it cannot be shaken by any conceptual fluctuation— and likewise, one by whom the mind and intellect have been offered to Me, the Supreme Self, in the manner previously explained.
He who is distinguished by such qualities is called My devotee; the intended meaning here is that such a collection of factors constitutes the perfection of the means for My worship. || 14 ||
Now, in the following verses, the words employed as qualifiers of the preeminent devotee are merely recited, since their meaning has for the most part already been explained:
"He from whom the world does not tremble, and who does not tremble from the world..."
He who is free from joy, impatience, fear, and anger—he too is dear to me. || 15 ||
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, free from distress, and has renounced all undertakings—that devotee of mine is dear to me. 16.
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced the fruits of both good and evil, and who is full of devotion—he is dear to me. 17.
He is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
he is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment.
One who is equal toward blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion—that man is dear to Me. (19)

The meaning of these adjectives is already established; however, the intended purport here has been stated previously: he who is endowed with such qualities as these—which are connected to the supreme yogis and serve as the causes for manifesting the state of having accomplished all that was to be done—he is my devotee. (15–19)
Now, concluding the chapter, he says:
"But those who worship this nectar of dharma as it has been described, full of faith, regarding Me as the supreme goal—they, being devotees, are exceedingly dear to Me. (20)
Those devotees who are intent upon my worship, who are dedicated to me, [should partake of] this nectar of dharma as it has been set forth—
this nectar consisting of right conduct centered on the worship of my own nature, which is the cause of immortality.
Those who worship—that is, they serve—the Reality through constant practice, they are exceedingly, most surely, dear to Me;

the meaning is that they are not separate from Me. Being of what nature do they worship? They are full of faith, cultivating faith which is the seed of all spiritual accomplishments; and for that very reason—

"Those for whom I am the Supreme": I alone, whose nature has been described as above, am the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, who is the ultimate goal to be attained through all means; those for whom I am thus the supreme and most excellent [goal], having attained the highest perfection which has faith as its root and results in absorption into Me—thus it is, Om. 20.

Where this very glory of the wish-fulfilling tree of devotion to the Blessed One blooms of its own accord— enticing even the minds of the virtuous, though they are devoid of longing for the pursuit of any worldly object—
the inhabitants of the Nandana grove, weary of their celestial wanderings, come there out of curiosity to behold it at all times.
O men of refined intellect, take refuge in this commentary on the twelve chapters as your sole ground of rest.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meanings of the statements, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.

Through the twelve preceding chapters, the entire reality of the subject matter—the purpose already introduced—has been stated almost in its entirety. It remains [to be discussed]... [text fragment ends].

There remains something yet to be said. Now, the very meaning already stated is being elaborated upon by the remaining five chapters for the sake of purification. And so, according to the sequence of action shown in the introduction:
Although the Supreme Lord is established in His single, ultimate nature as previously described, He—

solely for the purpose of His own incomparable play— manifests His very own singular self-nature by means of two branches, through the conceptualization of the division between the object of knowledge and the subject.
This great snare consisting of illusion (māyā), which she spread out,

remains having completely enclosed the entire wheel of transmigratory existence, manifesting itself through the distinction between objects and subjects and through the relationship between the body and the embodied soul; by her own will, it—

The Supreme Lord himself has taught the subject matter characterized by knowledge— whose nature is explained here and there throughout this entire treatise, which serves as the means for stringing together [the teachings] directed toward those persons he has chosen to favor— in that [work], through the distinction between the object and the subject.

For the purpose of unraveling that which remains [concealed], the seventh chapter, characterized by knowledge (*jñāna*), elaborates upon the subject matter; for therein, the very reality of the Supreme is [disclosed] through the distinction between the insentient and the sentient, preceded by the discernment of the expansion of *prakṛti* in its gross and subtle forms. Thus is the meaning of that [chapter].

The final resolution is established by demonstrating that the higher *prakṛti*, characterized as the reality of Brahman and taught in such passages as "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world" (7.6), is in its ultimate sense non-different from the two [other] *prakṛtis*, the higher and the lower.

Now, he begins the immediately following chapter for the purpose of determining knowledge as the means for uncoiling her, who exists in the relationship of body and embodied being; therein, first, having expanded upon those two— the body and the embodied being— ...

By providing an indication of the designation of the knowledge that is about to be explained, the Blessed One, while demonstrating its general characteristic, also briefly stated the essential nature of the intended knowledge: [The Blessed One said: (p. 277) [He who knows... etc.
This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the "field" (kṣetra). Those who know this call him who knows it the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). (1)

This body, established as being well-known to all cognizers, is called a "field" (kṣetra) because of its similarity to a field; it is described by the designation "field. Just as [the potentiality] of seeds such as grain situated within a granary or similar receptacle—

The field (kṣetra) is defined as that locus where the manifestation of specific productions— such as roots, trunks, branches, and stones— occurs with reference to the earth; likewise, it is the locus for the manifestation of those karmas accumulated within the latent deposit of karma (karmāśaya).

The body, which serves as the substratum for the manifestation of the specific results of maturation characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience, is also called this "field. Therefore, that which is experienced as the locus for the ripening of those actions should be understood as the body. And he who [knows] this field of such a nature—

One who knows—that is, one who understands—is known by those who know that [knowledge], namely those who know the true nature of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), as the "Knower of the Field. What is expressed by this? In this body, there exists for all embodied beings a twofold perception: through the sense of "I" (*ahantā*) and through the sense of "this" (*idantā*). Thus, [one perceives]: "I am a Brahmin..."

Through such expressions as "Yajñadatta," they determine the body by way of its identity with the self (*mahantā*); at other times, they determine it by way of its objectivity (*idantā*), as in "this is my body. Therefore, there certainly exists here some determiner who is the subject (*pramātā*). And that aspect which is perceived as the subject is the *kṣetrajña*.

The living being (jīva) is to be understood as consciousness (cetana). Thus, whatever in this body is perceived through its state of being an object of knowledge, solely by virtue of its relation to a knower, that should be known as a portion of the field (kṣetra). That which is perceived as the knower is to be known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Self (ātman). It is only to this extent [that the distinction is made].
Constant attentiveness is the cause of the knowledge that discriminates between the body and the embodied soul. Yet,

for all embodied beings whose vision of reality is obscured by *māyā*, this [attentiveness] does not awaken even in a dream, as they remain bound by the mere relationship between the object of cognition and the cognizer, which underlies all higher and lower worldly transactions.

To whatever extent the vision of reality has been opened for them solely by the power of the Lord’s grace—that alone is the object of this knowledge; such is the intended meaning. For it has been said: "Only certain yogins who know that [reality] perceive it. (1)

Now, one might object: "Has it not been established that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), there is only a single cognizer? Yet, in every field (kṣetra), the uncontradicted cognition of distinct experiencers remains firmly established.
To dispel this confusion regarding the contradiction with his own system, he says:
And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata;
that which is the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field is, in My view, true knowledge. (2)

Here, the single, non-deviating, and unique characteristic of the self has been stated as the mere quality of being a knower (*vedakatvamātra*). Therefore, it is established that the distinct natures belong only to the bodies— which are the objects of knowledge (*vedya*), mutually differentiated, and subject to various momentary states— and not to the self.
There is no plurality of the one ultimate Self, the knower who exists as the presiding principle by virtue of being merely the state of knowing,
even though it resides within all bodies, because it never deviates from the single characteristic of being the knower. As for that [distinction] which occurs in each body...
The perception of [the Self] as distinct through the delimitation of birth is nothing but the play of the inconceivable power of the Lord’s Māyā;
therefore, for the very purpose of dispelling that [delusion], this teaching is spoken by means of Arjuna for the sake of those who are awakened.
[It concerns] all fields existing through the distinctions of the fourteenfold creation of beings.

Know me alone— the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Supreme Self— to be present within all innumerable bodies. Just as, during the state of Māyā, the perception of the Knower of the Field exists merely through its awareness of the various parts situated within a single field, so too [is it here].

As the experiencer of the entire body, I alone am the one ultimate Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Therefore, that knowledge which consists of the correct realization of such a Field and Knower of the Field is alone intended by Me as "knowledge," and not that which is propounded by the Sāṃkhya and other systems.

The intended meaning is that the mere knowledge of the distinction between the body and the embodied soul is the ultimate, essential knowledge. Now, [the nature] of the field (kṣetra), which— though established in various forms through the differences of the various philosophical systems— is...

(p. 279) Since there is no difference in the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) consisting merely in being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*), when its true nature is to be established by relying on some particular system of philosophy,
[the author] does so by resorting to the Sāṃkhya system as it is well-known from the Vedas and other scriptures.
In order to introduce the essential nature of the field that is about to be explained, he says:
"Listen to me in brief concerning that field—what it is, of what kind it is, what its modifications are, from whence it arises, who it is, and what its inherent nature is. (3)
It has been sung by the seers in many ways, separately through various Vedic meters,
and it has been definitively established through the reasoned words of the Brahma-sūtras.
Understand in brief that field which was introduced as being knowable by the Knower of the Field—
meaning, what its designation is, as well as in what manner and by what variety of modes it exists; and also whatever object within that field is subject to modification.
Because it possesses a specific causal relationship, it is subject to modification, like a transformation; listen to that as well.
Likewise, listen also to how from that which is subject to modification, whatever object arises as a modification.
Furthermore, listen to who that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is, what his synonyms are, what his nature is, and what he is like.

Understand all of that as it is being stated in brief. In order to demonstrate that this subject matter is well-known through both Smṛti and Śruti, he says: it has been "sung" (gītam) in various ways—that is, in many forms—here and there in the Smṛti scriptures by the sages who are the authors of those Smṛtis. Likewise...

It was sung in various meters (*chandobhiḥ*)—in diverse forms according to the different branches of the Vedas—and for that very reason, in distinct sections (*prakaraṇa*). By the term "Brahmasūtra-words" (*brahmasūtrapadaiḥ*), the secret portion of the Veda known as Vedānta is meant; those which are its constituent words (*padāni*).

These are the intermediate sentences; by means of these, which possess logical reasons and are joined with rational arguments, it is "thoroughly ascertained," meaning a specific determination has been made. || 3-4 ||

Thus, by this [verse], the fact that the subject matter to be explained— which sets forth the field (*kṣetra*) and so on— is well-known from the Vedas, the Upanishads, and the Smritis has been stated. In that regard, concerning what was said— that "there is the field and there is the knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*)— the field is the body, and he who knows it is the knower of the field.

Having already stated their essential nature with the words "of whatever kind," etc., he says the following to state what remains: (p. 280) "The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest."
The sense faculties are eleven, and the objects of the sense faculties are five.
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the physical aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude—
this is declared to be the field (kṣetra) in brief, along with its modifications.
This field, consisting of a collection of entities such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, is joined with transformation;

because it grasps transformation, it is also briefly described as being joined with that which has become primordial nature (*prakṛti*). In this context, by the word "great elements," the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) themselves are meant, since they possess greatness in terms of pervasiveness and other qualities.

These are to be understood, since by means of half a verse the four categories that constitute the cause have been summarized. Among them, *ahaṅkāra*—the notion "I am"—is in some places expressed by the word *asmitā*.
*Buddhi* is well known as the principle of the Great (*mahat-tattva*), which is knowledge characterized by ascertainment. Likewise...

The unmanifest (avyakta) is primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of the three qualities (guṇas). These four, beginning with the gross [elements], have been specified in their causal order. Furthermore, the subtle elements (tanmātras) are the causes of the gross elements, such as earth and the rest. And the ego (ahaṅkāra) is divided into the categories of taijasa, vaikārika, and bhūtādi.

It is threefold. In this regard, it is the cause of the mind by virtue of its *taijasa* (fiery) nature, of the sense organs by virtue of its *vaikārika* (pure/transformative) nature, and of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) by virtue of its *bhūtātman* (elemental) nature; thus, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which consists of these three types of qualities (*guṇas*), possesses causality. However, some maintain that the sixfold group characterized by the ego and the subtle elements has its origin in me (*mattattva*).

Some say that the cause [of the world] is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) itself; thus, they establish the intellect (*buddhi*) as the cause. Furthermore, they state that the cause of the intellect is *prakṛti*—which consists of the three *guṇas* and is denoted by the term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
By thus explaining these four causal entities, the subject matter introduced as "that which undergoes transformation" (*yadvikāri*) is established.
This has been determined. For here, the Unmanifest (avyakta), with respect to its own domain of authority, is the root cause;

and egoity (ahaṅkāra), being an effect of the intellect (buddhi), is the cause of the sense organs and so forth; and the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi), being effects of egoity or effects of the intellect, are the cause of earth and the other gross elements.

Because they are the causes of all four [categories], they possess the quality of being subject to modification (*vikāritva*). Now, in order to set forth the category of effects (*kāryavarga*), he says: the five sense organs (*indriya*)—the five cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*) such as hearing and so forth, which are well known—and the five [organs] beginning with speech.

The organs of action (*karmendriya*) are also a reality (*tattva*), as is the mind (*manas*), which is the eleventh and consists of volition and conceptualization. Regarding the "five objects of the senses," although the term "objects of the senses" refers to sound and the other qualities of the elements, nevertheless, [it refers to] the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Since the perception of their own nature occurs through the perception of their own qualities, the term "objects of the senses" refers only to the gross elements; for this group of sixteen is a collection of modifications (*vikāra*), and it is exclusively an effect (*kārya*), not a cause (*kāraṇa*). Thus it is established according to the Sāṃkhya system.

This twenty-fourfold set of principles (tattvas) is established in the form of the body; because it is to be known by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), it is called the "Field" (kṣetra). Now, however, regarding the various collections of categories that have been formulated in other philosophical systems by relying upon their respective specific methodologies:
Since everything that exists does not transcend the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), it follows that according to our position, it is indeed the field (*kṣetra*).

To demonstrate this, he says "desire," and so forth. By some, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, and the like are accepted as attributes of the self; however, because they are objects of cognition, they are nothing but the field. Likewise...

The aggregate is the collection of the body, the senses, and so forth. Consciousness (*cetanā*)—derived from the sense that "by this [instrument] one perceives" (*cetayate*)—is knowledge, which is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the ego-sense (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) based on the maintenance of the vital breaths and other functions. All of this—

The purport of this half-verse, "it is indeed the field (*kṣetra*) because it does not transcend the state of being an object of knowledge," is as follows: how can the Self, whose sole nature is that of the subject (*pramātṛ*), be an object of knowledge (*prameya*); or how [can there be such a thing] for that [Self], whose essential character is defined as the synthesizing subject (*anusaṃdhātṛ*) established by the impossibility of all worldly transactions?

Many scholars have exerted great effort to refute various arguments, such as "it is impossible" or "how can that whose majesty is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth exist throughout one's entire life? And that [state] is the stage of the reality being established.
Because it concerns persons who have not yet transcended the state of having a doubtful intellect;
in this discussion of the established tenets (*siddhānta*), even one who possesses qualities such as pure faith manifested through the grace of the Lord,
is a specific type of person fit for instruction by one whose stainless wisdom is free from defects such as well-formed doubts.
When this [objection] is presented, there is no purpose whatsoever other than the clouding of the intellect; for,
toward a person who is relishing a perfectly prepared and delicious variety of food,
there is nothing beyond merely producing a distaste for the meal at hand by explaining the state of its preparation.

One should not follow the path of those whose souls are mocked by the ostentatious display of a dance of untimely scholarship, under the pretext that some benefit might arise; rather, one should consider the characteristics of the field exactly as they were introduced.
Thus much has been determined. 5–6.
Now, that which was introduced as "who he is" and "what his nature is"—namely, the definition of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)—remains to be determined. And so:
"And know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (13.2).
Thus, only the primary single *kṣetrajña* is intended;

his "object of knowledge," which I shall declare—beginning with the words "I shall declare that" (13.12)—he will explain at length by means of its defining characteristics. But for now, regarding such a *kṣetrajña*:

Regarding the field that has been described, in order to demonstrate that the very collection of qualities which serves as the cause for its manifestation— by means of which qualities the knowledge previously established as the primary form of perfect realization is revealed— is itself "knowledge," he says:
Humility, unpretentiousness, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-control. (7)
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism, and the contemplation of the evils of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering. (8)
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (9)
And unswerving devotion to me through the yoga of exclusive concentration;
the habit of dwelling in solitary places, and a lack of delight in the assembly of worldly people. (10)
Constancy in the knowledge of the inner self and the perception of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
that which is otherwise than this is ignorance. || 11 ||
For one who is prone to faults such as rivalry and the like,
the resolve to imitate the virtuous conduct practiced by other well-known persons is called *māna* (pride). And that [resolve] persists even after the act has been performed.
(p. 283) To bring about the fruit of falling into the abyss of saṃsāra through mere virtuous conduct is a great defect pertaining to those belonging to the asura creation; and so it has been said:
The fire-sacrifice of pride, the silence of pride, study through pride, and sacrifice through pride—
these four bring about fearlessness.
"Things not performed according to rule bestow fear" (Mahābhārata).

Thus, the four entities— namely the Agnihotra and others— which take the form of the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma), when performed as enjoined by the scriptures, first of all grant freedom from fear.

Indeed, the meaning of this verse is also that actions performed with a mind defiled by faults such as pride result, on the contrary, in great fear for the one who undertakes them. One who possesses such pride is "the proud" (*mānī*);
the state of being that is "pridedness" (*mānitvam*), and the absence of that is "humility" (*amānitvam*).

The quality called purity of intention (*śuddha-saṃkalpatva*) is termed "knowledge" because it is the cause for the manifestation of knowledge. In the same way, there is freedom from hypocrisy (*adambhitva*). For hypocrisy exists when one's intention is defiled by faults such as pride, and [one acts] merely for the sake of visible results.

The performance of virtuous conduct (*sadācārānuṣṭhāna*) means practicing dharma through hypocrisy. One who possesses that is a hypocrite (*dambhī*), a practitioner of false conduct; the state of being such is hypocrisy (*dambhitva*). The absence of that is non-hypocrisy (*adambhitva*), which means the performance of actions correctly; that too is as explained previously.

It is knowledge alone. Likewise is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). Violence (*hiṃsā*) is defined as the desire to kill living beings by one who is addicted to hatred, greed, and so forth, without regard for scriptural injunctions; its absence is non-violence.
This is the state of being free from malice toward all beings due to a heart moistened with natural compassion; that too is knowledge.

Likewise, forbearance (*kṣānti*) is the state of being unchanging in speech, mind, and action when one is being harmed by others, despite having the capacity for retaliation, due to the natural tranquility of the mind; that too is indeed knowledge (*jñāna*). Now, if non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and forbearance are knowledge, then how [is this so]?
It is said that for Arjuna— who had been accepted as a fit recipient for the instruction of the knowledge of reality—
while being enjoined to the performance of actions such as sacrifice and battle, the violence and impatience inherent therein were taught as things to be practiced. This is stated [as follows]:

For one who is established in the knowledge described above, violence and impatience—which exist as their own duties that must necessarily be performed—do not actually constitute violence, nor do they constitute impatience; this has already been stated previously. *Ārjava* is straightforwardness, the absence of crookedness, which is the cause for the activity of speech and mind in accordance with the heart.
That which they praise is this:
"Everything crooked is the station of death; straightforwardness is the station of Brahman.
That too is knowledge. Thus, these are the five dharmas.

They are born suddenly only for those who partake in the divine creation indicative of the grace of the Supreme Lord, and not for others whose continuity of good and evil karma is being exhausted and whose wisdom is capable of discerning the true nature of saṃsāra. And they...
For that person who has established [the teaching] in his heart, it serves as the root-continuum of the tree of knowledge.

When such a person is impelled by the power of grace through the cultivation of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth, the dharma known as "service to the teacher" or "propitiation of a true guru" arises; this is...
Knowledge. Indeed, this [knowledge] is a factor that serves as the trunk of the tree of the knower;
from it, these factors arise like branches and spreading twigs, namely:
a specific mental formation preceded by the mastery of the treatises, as well as [the cognition] regarding objects to be abandoned and to be adopted.
Discernment (*viveka*) is the inclination toward the practice of what is to be adopted, preceded by the rejection of what is to be abandoned, for one who has realized the true nature of reality.
When such qualities arise through the very service of the teacher (*ācāryopāsanā*), they stand in the place of sprouts and flowers.
Specific virtues, beginning with purity (*śauca*) and ending with the perception of defects such as birth and so forth,

emerge. In that regard, for one who has attained the qualification for the performance of specific rites and whose mind is attached to those various actions which are causes of well-being, and who is being bound by their qualities, the first is purity (*śauca*).
Name is a quality of all actions because they are preceded by it. And that is of two kinds:

external and internal. Therein, the external [name] consists of earth, water, and so forth, according to fixed procedures in dependence on the status of the qualified person, place, time, and other factors.

Purification (*mṛjā*) consists in the removal of impure substances, odors, smears, and so forth, up to the final cleansing. When external [impurities] have ceased, the unshakable conviction that "I am pure" is what they call internal purity (*bhāva-śuddhi*). And this purification pertains to those [actions] accomplished through body, speech, and mind.

Austerity (tapas) should be understood as an indicative term for other qualities such as self-study (svādhyāya), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth. Now, stability (sthirya) consists in the cessation of defects such as doubt regarding those matters that are to be practiced.

Immovability. And when that exists, there is self-restraint—the restraining or controlling of the self, that is, the internal organ, from prohibited objects. And from that arises dispassion toward the objects of the senses—whether perceived or revealed—due to seeing the defects such as decay and excess.
The state of being free from attachment and aversion, reaching its highest excellence, culminates even in the virtues of other sentient beings. When such a virtue exists, there is non-egoism—
the absence of the wicked conceit that "I am such a person"— or alternatively:

It is the cessation of the notion "I am" with respect to the body and so forth. And from that follows the observation—that is, the retrospective examination—of the great evil of suffering itself, which originates from defects such as birth and so on.
For example, the suffering of birth consists in the experience of unsurpassed afflictions, such as dwelling in the womb and so forth.

For one who has taken up a body, the suffering of death is inevitable; likewise, while the body exists, there is the suffering of old age, disease, and so forth. Thus, this state of being embodied is nothing but suffering throughout its initial, middle, and final stages. Therefore, having ascended the palace of discernment (*viveka*), one should investigate—both with respect to oneself and others—the nature of this condition.
He is patient. As it has been said:
"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man, beyond grief, looks down upon grieving people, just as one standing on a mountain peak gazes upon all those standing on the ground."

Thus, for one who is of such a nature, there is non-attachment (*asaṅga*), that is, detachment or indifference, toward specific ritual actions whose fruits are heaven and the like; likewise, there is non-clinging (*anabhiṣvaṅga*) toward the causes of perceived pleasure, such as children, wife, and home, which entails the renunciation of all possessions. And for one who has reached this state—
Equanimity amidst the occurrence of the desirable and undesirable— that is, when encountering pleasant or unpleasant objects—

consists in a state of mind free from internal fluctuations such as joy, grief, and the like. It is precisely within this collection of qualities, which serves as the site for the various sprouts and flowers of the tree of knowledge, that [this equanimity resides].

When [the state] has been accomplished, devotion—which stands in the place of the fruit—is my worship. Of what nature is it? It is unswerving, meaning free from any lapse. By what means? By "exclusive yoga" (*ananya-yoga*), that is, by means other than that which is distinct from my own nature as it has been described.
(286) "Connection with the object" (*vastu-yoga*) means a relation with something else; the absence of that is "non-connection with anything else" (*ananya-yoga*), by which [it is meant].

What is being said? The vision of all existents as non-different from my own nature is the primary devotion to me (*mad-bhakti*), which is the fruit of the tree of knowledge. For that is the fourth [kind of devotion].
The state of devotion consists in being a possessor of knowledge (*jñānitva*). As was stated previously:
"But the man of knowledge, I consider to be My very Self" (7.18).
And when that [state] exists, there is the practice of resorting to solitary places (*viviktadeśasevitva*), [which refers to] a solitary place.
