It is the habit of resorting to and dwelling in mountain caves, sacred riverbanks, and secluded dwellings— places devoid of any animate or inanimate object that could obstruct the tasting of the nectar of such unsurpassed devotional rasa—
and a lack of delight in social assemblies where the mind is distracted by worldly crowds and which are hostile to spiritual progress.

"Distress" means the avoidance of that [worldly attachment]. Likewise, "constancy in the knowledge of the supreme self" (*adhyātmajñānanityatva*) refers to one for whom the knowledge of the supreme self—that is, the realization of the nature of the Supreme Self—is constant and unerring; the state of being such is its "nature" (*tattva*). And when that [constancy] exists—

The vision of the object of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānārthadarśanam*) means the knowledge, the awakening, the self-reflective experience of the supreme state (*para-bhāva*), which is characterized by the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātmasvarūpa*). By the former term, one who postulates the attainment of knowledge, the latter term establishes that very [knowledge] as being already accomplished; it is that very [state].

The meaning is that "the vision of the goal" refers to the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that whose purpose is the goal and whose fruit is the goal; this constitutes unsurpassed perfection (*niruttarā siddhi*). These qualities, beginning with dwelling in secluded places and ending with the vision of the goal which is the purpose of the knowledge of reality, are the constituent factors of devotion in its state as a fruit; such is the totality of these attributes.

"Knowledge" (jñāna) has been explained; its meaning is clear. Therefore, whatever exists in a manner other than—that is, contrary to—the aforementioned collection of qualities, such as pride, hypocrisy, and so forth, all that should be understood as ignorance (ajñāna), which is the opposite of knowledge. And this [will be explained] further on.
In the context of narrating the creation of the gods and asuras, he will again describe the characteristics of knowledge and ignorance. (7–11)
And by means of such knowledge—
(I shall now) declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality.
That which is to be known (*jñeya*) is that which is to be understood as the fruit established by the aforementioned knowledge.

I shall now declare—that is, I will explain in detail—the reality characterized as the Supreme Self; having known that, having realized it, one attains—that is, pervades—the immortal, which is of an imperishable nature. [Objection: But how can that which is not perceivable by anything else...

How can that which has the nature of being the perceiver of all things be designated as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), like any other distinct entity determined by the notion of "this-ness"? True; its status as an object of knowledge is not possible from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
However, it is [so designated] during the stage of one who desires to ascend [to higher levels].

Because it consists of the distinction between the knower, the knowing, and the known, the term "the known" (jñeya) is applied to it figuratively; its status as "the known" is not intended in an ultimate sense. For its true knowledge is precisely the reflective awareness of it as one's own self, in the form "this is I."
In the same way, through the distinction [of "I" and "this"],
the realization of that single reality, characterized merely as the experiencer, is possible.
He states those very qualifications of it as follows: "The beginningless supreme Brahman is said to be neither being nor non-being. (12)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands encompassing all.
It appears to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses;
it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all; it is free from the gunas and yet the experiencer of the gunas.
It exists both outside and within all beings, as the unmoving and indeed as the moving;
because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible—that which is far away and yet near.
Undivided, yet existing as if divided among those who are divided;
it should be known as the sustainer of beings, as well as the devourer and the progenitor.
That is the light even of lights; it is said to be beyond darkness.
It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge, established in the heart of all. 17.
"What is that which is to be known?"— he indicates it by the designation "the Supreme Brahman.
Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*),
all things are established as being of the nature of Brahman, that which is currently [presented] as the object of knowledge...
That which appears is the lower [Brahman]; however, that whose nature consists solely of the knower is said to be the higher Brahman.

Of what kind is that? It is "without beginning" (*anādimat*). This object of knowledge, common to all knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), consisting of earth and so forth, exists as an established object of experience.

Likewise, it exists as the body for each individual knower (kṣetrajña), having been previously established as possessing a dual nature; being dependent upon causes, it has a beginning, and because its nature consists of coming and going, it is delimited by a prior limit; and therefore—

Even that which is delimited by its final limit is thus defined; however, the opposite of that—the Supreme Brahman—is said to be without beginning and to exist independently of any other cause. Furthermore, what is it like? It is not "existent" (sat).
For in this world, whatever is grasped as "this" by the external and internal senses is [only so perceived] by subjects under the influence of *māyā*.

It is apprehended as "existent" (*sat*). However, Brahman—because its sole nature is that of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and because it transcends the domain of all the senses—is not "existent" in that manner. Nor, on the other hand, is it called "non-existent" (*asat*). For even though everything apprehended as existent appears in such a way, it is precisely that [Brahman] which is the illuminator of all things.

How can that which is the cause of existence be said to be non-existent? For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that this [Reality], whose nature is the single ultimate subject (*paramārtha-sat-eka-pramātṛ*), possesses the form of the universe, he says "with hands and feet everywhere," and so forth. Those which belong to all the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*)...
The organs of action, such as the feet and so forth, and the organs of cognition, such as the eyes, ears, and so forth, which are established as the means for their respective actions and cognitions—
these are merely distinct manifestations of the power of that one Universal Self, who is the unique agent and knower.

The intended meaning is as follows: because it says, "It exists pervading everything," that single reality alone exists, pervading this entire world by way of being both the agent and the knower. For this very reason, it says, "it appears through the qualities of all the senses. Those [qualities] which, by virtue of their connection with various individual souls (*kṣetrajña*),...

It is so described because it illuminates— that is, makes manifest— the qualities and attributes of all the internal and external sense organs as they appear, such as their capacity to manifest objects like sound and the rest; yet it itself is devoid of all sense organs, for it does not possess them.

The meaning is that knowledge is dependent upon the restricted senses, like a *kṣetrajña* whose essential nature is delimited by what is manifested through *māyā*. Likewise, it is unattached because it is established solely in its own nature as pure consciousness, and thus [unaffected] by the object of knowledge which is of the nature of *prakṛti*.

It is unmixed with conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and yet it sustains all—that is, it supports and maintains everything. For within that reality, whose nature is distinct from the objects of knowledge (*vedya*), all this is established, since without it nothing whatsoever could attain its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) in relation to the qualities (*guṇa*).

It has emerged from sattva and the other [guṇas]— which consist of illumination, activity, and restraint, and whose functions are pleasure, pain, and delusion— and its essential nature is absolutely distinct from them;
for Brahman does not consist of impermanent pleasure and so forth, but is like the pure ether.
Although its own nature is absolutely untouched by various qualities such as sunlight, dust, or darkness,
it is nevertheless perceived as possessing those qualities by cognizers who lack inquiry into reality;
for in fact, because it is the enjoyer of the qualities, it experiences them as a perceiver of the qualities, but not [as their creator].
By those [limitations], its true nature is concealed. Therefore,

because it is the universal form whose own majesty is unconditioned, like space [which exists] externally as the object of knowledge for all beings— both moving and unmoving, such as jars and the like— it likewise exists internally.
And although it appears as the state of the knower, in ultimate reality that single reality is established as having the very nature of universal consciousness;
the designation of "external" and "internal" is caused merely by the intervention of cognitions such as the body. For this very reason:
He said: Because it is established solely in its own eternally immovable nature, it is "non-moving" (*acara*), being devoid of the quality of motion;

yet, because its power is eternally extended through its capacity to cognize all objects, it is "moving" (*cara*), as if having the habit of going. Likewise, because its essential nature is distinct from all objects that are to be apprehended as "this," [it is both moving and non-moving].

It is supremely subtle; and because of that subtlety, it is "unintelligible," meaning its essential nature cannot be determined as "this. For this very reason, since it is not an object of knowledge for any cognizers, it is "distant," being extremely remote. And yet, without it, nothing at all [could exist].
Because neither knowledge nor action is possible [in relation to it], it stands in close proximity to all things.

Likewise, while objects are divided—being mutually distinct as gods, humans, animals, and so forth—it remains undivided and of a single, non-different nature, consisting of the essence of universal consciousness. And yet...
And it exists as if divided, because it appears through differentiation; likewise,
that reality is the sustainer of all beings, because it is the sole cause for the persistence of each respective form.
It is the sustainer (*dhāraka*). Likewise, it is the devourer (*grasiṣṇu*), because it possesses the power of withdrawal and has the nature of consuming.

Likewise, it is the source of manifestation (*prabhaviṣṇu*), meaning it is the cause of maintenance, dissolution, and creation, because it is the cause of production. Likewise, it is light (*jyotis*), because it is the cause of illumination for lights such as the sun and others that illuminate.

It is the illuminator. For those [objects], although they illuminate the existence of the world, are themselves illuminated by the light of consciousness (*saṃvit*). Therefore, it is said to be "beyond darkness. Whatever is illuminated by another is, by virtue of its own non-luminous nature, of the nature of darkness (*tamas*). Consequently, that...

Reality (*tattva*) is supreme because it consists of the nature of illuminating everything; it is either preeminent or transcendent. Likewise, it is "to be known through knowledge" (*jñānajñeya*), meaning it is to be recognized as one's own self (*ātmatayā pratyabhijñeya*) by means of knowledge in its previously explained form. This is because it is accessible through knowledge (*jñānagamya*).

Without knowledge, it is likewise impossible to make [it] an object. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), it resides specifically as the cognizer within the heart—that is, the inner core—of every possible subject;
for in the state of accomplishment (*siddhyavasthā*), it is thus to be known through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). (12–17)
He summarizes:
"Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been declared in brief.
My devotee, having understood this, attains to my own state. (18)
Thus, by this much of the text, [it is shown that] the field consists of the great elements;
and by the passage beginning with "the body, consisting of the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*)," likewise—
Knowledge consists of the attributes beginning with humility (*amānitva*) and ending with the vision of the reality of the Truth (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*).

Likewise, [the verse] "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) in all fields" (13.2) indicates that the primary object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is the Truth (*tattva*) which is the essential nature of the Supreme Knower of the Field. This is the principal [point].
These three categories have been stated; for it is only through my grace that my devotee, being intent upon my worship,
becomes fit for this triad— namely, for attaining my state, which is the realization of my own essential nature.
Once reborn, he becomes capable. || 18 ||

Now, since this knowledge has been taught herein, by means of it the three categories characterized as primordial nature (prakṛti), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and the supreme self (paramātman) have been determined;
thus, he speaks in order to demonstrate them briefly and in sequence:
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
know also that the modifications and the qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti.

This very nature (*prakṛti*), whose form was explained in the seventh chapter as being in the state of an object (*viṣaya*), is now presented by way of its division into the state of the body (*śarīra*); likewise, that *puruṣa* who was explained as being in the state of the subject (*viṣayin*) and as the embodied one (*śarīrin*)— these two alone [are defined] by virtue of their mutual connection.
"Know" means understand that there is no prior limit (pūrvakoṭi) perceived for the relationship of identity between these two;

however, because of knowledge of the nature described above, there is indeed a final limit (antakoṭi). Thus, the intended meaning here is that the relationship between these two is beginningless (*anādi*), and not that their eternity is being established by treating them as equal counterparts.
Since *prakṛti* is an object of cognition, it possesses the nature of arising and passing away while remaining eternal as a continuous flow;

however, the *puruṣa*, being in the ultimate sense of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*), is eternally immutable (*kūṭastha-nitya*). For this very reason, [the author] says that the transformations such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* have as their sole inherent nature the state of being objects of cognition.
Know them to be born from primordial nature (prakṛti), having the primary matter (pradhāna) as their cause. || 19 ||
Having thus explained the nature of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* in general,

[the author now explains] how *prakṛti* is connected to each individual *puruṣa* by way of assuming various bodies, and how the *puruṣa* is likewise connected to each body by way of being the various *kṣetrajñas*.
To explain this, he says: "Nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause in the state of being the agent of cause and effect;
the person (puruṣa) is said to be the cause in the state of being the experiencer of pleasures and pains. (20)

The effect consists of the great elements and so forth; the causes are the external and internal sense organs. Thus, the aggregate consisting of the body and so on is denoted by the term "effect-cause" (*kāryakāraṇa*). Regarding its agency, *prakṛti*—the unmanifest (*avyakta*) whose nature is the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃpratyaya*) residing solely therein—is [the agent].
The cause is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa*). For she, being established as the body-self, is the basis for the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) residing therein.
Likewise, because pleasure and so forth—which are objects of experience—are to be enjoyed by the self... (p. 292) ...[she is] that [self].

The conceit of being an enjoyer [arises]; in that regard, because it possesses the nature of an experiencer, the *puruṣa* alone is the cause. When the notion of the *puruṣa* exists, there is the objectivity of the object of enjoyment—which consists of pleasure and pain—and the designation of the *puruṣa* as the subject. || 20 ||
Why is this?—For the person, situated in nature, experiences the qualities born of nature;
attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. (21)

Because the Puruṣa, abiding in Pradhāna— which has evolved into the form of a body consisting of various causes and effects within Prakṛti— and existing there by virtue of Māyā through the support of a corresponding degree of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra),
[perceives] the qualities (guṇas) such as Sattva and the others, which are born of Prakṛti and have arisen from Prakṛti.
It experiences—that is, it takes as its objects—those things transformed into the nature of pleasure and so forth, by virtue of being the knower (*vedaka*).

For the qualities of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as sound and the rest, having attained the state of being known in the form of pleasure and so forth, are the cause for the designation of the *puruṣa* as the subject (*viṣayin*). Thus, [the relationship exists] through the state of being the body and the embodied one.

The relationship between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* arises from non-discrimination (*aviveka*) through the state of being the object and the subject. Consequently, for this *puruṣa*, there is a firm connection with the *guṇas* consisting of the notions of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*), characterized by identifying with the body and with objects; this occurs while those [guṇas] exist.

In those births— which are the manifestations of the causes of origination in wombs where *sattva* predominates, or where *rajas* and *tamas* predominate— the cause and reason for their occurrence in the form of human beings and so forth is solely attachment to the *guṇas*, which has as its sole motive the absence of discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
The meaning is that this constitutes the state of transmigratory existence for the person. || 21 ||
Since the Supreme Reality abides in two ways within this body associated with various individual persons, he says: "The witness, the consenter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord."
And he is also called the Supreme Self (paramātman), the supreme person within this body.
Maheśvara is the Great Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, whose lordship is superior to that of all other persons; he is the Master, synonymous with the term *parabrahman*, who,
in relation to the persons manifested by his own *māyā*, is the witness and sustainer within this body.

"He is established as both the consenter and the enjoyer. Since the Puruṣa perceives the object presented as an object of vision through the sequence of Nature (prakṛti), Mahat, and Ahaṅkāra, he is called the "observer" (upadraṣṭṛ). Likewise, the body and so forth are merely the objects of vision.
Apprehending through the sense of "I," the Lord (bhartṛ) is the sustainer of cause and effect;

he alone is designated as such. Likewise, that which is conceived by Nature—that is, known, apprehended as an object of cognition, and existing as the domain of pleasure and so forth—the Puruṣa considers from behind; thus, he is the "consentor" (anumantṛ).

It is said: therefore, the designation of that very [Self] as the enjoyer is due to the superimposition of corporeality and subjectivity upon the *puruṣa* according to the Sāṃkhya method; in this regard, the cause is the absence of discrimination (*aviveka*), and that is rooted in *māyā*. However, when, through the dawning of knowledge (*vidyā*), the wisdom born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) manifests, [the superimposition ceases].

Then, that very person is designated as the Supreme Self (paramātman); he is described according to the continuity [of the teaching] as having the nature of Brahman, which is of the single essence of non-dual consciousness as previously established. || 22 ||
Thus, he states the fruit of the knowledge characterized by the discrimination between primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), and the Lord (īśvara):
"He who thus knows the person and primordial nature along with its qualities—no matter how he may conduct himself—he is not born again. (23)

The yogi who, in the manner thus described, knows the Puruṣa as existing in the form of various individual knowers (kṣetrajña) together with the guṇas existing in the state of objects consisting of pleasure and so forth— he, by virtue of knowing the ultimate reality of the three principles, is in every way and by every means...
Even while existing as a performer of those duties consisting of the specific dharmas of one's caste and the specific dharmas of one's stage of life,
and remaining as their practitioner, he is not born again— that is, he does not become subject to transmigratory existence—
because of the fire of knowledge described above, which [consumes] the causes for the production of transmigration.

Because of the burning away of those karmas that stand in the place of seeds. As it is said on page 294: "Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again, so too, once the afflictions have been burnt away by knowledge, the self is not produced again."
Thus, the meaning is clear. || 23 ||
And regarding this view of the Self, although the aforementioned knowledge alone is primarily the means, he says that it is nevertheless reached in some way even through other, secondary means:
"Some perceive the Self within themselves by means of the self through meditation."
Others by means of Sāṃkhya-yoga, and still others by means of Karma-yoga.
But others, not knowing this, worship having heard it from others;
they too, being devoted to what they have heard, surely cross over death.

Some, possessing the innate knowledge of reality (*sahajasiddhatattvajñāna*) and being recipients of the unsurpassed grace of the Supreme Lord, perceive the Self through meditation; they realize it by recollecting its nature as the aforementioned Brahman.
For this very reason, in order to demonstrate non-duality, he asks: "By what, and where, do they see?"
"They perceive the Self by means of the self within the self. What is meant by this? That in whatever locus, such as the heart, they perform meditation; by whichever internal organ they perform it;
and whatever they apprehend through that meditation—all that they reflect upon as being nothing other than the nature of the Supreme Brahman.

The purport is as follows: such is the supreme pinnacle of self-knowledge. At present, others who have not attained this much of a capacity perceive the Self through Sāṃkhya—that is, through knowledge consisting of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Others [perceive it] through Yoga, according to the methods set forth by Patañjali and others.
Others, however, perceive the Self through the yoga of action—a form of concentration consisting in the performance of their own duties while remaining established in the aforementioned knowledge.
Thus, two modes of self-knowledge have been presented, distinguished as higher and lower. Among these:

That which was described by the words beginning with "by meditation" as having the nature of pure knowledge alone is the state of one who has ascended (*ārūḍha*) among those engaged in action (*karmayogins*). As it has been said:
"For him alone who has thus ascended to yoga, tranquility (*śama*) is said to be the means. (6.3)

p. 295) Thus [it is said]. Although "by means of the yoga of action" implies a nature of synthesis (*samuccaya*), for those practitioners of the yoga of action, the stage of one who desires to ascend is characterized by action as the primary element; as it is said:
"For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga... (BhG 6.3).

Thus, as previously established by such statements, the supreme means (*para-upāya*) is twofold: through *sāṃkhya* and through *yoga*. The other [means] is the inference that leads to the realization of gross distinctions. Others, however, due to the absence of current fitness even for these two types of means, [proceed] in the manner already described.

Not knowing the Self through direct perception, yet possessing qualities such as purity to a certain degree, they hear from authoritative persons what has been seen or inferred by others; having thus ascertained it, they rely solely on scripture and worship—that is, they devote themselves to—that [Self]. They too are of such a kind.
Having become the field for the seed of accomplishment characterized by faith, they indeed transcend death and gradually attain the imperishable Self, because they are intent upon the true goal.
For both the real and the unreal are possible; [these people] are graced by knowledge.
Those deluded by illusion cling to the unreal as real, whereas those who are not so deluded cling to the real; they obtain a fruit exactly corresponding to that [clinging]. And thus it has been said:
"Both immortality and death are established within the body."
Through delusion, one meets death, even though immortality is established in truth.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 24–25.

In order to explain more clearly the very meaning already stated, he says until the end of the chapter: "Whatever being exists, whether stationary or moving, know that, O bull among the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field. (26)

To whatever extent there exists any being whatsoever— of whatever measure, innumerable, and endowed with any particular distinction— that constitutes the class of living creatures, all that belongs to *prakṛti* as it has been transformed into the form of the body of the field (*kṣetra*), and likewise to the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

Know— that is, understand— that [the soul] arises from the conjunction of the self, which is established through the conceit of possessing various bodies, with its cause being the mutual relationship that has proceeded as an beginningless continuity. What is meant?
The cause of this endless phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which consists of various moving and non-moving entities,

is its connection with *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* as a unity through the relationship of body and embodied being, due to their undiscriminated nature. Therefore, the first method is the discrimination between the body and the embodied being, as follows:

Because when the knowledge thus established has been well understood in the Self— whose true nature is distinct from primordial matter (prakṛti) as it has transformed into the state of a body— the delusion regarding the cognition of all knowers-of-the-field (kṣetrajña) ceases, due to the non-deviation from the single characteristic of being merely a knower (vedaka). || 26 ||
He says that the yogi becomes a possessor of right vision through the perception of the natural unity with the Supreme Self:
"The Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings..."
He who perceives the Imperishable within all things that are perishing—he truly sees.

He abides equally— without distinction— in all beings, whether moving or stationary, and though there are infinite particularities due to intermediate subdivisions within these two classes, He remains without change because He is devoid of modifications such as birth and the like, owing to His ultimate eternity.
The yogi who perceives the Supreme Lord— the independent Supreme Self— who is eternally present, as his own self through reflective awareness, directly realizes Him; he alone sees,
because he possesses the vision of the ultimate reality, which is the truly absolute state of the seer.
The meaning is that all those who perceive a plurality of selves as distinct from That [the Self] are perceivers of false objects.
In what kind of beings does one see what kind [of Self]? In beings that are perishing—that is, subject to modifications such as birth and so forth, ending in destruction—one sees the imperishable.
Not deviating from that single nature which consists solely in being the knower— that yogi, indeed, with the eye consisting of knowledge that has opened as previously described,
perceives his own essential nature as distinct from all objective aspects characterized by appearance and disappearance.

The direct realization of the Supreme Self—the sole characteristic of the knower—as the single reality (*ekatattva*) in all states, as one's own self, is called right vision (*samyagdarśana*); others, however, possess perverted vision (*viparītadarśana*). And that very person is "possessed of the Self" (*ātmavān*). || 27 ||
In this regard, he states the reason:
"For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not destroy the self by means of the self; therefore, one attains the supreme goal. (2.28)

Because, having made equal— that is, identical— in every respect the entire range of objects of knowledge consisting of primordial matter (*prākṛtabhāva*) by way of their common nature as universal consciousness (*sāmānyasaṃvidrūpatā*),
the Lord, the Master, the Supreme Self, remains established by his very nature as one who has correctly attained firm footing.

Seeing and recognizing the Self by oneself through one's own self as having the nature of reality, one does not destroy it; through non-recognition, one does not reduce that which truly exists to non-existence. What is meant is this: by means of the eye of knowledge thus explained...
He who does not perceive the Supreme Self as distinct from the field and the knower of the field is, in the primary sense of the term, a self-destroyer; as it has been said:
"He who represents the Self, which exists in one way, as being otherwise..."
What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self?
Thus [ends the section]. || 28 ||
And who is it that perceives such a nature of the Supreme Self? To this he says:
"He indeed sees truly who perceives that all actions are being performed in every way by Nature alone, and likewise perceives the Self as the non-doer. (29)

Nature (prakṛti), which is divided into the categories of the conscious and the unconscious, and which exists in two forms as previously explained— the higher and the lower— becomes bound by an beginningless relationship in the form of the field and the knower of the field solely through the power of the Supreme Lord’s will.
It fashions this entire manifold universe. Thus, in the seventh chapter, after explaining the nature of the two-fold *prakṛti*, it is said:
"Understand that all beings have this as their source" (7.6).
Thus; even in this chapter, this very same meaning has been stated by the verse beginning with "Whatever [is possible] in this world" (13.26). Therefore, by such a nature itself...

He who perceives— that is, correctly discerns— all actions, which are being performed and brought to completion by the mind alone, appearing as if connected to various bodies; such a yogi is thus [described].

In that manner, one should remain well-established at all times within one's own self alone— which is of the nature of Brahman, whose essence is truth, and which is pure consciousness— being, in the ultimate sense, a non-doer because of being uninvolved in all actions.
He perceives [the Supreme Self] as devoid of effort toward the accomplishment of effects distinct from its own nature. What is meant?

Just as the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) possesses agency through the conceit of non-difference from *prakṛti*, such is not the case for the Supreme Self. For His primary agency consists solely in the reflective awareness of His own nature.

The designation of agency and action attributed to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is figurative (*gauṇī*). Thus, this entire discourse regarding agent and action is based upon duality; and this duality is merely a manifestation of *māyā* and does not rest upon the reality of an objective entity. Therefore, [the attribution of action] to the one principle is based upon an effect that is distinct [from it].
The intended meaning is that agency is not real. || 29 ||

This being the case, in order to demonstrate that the supreme knowledge regarding the single reality characterized by the true Brahman manifests immediately after the discriminative knowledge of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, he says:
When one perceives the existence of beings as distinct yet unified in one place,
and likewise their expansion from that very source, then one attains Brahman.

At that time, the yogi attains Brahman; that is, he achieves absorption in the one reality, the supreme truth, the Paramātman as previously described. When? At the time when, through the purity born of discriminative knowledge, [he perceives] correctly.
The yogi, whose nature is that of the single, all-pervading Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) which is manifest, perceives the distinctness— the mutual differentiation—
of the various states of beings, both moving and unmoving, as being situated in one. That is, he perceives them as existing within the One.
One directly realizes that [the world] exists as being of the very nature of the Supreme Self, which abides as nothing but the manifestation of non-dual consciousness. What is stated by this?
That all entities are adorned by the seed-syllable of the word "light" (*prakāśa*).

When the yogi experiences that those things whose very acquisition of self-nature depends solely upon being manifest possess, in reality, the singular nature of being illuminated by another (the Light), and when he perceives everything as abiding in the One;

In the same way, when one perceives from that very same single reality an expansion consisting of manifoldness—the vast extent of its manifestations—then one attains Brahman. What is meant by this? It is that the yogi, whose mind is purified through mastery of the knowledge born of discrimination, [perceives] within a single reality...
One perceives the entire multitude of differentiated things as non-different from that [reality];

likewise, as that very single reality has emanated in the form of the diversity of all phenomenal existents, the delusion consisting in the perception of a plurality of natures in its entirety dissolves—this is the meaning. And thus, this is precisely the point.
It has been restated by some wise person:
"Whatever is suspected of being distinct does not differ from distinctness itself. (30)
Thus, although the characteristics of such a Supreme Self have been stated many times, he speaks of them again in this context:
"Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this Supreme Self is immutable."
O son of Kuntī, even while dwelling in the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted.

This Blessed One is the Supreme Self, the ultimate reality, whose true existence is by its very nature unimpeded everywhere and at all times; consequently, His abiding within every body is indeed uncontradicted.
Nevertheless, even while residing therein, He does not act, because He remains firmly established solely in His own singular, established nature.

It does not experience agency based on distinct effects; and since that is so, what talk can there be of experiencing the fruits of action? Thus it is not tainted. Because it is beginningless and the cause of all, and for that very reason devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatvāt*), having transcended the qualities which are characterized by arising and passing away.

Because its nature is distinct from those [qualities], it is imperishable (*avyaya*), meaning it is devoid of decay (*vyaya*), which is to say destruction. Although beginninglessness and imperishability have been stated of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) as well, nevertheless, because that [Knower] is bound by *prakṛti*, which consists of the qualities (*guṇa*), it conforms to the nature of those [qualities].

The quality of undergoing various states of arising and passing away is figuratively attributed [to the Self] as long as ignorance persists; however, even figuratively, this does not apply to the Supreme Self. Therefore, unlike the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), He possesses neither agency nor connection with the fruits of action. || 31 ||

(p. 300) And just as, despite its presence in all bodies, it remains free from contact with the stain characterized by connection to the fruits of karma, so too he speaks in order to demonstrate this by means of a simile:
Just as space, being all-pervading, is not defiled because of its subtlety, so the Self, though abiding everywhere within the body, is not defiled. 32.

Just as space— due to its subtlety and minuteness, being all-pervading, encompassing all things, and possessing a majesty unconditioned by space, time, and so forth— is not defiled by limited, pervaded entities, nor is it joined with its own attributes; |||

In the very same way, although this Supreme Self (paramātman) exists as all-pervading and is eternally present within every body— encompassing all infinite varieties such as gods, humans, animals, and so forth— it remains untouched by their attributes,
such as pleasure and pain, or birth and destruction.
It is not smeared—that is, it is not touched—by those [mental states] born from the conceit of being connected to the fruits of karma.
And so it has been said by a certain knower of Brahman:
"Just as when the space within a single jar is covered by dust, smoke, and so forth..."
In the same way, all living beings are not joined with pleasure and the other [feelings].
Thus [ends the section]. || 32 ||

Thus, even though there is an absence of contact with the fruits of action in every respect, because He possesses the attribute of being the illuminator that is not shared by anything else, He alone is the illuminator of the conventional distinction between the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña); to demonstrate this by means of another analogy, he says:
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world,
so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field.

Just as, in whatever manner this Blessed Sun, whose nature is directly perceptible to the entire world, alone and without companion illuminates the whole, undivided world— the universe composed of manifold states— and causes it to attain its own true form; in that very same manner...
This one Supreme Self, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who pervades all fields, illuminates the field. What is meant by this?
It is that although the objects to be illuminated are manifold, the illumination—which is an attribute of the Supreme Self—remains [unitary]. (p. 301) If...

The metaphorical designation of multiplicity is merely conventional; in the ultimate sense, however, there is only one [light] that illuminates all objects to be illuminated. And the relationship of analogy between the sun and the eye exists solely on the basis of their common nature as illuminators. For just as the sun [illuminates] entities...

The illuminator is not like the field-owner (kṣetrin). For instance, the sun is an illuminator merely by manifesting objects such as jars and cows that have acquired their own nature from some cause, but not by producing them; the field-owner, however, produces those very things precisely by bringing them to a state of manifestation. Therefore...
That it possesses the quality of being a producer has already been established previously. || 33 ||
Thus,
concluding this chapter with the determination of the three principles characterized as the field (kṣetra), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and the Supreme Self (paramātman),
he says: "In this way, the distinction between the field and the knower of the field [is seen] by the eye of knowledge."
And those who know the liberation from the nature of the elements go to the Supreme.

Those yogins who, in the manner thus described, [know] the lower *prakṛti* which has been transformed into the state of the field (*kṣetra*)— that is, the body— as well as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*),
who exists in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) supported by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) of various fields; [they do not fall].

They know—that is, they understand—the distinction, the difference, the mutually distinct essential nature of the two; by what? By the very eye of knowledge beginning with humility (amānitva) and ending with the vision of reality (tattvadarśana). Not only do they know the distinction between the two, but also the liberation from the material nature of beings (bhūtaprakṛti-mokṣa).

Those who know— that is, those who understand that liberation from this gross nature which has been described consists in not entering it again, and thus constitutes the absolute abandonment of bondage—
what is meant by this? [It is] regarding the field and the knower of the field.

The mere comprehension of their mutually distinct natures may occasionally occur through the cultivation of scripture and reasoning; however, liberation from *prakṛti* does not arise by that alone, for it occurs only through constant attentiveness to the nature of the Self as distinct from it. Therefore, it is stated separately:

"And the liberation from the nature of the elements. Such persons as these go to— that is, they attain— the supreme, unsurpassed reality, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is established in the seventh [chapter] as the "higher nature" (*parataraprakṛti*) and is characterized by non-difference from it.
They attain accomplishment; thus, Oṃ. 34.
Since enjoyment is indeed consumed by all living beings from this field— which is perpetually parched by the threefold suffering and utterly devoid of essence—
may that [enjoyment] flow for you from the thirteenth chapter, which is a dense mass of the nectar of consciousness.
She was sprinkled with the drops of nectar from his words, and she had brought forth the beauty of the fruit of liberation.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meanings of the statements, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. 13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter:
"And those who, at the conclusion of the thirteenth chapter, know the liberation from the material nature of beings... (13.34).

Regarding what was stated there, it is indeed asserted that *prakṛti*, having entered into the state of being a modification (*vikāra*) of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth, is designated by the term "the *prakṛti* of the elements" (*bhūtaprakṛti*). Consequently, it follows that there exists for her a causal reality consisting of *prakṛti*. And in accepting that [position],...
The doctrine of the non-duality of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmādvaita*) is contradicted by this scripture; for here,

reality is the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is firmly established in such a nature, characterized by supreme bliss arising from the reflective awareness of one's own essence as the eternal, unitary light of consciousness.

That which is designated by the term *parabrahman*— the one alone, established as ultimate reality through the non-contradiction of scripture, reasoning, and perception— is proven and demonstrated throughout this treatise;
of which...

The definition has been established by such passages as, "The Brahman without beginning, the supreme... (13.12). Consequently, how can the second principle called *prakṛti* be established as existing? What is its essential nature, or of what kind is it?

By what means is it known that his connection [to the world] is through the reality of the nature of the Supreme Brahman? Furthermore, since the material nature (*bhūtaprakṛti*) has been said to be twofold—by way of transformation as the body-self and as the object-self—how then can there be liberation for the Self? Is it by the absolute abandonment [of nature], or otherwise? In this regard:
First of all, the first alternative has not been accepted here; and thus it has been said:
"Because of being beginningless and devoid of qualities, this immutable Supreme Self, O son of Kuntī, though dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is tainted" (13.31).
"Thus,
even here in this world, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity" (5.19),
and so forth. By this [verse], liberation is shown to result from the absolute relinquishment of *prakṛti*, which has undergone transformation into the state of the body.

It has not been accepted. Likewise, even for that which has transformed into the state of being an object (*viṣaya*), an absolute avoidance is not intended. As it has been said: "But those who are free from passion and hatred, while engaging with objects through their sense-faculties... (p. 304)
One who has mastered the self attains serenity through the senses that are under one's own control.
Likewise,
O Bhārata, the ignorant act with attachment to action just as they do.

"A wise man, being unattached, should act thus, desiring the welfare of the world" (3.25), and so forth. In this way, how is liberation from *prakṛti*, which consists of the objects of the senses, [attained]?
That knowledge concerning the objects of both [the self and *prakṛti*] by which this is known is superior because of its subtlety; it is [taught] here and there.
Vowing to speak again even that which has been previously mentioned, the Blessed One said, prefaced by its praise:
"I shall further declare the supreme knowledge, the best among all forms of knowledge."
Knowing which, all the sages have attained supreme perfection from this state. || 1 ||

In the manner already described, I shall further— meaning again or even more extensively— declare with excellence that supreme, most eminent, and preeminent knowledge among all forms of knowledge concerning the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and other subjects, by means of the knowledge about to be expounded.

Because it will lead to the correct practice of the aforementioned forms of knowledge, this [knowledge] is the most excellent among them. For this very reason, he says: "Having known which, all the ancient sages, being self-controlled, attained supreme perfection—that is, the highest accomplishment characterized by the ultimate state of union."
They have emerged from this cycle of existence. || 1 ||
For this is the power of that knowledge:
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
they are not born even at the time of creation, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution. (2)
Having relied upon and properly grasped this knowledge which is about to be declared, other yogis as well, having attained my own nature— the non-difference from my being—
do not [undergo birth and death], even during creation and dissolution, unlike other individual souls (kṣetrajñas) who are devoid of this knowledge.
They come to possess the designations of "origination" and "destruction" because of the manifestation of their ultimate eternity.
Then, in order to explain this knowledge, he says: "My womb is the Great Brahman; therein I place the seed. (p. 305)
From that, O Bhārata, the origin of all beings comes into being.

That reality which has been established as existing in the form of the cause consisting of the primordial nature (prakṛti) and which was suspected to be distinct from the Supreme Brahman, is in fact not distinct from it in the ultimate sense; it is Brahman itself. However, it is "great" (mahat) in comparison to that [Brahman], because it is gross insofar as it is an object of cognition.

Being thus contemplated: because I, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, am the locus for the production of the world as a plaything, that [world] is my "womb" (yoni). Into that Great Brahman, which is in truth the womb, I place the embryo.
The meaning is: "I effect the transfer of my own vigor, which has consciousness as its characteristic. What is expressed by this?

While perceiving the nature of the Supreme Brahman, whose characteristics have been described, I cause the reality characterized as primordial matter (*prakṛti*) to appear; even though that [reality] possesses the quality of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Because there is no manifestation without entering into the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), it possesses the nature of Brahman; yet, because it has the nature of a delimited object of knowledge (*vedya*), it is gross.
Thus, the Great Brahman—consisting of "this-ness" (*idantā*) and being the sole cause of the manifold existence of the entire universe—is mine.

It serves as the womb for Him who delights in the desire to create the world; therefore, he says that from that very nature— which is indicated by the demonstrative pronoun "this"— there arises, that is, there occurs the birth, of all beings, both moving and unmoving, of all living creatures.

Thus, by this [verse], the supremely wondrous nature of the supreme Lord’s power of *māyā* has been demonstrated: that even while there is not the slightest deviation from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it manifests in the form of the manifold expansion of worldly phenomena (*jagadbhāvaprapañca*) in such a manner, as is to be understood by the fully awakened.
It is the state of being manifest. And this very nature, which consists of such a wondrous form, was previously explained while implicitly including it [in the statement]:
"For this divine illusion of Mine, composed of the gunas, is difficult to overcome."
"Those who take refuge in Me alone cross beyond Māyā.
(7.14) Thus [ends the section]. || 3 ||

(p. 306) Now, in order to clarify that very usage of words such as "womb" (*yoni*) which was employed here by way of encompassing the nature of worldly objects, he says: "O son of Kuntī, whatever forms are produced in all wombs..."
Of these, the Great Brahman is the womb; I am the seed-bestowing Father.

In all wombs— that is, in all fields (*kṣetra*) which serve as the substrata for the manifestation of entities and which depend upon females and so forth— those forms (*mūrtayaḥ*) which consist of the fourfold distinctions of configuration through the four modes of birth, such as being born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) and so on; these are the shapes (*ākṛtayaḥ*).
Of all those beings that come into existence—

that is, arise— the Great Brahman, whose nature is as previously described, is their primary source (*yoni*), characterized by the universal feature of "this-ness" (*idantā*) and consisting of primordial matter (*prakṛti*); and within that source—
I am the father because I bestow my own potency upon the seed characterized by consciousness (*saṃvit*). Just as a certain person,
such as a Brahmin, deposits his semen and thereby implants a fetus in the field of a woman who has been taken as a wife for the purpose of producing offspring, and yet—

"He attains another form; even so, without falling away from my own nature, I emit within the Great Brahman as described the seed characterized by consciousness, which is the cause of the world's existence.
Thus, by the mere fact of not falling away from one's own nature, the Self is designated as the "father," the "locus," and the "womb."

The manifestation of the gross Brahman is the description of the conscious aspect as the seed-cause for the emergence of manifold existence. For indeed, just as there can be no manifestation of the progeny of the male seed without a womb serving as its substratum, [so it is here].

Thus, the meaning is that for the Supreme Lord who desires to emit [the world], there would be an absence of the emergence of the playthings that constitute the world— namely, of the potency characterized as consciousness— were it not for Prakṛti, which consists of the gross Brahman whose nature is the mere non-apprehension of "this-ness" (evamidantā). || 4 ||

Thus, that which is apprehended as "this is so" is the very nature of the Self (*svarūpa*) itself, not some other entity whatsoever; its relationship with the other Brahman is characterized by the relation of the illuminated and the illuminator, and that [relationship] is non-dual luminosity (*prakāśādvaita*).

Without [the Knower], the state of being a manifest object cannot be established for that which is to be manifested, because it lacks the attainment of its own nature; thus, first, knowledge regarding primordial matter (*prakṛti*) has been explained. Now, concerning that [knowledge] which has thus come into existence—
Since liberation would be impossible for that which consists of the transformations of the elements and so forth established as the state of the body and so on,
knowledge whose object is the meaning of non-difference is now determined. In this regard,
that *prakṛti* whose nature has been explained appears in the form of objects belonging to the domain of the body.

It binds the embodied soul through its own transformations, such as *prakṛti* and the rest, so that liberation from it occurs only by avoiding them. However, the specific modes by which these [transformations] become objects of experience bind the embodied soul through the notions of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*); therefore, from those [modes], [liberation follows].
In order to demonstrate step by step that liberation consists in liberation from the nature of the real, He says:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities born of Nature, O mighty-armed one, bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body. (5)

Because it is eternal from the perspective of ultimate reality, the embodied self— which is imperishable and devoid of destruction, and likewise free from birth— is bound by the qualities known as *sattva* and so forth, which arise from the aforementioned *prakṛti*, whose nature will be described, and which bind in the manner that will be explained.
They render [the self] dependent, because it conforms to the properties of the superimposition of egoity upon the body, which undergoes destruction and origination. || 5 ||
To explain how these act as bonds, he describes their classification:
"In that regard, O sinless one, *sattva*, because of its purity, is illuminating and healthy; it binds by attachment to pleasure and by attachment to knowledge. (6)

Among those, the quality of *sattva* binds the being through attachment to knowledge— that is, that attachment which consists of the conceit "I know this" and absorption in that knowledge which is restricted to specific objects and dependent upon specific instruments; by means of that, it makes one subject to dependence.

Likewise, it binds through attachment to pleasure (*sukha*). Pleasure is the satisfaction that culminates in the cessation of the desire for other objects upon the attainment of various desired objects;
attachment to that consists in the support of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*), such as "I am happy" or "pleasure is mine."

Absorption (*tallīnatva*); by means of that, he brings [the object] under his control. Why? Because a sentient being (*sattva*) of such a nature is luminous (*prakāśaka*), since it is pure and its essential form is free from the stains characterized by obscuring darkness.
Therefore, it binds through attachment to knowledge because it is the cause for the manifestation of objects;

and because it is free from affliction—being devoid of passion (rajas) and thus free from the affliction consisting of the suffering of worldly activity—it binds through attachment to pleasure due to its subtlety. Attachment to knowledge has been explained previously. (6)
Likewise:
"Know that *rajas* is of the nature of passion (*rāga*), arising from thirst and attachment;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action. (7)

Know that the quality known as *rajas* is characterized by passion and consists of the desire for pleasure; therefore, it arises from craving and attachment. Because it has proceeded in an unbroken succession since beginningless time, "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is the thirst for the taste of sense objects, and "attachment" (*saṅga*) is the state of being solely dependent upon them; from these, its "origination" (*samudbhava*) is its birth.

Know that it is of such a nature. Passion (rajas), being of this very character, binds the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) through attachment to action. For one impelled by passion for action, there is activity characterized by the acquisition of desired objects and the avoidance of undesired objects; attachment therein is the state of being intent upon that.
By means of that [ignorance], which consists of the conceit of being the agent of determined actions, it brings about subjection to another. || 7 ||
Likewise:
"Know that darkness (tamas) is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings;
it binds them, O Bhārata, through negligence, laziness, and sleep. (8)
Furthermore, know that the quality characterized as *tamas* is born of ignorance;
because it is distinct from the quality of *sattva*, whose nature is luminosity, it arises from the absence of knowledge, and consequently,
it causes delusion for all embodied beings by producing a failure to comprehend the objects of knowledge.

That kind of darkness (tamas) binds the embodied soul through negligence— that is, through indifference toward the discrimination between the means and the end— as well as through laziness, which consists in a lack of exertion toward duties due to being devoid of the quality of passion (rajas) characterized by activity, and likewise through sleep, which is of the nature of delusion and involves the cessation of the power of all the senses.
It restrains; thus, the nature of the three qualities and the manner of bondage have been explained. || 8 ||
(p. 909) Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of that quality whose excellence arises when its own specific effect is present, he says:
"Sattva attaches one to happiness, O Bhārata, and rajas to action."
But darkness, veiling knowledge, engenders heedlessness.

When the effect of the quality of *sattva*, characterized by happiness, is present, *sattva* becomes attached and attains a state of perfect excellence. Likewise, when action, which is the effect of the quality of *rajas*, is present, *rajas* becomes attached. Similarly, when negligence, characterized as previously described, is present, *tamas* becomes attached. Having done what? Having [abandoned] knowledge.
Having veiled, that is, having obscured, the comprehension of the object. || 9 ||
Now, in order to demonstrate how these qualities function by mutually overpowering one another, he says:
"O Bhārata, Sattva increases by overpowering Rajas and Tamas; Rajas [increases] by overpowering Sattva and Tamas; and likewise, Tamas [increases] by overpowering Sattva and Rajas. (10)

Having overcome and suppressed *rajas* and *tamas*, the quality of *sattva* increases. What is meant by this? When *sattva* has increased and becomes powerful, then no other quality (*guṇa*) initiates its own effect. Likewise, having overcome *tamas* and *sattva*, the quality of *rajas* increases. Similarly...
Having overcome rajas and sattva, the quality of tamas increases. || 10 ||
Now, he states the indicative marks that manifest the increase of these qualities: "When light arises through all the gates in this body, one should know then that *sattva* has increased. (11)
Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and thirst—these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas. (12)
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion—these arise when Tamas has increased, O joy of the Kurus. (13)

When, at whatever moment in this body, knowledge— the perception of objects such as sound— arises by making the light manifest, clear, and free from doubt through all the doors, such as the ears and so forth; at that time...

One should know that when *sattva* has increased and accumulated because *rajas* and *tamas* have been overcome; likewise, when *rajas* has increased and accumulated because *sattva* and *tamas* have been overcome, these signs arise. Namely:

Greed (*lobha*) is the lack of cessation even when a desired object has been obtained; it is the state of being oriented toward activity for the sake of acquiring that object. Following that, "undertaking" (*ārambha*) means action—the process of acquiring that object. Likewise, even when some object has been obtained, there is the [pursuit] of objects belonging to other categories.
The non-ceasing of activities is the absence of tranquility. Likewise, *tṛṭ* means thirst, longing, or passion (*rāga*).

Similarly, when darkness (*tamas*) has increased and gained strength by overpowering the qualities of goodness (*sattva*) and activity (*rajas*), these signs arise. For example, there is a lack of illumination due to the suppression of the quality of goodness.

The absence of illumination is the non-perception of objects. Likewise, due to the suppression of the quality of *rajas*, there is a lack of activity, which is the absence of action. Consequently, because they have increased of their own accord, negligence (*pramāda*) and delusion (*moha*) possess the characteristics previously described. (11–13)

Now, in order to demonstrate that these [qualities] are indeed causes of bondage by indicating the attainment of specific other worlds when their increase occurs and the departure of the vital breath takes place, he says:
"When the embodied soul meets its dissolution while sattva is predominant..."
Then he attains the stainless worlds of those who possess supreme knowledge. || 14 ||
Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action;
likewise, dissolved in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.

When, at which time, the quality of *sattva* has increased and become powerful, the embodied being (*dehabhṛt*) undergoes dissolution— that is, receives the designation of destruction— then he goes to the worlds, the celestial realms, belonging to those who possess supreme knowledge, the gods, and others of exalted wisdom.

Because it consists of the quality of *sattva*, one attains states that are stainless and pure, and there receives the designation of being born [among them]. Likewise, when *rajas* has increased, having dissolved [into it], one is born among mortals who are attached to action—those primarily characterized by the quality of *rajas* and intent upon various specific activities. In the same way...
When *tamas* has increased, having dissolved away, one is born in deluded wombs—among animals, stationary beings, and the like—which are dominated by *tamas*. || 14, 15 ||

(p. 311) At the time of departure, in order to specify the results corresponding to the increase of the qualities such as *sattva*, he says: "They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by *sattva*;
the fruit of *rajas*, however, is suffering; and the fruit of *tamas* is ignorance. (16)

When there is an increase in the quality of goodness (*sattva*) resulting from well-performed action— such as sacrifice and other specific rites— that has been properly executed according to the scriptures, its fruit arises as *sāttvika*, originating from the quality of *sattva*; it is stainless, pure, and consists of the nature of distinguished knowledge and bliss.

The remainder [is as follows]: When *rajas* increases, the fruit is suffering because the mind is afflicted by doubt and other such defects; the meaning is that whatever action is performed when there is an absence of purity through qualities such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, being characterized by worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), results only in suffering. It is exactly the same for *tamas*.
When there is an increase [of passion], the fruit of an action performed with a mind corrupted by delusion (*moha*) and the like—
namely, an action applied in a manner contrary to the injunctions of the scriptures— is ignorance, which is indeed delusion itself.
He states this very point in brief:
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas* indeed arises greed;
from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance itself. (17)

The meaning of this verse is clear. The purpose of this detailed exposition— presenting the distinctions among the individual natures, collective forms, functions, and fruits of these qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest— is to demonstrate that in all their states, they possess only the nature of being objects of cognition (*vedya*).
It should be understood thus. || 17 ||
And he states its purpose:
"Those established in sattva go upward; those characterized by rajas stay in the middle; those established in the activity of the lowest quality, the tamasic, go downward. (18)
When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities,
and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains my state of being.
The two verses [18 and 19] have clear meanings.
Having transcended these three qualities that arise from the body, the embodied soul, liberated from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, attains immortality. (20)

All entities that exist in the form of modifications of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), having transformed into the state of body, sense objects, and so forth, arise from the body; for when the body exists, they arise as consisting of body and sense objects, and thus they attain their perceptibility through that very [body] as their essence. Therefore, these...

Having transcended— that is, having completely passed beyond— the three qualities (guṇas), beginning with sattva, whose nature has been explained, by distinguishing them from one's own self which has the singular nature of being the knower; the embodied one, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), because of that very distinction, is free from the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, and thus possesses the nature of pure consciousness alone.

One whose fundamental ego-sense is firmly established, being liberated and freed from birth, death, old age, and suffering— along with the afflictions of arising, destruction, and transformation— which are bound to the states of the body and other things composed of the *guṇas*,
attains and reaches the immortal Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self.

The meaning is that it attains non-difference from that. What is stated by this? Liberation from the primordial nature (*bhūtaprakṛti*) consists in the cultivation of the soul’s innate, distinct nature from the qualities (*guṇa*) whose true form has been explained; it does not consist in [liberation] from that [nature] which takes the form of the body, objects, and so forth.
Liberation is merely the removal [of suffering]. || 20 ||
Then Arjuna, desiring to know specifically the nature of that which transcends the qualities (guṇātīta), said: "By what marks, O Lord, does one transcend these three qualities?
What is his conduct, and how does he go beyond these three qualities? (21)

By what signs, indicators, and characteristics does one become transcendent over these aforementioned qualities—that is, become liberated from them? And as for one who has transcended the qualities, what is his conduct, what is his behavior—this is the meaning. And in what manner does he transcend, or go beyond, these qualities?
What is the method for attaining the state that transcends the qualities? || 21 ||
For the purpose of resolving these three questions, the Blessed One spoke this reply:
"O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, and even delusion when they have arisen, nor does he long for them when they have ceased. (22)
He who remains sitting like one indifferent, not shaken by the qualities;
he who, knowing that "it is only the qualities that move," remains steady and does not waver—(23).
He for whom pleasure and pain, as well as sleep, are equal; to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same;
who regards the pleasant and unpleasant as equal; who is steadfast; and to whom censure and self-praise are equal. (24)
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the parties of friend and foe, and who renounces the fruits of all undertakings—he is said to have transcended the qualities. 25.

The connection is as follows: such a person, distinguished by the specific qualities set forth in these four verses, is said to have transcended the gunas. Who is he? He is one who does not feel aversion toward these objects that have come forth—that is, which are fully manifested—because they are contrary to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), nor does he feel attachment toward them.

The meaning is that he "frequents" [them]. Likewise, the meaning is that he does not pray, "May these remain inactive, having failed to attain their function. He asks, "Which are those? and answers: the "manifest," which is the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of knowledge and so forth that reveals the increase of the quality of *sattva*; likewise, "activity" (*pravṛtti*).

Likewise, activity (*kriyā*) is the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the quality of passion (*rajas*), and similarly, delusion (*moha*) is the characteristic mark of the quality of darkness (*tamas*), consisting as it does of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Regarding these things—
which serve as signs of the increase of the qualities such as *sattva*, and which are either causes for engagement or causes for withdrawal— [one should observe them].

Because he is established in his own eternally unchanging nature, he who is not covered by passion and aversion even in the slightest degree is said to have transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*). This is the primary sign of the existence of one who has transcended the qualities. This definition of one who has transcended the qualities has been stated [here], and that which will be stated [later] is in the second [chapter].
What has been established here in the context of describing the characteristics of steady wisdom (*sthiraprajñatva*) should also be applied here.

Now, it may be argued: "Indeed, activity (*pravṛtti*) and delusion (*moha*), being present in active states, are objects of aversion to you because they increase *rajas* and *tamas* and are characterized by a lack of luminosity."

For the yogin, however, since illumination (*prakāśa*) has arisen as a sign of the increase of *sattva*, how could it be an object of aversion? For it has been said: "He who does not hate illumination and activity is one who has transcended the qualities.
To this it is replied: here, for the yogin engaged in practice, even the sign of *sattva* is like the signs of *rajas* and *tamas*.

That which is of the nature of light, when it is active, becomes an object of aversion because it is subject to negation. And so, in the *Pātañjala*, after describing the nature of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), it says:
"And since this discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) consists of the quality of *sattva*, it is non-perverted; therefore, in that [discernment]..."

It has been said that "the dispassionate mind restrains even that manifestation. However, this specific distinction is stated for the practitioner of action (karmayogin) who has ascended to the state of transcending the qualities (guṇātīta):
namely, that he does not hate even when activity manifests, nor does he long for its cessation.
For if that were the case, because of the persistence of aversion and attachment, the state of transcending the qualities (*guṇātītatā*) would not be possible. Therefore,

he is one for whom aversion and attachment do not arise toward light and the other [qualities], whether they have emerged or subsided, as things to be rejected or accepted, since his consciousness has not fallen away from its pure nature.

"He is said to have transcended the qualities"; this means that these are the marks of one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta-liṅga*). He states another mark of such a person in the passage beginning with "sitting like one indifferent" (*udāsīnavad āsīnaḥ*). One who is not shaken by the qualities, whether they are active or withdrawn, and is not displaced from his own true nature (*svarūpa*), is one whose essential character is to have transcended the qualities. Why is he not shaken?

He states a qualification containing a reason: "sitting like one who is indifferent. One who, because his mind is not mixed with another's occurring pleasure or pain, remains established in himself, changeless, and observes from a neutral standpoint—he is called "indifferent" (*udāsīna*). He [the yogi] is exactly like that.

Remaining changeless and resting in his own nature, as if indifferent to the activity and cessation of illumination and the other [qualities] belonging to another, the qualities simply function while undergoing their activity. He who remains as a knower and perceiver to this extent abides in his own state; for this very reason, he does not stir from his true nature.

"He moves; he is said to have transcended the qualities (guṇātīta); this is his characteristic"—this is the meaning. By this, the answer has been given to the question: "By what characteristics does one transcend the qualities? He states the answer to the question "What is his conduct?
with the words "equal in pain and pleasure," and so forth. [The compound] "duḥkhasukhasvapnāḥ" means...

The functions of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* have been described. One who is "equanimous" (*sama*) is so called because these qualities are perceived by him as equal, without distinction. His conduct is such that he does not delight in pleasure, does not loathe pain, and is not deluded even in sleep. He is the same toward both the parties of friend and foe.

p. 315) This much, up to this point, is the answer to the question "What is his conduct? in this very manner. And as for the question "How does he transcend these qualities?", he provides the answer beginning with "All," etc., regarding all undertakings.

Because he is intent upon the worship of his own Self— which is fearless, filled with unsurpassed innate bliss— he is a renouncer (*tyāgī*), meaning one who abandons (*varjayitā*) the fruits characterized by the attainment of enjoyments such as heaven, due to being free from all desire for rewards (*nirabhisandhānatva*). This applies to the undertakings of actions such as sacrifice, austerity, and charity.

The meaning is that the injunction characterized by the performance of one's own duties as taught in the scriptures— being grounded in knowledge and devoid of attachment to the fruits— is the cause for attaining the state of being beyond the qualities (guṇātītatva). || 22–24 ||
He states the supreme method for attaining the state beyond the qualities (guṇātītatva):
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion, having transcended these qualities, becomes fit for the state of Brahman. (26)

And he who serves Me— whose nature has been described as it is— with the yoga of devotion that is unswerving, free from deviation toward other objects distinct from Me, and in the form of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the four kinds previously explained;

Having worshipped according to the injunctions appropriate for each stage, beginning from the state of being afflicted and ending with the state of possessing knowledge, he— having reached the supreme limit and having transcended these aforementioned qualities—
becomes fit for *brahmabhūya*, that is, for the state of Brahman; he becomes Brahman itself, whose nature has been described as such.

The phrase "he becomes" means that he has now crossed over the great ocean of the delusion of duality, which is otherwise difficult to traverse by other means; for, through the aforementioned sequence,
he has realized me, the Supreme Self, whose nature is the non-dual pure consciousness of the Supreme Brahman.

For the yogin whose consciousness is perfectly rested, not even the slightest thing in the form of a quality remains as a separate, distinct entity. This is because my own essential nature, which has been explained as the ultimate reality, appears as "this" only through the power of my inconceivable *māyā*.
Just as that which is being perceived attains the nature of an entity called "prakṛti," in the very same way, these my real attributes, when not being perceived,
come to be designated by the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth. And thus, my attribute known as "illumination" (prakāśa)—
[He] is of the nature of a light consisting of consciousness that is eternally manifest and independent of any external object to be illumined. (p.

316) By being dependent upon external, limited objects of illumination, and because it conforms to their nature, it appears as if it has attained limitation and receives the designation of the quality of *sattva*. Thus...

My attribute (*mad-dharma*), although its essence consists of the activity characterized by the mere experience of one's own nature (*svarūpa-anubhava-mātra-lakṣaṇa-kriyā-ātmā*), receives the designation of the *rajas* quality (*rajo-guṇa*) because it is directed toward external, limited objects of illumination. Likewise, that which is the innate and eternal state (*sthiti*) within my majesty, which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth— that very same [state]...
By virtue of being established upon distinct substrates, it receives the designation of the *tamas* quality, which is characterized by restriction. Thus,

through the variety of its reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the power of *māyā*, whose sole function is the activity of creative ideation (*bhāvanā*), manifests this most wondrous world consisting of the conceptual diversities of the states of the qualities of *prakṛti* and so forth.

Painting the portrait of the three worlds, she deludes all embodied beings; yet, when she is set aside by the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) expanding in the form of devotion (*bhakti*), then only the one ultimate reality, Brahman itself, remains. Therefore it is said: "He who serves me through the yoga of devotion..."
"He becomes fit for becoming Brahman. || 26 ||
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss. (27)
Because I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Brahman as described and of the supreme reality— that is, I am established as conforming to the very nature of that reality through non-deviation from it—
since it has been stated that Brahman alone exists in the form of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Field (*kṣetra*), and so forth.

Nevertheless, by being grounded in the reality delimited by that [Ātman], it conforms to its very nature and is established everywhere. Of what kind of Brahman am I the foundation? Of the immortal and the imperishable—that is, of that which is devoid of *vyaya*, a modification characterized by decay or diminution; for this very reason, it is "immortal."

Of that which exists eternally. Not only am I the foundation of Brahman, but I am also the foundation of its eternal attribute, which consists of the nature of consciousness and light; likewise, I am the foundation of that innate bliss, the absolute happiness, which requires no external cause.

I am the foundation. What is meant is this: that Supreme Brahman, whose nature consists of luminosity, bliss, and immutability—that is I, to be attained by means of this one single method characterized by devotion. Om. || 27 ||
By means of those worthless coins made of tin, lead, and copper-stained base metals— such as *sattva* and the rest—
which people employ while trading in the long marketplace of saṃsāra and thereby experience misfortune,
[the author] has achieved success regarding this "mercury" (*rasa*) which is the subject matter of the fourteen great chapters.
May they, having been led to the ultimate reality, bestow upon you imperishable prosperity in an instant.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Bhagavadgītā-vivaraṇa* titled *Sarvatobhadra*, consisting merely of the connection of the meaning of the statements, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. 14.
